redemption-18-year-old-bourbon-alan-kenn:
“I want feelings and vibes, songs this reminds you of, or a collection of memories,” Alan Kennedy tells us. We’re sitting in a conference room in Kentucky, an intimidating lineup of 74 barrel samples of 18 year old bourbon is neatly arranged in front of Kennedy, Redemption’s master blender, to craft upcoming releases.

Kennedy sets a few ground rules. He doesn’t want us to identify flavors of marzipan, vanilla, or petrichor. He wants to hear what a whiskey evokes, not a formal review. “Shout out everything that you're feeling after a sip,” he says.

Our assignment today is twofold. First, we’re to identify barrels for the 2027 blend of Redemption’s 18 year old bourbon. Kennedy is open to finding several blends for the younger release: “If we find good groupings, we can do two or three different separate batches of 18 years,” he says. The samples will help determine how many distinct whiskeys he has to work with. Approximately 30 barrels will need to be allocated, with enough aging potential to become Redemption’s first 21 year old, potentially arriving in 2029.

Let’s hope my palate doesn’t pack it in early; this is easily the highest volume of samples I’ve ever tried in a single sitting. Over the day, my notes include “toothpaste vibes,” “Boy Scout camp,” “If you had AI make generic bourbon,” “Outback Steakhouse,” and “A man wearing a suit on an airplane.” Odd as they seem, Kennedy’s pleased. “We can work with those,” he says. “As a sommelier, I learned early on that your tasting notes influence what other people taste,” he explains. Ask for vanilla, and you’ve already led the witness. “Connect it to memories and feelings or music or art; there’s more there.”

One Lot, Several Personalities

Redemption introduced its Ancients series in 2017, returning to the collection in 2025 with an 18 year old bourbon drawn from 69 barrels. That release yielded approximately 2,400 bottles at 103.4 proof, priced at $400. It returned in 2026, providing the immediate predecessor to the whiskey we’re helping Kennedy assemble.

Today’s samples come from lot 08F30, distilled in a single day at MGP in Indiana in 2008, using a mashbill of 75% corn, 21% rye, and 4% malted barley. They entered Independent Stave Company barrels with a No. 3 char at 120 proof, and were stored together in a row on the third floor of an MGP Indiana warehouse. The inventory predates current owner Deutsch Family Wine & Spirits’ 2015 acquisition of Redemption, but was included with the sale. Kennedy has spent the past three years sampling it.

Many of the 74 samples’ proofs register in the 80s, while 22 exceed 100. Kennedy attributes the low readings to humid maturation conditions in Indiana; the barrels moved to Kentucky about a month before our tasting. “There were some beautiful whiskeys in this that were naturally in the 80s, and I’m excited to show that,” he says. “In the time of hazmats, this is the reverse.”

Despite their shared inception, the barrels have matured to show radically different profiles. Number 23, now 81.77 proof, is juicy and cotton-candy sweet, yet dry. Barrel 49, at 85.5 proof, suggests eucalyptus, peppermint, then Listerine, and No. 25, at 96.79, smells like buttercream frosting dusted with cinnamon. Kennedy keeps pushing us for vibes, so we deliver. Barrel 53, at 85.03 proof, is a “freshly talcumed baby’s bottom,” 59, at 100.8, is “economy plus; basic but you get an extra free drink and a little more leg room,” especially compared to No. 15, which at 105.3 proof is “a business class blender, with swagger; someone who wears a suit on the plane.”

From Strawberry to Mouthwash

My more esoteric notes aside, samples do naturally sort themselves into categories as the day progresses. Seven barrel samples land squarely in the bakery case, suggesting pie crust, frosting, graham crackers, and cinnamon cereal. Counting fruit candies, caramel, and other sweets, that barrel pool widens to 19. A recurring theme in that pastry shop set is strawberry; it shows up about 12 times.

At the opposite end of the spectrum, a slew of barrels lean herbaceous. Eight barrels show explicit mint or menthol notes, ranging from dark chocolate with mint to my less welcome mouthwash impression. “Grouping comparative flavors together is good,” says Kennedy. “When you’re blending, you want to have a central idea, but you need to contrast that to give it more depth. If it was all strawberries, okay, fine. But strawberries with mint and leather? Now it starts to build. It’s the different hues that come together to make a painting perfect.”

We identify five barrels that are clearly ready and need to leave the wood. Another six are marked as blending components, including some I wouldn’t choose to drink alone. Number 50, for example. At 101.3 proof, it’s tight and tannic, with leather and mint chocolate, but Kennedy sees how its length and darkness could deepen brighter, fruitier whiskey. Three barrels are written off as not viable—too astringent or otherwise faulty. The majority are in good shape, and though it takes us more than six hours, we finally finish tasting the sample lot.

Kennedy is pleased by the session work. “Your memories and mine all came together and influenced each other,” he says. “But there are group memories we can share and relate to, and that makes a better whiskey.”

Which Barrels Make It to 21?

Barrel 41 is bright, fruity, and floral, prompting a question: “Can it hold a little more oak?” It becomes an early candidate for a 21 year. Overall, our group flagged 23 barrels that could benefit from more aging. Take No. 58, at 85.83 proof, the recipient of my “AI’s attempt at generic old bourbon” description. Kennedy agrees there’s nothing wrong with it; however, there’s no serious defect, and he sees it as a component that could fit into several combinations without disrupting them. “Let’s age it up,” he declares, scribbling in his notebook.

While Kennedy hopes to carry roughly 30 barrels forward, reaching that age won’t ensure a release. “It wasn’t a guarantee that I would do a 21,” he says. “The barrels we tasted were going in the right direction, but they’re not there yet.” He wants further development while preserving the candy notes, working with Castle & Key’s team on warehouse placement and reassessing them about every six months. “I have hope, and I’m optimistic,” he says. “But if it shouldn’t be done, we won’t do it.”

Pastry Shops and Kentucky Snow Days

What’s definite is a 2027 Redemption 18 year old release, something he’s currently working on. “Blending is an art form that’s been around for way too long to only be worried about the chemical structure of the product,” Kennedy tells me. That’s why he prefers to connect flavors to moments or emotions. “There’s more there; it’ll have more soul this way,” he says.

His takeaway from the 74 samples we tried was “three completely different maps of flavors” in the inventory: fruity candy; brown sugar, cinnamon, and crème brûlée; and the dusty character of older bourbon. The candy notes connect to his life as a father. He has children ages 5 and 9, one adventurous about food, the other less so. Sweets bring them together, and his eldest is fascinated by a New York shop that makes pastries that resemble the fruits inside them. “Those flavors are a deep part of my life,” he says. “Exploring life and food experiences through these things in my life right now.” 

The baking flavors evoke another setting: Watching snow fall in Kentucky, bourbon in hand, old-school R&B playing. “It’s the warmth and the comfort,” he says. “Brown sugar, cinnamon, ginger, dark chocolate notes.” He’s weighing whether those directions deserve simultaneous releases or separate years, explaining that he wants to tell “the right story at the right time.”

How Does This Batch Compare to the 2026 Redemption 18?

Kennedy says this lot of barrels is similar to the 50 that comprise the 2026 Redemption 18 year old, with “maybe a little more cherry.” Bottled at 102.85 proof, “I had a suspicion when I tasted it,” he says of the 2026 18 year. Much of what he loves is “how much corn shows, with the fruit notes coming through naturally, and the lighter characteristics brought by aging but not diminished by the wood,” he says. “A real highlight of how things can age correctly.”

In my glass, the 2026 Redemption 18-year bourbon delivers perfectly. It’s round, juicy, and bright, offering cherry Blow Pop, vanilla wafer, and salted caramel on the nose, grounded by mushroomy rickhouse funk. The palate is full of syrupy maraschino juice, cherry-pie filling, flaky butter pastry, and cinnamon sugar. Its long finish recalls a final forkful of pie, caramelized browned crust and juicy filling together. It’s one of the most delicious 18-year bourbons I’ve ever had.
wood-ear-telluride:
Japanese whisky has a distinctly Scottish pedigree, having long been inspired and influenced by scotch whisky-making. But in the heart of the Rocky Mountains, Wood Ear Whiskey Lounge & Noodle Bar is putting a uniquely Western spin on the genre.

Telluride is one of the country’s top ski destinations, but also one of the few ski towns that stays busy and vibrant year-round, with extensive hiking and biking, plus a nonstop series of high-profile music, arts, and film festivals. Wood Ear sits right on the town’s main street, Colorado Avenue, in a historic former 19th-century tavern that still showcases the original 1860 Brunswick bar, carved from mahogany, oak, and white tiger pine, with 12-foot French mirrors. In this Old West ambiance, owner Matthew Arnold has created a fun mashup of all things Japan, Texas, and Colorado. He spent years in the restaurant and bar trade in his native Texas before moving to Telluride in 2018 to open Wood Ear. He imports post oak from the Lone Star State to fire his large offset smoker, where he makes classic slow-smoked Texas beef brisket and pulled pork shoulders. These make up some of the most popular dishes on the menu, including the bestseller, Pork on Pork Ramen, a combo of barbecued pulled pork and braised Japanese-style pork belly (chasu), with ramen noodles, roasted corn, cabbage, soft egg, and the namesake wood ear mushrooms in a chicken and pork broth. Another can’t-miss dish is the smoked brisket nigiri: sliced strips of brisket atop vinegared rice in the form of traditional nigiri sushi, a brilliantly delicious idea that pairs very well with whiskey and seems long overdue (there’s also a beef brisket ramen).

This same multicultural approach carries over to the bar, where an impressive display of Japanese whisky sits on shelves alongside several dozen bourbons and a healthy slate of Texan whiskeys, including bottlings from Balcones and Garrison Brothers. There's also a curated list of about 20 mezcals, including several Del Maguey offerings. All spirits are offered in 1 and 2-ounce pours with a 50% discount for the larger size, so for instance, hyper-local Telluride Whiskey is $12/$18, and Del Maguey Chichicapa is $18/$27. The selection also offers several other Colorado whiskeys, including 291 Distillery from Colorado Springs and Peach Street from Palisade. The 40-plus domestic whiskeys start with Sazerac Rye ($10/$15) and run up to WhistlePig The Boss Hog VII, XI and XII, each $140/$210. It also carries a dozen Japanese and about 10 scotch and Irish expressions.

But a big focus of Wood Ear is tasting flights, especially for Japanese whiskies, some of which are highly allocated in Colorado. “When we opened, I wanted to get every Japanese whisky I could, and our spirits list got up to about 300, but we decided to stock only what we could display behind the bar, and based on what was selling, we are now down to about 200,” explains Arnold. “We also focus on cocktails and opened with over 80 house cocktails; now we are down to about 60.” His Japanese introductory flight features 3/4 ounce pours of Mars Iwai, Suntory Toki, and Nikka Coffee Malt for $34; a Nikka flight of Taketsuru, Yoichi, and Miyagikyo is $58; Suntory with Yamazaki Reserve, Hakushu Reserve, and Hibiki Harmony is $96. The top-of-the-line offering is the “High Roller Flight,” with Nikka 21, Hakushu 21, and Yamazaki 18 for $300. There are also flights of Colorado’s 291, Michter’s, Balcones, and Jefferson.

Despite a multi-page cocktail list, the bestseller is the Wood Ear Old Fashioned ($18), accounting for about 15% of all drink orders. It uses Basil Hayden bourbon, house-smoked orange bitters, brown sugar, and a grind of black pepper, topped with a cherry, for an experience Arnold describes as evocative of a “wood-burning stove in a cabin in the woods.” Other interesting whiskey cocktails include the Samurai Sword, their take on a Penicillin (Mars Iwai 45 whisky, lemon, honey, and ginger, $22), and the Palisade Sour (Peach Street bourbon, egg white, lemon, simple syrup, and red wine, $22). The offbeat fusion approach is a refreshing change from Telluride’s many Old West saloons, but Wood Ear’s ultra-creative cuisine and interesting bar menu would stand out in just about any location.
jacobs-pardon-bourbon-review-tasting-not:
Jacob Pardon master blender F. Paul Pacult worked through 73 trial blends over five weeks for the brand’s first bourbon—and he kept coming back to blend number 46, time and again. Still, he pressed on. “I can find something better than 46,” Pacult recalls thinking. After 27 further attempts, he realized, “I could not.”

The result is Jacob’s Pardon bourbon, a nationally available, four-grain, 90-proof blend priced at $60. Its components come from MGP in Indiana, Jackson Purchase in Kentucky, and Middle West in Ohio. Pacult calls it “an ultimate heartland whiskey. I wanted to find a bourbon that would be a crowd pleaser, but I also wanted it to be very individual,” he said.

As Whisky Advocate reported when Jacob’s Pardon launched in 2020, Marc D. Taub, president and CEO of Palm Bay International (Jacob’s Pardon’s parent company), and his son Jake built the brand around presidential pardons granted to their bootlegging relatives. The family chose sourcing and blending over building a distillery, extending its earlier history in rectifying. Earlier releases included an 18 year old American light whiskey and a blend incorporating Tennessee whiskey.

“But the American whiskey business centers around bourbon,” Taub says. “And that needs to be something we offer, though if we enter the bourbon category, we wanted to have something that was a bit different.” So, he tapped Pacult to assemble it. Pacult, a longtime spirits writer and alcohol consultant who’s worked with brands like Louis XIII cognac, said that “bourbon’s a funny animal, because it can be disappointing at times” by not having enough character. He sought character without sacrificing versatility—something that must work in a cocktail without overlooking neat pour enthusiasts.

“The MGP was the foundation,” Pacult says, noting that its 7-year bourbon appeared in every trial batch to establish the blend’s backbone. “It was easy to build upon that.” Next came 4-year high-rye bourbon from Jackson Purchase, “which is the one that brings the fruit,” he says. “I kept coming back to black cherry and black raspberry.” Middle West’s 4 year old wheated bourbon added silkiness as Pacult gave mouthfeel as much consideration as flavor.

Pacult melded the components in varying amounts throughout the blending process, with Pacult’s wife, Sue, having a hand in the final selection. “She’s not a bourbon enthusiast, but she walked into my office and said, ‘What is that fantastic aroma?” he recounts. That sample was number 46. “I did the blending, but Sue did the confirmation,” he quipped.

The combined grain recipe is 72% corn, 16% rye, and 6% each wheat and malted barley. “So does the corn dominate? No, I don’t think so,” says Pacult. He’s correct. The final blend is well-balanced, with none of the individual elements shouting down another. It has ample dark fruit on the soft, sweet nose, plus a light rye spice. It’s got an appealing candy bar vibe, with caramel, chocolate, and malt notes rising.

It’s an easy sipper, with a velvety mouthfeel and a light grip. On the palate, more candy bar mingles with black raspberry and stone fruit. The medium-length finish brings dark chocolate and cherry. Pleasing as a neat pour and sturdy enough for a cocktail, it delivers on Pacult’s original brief. Number 46 was the ideal iteration. The other trial blends only helped him realize it.
old-forester-tribute-series-12-year-bour:
Old Forester is arriving on shelves in a new shape. Its new Tribute Series, a 12 year old bourbon bottled at 115 proof, is housed in a stylish, elongated mid-century modern decanter. Available in limited quantities nationwide beginning October 15, the annual series revives a chapter of Old Forester’s history when its whiskey’s packaging was meant to be beautiful enough to earn a permanent place in the drinks cabinet.

According to Old Forester, Tribute combines older stocks through batching, rather than relying on a single barrel or single lot. "By bringing together some of our most mature whiskey and drawing inspiration from an important chapter in our design history, we've created an expression that honors where Old Forester has been while showcasing what makes our whiskey distinctive today,” said Caleb Trigo, Old Forester’s assistant master distiller.

That production process, higher proof, limited availability, and elegant packaging come at a substantial price: Tribute’s suggested retail price is $300. If Birthday Bourbon, Old Forester’s flagship allocated product, is any indication, expect the price to increase exponentially once Tribute hits the secondary market. Birthday Bourbon is priced at $200, though it frequently moves for $450-plus.

Tribute Series isn’t Old Forester’s most expensive whiskey. That title goes to its 150th Anniversary Brown-Forman decanter, released in 2023. A 12.5 year old bourbon, it had a scant 650 bottles produced, with only 150 bottles offered publicly for a whopping $2,500 each.

According to the distillery, the Tribute Series “opens with aromas of warm caramel, sweet leather, golden raisins, and dark cherries. On the palate, cherry and candied walnuts evolve into sweet cinnamon and cardamom, followed by a long finish of toasted oak, peppercorn, cherry preserves, and black tea.”

Decanters aren’t merely a hollow nostalgia play by the Kentucky distillery. The brand’s first upgraded containers ran from 1950 through 1953 and were designed by Ernst Spuehler. From 1954 through 1969, Raymond Loewy oversaw the design process, including that of the famous 1957 “Sputnik” model.

Tribute becomes the latest Old Forester launch this year. March saw the addition of High Angels’ Share rye to its experimental 117 Series ($65), while July’s Triple Char ($65/375 ml) became the first Old Forester expression made entirely from whiskey distilled at its Main Street facility.

For the average drinker, the immediate question is whether the $300 price tag is worth it. At $25 per year of age, it’s a considerably more expensive option than many of its 12-year counterparts. Consider Knob Creek 12, $60, which earned 95 points from us and second place in our 2020 Top 20. While Weller 12, a 91-point inclusion in our 2026 guide to 12 year old bourbons, has a $70 suggested retail price, markup puts it around $200. Still, with collector fervor showing few signs of slowing, don’t bet on Tribute Series gathering dust on a store’s shelf.
new-whiskeys-from-bookers-jack-daniels-a:
It's an American whiskey-heavy week for new releases, kicking off with the latest batch of Booker's. Joining it is a wheater from New Riff, two new bourbons from Iron Smoke, and a high-rye bourbon from Liberty Pole. Elsewhere, Jack Daniel's has debuted another Single Barrel Special Release rye, Pursuit United has a new double oak rye, Chattanooga Whiskey has its first-ever Tennessee whiskeys, and Penelope has the fifth iteration of its collaborative blend with FCancer. Overseas, Bowmore has partnered with a New York-based design firm on two new single malts. 

Booker’s 2026 Batch No. 3 The Southern Thunder Batch Bourbon

ABV: 63.65%
SRP: $100
Availability: Limited

The third Booker’s batch of the year has arrived. It comprises five different production dates, with the youngest at 7 years old, stored throughout five seven-story warehouses. The barrel breakdown is as follows:

  • 23% matured on the 5th floor of warehouse 3
  • 21% matured on the 3rd floor of warehouse G
  • 22% matured on the 6th floor of warehouse 6
  • 20% matured on the 4th floor of warehouse 4
  • 14% matured on the 4th floor of warehouse M

As with every new batch of Booker’s, this one comes with a story about its namesake, late master distiller Booker Noe. Many who knew Booker described him as “Southern thunder,” because of his deep, booming voice.

Jack Daniel’s Single Barrel Special Release Coy Hill Rye (2026 Release)

ABV: 64.35%–74.25%
SRP: $90
Availability: Nationwide

Jack Daniel’s latest Single Barrel Special Release has arrived. This year’s edition is another rye, following in the footsteps of last year’s debut of Tanyard Hill. These barrels were distilled in 2016 and aged for 10 years on Coy Hill—the highest point of elevation at the distillery—in Barrelhouses 1–13. It uses Jack’s signature rye mashbill of 70% rye, 18% corn, and 12% malted barley, and it underwent the Lincoln County process.

Chattanooga Whiskey Bad Chattanoogan Tennessee Whiskey

ABV: 50%
SRP: $65
Availability: Limited

For its first Tennessee whiskey, Chattanooga Whiskey stayed true to its experimental roots, finishing it with toasted maple wood records (yes, you read that right). The straight Tennessee whiskey is made from three high-malt mashbills, maple charcoal mellowed, and aged 4 years in oak. After this initial maturation, the whiskey was transferred to barrels along with records cut from solid sugar maple; they were toasted for a day and laser-engraved with two original tribute songs about the distillery written by Chattanooga Whiskey creative director Rich Abercrombie, who also fronts the Dollars Family band. The whiskey was finished for 30 days.

Bad Chattanoogan comes in two editions: Side A, “Bad Chattanoogan,” and Side B, “City I Love.” Each bottle comes with a playable four-inch Tiny Vinyl hangtag featuring both original songs. The whiskeys are available at seelbachs.com and at Tennessee retailers.

Given that Chattanooga is a Tennessee-based distillery, it may come as a surprise that this is its first Tennessee whiskey; until now, it had forgone the Lincoln County Process, the hallmark of Tennessee whiskey.

New Riff 6 Year Old Bottled in Bond Wheated Bourbon

ABV: 50%
SRP: $60
Availability: Limited

Newport, Kentucky-based New Riff has unveiled a new wheated bourbon. The mashbill—65% corn, 18% floor-malted wheat, 10% unmalted wheat, and 7% dark wheat—is likened to a beer recipe, drawing on the distilling team's brewing background. The use of floor-malted wheat, a labor-intensive process, is intended to lend the bourbon greater depth and a more robust character. Bottled in bond without chill filtration, the release is available exclusively to New Riff's Whiskey Club members, with pickup at the distillery. 

Penelope FCancer 6 Year Old Blend of Straight Whiskeys (Batch 5)

ABV: 50.5%
SRP: $80
Availability: Nationwide

Now in its fifth year of collaboration with FCancer, Penelope Bourbon has released its annual limited-edition whiskey, this year a 6 year old blend of straight bourbon and American malt whiskeys. Distilled at parent company MGP's distillery in Lawrenceburg, Indiana, the whiskey features a four-grain mashbill of 64% corn, 20% rye, 1% malted rye, and 15% malted barley. Previous releases have featured blends of straight whiskeys, while last year's Batch 4 also included a cask-strength iteration. The brand has pledged $250,000 to the nonprofit that advocates for cancer prevention and early detection.

Pursuit United Extra Special Double Oak Rye

ABV: 63.1%
SRP: $150
Availability: Limited

Louisville-based Pursuit Spirits has debuted Pursuit United XS Double Oak, a new series featuring extended secondary maturation in custom-built barrels. The inaugural release is a barrel proof rye, blending straight rye whiskeys from Bardstown Bourbon Company and Sagamore Spirit before undergoing almost 2 years of additional maturation in American oak barrels from Seguin Moreau's Napa cooperage. The barrels feature a no.-3 char and toasted heads, a combination previously used in its single barrel release, Episode 063. This release is just 720 bottles, with 92% allocated to existing Pursuit’s club (P. Club) members and the remainder reserved for new members who join in person at the brand's Whiskey Row location in Louisville.

Iron Smoke Barrelhouse Collection: 5 year old Maple Barrel Finished Bourbon

ABV: 50%
SRP: $75
Availability: Limited

Iron Smoke Barrelhouse Collection: 10 year old Bourbon

ABV: 57.5%
SRP: $130
Availability: Limited

Fairport, New York distillery Iron Smoke is celebrating its 15th anniversary with a trio of new whiskeys. The first two whiskeys have just been released, including a 5 year old bourbon that finished in maple syrup barrels, and an ultra-aged 10 year old bourbon. The third whiskey, an 8 year old double-oaked bourbon, is expected to launch next month.

Alongside the anniversary, Iron Smoke is celebrating another milestone. Last month, the brand purchased its longtime 20,000-square-foot production space in Fairport. The deal was part of a larger $3 million investment, which aims to upgrade the distillery while increasing its production capacity.

Liberty Pole Spirits High Rye Bourbon

ABV: 50%
SRP: $55
Availability: Limited

Pennsylvania-based Liberty Pole Spirits has introduced a new bourbon to its core range. This one has a “barely legal” mashbill of 51% Bloody Butcher red corn, 40% rye, and 9% malted barley. Co-founder Jim Hough says the goal was to give the rye grain a larger role in the whiskey’s flavor profile, and he recommends tasting it alongside the brand’s wheated bourbon, which uses substantially more corn. Similar to that whiskey, the newcomer was aged 4.5 years.

 

Bowmore Captivo Oak Voyage scotch single malt

ABV: 50.8%
SRP: $350
Availability: Limited

Bowmore Captivo Sherry Cask Pursuit scotch single malt

ABV: 51.8%
SRP: N/A
Availability: Global Travel Retail exclusive

The Bowmore Captivo Collection, comprised of two limited edition single malts, is rooted in collaboration. In creating the new whiskies, the Islay distillery partnered with New York-based design studio Snarkitecture—a somewhat unlikely pairing for a whisky distillery, but chosen for what Bowmore refers to as like-minded “craftsmanship, creativity, and pursuit of discovery.”

The 20 year old Oak Voyage spent two decades in bourbon barrels before being finished in American oak oloroso sherry butts. It’s a U.S. exclusive and will be available starting in November. Sherry Cask Pursuit features a heavier sherry influence; it matured first in Spanish oak oloroso sherry casks and bourbon barrels, and was finished in oloroso hogsheads. As a Global Travel Retail exclusive, it will be available in Taipei and Hong Kong later this year, and in international markets slated for further down the road.

Snarkitecture’s influence is in the whisky’s packaging; co-founder Alex Mustonen visited Islay, drew inspiration from the island’s terrain and the distillery, and created a multilayered portal design for both the box and the label.
whiskey-and-tequila-halloween-cocktails:
Whether you’re throwing a costume party or keeping it low-key this year, a festive cocktail is the perfect way to get into the spirit. 

First, choose your drink: Are you in the mood for something whiskey-based or maybe a tequila tipple? Either way, there’s something for everyone. In addition to warming fall flavors like apple, pumpkin, sage, and cardamom, some of these drinks have a pop of spooky color—think blood red or jet black—from ingredients like blackberry, blood orange, black lava salt, red wine, and amaro, making them all the more appropriate for the holiday. 

Poison Apple

Joann Spiegel, director of operations at Cocktail Kingdom, created for The Haunting pop-up bar

  • 1 oz. rye whiskey
  • 1 oz. apple brandy
  • 1/2 oz. fino sherry
  • 1/2 oz. bitter apple syrup (recipe below)
  • Dehydrated apple slice, for garnish

Stir all ingredients with ice and strain into a rocks glass over a large ice cube. Garnish with a dehydrated apple slice.

Bitter Apple Syrup

  • ½ cup turbinado sugar
  • 1/3 cup apple cider
  • 2 ½ tsps. white miso
  • 1 Tbsp. Angostura bitters
  • 1 Tbsp. Bittermens Elemakule Tiki bitters

Combine sugar and apple cider in a small saucepan over low-medium heat. Warm until sugar is dissolved, whisking frequently. Remove from heat and whisk in miso until fully incorporated. Allow to cool completely, then stir in both bitters. Strain through a fine-mesh strainer into a clean jar or bottle. Store in refrigerator up to 2 weeks. Shake before each use.

Hallowed Be Thy Grove

Cole Johnson, beverage manager at The Edison at Disney Springs in Orlando

  • 1 oz. Dos Hombres blanco tequila
  • 1/2 oz. Dos Hombres mezcal
  • 1/2 oz. crème de mûre
  • 1/2 oz. bourbon barrel-aged maple syrup
  • 1/2 oz. lemon juice
  • 1/4 oz. lime juice
  • 2 dashes Fee Brothers Cardamom bitters
  • Blackberry, for garnish

Add all ingredients to a shaker and shake vigorously. Double strain into a chilled coupe and garnish with a skewered blackberry.

The Severed Sun

Joann Spiegel, director of operations at Cocktail Kingdom, created for The Haunting pop-up bar

  • 1 1⁄4 oz. Kentucky straight bourbon
  • 1⁄2 oz. artichoke amaro
  • 1⁄4 oz. elderflower liqueur
  • 1 1⁄2 oz. acidified grapefruit juice (recipe below)
  • 1 oz. ginger and sage syrup (recipe below)
  • 1 oz. Lambrusco

Add all ingredients except Lambrusco to a cocktail shaker and fill with ice. Shake and strain into an ice-filled Collins glass. Float Lambrusco on top.

Acidified Grapefruit Juice

  • 2 cups grapefruit juice
  • 2 tsps. citric acid

In a non-reactive container, combine grapefruit juice and citric acid, and whisk until the acid dissolves. Bottle and refrigerate up to 2 weeks.

Ginger and Sage Syrup

  • 1 cup sugar
  • ¾ cup water
  • ¼ cup ginger juice
  • 25-30 fresh sage leaves

In a medium saucepan, combine sugar, water, ginger juice, and sage leaves, and bring to a boil. Reduce heat and simmer for 10 minutes. Remove from heat and let the mixture infuse for at least 30 minutes, up to 1 hour. Strain through a bouillon strainer into a bottle and refrigerate up to 2 weeks.

The Doctor

Salt Wood Kitchen & Oysterette in Monterey, California

  • 2 oz. bourbon
  • 1 oz. lemon juice
  • 1/2 oz. Demerara syrup
  • Dash Angostura bitters
  • 1/4 oz. Averna amaro (preferably kept in a vial until serving)

Shake all ingredients except Averna and strain into a coupe. Slowly pour in the Averna.

Black Widow

Nicholas Miller, executive chef at Tropicado at La Concha Key West, Autograph Collection hotel in Key West

  • 11/2 oz. Milagro reposado tequila
  • 3/4 oz. Solerno blood orange liqueur
  • 3/4 oz. fresh lime juice
  • 3/4 oz. blackberry-jalapeño simple syrup (recipe below)
  • 2 blackberries, plus 1 more for garnish
  • 1 thin jalapeño slice, plus 1 more for garnish
  • Black lava salt, for rim

Half-rim a double rocks glass with black lava salt and fill with fresh ice. In a shaker, gently muddle 2 blackberries and 1 jalapeño slice with the blackberry-jalapeño syrup. Add tequila, Solerno, and fresh lime juice. Fill with ice and shake vigorously for about 10-12 seconds. Double-strain into the ice-filled rocks glass. Garnish with one fresh blackberry and one jalapeño wheel.

Blackberry- Jalapeño Simple Syrup

  • 1 cup water
  • 1 cup granulated or Demerara sugar
  • 1 cup fresh blackberries
  • 1 cup deseeded and sliced jalapeños
  • ½ Tbsp. fresh lime juice

Combine water, sugar, blackberries, and jalapeños in a medium saucepan. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves. Do not boil. Lightly muddle blackberries and simmer gently for 8–10 minutes. Remove from heat and steep for 5-10 minutes. Strain through a fine-mesh strainer, then strain again through cheesecloth. Stir in lime juice. Cool, bottle, and refrigerate for up to 3 weeks.

Bone Temple

Erin Hayes and Kelsey Ramage, co-founders of Black Lagoon pop-up bar

  • 2 oz. Teremana blanco tequila
  • 1/4 oz. Lustau amontillado sherry
  • 1 oz. spiced oat orgeat (recipe below)
  • 3/4 oz. tart cherry juice
  • 1/4 oz. lime juice
  • 1 dash absinthe
  • 2 dashes Bitter Queens tobacco bitters
  • Lime wheel and cinnamon stick, for garnish

Whip shake all ingredients with crushed ice and pour into a tiki glass. Top with more crushed ice, lime wheel, cinnamon stick, and drink umbrella (optional).

Spiced Oat Orgeat

  • 2 cinnamon sticks, broken up
  • 4 ½ tsps. pumpkin pie spice
  • 2 cups oat milk
  • 2 ½ cups caster (superfine) sugar
  • ¼ tsp. salt
  • 3 drops vanilla extract

Add cinnamon sticks and pumpkin pie spice to a pot. Toast over medium heat until fragrant. Add oat milk and bring to a simmer. Remove from heat and strain through a coffee filter. Add caster sugar, salt, and vanilla extract, and whisk to dissolve. Bottle and refrigerate up to 2 weeks.
best-london-whisky-cocktail-bars:
For a city with a legendary drinking culture, London’s pubs and bars often shut down just as the evening is getting good. Fortunately, the Shoreditch neighborhood caters to late-night denizens and the “sure, one more” crowd. Over the past decade, this corner of East London has become one of the city's most interesting nightlife districts, with ambitious cocktail bars that compete with the world's best. Whisky is particularly well represented, whether it's a bourbon cocktail served in a tin can or a scotch concoction finished with a red-hot poker. I spent 36 hours drinking my way around Shoreditch and its neighboring enclaves. Here are five bars worth seeking out—and what to order when you get there.

The Cocktail Trading Co.

68 Bethnal Green Road, E1 6GQ


Come for the playful (and delicious) cocktails, stay for the great vibes. The Cocktail Trading Co. is the kind of cocktail bar where the bartenders are having as much fun as the customers. The current menu is structured as a calendar you flip through, with a different beverage per month. Start with the Corn on the Cobbler, created by general manager Tris Carvalho. This melds Evan Williams Extra Aged and Mellow Corn with sweetcorn syrup, honeydew cordial, and a house sherry blend. Served in a corn can and topped with popcorn, it’s an easy sipper that disappears too quickly.

Follow it up with the Ikigai Drive-By, combining Suntory Toki, Maker's Mark, pine and bergamot liqueur, vanilla and cacao bitters, and dandelion-root tea syrup. It arrives inside a flask concealed in a fake self-help book, and you pour it yourself. Personal introspection has never tasted so delicious. Let assistant general manager Thomas Mialhe make you a custom beverage for your third round, or ask barman Dan Williams for one of his Espresso Martinis made with cognac or bourbon to close out the night. If you’re lucky enough, Williams may treat you to the house send-off: a Pickleback made with house-made brine.

Seed Library

100 Shoreditch High Street, E1 6JQ

If you don’t make a reservation, prepare to wait to get into this enclave tucked inside the One Hundred Shoreditch hotel. The brainchild of Ryan Chetiyawardana, better known as Mr Lyan, Seed Library pairs a clean aesthetic with cocktails that are far more complex than their short ingredient lists suggest. There’s also an excellent soundtrack, courtesy of a DJ spinning vinyl.

Orchard flavors seem to be a recurring theme on the current menu. They’re present in the Golden Spring Fix, which combines Maker's Mark, amaretto, elderflower, apple-cured egg yolk, and lemon. And in the Beeswax Old Fashioned, which uses Monkey Shoulder, sugar, bitters, and beeswax to reimagine an old standby. 

There’s also the decadent Koji Hardshake, made with Johnnie Walker Blue Label, miso, koji, cream, sugar, and lemon, a Whiskey Sour turned inside out, with savory fermentation adding depth to the whisky. Want to branch out from whisky? The Dirty Mezcal Martini combines Del Maguey with dry vermouth and fermented tomatillo, creating earthy, crisp flavors in each sip.

The Sun Tavern

441 Bethnal Green Road, E2 0AN

Bartenders from other venues on this list hang here for a reason. The Sun Tavern has the easygoing atmosphere of a neighborhood dive, with a cocktail program that punches well above its weight. It maintains London's largest Irish whiskey selection (including plenty of rare and vintage bottlings) and what it describes as the world's most extensive collection of poitín, Ireland's historically illicit spirit.

The cocktail program here is more classical than experimental, but the menu is still as diverse. On the more imaginative side, you’ve got the Soi Cowboy, with Dewar's 12 year, Desi Daru mango-infused vodka, Thai milk tea, and coconut; a refreshing long drink that draws inspiration from across the globe. The Irish Coffee—Crested 10 whiskey, coffee, and cream—is tasty, but the Belfast Coffee is the winner. Made with Ban poitín, cold brew coffee, cream, demerara, and nutmeg, the poitín adds an earthy, fruity flavor that’s unexpected but quite cohesive. 

FlipDog

104–122 City Road, EC1V 2NR

Founded by Ukrainian hospitality entrepreneurs Artem Skapenko and Alex Kostenyuk, this lively bar approaches drinks with a flourish. FlipDog takes its name from an old cocktail-making technique involving a red-hot iron poker, which it showcases in its Morning on the Platform. That drink combines sesame-infused bourbon, peated scotch, amaretto, oloroso sherry, and coffee, then finishes it with a poker heated to approximately 1,200°C. Next, opt for The Half Pint, which disguises Johnnie Walker, Nixta corn liqueur, sherry, and citra hops as a small beer, complete with a foamy head. It's an inventive twist for whisky drinkers who’ve seen everything.

A Bar With Shapes for a Name

232 Kingsland Road, E2 8AX

When iconic bartenders become obsessed with the Bauhaus art movement, you get one of London's most interesting drinking establishments. Founded by industry veterans Remy Savage, Paul Lougrat, and Maria Kontorravdis, this minimalist Haggerston bar substitutes geometric symbols for a conventional name. (Yes, seriously.) It earned the No. 35 spot on The World's 50 Best Bars list in 2023 and remains the late-night cocktail hotspot because it’s open until 4 a.m. and the cocktails always hit.

Try the Bogler, which combines Buffalo Trace bourbon, shiso, sesame, and lemon for a savory, citrus-bright experience you’ll order on repeat. Or the Atlas, which combines Redbreast 12 year old Irish whiskey with dulce de leche, Amaras Espadín mezcal, and tonka. While spirit-forward, it has a measured sweetness that keeps it balanced. For something lighter and more crushable, the Warp/Weft brings together Suntory Toki, banana, and flaxseed in a silky sipper. Sidle up to the bar and go off-menu by asking the staff—each clad in chromatic coveralls—for something different. I did and was served a banana-and-bourbon Highball riff that was a stunner.

knob-creek-21-johnnie-walker-festive-ble:
Aged liquid seems to be a running theme in this week’s list, which is headlined by the return of Knob Creek 21—the oldest whiskey ever released by Jim Beam—following its debut last year. It’s joined by a new 12 year old from Barrell that explores special French oak casks, a 10 year old from Missouri-based Holladay Distillery, a 10 year old permanent release from independent bottler Copper & Cask, a commemorative release from Wyoming Whiskey, and new bourbons from Koopers and Ghostwood. Looking abroad, Johnnie Walker has a new blend to celebrate the Indian festive season, Dalmore is set to debut a new 18 year old Cigar Malt Reserve spin-off, Teeling taps Venezuelan rum casks for its latest creation, and Indri explores ruby port casks for this year's Diwali Collector’s Edition.

Knob Creek 21 year old Bourbon (2026)

ABV: 50%
SRP: $250
Availability: Nationwide

Last year, Jim Beam rolled out the oldest whiskey in the distillery’s history—a 21 year old Knob Creek bourbon that was distilled by Fred Noe in 2004. Now the distillery is back with a fresh batch, available for a limited time at retailers nationwide. Like its predecessor—and many of the other expressions in Knob Creek’s lineup—this was bottled at 50% ABV.

Barrell 12 year old French Toast(ed) Bourbon

ABV: 53.62%
SRP: $160
Availability: Limited

The newest blend in Barrell’s Red Label Series—which highlights finished whiskeys with age statements—was aged in French oak casks of varying toast levels. The liquid is comprised of 12 to 17 year old bourbons from Kentucky, Indiana, Tennessee, and Wyoming, finished in Grand Chauffe French oak barrels. (Grand Chauffe is a method by which the barrels are subject to low heat over a longer period of time, yielding deeper flavors.) The supporting cast of French oak casks rounded out the blend with additional dimension and layers of flavor. Finishing time varied from 5 to 39 months.

Barrell 12 year old French Toast(ed) is available online and at retailers nationwide.

Ben Holladay 10 year old Bourbon

ABV: 55.5%
SRP: $125
Availability: Limited

In celebration of its 170th anniversary, Weston, Missouri’s Holladay Distillery has released a 10 year old Ben Holladay, its oldest bourbon to date. It’s crafted from the original Ben Holladay bourbon mashbill of 73% corn, 15% rye, and 12% malted barley. It will debut at the distillery at 10:00 a.m. on Saturday, October 17th, with a limit of one bottle per person.

Although the distillery was founded in 1856 and survived Prohibition, by 1985 it was mothballed amid a slumping American whiskey market. Private investors bought the site in 1993, but didn’t restart whiskey operations; that would come 23 years later in 2016, when the distillery underwent a $10 million renovation. Upon completion, it began distilling bourbon once more, led by master distiller Kyle Merklein. 

Wyoming Whiskey Queen of the Tetons Second Edition

ABV: 49.5%
SRP: $80
Availability: 1,000 bottles; online, at the distillery, Wyoming retailers

The second release of Wyoming Whiskey’s Queen of the Tetons, a bourbon that pays homage to Grizzly 399—a bear killed by a car in October 2024—is a blend of just eight barrels. Bottled at 99 proof, the whiskey is made from Wyoming-grown grains and distilled, aged, and bottled in-state. A new documentary film, “399 Forever,” is being released alongside the bourbon, available on Amazon Prime Video beginning today. As part of the release, Wyoming Whiskey will donate $5 from every bottle of Queen of the Tetons Second Edition sold to the Grand Teton National Park Foundation, which supports grizzly education, conservation, and research programs in the park.

Copper & Cask X Barrel Proof Bourbon

ABV: 58.2%
SRP: $70
Availability: Nationwide and online

Independent bottler Copper & Cask has released its first permanent release, a barrel proof bourbon aged 10–12 years. This expression, created by barrel master Stephen Corrigan, comprises 45 barrels of low-rye (21%) and high-rye (36%) MGP bourbons. The barrels were aged in various locations prior to blending, including Indiana, Kentucky, and at Copper & Cask’s own outpost in Rhode Island.

Ghostwood 3 Brothers Bourbon

ABV: 40%
SRP: $49
Availability: Online and select Texas retailers

Bozeman, Montana-based whiskey brand Ghostwood has introduced a new three-grain bourbon. This one was distilled in Indiana with a mashbill of 60% corn, 36% rye, and 4% malted barley. It was aged for 6 years in No.-4 char barrels and bottled in Columbus, Illinois, at 80 proof. According to founder and master blender Lucas Perks, this expression was inspired by memories of sitting by the campfire and telling ghost stories with his brothers.

Koopers Whiskey The Prodigal Son Bourbon

ABV: 47.2%
SRP: $61
Availability: Online, at the Koopers tasting room, and select retailers

Texas blending house Koopers has a new bourbon that celebrates coming home for the holidays and toasting cherished memories. The newcomer is a blend of four mashbills, including high-rye, low-rye, and wheated recipes. The stocks were sourced from Green River, OZ Tyler, and Lux Row distilleries, and were aged 4–6 years.

Bruichladdich The Laddie Rye (2026) Scotch Single Grain

ABV: 50%
SRP: $60
Availability: Select retailers nationwide

Last year, Bruichladdich debuted a new single grain expression touted as a Scottish take on American-style rye whiskey. Now the distillery has released a follow-up that has a slightly different recipe. At 6 years old, the newcomer is just a bit younger than the original. It was distilled entirely from Islay rye and barley harvested in 2019 and aged in a mix of first-fill bourbon barrels and second-fill American Virgin Oak casks. Unlike the original, which used toasted and uncharred oak, the new batch includes a selection of de-toasted and re-charred bourbon barrels.



Johnnie Walker Blue Label Festive Blend blended scotch

ABV: 40%
SRP: $220
Availability: Limited; imported by Diageo USA

Johnnie Walker is no stranger to limited-edition packaging, but its new Festive Blend offers something more substantial: A whisky created specifically for India’s festive season. Developed by Johnnie Walker master blender Dr. Emma Walker, this limited edition was drawn from older stocks to create a balanced, spicy flavor profile designed to complement the cuisine of the Indian festive table. The release continues Johnnie Walker’s collaboration with Indian couturier Rahul Mishra, whose design brings a contemporary dimension to the brand’s celebration of Indian culture and festive traditions.

The release continues a broader theme in Walker’s work to evolve Blue Label through blending with purpose. The 93-point Johnnie Walker Blue Label Elusive Umami explored whisky’s relationship with gastronomy in collaboration with chef Kei Kobayashi, with a recommended pairing with Oscietra caviar, while the 94-point Johnnie Walker Label Azure was designed with coastal dining and seafood in mind. Now, Festive Blend draws inspiration from India's spices and celebratory traditions.

Dalmore 18 year old Cigar Malt Signature Reserve Scotch Single Malt

ABV: 46%
SRP: $400
Availability: Nationwide starting in November

Dalmore announced that it will add a new expression to its core Signature Range starting next month. The newcomer is purpose-built for pairing with cigars, following the success of the distillery’s Cigar Malt Reserve expression. It was aged for 16 years in bourbon barrels before finishing in a series of four casks—matusalem sherry, marsala, cabernet franc, and cabernet sauvignon. The latter three of those were French oak casks. The final whisky was bottled at 46% ABV with natural color and no chill filtration.

Teeling Small Batch Santa Teresa 1796 Cask Finish Blended Irish

ABV: 46%
SRP: $50
Availability: Limited; imported by Bacardi

Teeling adds a Venezuelan rum twist to its Small Batch series with this limited-edition release, swapping the Caribbean rum casks typically used for its flagship blend for solera casks from Santa Teresa 1796 to add depth and character. The collaboration brings together two producers with deep heritage; the Venezuelan rum producer has roots dating back over 200 years, while the Teeling family’s whiskey-making history in Dublin stretches back to 1782. The collaboration was developed through close partnership between Teeling’s master distiller Alex Chasko and Santa Teresa 1796 master blender Nancy Duarte, exchanging expertise, casks, and insights throughout the maturation process. The expression arrived in select European markets in September and is expected in the U.S. by early 2027.



Indri Diwali Collector’s Edition 2026 Ruby Port Cask Indian single malt

ABV: 58.5%
SRP: $275
Availability: 540 bottles for the U.S.; imported by ImpEx Beverages Inc.

Indri master blender Surrinder Kumar matured this year’s 2026 Diwali Collector’s Edition in ruby port casks. Now in its fourth year, the series pairs distinctive cask maturation with specially commissioned packaging. This edition’s artwork by Indian designer Krsna Mehta draws on royal heritage and traditional miniature paintings. Diwali, the Festival of Lights, celebrates the triumph of light over darkness. The series debuted in 2023, earning 92 points, with the first two annual expressions featuring peated malt matured in sherry casks, though with subtle differences in ABV and cask types, before the 2025 edition turned to marsala wine cask maturation.
lost-lantern-george-dickel-collection:
From its rustic outpost in Vergennes, Vermont, Lost Lantern has bottled a wide variety of whiskeys from distilleries across the country (all 50 states, in fact). The independent bottler has primarily worked with craft whiskey makers, though some bigger distilleries such as High West and New Riff have also appeared in Lost Lantern releases. The company is now featuring a bigger name: Tennessee’s Cascade Hollow and its George Dickel brand, in Lost Lantern’s first collection dedicated to a single distillery.

When Lost Lantern founders Nora Ganley-Roper and Adam Polonski met with Nicole Austin, director of American whiskey liquid development at Diageo (parent company of Dickel), who, prior to taking on that role, had served as Cascade Hollow’s general manager and distiller since 2018, she was keen on sharing a different side of Dickel with them. “We knew that Dickel had a number of unique projects and experiments hidden in their warehouses, but honestly wouldn’t have known what to ask for,” says Polonski. “We asked Nicole what whiskeys she was particularly excited about and didn’t necessarily have immediate plans for—the kinds of whiskeys that would both excite folks who already love George Dickel, and intrigue folks who are more used to the small distilleries we usually work with.” The resulting Lost Lantern collection ranges from Tennessee whiskey (Dickel’s bread and butter) to light whiskey, non-charcoal filtered bourbon, and the first-ever bottled iterations of Dickel rye and wheat whiskey. 

The three most widely available whiskeys in the George Dickel Collection are part of Lost Lantern’s Single Distillery Series, which emphasizes blends and has also included releases from Balcones, Whiskey Del Bac, and New York Distilling. Ganley-Roper, Lost Lantern’s head blender, created the blends with input from Polonski and Austin in the early stages, developing prototypes while visiting Dickel and then scaling them up in Vermont. Among the new whiskeys in the Dickel Single Distillery Series is Fabled Forest ($100), a Tennessee whiskey that’s bottled at a cask strength of 46.6% ABV. (Middle Tennessee is one of the few places in the U.S. where a whiskey’s proof will go down over time, due to persistent humidity in the warehouse.) It’s a blend of 7 barrels aged between 11 and 18 years, with about a quarter of the blend coming in at 18 years old.

Next up is Wild Woodland Tennessee straight rye ($80), which is comprised of 5 barrels of 7 year old whiskey and bottled at 59.15% ABV. It marks the first release of Dickel’s own Tennessee-distilled rye; previously, the distillery’s ryes have all come from Indiana’s MGP.

The Dickel Single Distillery Series rounds out with Golden Grove Tennessee straight wheat whiskey ($80), a blend of six barrels at 60% ABV; like the rye, it’s also the first release of such a whiskey from Dickel. There are 815 bottles of Fabled Forest, 665 of Wild Woodland, and 677 of Golden Grove, available online at lostlanternwhiskey.com and seelbachs.com; at retailers in California, New York, Massachusetts, and Illinois; and at the Lost Lantern Tasting Room.

In addition to the three Single Distillery Series whiskeys, there are a bevy of single barrel releases, which are far more limited. There are seven unique Dickel single barrels in total:

  • George Dickel 11 year old Tennessee whiskey; made from 84% corn, 8% rye, and 8% malted barley (2 barrels)
  • George Dickel 18 year old Tennessee whiskey; made from 84% corn, 8% rye, and 8% malted barley, and bottled at 40.3% ABV. The oldest whiskey Lost Lantern has ever released (3/4 barrel)
  • George Dickel 10 year old bourbon—not charcoal mellowed; made from 75% corn, 21% rye, and 4% malted barley (2 barrels)
  • George Dickel 10 year old Tennessee whiskey Groovy Staves; aged for 10 years in a barrel made with grooved staves to maximize wood contact (1 barrel)
  • George Dickel Tennessee 7 year old rye; made from 84% rye, 8% corn, and 8% malted barley. The first standalone release of Dickel’s Tennessee-distilled, charcoal-filtered rye, though it previously appeared as part of a collaborative blend made with Colorado-based Leopold Bros. (4 barrels)
  • George Dickel Tennessee 7 year old wheat whiskey; made from 100% wheat (2 barrels)
  • George Dickel Tennessee 8 year old light whiskey; made from 84% corn, 8% rye, and 8% malted barley. Another previously unreleased style from Dickel. (2 barrels)

The single barrel whiskeys are available exclusively through individual retailers; visit lostlanternwhiskey.com for information on where to find each one.

As Lost Lantern’s star and scope continue to rise, Polonski and Ganley-Roper expect their mission to remain the same. “Most of our partners will always be small distilleries…we are open to working with other major distilleries, but we need to be able to do it with full transparency, working closely with their team, as we did with Nicole,” says Polonski. “And we need to have something to add: something that Lost Lantern can say or share about the distillery that will excite and surprise people, even people who already love that distillery and know it well.”
macallan-fine-and-rare-1926-60-year-old-:
On October 9th, Sotheby’s sold the ninth bottle of Macallan 1926 60 year old to break a million dollars at auction. Held at the Macallan Distillery, Sotheby’s achieved a hammer price of £1.7 million for Macallan Fine & Rare 1926 60 year old. This met Sotheby’s low pre-sale estimate, but fell just shy of the record hammer price of £1.75 million set by Sotheby’s for the Macallan Valerio Adami 1926 60 year old in 2023.


With buyer’s premiums added, the equivalent price in U.S. dollars was $2,810,874, the favorable exchange rate putting this figure ahead of the equivalent value of the 2023 sale of the Valerio Adami label. Sotheby’s recognized both auctions were conducted in the UK, so with a hammer price falling £50,000 short, this does not represent a new record. Nor, after a three-year wait, did it break the $3 million barrier. It is, however, a new record for the Macallan Fine & Rare 1926 60 year old label, beating the earlier record set in 2019, and a fitting way to mark the centenary of its distillation.

After maturing for six decades, just 40 bottles of The Macallan 1926 were drawn from a single sherry-seasoned oak cask (No. 263) in 1986, representing the oldest vintage bottled by Macallan. A maximum of 14 were decorated with the Fine and Rare label, 12 were designed by Sir Peter Blake, and a further 12 by Italian artist Valerio Adami. Irish artist Michael Dillon hand-painted one bottle, and the other is the last unlabeled Macallan 1926 60 year old in existence. The Macallan Fine & Rare 1926 60 year old was released in 2002, becoming the foundation of Macallan’s iconic Fine & Rare collection. 

The auction of private collections predominantly featured Macallan distilled and bottled in the 20th century, including Macallan Anniversary Malts, Gran Reserva, and Red Ribbon releases. Two-thirds of the hammer prices exceeded the high estimates for the lots, and 100% of lots sold. Macallan 1986 Romantica Collection was Lot 1, a three-bottle set created by Macallan exclusively for the sale in honor of the centenary of Macallan 1926 60 year old. Inside each bottle was Macallan 1986 40 year old drawn from a single sherry-seasoned European oak cask No. 9925, and bottled at 42.6%, the same strength as the Macallan 1926 60 year old bottled in 1986. Macallan commissioned the three original Macallan 1926 60 year old artists, namely Valerio Adami, Sir Peter Blake, and Michael Dillon, to create an original work celebrating the passage of time from 1986 to 2026. They were presented in a bespoke presentation cabinet containing remarkable artifacts from the creative process, including Valerio Adami’s paintbrush, original collage elements from Sir Peter Blake, and a preliminary sketch from Michael Dillon. The set sold for a hammer price of $171,959, with proceeds split between three charities selected by the artists.

Additional sale highlights included a full set of Macallan in Lalique decanters from the Six Pillars collection which garnered an impressive $370,374, far above recent bids for individual bottles. A bottle of Macallan 1937 The Golden Age of Travel – The Ocean Liner sailed off with a hammer price of $112,435. This is a rebottling from 2015, so the liquid inside is only 34 years old, but only 50 bottles were released. Then there was the return of the once record-breaking bottle No. 3 of Macallan The Reach 81 year old; a one-of-one release from 2022 with a red-lined case that Sotheby’s previously sold in October 2022 for $270,487 direct from Macallan, with proceeds going to charity. Four years later, the one-of-one edition, the oldest Macallan in the sale, only reached a hammer price of $138,890, 56% lower than its last appearance (hammer price fell from £240,000 to £105,000).

The sale has done much to shore up the Macallan secondary market, one of the partnership’s aims, and brought the auction to the distillery, reaffirming demand for its most coveted historic bottlings. Yet, three years on from the Macallan 1926 60 year old record, the failure to surpass that benchmark, coupled with the conspicuous absence of the Red Collection, TIME:SPACE, Folio, and other significant series from the past decade, suggests greater caution remains over the value of contemporary Macallan releases. Whether this renewed focus on historic bottlings will translate into stronger results for modern releases at future auctions remains to be seen. The 56% fall in the hammer price of the one-of-one Macallan The Reach 81 year old offered a more sobering reminder that, despite the strength of its auction heritage, the distillery has yet to resolve all its secondary-market challenges.

russells-reserve-camp-nelson-d-2026-revi:
For four years, Russell’s Reserve has explored the influence of warehouse location on whiskey maturation by narrowing its focus. Each installment of its coveted Single Rickhouse Collection has drawn barrels from one or two floors at a specific location in its Camp Nelson warehouse complex to showcase how differences in elevation, airflow, and temperature can shape a bourbon’s character. For the fifth release, master distiller Eddie Russell flipped that approach, drawing barrels from five floors of Camp Nelson D to create a rye flavor profile.

Meet Russell’s Reserve Single Rickhouse 2026 Camp Nelson D, a 120.8-proof bourbon that Russell says tastes remarkably like a rye whiskey.

The Single Rickhouse collection debuted in 2022 with Camp Nelson C, selected from floors three and four, considered the warehouse’s sweet spot. Camp Nelson F followed in 2023, with barrels from the fourth and fifth floors, where abundant airflow influenced maturation. In 2024, Russell turned to the sixth floor of Camp Nelson B, where greater exposure to heat and sunlight produced pronounced honey and char notes. Last year’s Camp Nelson E explored whiskey matured on the fifth floor of a cooler, more shaded warehouse. Bottled at 128 proof, it became Single Rickhouse’s highest-proof release to date.

Camp Nelson D takes the experiment a step further, exploring what happens when whiskey matured under different conditions throughout the same building is brought together. Built in 1946, Camp Nelson D occupies an elevated, west-facing position on the property, relatively isolated from neighboring warehouses. That location allows strong, consistent airflow through the building, creating an aging environment distinct from those previously featured in the series.

“Camp Nelson D was the first rickhouse I ever worked in at Camp Nelson when I started as a union employee 45 years ago, so coming back to it for this release meant a lot to me,” Russell said in a statement. Rather than concentrating on a particular section of the warehouse, Russell and his team selected barrels from floors one, three, four, five, and six, the broadest vertical selection in the collection’s history. The decision was driven by what they discovered during tasting, particularly in an unlikely location: the ground floor.

“We don’t typically draw from the first floor,” Russell says. “But some of the barrels we tasted down there contributed an earthy character that helped build the spicy, rye-like profile we found ourselves chasing. Once we realized what was developing, we leaned into it. This is the first Single Rickhouse release where, tasted blind, you'd bet it was a rye.”

That’s a notable transformation for a bourbon made with Wild Turkey’s standard mashbill of 75% corn, 13% rye, and 12% malted barley. According to the distillery, Camp Nelson D opens with aromas of baked fruit, apple, vanilla, and baking spices, followed by cinnamon, clove, stone fruit, and rye bread. Pepper, spicy oak, and lingering rye spice appear during the medium-length finish. (We’ll update this story with our tasting notes shortly.)

Non-chill filtered and bottled at barrel proof, Camp Nelson D adds another dimension to the collection’s ongoing examination of whiskey terroir. Whereas previous editions showed how individual locations within a warehouse could produce distinctive flavors, this release explores how those differences can be combined to create something greater than the sum of their parts.

Russell’s Reserve Single Rickhouse 2026 Camp Nelson D is available in limited quantities at select U.S. retailers and the Wild Turkey Distillery visitor center for a suggested retail price of $300.
the-long-orchard-whiskey-cocktail-recipe:
American single malt whiskey continues to gain popularity, not only because it's delicious on its own, but also because it makes a layered yet balanced foundation for cocktails.

“American single malt has enough character to remain clearly present in a drink,” says Jason Hedges, corporate beverage director of LT Hospitality at the Eventi Kimpton Hotel in New York City. “Malted barley brings texture, toast, fruit, and a distinctive grain-driven richness, while American oak can contribute caramel, vanilla, and spice. It gives a bartender many of the qualities associated with classic malt whisky, but often with a broader and more distinctly American flavor vocabulary.”

Hedges recommends building around those qualities rather than covering them up. Try his Long Orchard, a “restrained, spirit-forward” drink built around the flavors of a late-fall orchard: dark fruit, weathered wood, cool air, and deeper sweetness. It's malt-forward with layers of dark cherry, caramelized sugar, orange oil, and warming spice. “The demerara gives it a rich, rounded texture, while the bitters provide enough structure to keep the drink dry and composed. The cherry sits in the background, drawing out the whiskey's fruit without turning the cocktail sweet or overly flavored,” he says.

The Long Orchard

  • 2 oz. Stranahan's Blue Peak (or other American single malt)
  • 1/4 oz. rich demerara syrup (recipe below)
  • 1 tsp. Rothman & Winter Orchard Cherry liqueur
  • 4 dashes Angostura bitters
  • orange twist for garnish

Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice. Stir about 25 revolutions, then strain over a large cube in a rocks glass. Garnish with orange twist.

Rich Demerara Syrup

  • 1/4 cup water
  • 1/2 cup sugar

Combine water and sugar in a small saucepan over low heat. Warm gently, stirring frequently until sugar completely dissolves, about 2 minutes. Don't allow mixture to boil. Remove from heat and let cool. Transfer to an airtight container. Keep refrigerated for up to 1 month.
high-west-midwinter-dram-14-russells-res:
This week sees a series of special releases from distilleries on both sides of the pond. The lone scotch comes from Isle of Skye, which has introduced a new whisky finished in magma stone-toasted casks. In the U.S., the latest release in the Russell’s Reserve Single Rickhouse series is here, High West has another act of A Midwinter Night’s Dram, Buzzard’s Roost is back with its Cigar Blend bourbon, Keeper’s Heart has debuted its first rye, and Maker’s Mark has launched the World Wood Collection. And from Oklahoma’s Wanderfolk Distillery is a new blended bourbon.

Isle of Skye Magma Stone Toasted Cask Finish Blended Scotch

ABV: 46
SRP: $47
Availability: Nationwide at Total Wine & More

Isle of Skye Whisky pays homage to its home with this latest blend, which underwent secondary maturation in a magma stone-toasted cask. Why magma stone? Skye, the largest of Scotland’s Inner Hebrides islands, formed in part by volcanic activity that shaped its mountains and rock formations over millions of years and left plenty of magma stone (about three-quarters of the island’s surface). The finishing casks were toasted with heated volcanic stone—a controlled process said to distribute toast more evenly throughout the barrels. The new blend, while limited, is available nationwide at Total Wine & More stores.

This isn’t the first magma-toasted barrel-finished whisky. Others have included Talisker Magma 47 year old single malt, Talisker Molten Seas 14 year old, and Dewar’s 21 year old Magma Stone Toasted blended scotch. All three were similarly finished in casks that were toasted with magma rocks (Talisker’s came from its home base of Skye, while Dewar’s sourced its volcanic stone from Iceland). The practice of using heated rocks to toast barrels comes from the wine world, and dates back to the early 2000s, when Maison Moussié cooperage founder Thomas Moussié started experimenting with heated rocks as a cask-toasting tool. He patented the lava stone-toasting process in 2018.

Russell’s Reserve Single Rickhouse Bourbon 2026: Camp Nelson D

ABV: 60.4%
SRP: $300
Availability: Limited

For the fifth release of the terroir-driven Russell’s Reserve Single Rickhouse series, master distiller Eddie Russell turned to Camp Nelson D, one of Camp Nelson's highest-elevation rickhouses (one of three maturation sites Wild Turkey owns). Rickhouse D, one of five rickhouses on the Camp Nelson property, was built in 1946. It sits on the western side of the site, experiences consistently strong airflow, and represents the highest-elevation rickhouse ever featured in the Single Rickhouse collection. The rickhouse also holds a special place in Russell’s heart—it was the first site he worked at when he joined Wild Turkey 45 years ago.

In creating the new whiskey, Russell pulled barrels from floors one, three, four, five, and six of the seven-story rickhouse—incorporating more floors than any previous Single Rickhouse release. Russell describes the resulting bourbon as earthy, with a “spicy, rye-like profile” that’s rounded out by notes of baked fruit, vanilla, and stone fruit. Russell’s Reserve Single Rickhouse 2026: Camp Nelson D is available across the U.S. in limited quantities, and at the Wild Turkey visitor center in Lawrenceburg, Kentucky.

High West A Midwinter Night’s Dram Act 14

ABV: 49.3%
SRP: $125
Availability: Limited

The latest chapter of High West’s A Midwinter Night’s Dram is a blend of 4 to 10 year old straight rye whiskeys that’s finished in a combination of ruby port, tawny port casks, oloroso, amontillado, and Pedro Ximénez casks—the first time sherry casks have been used for the whiskey’s secondary maturation. The components of the blend (which is High West’s Rendezvous Rye) are 95% rye, 5% malted barley from MGP; 80% rye, 20% malted rye distilled at High West; and 64% rye, 30% corn, and 6% malted barley from Bardstown Bourbon Co. A Midwinter Night’s Dram Act 14 is available at the High West General Store in Park City, Utah, and online. Of the nine A Midwinter Night’s Dram releases we’ve reviewed, seven have scored 90 points or above.

Buzzard’s Roost Cigar Blend Bourbon (2026 Edition)

ABV: 52.5%
SRP: $85
Availability: Nationwide

Another edition of Buzzard’s Roost Cigar Blend bourbon is here. The new whiskey follows the same path as its forebear: a mashbill of 60% corn, 36% rye, and 4% malted barley, and is double-oaked, aged first in new oak, then finished in the brand’s standard lightly charred, heavily toasted barrels. While the bourbon has national distribution, it’s also available at the Buzzard’s Roost tasting room and microdistillery on Louisville’s Whiskey Row, and online. Buzzard’s Roost launched its cigar blend program with a rye in 2022 and has since alternated between bourbon and rye releases each fall.

Keeper’s Heart Triple Pot Distilled Straight Rye

ABV: 48%
SRP: $50
Availability: Nationwide

The second release in the Keeper’s Heart Triple Pot Distilled range is a rye, made from a mashbill of 90% rye and 10% malted rye, all sourced from the Midwest, and triple distilled in copper pot stills. The triple distillation, not often seen in American whiskey, is spearheaded by master distiller Brian Nation, an Irishman (former master distiller at Midleton Distillery) who has melded the whiskey-making traditions of Ireland and the U.S. at the Minneapolis -based O’Shaughnessy Distilling Co., the home of Keeper’s Heart. The new rye will be available next month, both in stores and online.

The first whiskey in the distillery’s Triple Pot Distilled series, American Pot Still, debuted last year. That whiskey was a blend of malted and unmalted barley and underwent triple distillation in the distillery’s copper pot stills.

Tallbird Blend of Straight Bourbons

ABV: 46.5%
SRP: $25
Availability: Limited

Guthrie, Oklahoma-based Wanderfolk Distillery has introduced a new blended bourbon. Tallbird, whose name is a nod to the nickname given to aircraft during sonic boom tests throughout the 1950s and ‘60s, is comprised of 7 year old bourbons sourced from Kentucky’s Bardstown Bourbon Co. and Tennessee-based TN Distilling. Once in Oklahoma, blending was overseen by head distiller Jeffrey Cole. At just $25, Tallbird is a real bargain. It’s available on Wanderfolk’s website and in Arkansas, Kansas, Missouri, Nebraska, and Oklahoma. The distillery is opening a tasting room later this fall.

Maker’s Mark World Wood Collection Expedition 01 Bourbon

ABV: 47.5%
Price: $85/liter
Availability: Limited

Maker’s Mark has launched the World Wood Collection, a Travel Retail-exclusive series with a triple oak-finished bourbon as its inaugural release. Expedition 01 marks the first use of Japanese mizunara oak staves in the label’s history, alongside French and American white oak. The parcels were individually finished, each barrel containing only ten staves of its respective wood, before blending. The release builds on Maker’s Mark’s longstanding approach to oak as more than just an aging vessel, spotlighting its role in shaping the final whiskey. Bottled at 47.5% ABV, it comes in a 1-liter bottle, available exclusively through Avolta retail outlets at New York (JFK), London (LHR), Istanbul (SAW), Perth (PER), and Bengaluru (BLR) airports.
tequilas-aged-or-finished-in-wine-barrel:
The majority of aged or finished tequilas are matured in bourbon or new oak barrels, as these are the most widely available. The flavors they produce—vanilla and toasted coconut, among others—certainly go well with most tequila taste profiles. But some producers have set their sights on other barrels, including wine, echoing a popular practice in the whisky world.

Among the first wine cask-matured tequilas available in the U.S. was Código Rosa blanco, a Napa Valley cabernet sauvignon-aged tequila introduced in 2016. In eschewing new oak and bourbon barrels for its aged tequilas (its reposado, añejo, and extra añejo are also aged in red wine casks), Código co-founder Federico Vaughan says he became committed to unlocking another level of complexity that couldn’t be achieved otherwise. “When we started Código, we quickly realized that most producers were using whiskey barrels simply because they were readily available, not because they were the best choice for tequila,” he reasons. “Aging [should bring out] a depth of aroma and flavor that you simply cannot achieve with an old whiskey barrel, especially when the goal isn’t to mask the agave, but to complement it.”

Código experimented with several grape varietals and oak origins before landing on Napa Valley cabernet sauvignon barrels made of French oak. Codigo’s Rosa spends 1 month in cabernet casks, and its pale pink hue resembles that of Provençal rosé. Vaughan says the tequila’s flavors are just as delicate as its color. “There are beautiful layers of dark fruit—ripe cherry and raspberry—subtle floral notes, and a gentle earthiness that adds wonderful depth,” he says. “And what makes Rosa so distinctive is that those wine characteristics don’t overwhelm the agave—they elevate it.”

In the years following the introduction of Código Rosa, rosa tequilas have become much more a fixture—the soft pink color has proven as alluring in tequila as it has long been in wine. Others who’ve thrown their hat into the rosa ring include Cazcanes, which has a Napa Valley cabernet sauvignon-aged reposado; Calirosa, with an extra añejo aged in California red wine barrels for 5 years; and Komos Reposado Rosa, aged in French oak red wine barrels for 2 months. Don Julio also has a rosa, finished for 2 months in ruby port.

Like Vaughan, Escasa Tequila master distiller Grace Gonzalez has found that wine barrels work well with tequila’s agave characteristics, not stripping or outshining them. With Escasa, introduced last fall, she melded her love of albariño wine with tequila, finishing the brand’s reposado in Spanish oak albariño casks for 4 to 6 months. While the tequila is lighter in color—those white wine barrels don’t have much color to transfer—the flavor profile shows up strong. Gonzalez describes the reposado as “herbal and high in minerality, balanced by citrus and acidity,” and calls it “the perfect marriage between wine and tequila.”

Aside from the complementary flavors imbued by wine barrels, Vaughan also praises the barrels’ integrity. “Because wine has a low ABV compared to spirits like whisky or fortified wines, the grain of the barrel remains strong after aging,” he explains. “Whisky barrels, on the other hand, have already given so much of themselves to the spirit, the oak is essentially exhausted.” Código hasn’t yet experimented with other wine barrels, but Vaughan isn’t ruling it out, as long as the barrel’s influence complements the agave, it’ll be considered.

Wine Barrel-Influenced Tequilas to Try

Aged in Napa Valley cabernet sauvignon barrels for 82 days

92 Escasa Reposado, 40%, $120

Aged in albariño casks from Spain’s Rías Baixas region for 4 to 6 months

92 Mi Campo Wine Barrel Aged Blanco, 40%, $25
