Rested in Napa Valley cabernet sauvignon barrels for 1 month
boston-travel-guide-for-whisky-lovers:
In this semiquincentennial year, American history is front and center, and few cities lay claim to as much of it as Boston. Ever since the Pilgrims landed at nearby Plymouth Rock in 1620, a long list of important historical events has unfolded here, from the Boston Tea Party and Paul Revere’s ride to the nation’s first public school and city park. Today, it offers visitors a unique blend of New England traditions and living history, along with top-flight whisky venues. And the city’s small geographical footprint makes it even more desirable. Boston Logan Airport is less than three miles from downtown, and Amtrak serves the city’s central train stations. Once you’re here, Boston is compact and mostly walkable.

Day One

Get into the Boston spirit and walk the Freedom Trail, a 2.5-mile path that links 16 key historic sites, including Old North Church, where Paul Revere’s famous “One if by land, two if by sea” lanterns were hung; the Granary Burying Ground, where Revere, Samuel Adams, and John Hancock have their final resting places; and the USS Constitution. The Freedom Trail begins at Boston Common, America’s first public park, founded in 1634, and the adjacent Boston Public Garden, where you can ride the pond in the famed Swan Boats.

Grab lunch (Wednesday to Sunday) at Buttermilk & Bourbon in the heart of the Back Bay, three blocks from the Garden. In addition to the signature buttermilk-fried chicken, specialties include warm honey- glazed biscuits with pimento cheese, New Orleans-style barbecued shrimp, and crawfish arancini, all washed down with whiskey cocktails like the Honey Butter Old Fashioned, made with brown butter-washed private barrel Maker’s Mark, honey, and Angostura bitters. There’s a concise but well-curated whisky list. Highlights include Eagle Rare 10 year old ($16/2 oz.) and the house private barrel Maker’s Mark ($17).

The city’s top waterfront lodging is Boston Harbor Hotel, which has a gorgeous setting on Rowes Wharf, with direct ferries to and from Logan Airport. The location is ideal—a short walk from the North End, Faneuil Hall Marketplace, and the Seaport District. Boston Common is also close, and ferries to Boston Harbor Islands National Park are less than a five-minute stroll. But the main draw for whisky lovers is The Dark Bar (from 4 p.m. daily), one of the best in the city. Inspired by Boston’s Colonial history, the cocktail menu has traditional 17th to 19th century punches, plus historic spin-offs like Fizzes, Sours, and Juleps, including a Whisky Punch made with Macallan 12 year old, lemon juice, Drambuie, and allspice dram. The spirits list has about 120 whiskies, including many rarities: Pappy Van Winkle 23 year old ($745/2 oz.), Macallan 30 year old ($755), and Laphroaig 34 year old Ian Hunter Book 5 ($385). More affordable options are available, even for unusual selections like Ireland’s Dunbrody Bourbon Cask ($19).

But that’s just the start. If you really want to splurge, The Dark Bar is one of the few places in the world where you can try Balvenie 60 year old, distilled in the first year of legendary malt master David Stewart’s tenure, with only 71 bottles ever made. A 1.5-oz. pour runs $12,500. The Dark Bar also offers “The Barrel Tasting Experience,” four 1-oz. pours of its rotating private cask bottlings and a classic Manhattan or Old Fashioned made using your favorite of the flight. This must be pre-booked, but is available Tuesday through Saturday, 5-10 p.m.

If you’re looking for an upscale but more modestly priced hotel, try The Liberty in the popular and walkable Back Bay. It’s an architectural masterpiece converted from an 1851 jail. Touches like cell doors and observation catwalks have been left in place, but instead of cells and a mess hall, there are comfortable guest rooms and one of Boston’s best slates of restaurants and bars. Riding the trend of “experiential travel,” The Liberty has a magic show and frequent lobby activations, with craft artisan stands, local food, wine, and spirits tastings, live music, and other pop-ups. Among the venue’s restaurants is Scampo, an Italian spot with elaborate homemade pastas and signature lobster pizza by celebrity chef Lydia Shire, plus several bars.

For a happy hour snack and libation, hit Vermilion Club in the heart of downtown. It’s a full-service high-end restaurant, but from 3-6 p.m. Monday through Friday, the bar serves discounted New England seafood specialties like clams casino, fried calamari, and even $1 oysters. While 70-plus whiskies are offered, the focus is on cocktails, headlined by the house Manhattan: private cask Knob Creek bourbon, Inniskillin Cabernet Franc ice wine, and house bitters ($18).

Then head to Bully Boy Distillers in an industrial part of the Roxbury neighborhood. Bourbon is its flagship product, and they make three styles: a high-rye (23%) bottled in bond, a high-wheat (30%) straight, and a limited single barrel Experimental Series, along with an American straight whiskey. Tours and tastings are available. Flights of its two permanent bourbons and American whiskey are offered ($13/3 1-oz.), along with both classic and creative cocktails. They always have three rotating barrel-aged seasonal whiskey cocktails. Be prepared to settle in and chat with the passionate staff.

New England is famous for its seafood, and no trip to Boston is complete without sampling dishes like clam chowder, haddock, and shellfish. Head to Seamark Seafood & Cocktails, which also doubles as your evening’s entertainment, as it’s located in Encore Boston Harbor, one of the largest and liveliest casino resorts in the Northeast. You can try your luck at gaming, enjoy DJs and live music, or even the occasional title fight, and then head to dinner.

Not many seafood specialists have the kind of whisky program you’ll find here, with over 100 selections, but don’t overlook the delicious specialty cocktails, like the Mr. Lee Manhattan (Nikka Coffey Grain, Lillet Blanc, and orange bitters) or the B-Town Old Fashioned (Michter’s US*1 straight rye, Bacardi Reserva 8 year old rum, Vermont maple syrup, and chicory pecan bitters). There’s a full raw bar with local oysters and clams, plus a menu of New England classics, including clam chowder, lobster bisque, spicy fried calamari, and baked haddock, along with wagyu steaks for surf & turf.

There are few upscale seafood spots with this much whisky, but even fewer with a hidden speakeasy. Old Wives’ Tale is inside Seamark and has its own list of specialty cocktails, as well as everything on the main menu. Pop in after dinner and try a Japanese spin on a Sazerac with Toki, Okinawan black sugar, Peychaud’s bitters, and absinthe, or an Old Wives’ Tattletale, mixing Glenlivet 12 year old and Ardbeg 10 with wildflower honey and bitters.

Day Two

Tatte Bakery & Café began with a pastry chef selling her creations at the city’s Copley Square Farmers Market. While it has since expanded to Washington, D.C., the small chain remains a local favorite, with locations throughout the city, including Charles Street and High Street near Boston Harbor Hotel. The pastries are delicious, but there is also a full breakfast menu, from oatmeal to shakshuka to breakfast sandwiches.

Take a walk around Faneuil Hall, the pedestrianized historic waterfront area that includes shops, street performers, and Quincy Market, full of local eateries, as well as the immediately adjacent North End, Boston’s “Little Italy.” If you still have an appetite, grab a cannoli at one of the neighborhood’s famous rivals, Mike’s Pastry or Modern Pastry, just down the block from each other on Hanover Street.

Then head to the Seaport District and stop at the Boston Tea Party Ships & Museum, a kitschy but very popular attraction with costumed staff who provide an interactive experience as you relive the Boston Tea Party. You even get to dump tea into the harbor off the 18th-century ship.

The Seaport is a new mixed-use pedestrian area with lots of shops, restaurants, offices, entertainment, and a large collection of outdoor art. It has venues for live music, comedy, pickleball, ice skating, and the first F1 Arcade in the country, using high-tech race simulators. But for whisky lovers—and barbecue fans—the highlight here is The Smoke Shop BBQ by Andy Husbands. The namesake owner is an award-winning pitmaster and author of five cookbooks. Smoke Shop, with six locations in the greater Boston area, is a four-time winner of Boston Magazine’s Best Barbecue award. The food is great, but the whisky list is even better, claiming to have New England’s largest American selection, with around 300 expressions at the Seaport location (the suburban Assembly Row spot has the most, around 430). All locations feature the signature Smoke Shop Old Fashioned using brisket-infused Jim Beam, house-smoked simple syrup, and Angostura and Regan’s orange bitters, served in a smoked glass. The group currently has 14 private casks, though not all are available at every location.

The “Rare & Allocated” section has nearly 100 entries, from Pappy Van Winkle 15 ($100) to oddities such as Legent Yamazaki Cask Finish blend ($60), Blue Run Blue Sizzle and STK 8 year old bourbon ($55), and Lock, Stock & Barrel 13 year old rye ($23). On the regular list there are many at $14 or less, including Castle & Key Small Batch, David Nicholson Reserve, and Basil Hayden Toast bourbons. There is always a $10 Whiskey of the Week, along with monthly whisky dinners.

If you’re not a fan of barbecue or just want more whiskey, a few blocks away is Trillium Fort Point’s taproom, roof deck, and outdoor patio. Trillium is a brewery but also has a distillery, one of the largest in the Northeast, in Canton, 20 miles outside Boston. Here, head distiller Kyle Wortz (formerly of Utah’s High West) uses estate-grown barley and corn from its 170-acre Connecticut farm to produce Wake Robin whiskeys, with several bourbons and ryes and a soon-to-be-released American single malt. You can try all the spirits and beers here at this 500-seat facility. They offer whiskey flights of three 1-oz. pours for $22 and house cocktails like the Blood Orange Bourbon Punch ($15). Nantucket-based Cisco Brewers also operates a seasonal outdoor beer garden in the Seaport, and Island Creek Oysters Raw Bar—a legendary aquaculture farm outside the city, many chefs believe to be the world’s best—has a year-round (weather permitting) outdoor raw bar.

Boston Harbor Distillery sits south of downtown in the Dorchester neighborhood, in an 1859 brick industrial building that once housed the Putnam horseshoe nail factory. Founder Rhonda Kallman was also one of the founders of Boston Beer Company. The tours ($20 and $50)—often personally led by Kallman—start with a lengthy tasting. There is a full cocktail bar and gift shop on-site.

The signature product is Putnam American single malt, aged 3.5 years in wine barrels from Napa’s Silver Oak winery, which is also available as a 4 year old bottled in bond. There are several ryes (straight, cask strength, and red wine barrel finish), as well as a spicy hot pepper and rye concoction called Demon Seed that’s made for cocktails, pre-made bottled Old Fashioneds with Vermont maple syrup, and a line of spirits distilled from seasonal batches of Samuel Adams beer, like an Oktoberfest brewed especially for the distillery.

A fairly new addition to the Boston entertainment scene is acclaimed Australian magician Christopher Wayne’s Saturday (and occasional Friday or Sunday) shows at Boston’s Theater of Magic in the Liberty Hotel. The 90-minute performances, with basic cocktails available, are a fun and different highlight of a Boston visit, with reservations mandatory. Then it’s time for dinner.

Steakhouses and whisky have a deep history together, and the leading independent steakhouse in Boston has long been Grill 23 since its opening more than 40 years ago. Make reservations early, as it books up quickly. The expansive menu ranges from classics like wedge salad, French onion soup, hash browns, steak frites, and prime New York strip to Japanese wagyu and 100-day ultra-dry-aged rib eyes. It has a long whisky list, complete with cocktails and flights, along with the highest possible Wine Spectator Grand Award of Excellence for its encyclopedic list.

There are 15 whisky flights, with prices starting at $25, each with three 1-oz. pours, including brand horizontals (Laphroaig, Glenmorangie, Glenfarclas, Mars, Kujira, Michter’s, and WhistlePig); regions, such as the Far East (Hatozaki Small Batch, Hakushu 12, and Matsui-Shuzo The Kurayoshi 18, $52); and age, (25 year old Bowmore, Macallan, and Balvenie, $269 each), and more.

Then there’s the main list of close to 250, with over 60 bourbons including Van Winkle 12, 15, and 23 ($85, $198, $340/2 oz.) and Michter’s Celebration sour mash, a blend of straight whiskeys from 12 to over 30 years old ($1,205). There are 30 ryes, a smattering of Irish whiskeys, and around 80 scotch single malts, from Glenturret Triple Wood at $12 to Glenfiddich 44 year old 1975 at $905. There are a dozen blended scotches, and an impressive list of nearly 40 Japanese, including eight from Chichibu’s Ichiro’s Malt Card lineup alone. It’s a wonderful grand finale to your Beantown visit, and you won’t leave hungry—or thirsty. But if you do, there’s one more chance: Boston Harbor Distillery has a cocktail lounge, restaurant, and bottle shop at Logan Airport in Terminal E.
japanese-inspired-whisky-cocktail-recipe:
Japanese bartending has long been admired for its exacting technique, impeccable hospitality, innovation, and intention for cocktails to be savored, not rushed. No longer confined to Tokyo, this Japanese approach to cocktails has taken root in the U.S., where Japanese cocktails continue to flourish—particularly in New York City, from long-standing destinations like Bar Goto and Bar Moga to newcomers including Cocktail Omakase and Bar Orai. 

On bar menus, Japanese whisky usually shows up in elevated Highballs, dual-spirit drinks, and rare bottlings at venues like Teruko, located beneath the storied Hotel Chelsea, home to over 350 expressions. Beyond the whisky itself, bartenders are increasingly drawing from Japan’s pantry. Ingredients such as shochu, nori, and shiitake mushrooms add savory depth to classics, speaking to the growing trend of savory cocktails, while others like osmanthus lend a delicate aromatic touch. 

At the core of Japanese cocktail culture is omotenashi, the philosophy first used to define hosting tea ceremonies in the 16th century. The word itself–omote meaning “public face” and nashi, meaning “nothing,” together means “no front, no back,” or no pretense. In a bar setting, this means extending hospitality beyond merely serving drinks to thoughtfully anticipating a guest’s needs. The philosophy carries through every aspect of the cocktail experience, with every ingredient, garnish, and technique carefully considered. These recipes showcase how leading Japanese-inspired bars reinterpret classics through technical precision, balance, and distinctly Japanese ingredients. 

Sushi Sazerac

Cocktail Omakase, which opened in spring 2026 in partnership with Tokyo's Bar Libre, takes its cues from the sushi omakase experience, where the chef selects the menu. For head bartender Mat Resler, one drink that inspired the concept was a Sushi Sour shared by Cocktail Kingdom Group owner Greg Boehm and his wife, Jessica, after the couple’s trip to Japan. "My wheels started to turn, and phonetically, Sushi Sazerac sounded great," Resler says of the cocktail's creation.

The drink, he says, needed to retain the backbone of a Sazerac’s profile, balancing strong, sweet, bitter, absinthe, and lemon oil while introducing unmistakable umami flavors. He settled on a base of nori-infused rye and Japanese barley shochu. At the bar, toasted buckwheat tea (soba cha) adds an extra layer of toasted sweetness to the demerara syrup, but it’s just as delicious without. Poured from a fish-shaped flask at the bar, it’s just as compelling poured directly into a rocks glass at home.

  • 1 oz. Nori-infused Rittenhouse rye (recipe below)  
  • ¼ oz. demerara syrup (2 parts sugar, 1 part water) 
  • ¼ oz. Campari 
  • ½ oz. Ichiko Shinwa shochu 
  • 2 dashes aromatic bitters 
  • Lemon peel, for aromatics 

Twist a lemon peel and coat the rim of the glass with lemon oil. Pour all ingredients into the glass and add one large ice cube. 

Nori-infused whiskey 

  • ½ nori sheet
  • 250-ml Rittenhouse rye 

Crush the nori sheet and add to a large container with the rye. Macerate for 2 hours, stirring often. Strain through a fine-mesh sieve, discarding the nori. Keep refrigerated for up to 6 months in a sealed container.

Kinoko Old Fashioned

At Teruko, the Kinoko Old Fashioned transforms the classic into an umami-driven libation. Beverage director Brian Evans pairs mushroom-infused Japanese whisky with high-proof bourbon, vetiver liqueur, maple syrup, bitters, and awamori (a distillate made from Thai rice and koji) for a drink layered with earthy woodsy flavors. The awamori provides a savory canvas, while maple syrup provides subtle sweetness. The umami and chocolate bitters echo the rich funk of the shiitake-infused whisky. 

  • 1 oz. Shiitake-infused Japanese whisky (recipe below) 
  • ¾ oz. Maker’s Mark cask strength (or other high-proof bourbon)
  • ¼ oz. Yokka Koji awamori
  • ¼ oz. Vetiver liqueur 
  • 1 tsp. Maple syrup
  • 2 dashes Japanese Bitters Co. umami bitters
  • 1 dash Scrappy's chocolate bitters
  • Grapefruit peel, garnish 

Combine ingredients in a rocks glass and stir 15 rotations with a large ice cube.  Express a swath of grapefruit peel approximately 3 inches from the surface of the cocktail, then drop expressed peel into glass as garnish.

Shiitake-infused Japanese Whisky 

  • 250-ml Suntory Toki whisky
  • 2 dried shiitake mushrooms

Combine ingredients into a non-reactive, sealable container and infuse at room temperature for two days (stirring after one day), then strain through a mesh strainer, pressing on the mushrooms to extract maximum flavor. Discard mushrooms.  Filter the infusion back into the bottle and store in the refrigerator for up to 1 year. 

Eau de Osmanthus

Created by Rio Azmee, creative director at Stone and Soil, this cocktail takes its inspiration from the art of blending perfume, using two delicate ingredients often used in the practice–oolong tea and osmanthus.  Together, they lend floral aromas, with notes of stone fruit and a honey-like finish, according to Azmee. At the bar, guests choose between two types of infused Japanese whiskies: Hibiki Harmony or Toki. Its simple build is akin to an Old Fashioned, with a high ratio of spirit, lightly sweetened, and kissed with citrus. 

Osmanthus is available online, at Asian supermarkets, or tea shops. If you can’t find it, jasmine tea, chamomile, or more oolong tea are good substitutions.  

  • ¼ cup Oolong tea-infused Hibiki Harmony or Toki 
  • ⅓ oz. Osmanthus Syrup (recipe below) 
  • 2 dashes Scrappy's Bitters Black Lemon

Stir together all ingredients in a rocks glass with a large ice cube. Garnish with lemon peel. 

Osmanthus syrup 

  • ⅓ cup sugar 
  • ⅓ cup water 
  • 3 tsp. Dried Osmanthus flowers, or Jasmine tea 

Bring sugar and water to a boil in a small saucepot. Turn the heat to a simmer and add the osmanthus, infusing for 3-5 minutes. (If using jasmine tea, immediately strain out and discard tea leaves.) Let steep off the heat for 10 minutes. Strain, let cool before use. Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks. 

Whisky Highball

The Japanese Highball may appear simple, but at Bar Goto, it becomes an exercise in ensuring each element shines. Owner Kenta Goto pays close attention to dilution, temperature, carbonation, and whisky selection to create a balanced cocktail. Two Japanese whiskies, Blend Tokie and single malt Kanosuke, are the cocktail’s backbone. 

His biggest tip for making one at home? Using whisky kept in the freezer before building the drink to ensure the drink stays ice cold. It slows dilution and preserves the crisp carbonation that defines a proper Japanese highball. 

  • 5½ tsp. Suntory Toki, chilled, ideally in freezer
  • 2 tsp. Kanosuke single malt, chilled, ideally in freezer
  • 4 oz. club soda, chilled

Fill a highball glass with ice cubes or an ice spear. Pour the chilled whisky into the glass and top with the chilled club soda. If the whisky is not chilled, add the chilled club soda first. With a barspoon, lift the ice gently to blend. 

Prelude

Created by the team behind Bar Moga, a 1920s-era Japanese cocktail bar with creative pours and live jazz, this drink was designed as an opening note, or aperitif for the evening. “The Woodford Reserve provides the structure, warmth, and oak backbone that grounds the drink, while lavender brings an airy elegance, with a hint of soft almond from the Crème de Noyaux to round out the finish,” says bar lead Simon Xi. 

The attention to detail extends to the ice. Bar Moga uses Kuramoto Ice from Kanazawa, Japan from a producer established in 1923, the same era that inspires the bar. The water is carefully filtered before being slowly frozen for an average of 72 hours, a process that removes most of its minerals and reduces its hardness from around 40 to just 3 to 4. The result is exceptionally clear, pure ice, with each piece cut by hand to fit the glass and cocktail. “For us, ice deserves the same care as every other ingredient,” says beverage coordinator and head chef Shintaro Eleazar Tozzo.

  •   1 oz. Woodford Reserve
  •   ½ oz. Cocchi Americano Bianco
  •   ¼ oz. Suze
  •   ¼ oz. Crème de Noyaux (or amaretto liqueur)
  •   ¼ oz. lemon juice
  •   ¼ oz. honey
  •   2 dashes lavender bitters 
  •   1 ½ oz. soda water

Shake all ingredients in a shaker except the soda water. Pour into a highball glass with ice. Top with soda water. Stir lightly and serve.

Penicillin 

Sam Ross’s modern classic keeps its bones in this version from Bar Orai, a Japanese-style vinyl listening bar located in Midtown East Manhattan. The vital ingredients–honey, ginger, lemon–remain the same, but are anchored by a Speyside single malt heavy blend finished in mizunara, the prized Japanese oak that’s a popular finishing cask for a variety of whiskey styles. Instead of the classic Islay malt floating on top, this version threads smoky scotch into the honey-ginger syrup. “The Japanese oak, not Japanese whisky, does the talking here. A Scotch classic wearing a Japanese accent,” owner and creator Joseph Moon notes of this version.  

  • 2 oz. Chivas Regal Mizunara
  • ¾ oz. Fresh lemon juice
  • 1 oz. Honey ginger scotch syrup (recipe below) 
  • Candied ginger garnish

Add the whisky, lemon juice, and syrup to a shaker. Fill with ice and shake until well chilled. Double strain into a rocks glass over a large ice cube. Garnish with a piece of candied ginger.

Honey Ginger Scotch Syrup 

  • ½ cup honey 
  • ½ cup water 
  • 2 inch knob fresh ginger, chopped 
  • ¼ cup + 2 Tbsp. Laphroaig 10 year old scotch 

Bring all ingredients to a boil in a small pan over medium heat, until the honey is dissolved. Let sit for 30 minutes. Strain ginger and whisk in the scotch. Refrigerate in an airtight container for 1 month.
what-is-sangrita:
Historically a juice-based drink, sangrita is a well-loved complement to tequila in Mexican culture. This alcohol-free juice-and-spice blend is often served alongside straight tequila to cleanse the palate between sips. Sangrita can sharpen the agave notes and balance the alcohol’s heat, revealing layers of flavor that otherwise might be missed.

Its origin began with traditional Mexican breakfasts. Mexicans often eat a citrus-based fruit salad that’s seasoned with chile powder in the morning, and the juices from that dish would be saved and sipped later in the day alongside tequila. The earliest versions were usually centered around citrus and pomegranate, sprinkled with chile powder and salt. Newer versions have shifted toward a tomato juice base with citrus and chile components. Literally, sangrita means “little blood” in Spanish, a nod to the drink’s color, derived from pomegranate or tomato.

While it’s widely embraced in Mexico, sangrita is virtually unheard of in the U.S., despite tequila's popularity. This is due to how Americans consume tequila versus Mexicans. “In the U.S., tequila’s rise has largely been driven by cocktails—especially Margaritas—and by a sipping culture that’s focused on neat pours or flights, and sangrita doesn’t fit neatly into either of those trends,” says Mexico native and chef Richard Sandoval, founder of Richard Sandoval Hospitality, the operator of 60 restaurants and bars globally. Sandoval has been dubbed the “father of modern Mexican cuisine” and he’s a torchbearer for Mexican and Latin culture. His restaurant empire includes numerous authentic Mexican concepts, but most don’t serve sangrita, though he says he’s considering incorporating it into guided tasting experiences, where staff would explain what sangrita is and how to properly appreciate it alongside tequila.

“Sangrita requires explanation, intention, and a slower pace, which is not always how tequila is consumed in American bars,” Sandoval explains. “Sangrita is about balance. It enhances tequila rather than masking it, offering acidity, spice, and freshness that reset the palate and highlight agave character. Its purpose has always been to complement tequila, not to act as a chaser in the American sense.”

Sangrita does pop up on a few tequila menus in the U.S. Órale Mexican Kitchen, with two locations in New Jersey, offers sangrita with its tequila flights. Beverage director Marcelino Figueiras notes that while sangrita isn’t well-known stateside, it’s a key part of the agave drinking experience at his venues.

“Our goal isn’t just to serve tequila, but to respect where it comes from and how it’s traditionally enjoyed,” Figueiras says. “Sangrita lets us present tequila in its full context. It’s about experience, education, and connection. It allows us to introduce people to something new while honoring the culture behind tequila.”

Figueiras says most of his customers who try sangrita with their tequila appreciate it, and the response has been overwhelmingly positive. Even guests who don’t understand it, or who initially confuse it with wine-based sangria (which Figueiras says happens often but opens the door for conversation), come around when they hear about sangrita’s history and purpose. Órale’s sangrita recipe includes tomato, orange, and lime juices with a blend of ground chile de árbol, cumin, and chile morita.

“Sangrita is a way to experience tequila the way Mexicans have for generations, and it gives people a chance to enjoy tequila in a more traditional way,” Figueiras says. “Offering sangrita is about elevating the agave conversation and giving guests a more complete understanding of the spirit and culture that birthed it. As American consumers become more educated and seek authenticity and depth, sangrita’s relevance will continue to grow. It feels like a natural step in the evolution of agave culture here.”

Sangrita Recipe

Órale Mexican Kitchen's Sangrita

  • 1 3/4 cups tomato juice
  • 1 3/4 cups fresh San Marzano tomatoes (peeled, roasted, puréed, and strained)
  • ½ cup fresh orange juice
  • 6 Tbsp. fresh lime juice
  • 3 Tbsp. grenadine
  • 1½ tsp. Maggi sauce
  • 1½ tsp. Worcestershire sauce
  • Pinch of salt
  • Pinch of freshly ground black pepper Pinch of signature spice blend (equal parts dried and ground chile de arbol, cumin, and chile morita)

Combine all ingredients and mix thoroughly using an immersion blender to ensure the flavors are well integrated. Serve in 2-ounce pours in a Vaso Veladora glass garnished with a fresh orange wedge. Store in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days.
whiskyfest-new-york-2026-seminar-lineup:
This year’s WhiskyFest New York takes place on Friday, November 20th at the Marriott Marquis. In addition to the usual spectacular evening of whiskies, tequilas and other spirits offered at the Grand Tasting, this year’s event will feature a special afternoon seminar session that will showcase some of the most rare, coveted ultra-aged bottlings in the whisky world.

The seminar kicks off at 2 p.m. and concludes just before 5 p.m., presenting a lineup of tastings that includes a ghost distillery bottling from Littlemill, a 50 year old Dewar’s, a 40 year old Highland Park, two prized Irish whiskeys from Midleton Very Rare, and three bottlings of Yamazaki Japanese whisky. Not to be outdone, Michter’s will be on hand to pour its 20 year old bourbon, as well as the Bomberger’s expression from its Legacy Series. If you’re curious about the value of the whiskies being poured, it  adds up to more than $10,000 worth of whisky. The seminars will be led by the whisky makers and educators for each expression, alongside Whisky Advocate editors.  

Setting The Stage

•Loch Lomond Group will present Littlemill 33 year old, from the “ghost” distillery of the same name from the Lowlands of Scotland. Littlemill’s stills ran dry in 1994, and the site was destroyed by fire in 2004.  Loch Lomond Group owns the remaining barrels, which are rarely tasted at public events. Loch Lomond master of whisky Andy Westley will lead this tasting along with Whisky Advocate senior editor Julia Higgins. Loch Lomond will also be pouring Glen Scotia 25 year old, giving attendees a chance to taste an ultra-aged Campbeltown scotch. 

•For Irish Distillers, master distiller Kevin O’Gorman will be on hand to taste through two of Midleton’s top expressions: Midleton Very Rare 2024 Vintage and Midleton Very Rare Barry Crockett Legacy, a single pot still whiskey that honors one of Midleton’s most venerable master distillers. O’Gorman will be accompanied onstage by Whisky Advocate contributing editor Jonny McCormick.

•For Michter’s, owner Joseph Magliocco will present the Bombergers and Michter’s 20 year old expressions, alongside master of maturation Andrea Wilson, accompanied by Whisky Advocate editor-at-large David Savona. Magliocco, who famously bought the trademark for $245 back in 1997, has built Michter’s into an American whiskey icon and is widely considered one of the modern whiskey era’s great visionaries.

•For Dewar’s, master blender Stephanie Macleod will present two ultra-aged expressions: Dewar’s 38 year old, and a recently bottled 50 year old expression, which has never been tasted in public. The 50 year old is the oldest Dewar’s whisky ever released. Macleod will be accompanied by Jonny McCormick, who will also be joined onstage by the other Whisky Advocate editors.         

                                

•Japanese whisky Yamazaki will focus on some of the key barrel types that contribute to the taste profiles of its most renowned expressions, with tastings of its Yamazaki Spanish Oak, followed by its 18 year old and 18 year old Mizunara. Leading will be House of Suntory’s Keli Rivers and Whisky Advocate contributing editor Jonny McCormick.

•Highland Park will be presenting its 30 year old and 40 year old scotch single malts. Both show the delightful effects of sherry on ultra-aged scotch, which melds with Highland Park 's subtle peat smoke to create its unique Highlands profile. This tasting will be led by Highland Park specialist Rose Robinson, accompanied by David Savona.

The entire afternoon session will run from 2 to 4:45 p.m. There will certainly be lots of discussion about which whiskies are everybody’s favorites. One thing for sure is that there will be lots of competition in this once-in-a-lifetime tasting session! Click here for more information.
milam-greene-unabridged-volume-5-review:
Milam & Greene isn’t interested in keeping its annually released Unabridged bourbon consistent. For the fifth chapter, the Texas whiskey maker has changed the recipe and turned up the proof.

Unabridged Volume 5, out now, brings together seven straight bourbon components from Kentucky, Tennessee, and Texas, ranging from 6.5 to 10 years old. Bottled non-chill filtered at 60.8% ABV, it’s the highest-proof Unabridged yet from the Blanco, Texas, distillery. Only 650 cases will be released, which each bottle retailing for $95. 

The series launched in 2022 as an annual showcase for Milam & Greene’s blending program, using bourbons of different ages, mashbills, origins, and climates as its palette. Volume 1 combined 38 barrels aged from 2.75 to 14 years, while Volume 2 grew to 56 barrels spanning from 2 to 16 years. Volume 3 blended 49 barrels, before Volume 4 shrank to just eight barrels aged 5 to 10 years.

For Volume 5, the blend size again grows, though this time the complexity comes from seven distinct components rather than a massive number of individual barrels. Kentucky bourbon accounts for 88% of the blend, led by 34% 6.5 year old made with malted rye and 31% 8 year old. The remainder includes 9.5, 7.8, and 7 year old Kentucky bourbons, 10 year old Tennessee bourbon, and 7 year old Texas bourbon made with malted rye.

“Managing the marriage of seven distinct mashbills, including our unique malted rye bourbon, required meticulous precision,” master whiskey maker Rikk Munroe said on the company’s website. After blending, the whiskey underwent what Milam & Greene calls “Texification,” using the temperature swings of the Texas Hill Country to marry the components before bottling. The company also used the technique on Volume 4, though here there are considerably more variables to reconcile.

What’s perhaps most interesting is how approachable Unabridged Volume 5 is at the 121.6 proof. It noses and drinks far softer, closer to something around 107.

In the glass, it’s deep ruby with thick legs, while the nose is big, dark, and confectionery without coming across hot. Brown sugar, caramel, and molasses appear alongside dark chocolate and tobacco, giving the whiskey the character of a decadent candy bar. Stone fruit follows, with the malted rye emerging toward the back.

The palate is similarly deceptive. It’s heavyweight but velvety and silky, opening with macerated cherries before concentrating toward the back of the palate. A rich cherry-syrup quality develops, balanced by enough oak and barrel spice to keep the sweetness from becoming cloying. Some drying structure emerges, along with cinnamon and baking spices, followed by a decent Kentucky hug as the whiskey goes down. The finish is medium-long and remains sweet, with fruit, settling on cherry cobbler.

That makes Volume 5 an interesting inversion of what its specs suggest. It's the highest-proof Unabridged and one of the series' more complicated blending exercises, yet neither quality makes the finished whiskey feel aggressive or disjointed. The biggest Unabridged release yet may also be one of the easiest to “read.”
football-themed-whiskeys:
Football season is off to a roaring start and whiskey brands are getting in on the fun, offering team-branded bottles and game-day festivities. Big names like Jameson and Jim Beam have official NFL partnerships, while Heaven Hill’s Evan Williams is leading the pack in college football with limited-edition bottles celebrating five universities. Regional whisky makers are also showing their team spirit, including Iowa’s Cedar Ridge, Colorado’s Laws Whiskey House, and Pro Football Hall of Famer Charles Woodson’s Woodson Whiskey, which has teamed up with his alma mater, the University of Michigan.      

Giants fans might still want to pour this year's Eli Manning Bold Pick from Knob Creek, but there’s also a fresh lineup of football-themed whiskeys to explore. We've rounded up 14 options to toast your favorite team this season.

Jameson Irish Whiskey x NFL 

ABV: 40%
Price: $25
Availability: Nationwide 

This summer, Jameson Irish Whiskey was announced as the Official Spirits Sponsor of the NFL. While there isn’t an NFL-themed labeled expression, Jameson is focusing on local market gatherings, bar events, and branded spaces at major events like the Super Bowl. Fans can also get back on their Jameson pours by submitting their bar tab online, with Jameson on the receipt in participating states. 

Jim Beam NFL Bourbon: Seattle Seahawks, Dallas Cowboys, and Kansas City Chiefs bourbon

ABV: 40%
Price: $15-19
Availability: Select local retailers

Jim Beam is bringing the team spirit to the 2026 NFL season with three limited-edition bottles celebrating its official partners: the Seattle Seahawks, a partner with Beam since 2021, and recent partners as of 2025, the Dallas Cowboys and Kansas City Chiefs. Each bottle features the brand’s signature white label Kentucky bourbon, aged 4 years and bottled at 40% ABV, in commemorative packaging bearing the respective team’s logos. The releases accompany Jim Beam’s new “Hit the Beam” campaign, which celebrates football’s infamous “doinks,” when a field goal kick narrowly misses the goalpost, hitting the beam. 

Woodson Whiskey x Michigan Football Champions x 12 5 Year Old Kentucky bourbon 

ABV: 45%
Price: $79
Availability: Select retailers

Launched this month by Pro Football Hall of Famer Charles Woodson’s whiskey brand, this limited-edition bourbon celebrates the University of Michigan's 12 national football championship titles from 1901 to 2023. Woodson himself is part and parcel of this legacy, bringing home a national championship for Michigan during his legendary 1997 season. This 5 year old bourbon has a high-rye mashbill (70% corn, 21% rye, 9% malted barley). Each bottle features a cork engraved with Michigan’s football helmet. 

Since its launch in 2020, the brand has celebrated several milestones close to the founder's heart. In April, it released a commemorative 6 year old bourbon honoring Michigan’s 2026 national championship in basketball. As an extension of his stamp on the sport, the label also is the official partner of the Pro Football Hall of Fame, a partnership that kicked off last year with a cognac-stave finished bourbon. 

Cedar Ridge × Iowa Hawkeyes 1847 bourbon 

ABV: 47%
Price: $55
Availability: Iowa retailers and online 

Iowa craft distiller Cedar Ridge launched 1847 Bourbon (and 1847 Vodka) in tandem with the University of Iowa's collegiate athletic division, Iowa Athletics, in August. Named for the university’s founding year, the bourbon is Cedar Ridge’s signature mashbill of 74% Iowa-grown corn, 14% rye, and 12% malted barley. Each bottle sports the Hawkeyes’ iconic Tigerhawk logo and co-branded University of Iowa packaging. Cedar Ridge became the Iowa Athletics’ first official spirit sponsor in 2024, but this marks the first official expression release with the university.  

Evan Williams 2018 Vintage Single Barrel Collegiate Edition Collection

ABV: 43.3%
Price: $35
Availability: Exclusively in participating university markets, Evan Williams Bourbon Experience  

In September, Evan Williams announced the return of its highly limited Single Barrel Collegiate Edition bottles (up from five to six in total), each from an individual barrel with respective logos for: The University of Alabama, The Ohio State University, University of Oklahoma, University of Oregon, University of South Carolina, Syracuse University. Distilled and barreled in 2018, each bottle features a custom wax dipped bottle top in one of the university’s primary colors. The collection is part of Evan Williams’ Bourbon Nation, which launched in 2024 with ESPN sportscaster Molly McGrath as its spokesperson to celebrate the traditions of college fandom. 

Breckenridge 40th Anniversary “The Drive” Limited Edition bourbon blends collection  

ABV: 43%
Price: $45
Availability: Limited 

Now in its 6th year of partnering with Colorado’s Broncos, Breckenridge Distillery has unveiled a trio of limited edition bottles to mark the 40th anniversary of “The Drive:” a legendary 98-yard possession from the Broncos in the 1986 AFC Championship Game. The collectible bottles come in blue, white, and orange labels. Since launching in 2021, the label has opted for blends for most of the annual releases, with availability online and at Colorado retailers.  

Gold Bar Whiskey Limited Collector’s Retro Edition Wine Cask Finished bourbon 

ABV: 42.5%
Price: $70
Availability: online and California retailers  

San Francisco’s Gold Bar Whiskey, located on Treasure Island in San Francisco Bay, is now in its seventh year as the official whiskey sponsor of its hometown team, the 49ers. Part of the Joe Montana Collection, this limited-edition four-grain bourbon is aged 4-plus years and finished in red wine casks for 5 to 6 months. The release celebrates four decades since the 49ers’ 1985 Super Bowl victory, one of four championships Montana helped bring home during his tenure with the team. Each bottle comes with one of five can koozies shaped like the team’s iconic 1980s gold satin jackets. Fans can also personalize their bottles with a custom engraving.

Philadelphia Eagles x BOTLD Bird Gang “The Vet” Straight bourbon 

ABV: 43%
Price: $38
Availability: online, select Philadelphia retailers

While partnerships are the norm for most football-themed whiskies, this one stands out as a collaboration directly involving an NFL team-owned whiskey. In 2023, the Philadelphia Eagles launched Bird Gang Spirits with Philly-based producer BOTLD, debuting a trio of bourbon, tequila, and vodka. This year’s limited-edition bourbon commemorates the 55th anniversary of Veterans Stadium, the Eagles’ former home, with packaging nodding to the team’s iconic Kelly-green uniforms worn between 1935 and 1995. The whiskey is aged for at least 3 years.

The team has since expanded its lineup with a World Championship Collection celebrating the Eagles’ victory in Super Bowl LIX. Released in 2025, the collection features a single barrel straight rye, American single malt, and single barrel Kentucky straight bourbon, alongside an Irish whiskey distilled, blended, and aged in County Cork, Ireland.

Sagamore x Baltimore Ravens Darkness Falls 8 year old bottled in bond rye 

ABV: 50%
Price: $59
Availability: Limited  

Sagamore Whiskey has released the 4th edition of its limited-edition Ravens bottle series, this one paying homage to the football players’ new all-black matte helmets which feature black talon stripes and two-toned black logo. The bottle, which uses a 2018 vintage of a pair of high-rye and low-rye mashbills, is adorned with the same charcoal and black tones. 

Teeling x Notre Dame Small Batch Blended Irish whiskey (Green Jersey Edition) 

ABV: 46%
Price: $35
Availability: Limited 

Teeling has been Norte Dame’s official sponsor since 2023, releasing limited edition bottles annually. This year’s Green Jersey Edition features Teeling’s signature Small Batch whiskey initially aged in bourbon barrels before finishing in Central American rum casks for up to 12 months. It follows last year’s 91 point scoring release with the same cask finish. The bottle carries a green embossed Notre Dame logo and a gold cap inspired by the team’s football helmets. It’s currently available at the Notre Dame stadium, arenas, and select retailers. 

Across the pond, Teeling has also extended its sponsorship of the Aer Lingus College Football Classic, the Dublin home for American College football, through 2028. It has unveiled Phoenix Twist, Teeling’s first ready-to-drink cocktail, made with the label’s Irish whiskey, ginger, and yuzu. 

Boot Hill Distillery Wabash Reserve: 1863 Edition 6 Year Old bourbon      

ABV: 45%
Price: $80
Availability: Online and select Kansas retailers

Dodge City, Kansas-based Boot Hill Distillery is celebrating its partnership with Kansas State University Athletics with the fourth edition of Wabash Reserve, the Wildcats’ officially licensed bourbon. Named for the university’s founding year, 1863, this three-grain bourbon is aged for over 6 years, making it one of the distillery’s oldest releases. Crafted by distillery owner, CEO, and K-State alumni Hayes Kelman and his family-owned label  using grain grown on the distillery’s fifth-generation family farm, the limited-edition bourbon continues a partnership that kicked off in 2021, with the latest edition left to age nicely since the previous edition’s release in 2023.     

Crown Royal Fine de Luxe Limited Edition University of Georgia Bulldogs 2026 Season Blended Canadian whiskey 

ABV: 40%
Price: $25
Availability: Limited; Georgia retailers only 

Crown Royal has been the Peach State’s beloved college team, the Georgia Bulldogs, since last 2025, when it rolled out a Fine De Luxe bottle packaged with red embroidered bags with the “G” logo. It continued the same packaging this year. The run is highly limited, with online stock sold out, and some stock still available from regional sellers. 

Indiana Whiskey Co. Domer Nation ’26 bourbon

ABV: 42%
Price: $60
Availability: Online and at the distillery 

South Bend-based Indiana Whiskey Co. unveiled its 2026 Domer Nation Game Day bourbon. Founded by Notre Dame alumni, the distillery collaborated with the university’s design students on the limited-edition collector’s bottle celebrating the Fighting Irish. Bottled at a special 42% ABV, the bourbon is available online and at the distillery’s tasting room. The brand is also hosting tailgate events ahead of Notre Dame’s home games throughout the season.

Laws Whiskey House × Colorado Buffaloes Ralphie’s Reserve bourbon 

ABV: 45%
Price: $45
Availability: Online, Colorado retailers

As the official partner with Colorado University Athletics since 2024, Denver-based Laws Whiskey House crafted Ralphie’s Reserve, now in its third year.  Though the partnership represents the entire athletic department, this bottle was launched specifically to be enjoyed at tailgates and watch parties for the football season. A portion of the proceeds from every bottle sold directly supports the Ralphie Live Mascot Program, helping fund the care of the university’s living buffalo mascots and American bison education. Laws also has a more limited release, Black & Gold, a 10-barrel batch including one re-barreled from the previous year’s blend. It’s $80 and available online and in Colorado retailers. 

Elijah Craig × Kentucky Wildcats Single Barrel Kentucky Straight bourbon 

Earlier this month, Heaven Hill announced two partnerships with the University of Kentucky: Evan Williams, as mentioned above, and Elijah Craig. Although the label has yet to release details, co-branded bottles are coming soon. Elijah Craig is slated to bring its name specifically to UK’s homebase facilities, along with a rebrand of what was formerly the Mezzanine Club to “Elijah Craig Club” at Kroger Field, the home of the Kentucky Wildcats. The inaugural release is slated to feature an Elijah Craig barrel personally selected by UK athletics director Jason “J” Batt to mark the launch of the partnership and his first football season at the University.
taketsuru-pure-malt-essentials-series-de:
Nikka Whisky is debuting a five-year series of annual limited edition Japanese whiskies leading up to the 30th anniversary of Taketsuru Pure Malt in 2030. The range is named after Masataka Taketsuru, widely regarded as the father of Japanese whisky, who studied whisky making in Scotland over a century ago and then brought his knowledge and skills back to Japan. He became the first distillery manager of Yamazaki Distillery, later setting out on his own to found Yoichi Distillery and Dai Nippon Kaju (the Great Japanese Juice Company). They made apple juice, and later, apple wine, changing the company’s name to Nikka Whisky, a portmanteau of the juice company name, once whisky became its main business.

Each whisky in the collection will explore the essence of Taketsuru Pure Malt, a blended malt made from single malts from Nikka’s Yoichi and Miyagikyo Distilleries, with each release built around a distinctive theme.

Taketsuru Pure Malt Essentials 2026 contains rare batches of single malts distilled at both Yoichi and Miyagikyo in 2000, the year Taketsuru Pure Malt was launched. These stocks are particularly scarce because Nikka had slashed production for a number of years as Japan’s domestic whisky market entered a long decline with the collapse of the economic bubble and the rise of shochu.

The theme of the inaugural Taketsuru Pure Malt Essentials release spotlights Yoichi’s character through skillful blending, while respecting the boundaries of a blended malt. Each Essentials release will have its own label: Yoichi is reflected in the distillery’s traditional indigo-blue label for the collection’s debut. Taketsuru founded Yoichi in 1934 on Japan’s northernmost island, Hokkaido, chosen for an environment surrounded by the Sea of Japan and snowy mountain peaks that offered conditions similar to Scotland. The landscape reminded Taketsuru of Campbeltown, where he studied whisky making in Scotland from 1918 to 1920. The direct coal-fired pot stills have straight necks and descending lyne arms leading to worm tubs—techniques intended to produce a robust, oily, characterful spirit, as the higher temperatures on the wash result in deeper caramel and complex toasted notes. Today, Yoichi produces a broad range of flavor profiles through variations in yeast strains, fermentation times, peat levels, cut points, cask types, and maturation conditions. Yoichi has a small on-site cooperage, not as large as their cooperages at Miyagikyo Distillery or Nikka’s Tochigi Aging Cellar on Honshu, but they fill a wide variety of casks, including bourbon, new oak, sherry, refill, rejuvenated, and Japanese mizunara oak. As a result, Nikka’s blenders have a wide range of component whiskies from Yoichi to work with. The first single malt release from Yoichi Distillery, called Single Malt Hokkaido, arrived in 1984, followed by the release of Single Malt Yoichi in 1989. Modern single malt expressions, such as Yoichi 10 year old, are still complex blends of different styles of whisky produced at one distillery.

When Taketsuru Pure Malt 12 year old was introduced in 2000, Nikka’s blenders were seeking a balance of pleasant peat, sherry cask influences, malty richness, and a smooth mouthfeel. As part of its launch, company opened a series of pop-up Taketsuru bars across Japan, encouraging retailers, bar owners, and curious whisky enthusiasts to discover the new expression.

The Taketsuru Pure Malt range subsequently expanded to include 17, 21, and 25 year old expressions, as well as three limited-edition 21 year olds released for Nikka’s 80th anniversary in 2014. Nikka entered the U.S. market in 2012, with Taketsuru Pure Malt 12 year old among its early releases. Those age statements were eventually phased out, leaving only a non-age stated expression, as Nikka faced dwindling stocks following the production cutbacks of the 1990s, just as Japanese whisky was experiencing a surge in global popularity.

This isn’t Nikka’s first anniversary countdown series. The company previously released the experimental Nikka Discovery Series ahead of its 90th anniversary in 2024, culminating in the 96-point Nikka Nine Decades. Taketsuru Pure Malt Essentials 2026 is bottled at 43%, the same strength as the original Taketsuru Pure Malt, and meets the Japan Spirits & Liqueurs Makers Association (JSLMA) guidelines for a Japanese whisky. The blended malt emphasizes the rich maltiness of the mature stocks and Yoichi’s characteristic peaty notes while retaining the balance of single malts that defines Taketsuru Pure Malt. Priced at $249, 1,200 bottles are allocated to the U.S. market.

Karuizawa moved up to lead the 2026 auction list as September’s 20 highest hammer prices totaled $1,139,934. As we enter the final quarter of the year, the list has outperformed 2025 in 6 out of 9 months in 2026, and September produced the third million-dollar month of the year. The list’s combined value is over $1.5 million ahead of the same point in 2025, showing a growing confidence in the secondary market. While there is no Distillers One of One auction this year, October is set to deliver plenty of thrills as Sotheby’s will host a magnificent sale direct from Macallan Estate, with additional sales of rare Japanese whisky and scotch in Hong Kong.

Sotheby’s sale of the unique bottle of Karuizawa 1960 52 year old for a hammer price of $500,000 helped the closed distillery edge past Macallan, becoming the fourth brand to lead the table in 2026. Japan is the first whisky-producing nation to have topped the table with two separate brands, after Yamazaki led the table in June. Karuizawa has delivered one in nine bottles on the list so far this year, and its average hammer price for bottles on the list is 2.5 times higher than Macallan’s. Despite slipping to 2nd place, Macallan had the most entries on the list in September, taking six slots with whiskies aged from 50–74 years. Van Winkle and Old Fitzgerald made solid gains in September too, with a bottle of Very Very Old Fitzgerald 1950 18 year old Blackhawk taking $84,900 (Sotheby’s sold a bottle of this for a hammer price of $90,000 in January). The Johnnie Walker Collection at Whisky Auctioneer was led by a bottle of John Walker & Sons Old Highland Whisky, which sold for $13,370.

Karuizawa is unlikely to hold on to the lead of the table for long. The Sotheby’s sale from Macallan Estate includes the first bottle of Macallan Fine & Rare 1926 60 year old to come to auction since the Sotheby’s sale in 2019, where it set a world record. It’s been more than 1,000 days since the last million-dollar Macallan bottle sold in November 2023, and a strong result will be crucial if Macallan is to defend its position at the top of the table for 2026. Additionally, the upcoming Sotheby’s sale includes Macallan The Reach 81 year old, a complete set of the Six Pillars Collection, and much more. Whisky Auctioneer has a strong selection of Bowmore whiskies, including Bowmore x Aston Martin 1968 Arc-54, Black Bowmore 1964 50 year old The Last Cask, and a Black Bowmore 1964 First Edition. The sale also includes the auction debut of the 97-point Ardbeg The Abyss and a bottle of Glenlivet Eternal Collection 56 year old. Let’s not forget that the six highest hammer prices of the year so far have all been for Japanese whiskies, so further rare Yamazaki and Karuizawa bottlings at Sotheby’s Hong Kong sales could keep competition for control of the table continuing through the end of the year. Buckle up for October; it’s about to get busy.

whiskyfest-new-york-2026-ticket-options:
Whether you’re an occasional sipper or a dedicated enthusiast, WhiskyFest New York 2026, taking place on November 20th at the Marriott Marquis in Times Square, is an event you won’t want to miss. There are four separate ticketing options: you can choose an all-day pass, Premium Admission, Seminars only, Seminar Package, or All-Access ticket; it’s sure to be memorable. WhiskyFest offers an opportunity unlike any other to gather with fellow whisky enthusiasts, taste extraordinary pours, learn how they were made and the traditions behind them, and discover new expressions to guide the next steps on your whisky journey. Which ticket is right for you? 

WhiskyFest Premium Admission

Premium Admission offers access to the Grand Tasting (6:30 to 9:30 p.m.), featuring over 100 whiskies, tequilas, and other spirits; cigar giveaways (note: smoking is not permitted at the event); and a gourmet buffet. All ticket holders receive a tote bag that includes a Glencairn tasting glass. Attendees will be the first to know Whisky Advocate magazine’s Whisky of the Year, as it will be announced here first!

WhiskyFest Seminars Only

Held from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m., WhiskyFest New York Seminars include a lineup of once-in-a-lifetime whiskies from ultra-aged to a pour from a closed distillery to unicorn expressions. Presented by distillers, blenders, and brand representatives, the afternoon will offer unforgettable whiskies and immersive education spanning Michter’s, Dewar’s, Yamazaki, Midleton, Littlemill, and Glen Scotia.

WhiskyFest Seminar Package

Want to attend the Seminars and the Grand Tasting? This is the ticket for you! Immerse yourself in the intimate afternoon seminar experience and the evening tasting event with this discounted ticket option. Plus, Seminar Package ticket holders get early VIP access to the Grand Tasting, beginning at 6 p.m.

WhiskyFest All-Access Package

Still thirsty for more? No problem! All-Access tickets include the Seminars, the Grand Tasting with VIP early admission, and entry to an intimate lounge that will be serving pours not available at the Grand Tasting, including but not limited to Double Eagle Very Rare, Hibiki 30 year old, Glenfarclas 35 year old, and Port Ellen 1975 Signatory Vintage, to name a few. This ticket includes everything that WhiskyFest New York 2026 has to offer!

WhiskyFest New York 2026 Pre-Event Checklist

__ Submit your time off for November 20th.

__ Buy your ticket.

__ Tell your friends, family, and/or whisky tasting club to buy their tickets before they sell out.

__ Make hotel reservations (take advantage of the WhiskyFest room block reduced rates while they last at the New York Marriott Marquis here) or arrange transportation to and from the event.

__ Check the WhiskyFest website for updates and prioritize the pours you want to taste.

__ Download the WhiskyFest app available now in your preferred app store.
glenfiddich-aston-martin-16-year-whisky-:
Aston Martin doesn’t bring the same Formula One car to the track each season. Glenfiddich doesn't see a reason to bring back the same whisky, either.

For the second release in its partnership with Aston Martin’s Formula One Team, Glenfiddich has returned with another 16 year old Speyside single malt at 43% ABV, but almost everything apart from the age statement and proof has changed. The new limited edition Glenfiddich & Aston Martin Formula One Team 16 year old Release No. 2 uses five different cask types and arrives with an SRP of $80.

That's a significant departure from the inaugural release, which debuted last year following the brands' partnership announcement in late 2024. That whisky leaned heavily into American oaks, aging in a combination of virgin American oak, bourbon barrels, and American red wine casks. The resulting single malt was correspondingly oak-forward. When we reviewed it in 2025, we found the 93-point single malt had pine and fresh oak on the nose, which gave way to brown sugar, baked apple, pineapple, and candied berries, with a syrupy texture and drying oak on the palate.

Release No. 2 takes a broader approach. Glenfiddich malt master Brian Kinsman built the whisky from stocks aged or finished in first-fill bourbon barrels, port pipes, oloroso sherry casks, wine casks, and a smaller contribution from fino sherry butts. “For this expression, I combined the influence of five distinct cask types, each contributing its own character, texture, and depth,” Kinsman said in a press release. “The art lies not in the individual components, but in bringing them together in a way that feels perfectly balanced.”

Kinsman’s five-cask construction is inspired by legendary F1 designer Adrian Newey, now managing technical partner at Aston Martin Formula One Team. The brands draw a parallel between Newey's manipulation of aerodynamic forces around a car that doesn’t yet exist and Kinsman's work designing whisky that won’t be ready for years; both seek exemplary results “through the mastery of the unseen.” It's an elaborate metaphor for maturation, but the glass offers an interesting comparison: Release No. 2 tastes markedly different from its predecessor.

The nose opens with caramel and vanilla alongside cooked and macerated orchard fruits, orange citrus, sticky toffee, cinnamon graham cracker, worn leather, and dried tobacco. A light floral character—reminiscent of honey blossom—also appears and, along with the orchard fruit, makes the whisky immediately recognizable as Glenfiddich. It’s layered and complex without feeling busy.

It's medium-weight on the palate and initially sweet, with orchard fruit arriving before barrel spice begins working toward the back of the tongue. Spiced apple cider garnished with a singed cinnamon stick comes to mind, followed by stewed pear, caramel, and another lift of floral character. It has considerable breadth, but it remains light on its feet and remarkably easy to drink. The oak arrives most clearly on the finish, but it's aged, soft, and restrained rather than drying, followed by a final sweet pop of stewed fruit. It’s well-executed. The five different cask influences work together instead of competing.

Same age, same proof, same Formula One partner, entirely different setup. In racing, they call that development.
little-book-infinite-III-and-bookers-res:
A couple of years ago, Beam master distiller Freddie Noe debuted two higher-end spin-offs of both Booker’s and Little Book. For Booker’s, it was called The Reserves, and it launched with a blend of 8 to 14 year old bourbons and then followed up last year with a tequila-finished bourbon, marking the brand’s biggest change in decades. The new Little Book series, meanwhile, was named The Infinite; both editions thus far have included bourbons made by three Beam master distillers, including Noe, his father Fred, and his grandfather Booker. The third editions of both The Reserves and The Infinite have now hit the market.

Booker’s The Reserves rye 2026

The newest release within The Reserves is a rye. Historically, Booker’s has focused on small batch bourbons, but there was one notable rye released in 2016: Booker filled 100 barrels of rye in 2003, a year before he passed, which then aged for 13 years in Jim Beam warehouses D and E. That whiskey was named our 2016 American Whiskey of the Year, and we cited it as one of the best whiskeys Booker ever made.

The Reserves 2026 recalls this whiskey, but it also takes inspiration from the apple wine that Booker would make each winter; his recipe included apples, bourbon barrels, and cinnamon, while the new whiskey, a 6 year old rye, is finished in apple brandy casks and infused with cinnamon sticks. Given that The Reserves is the most ultra-limited of Booker’s releases, the incorporation of cinnamon sticks into the barrels might come as a surprise—after all, who could blame you if you associated cinnamon-flavored whiskey more commonly with the likes of Fireball, or even Beam’s own Jim Beam Kentucky Fire. But Beam is making The Reserves 2026 sound like an apple pie, with notes of bright apple, sweet caramel, vanilla, and cinnamon baked apple throughout. 

As with all Booker’s whiskeys, this one is bottled at cask strength, coming in at 62.55% ABV. It’ll be available in limited supply nationwide for $130.

Little Book The Infinite Edition III blend

Now in its third year, Little Book The Infinite continues what its two predecessors started. Edition III begins with a base of both Editions I and II—the former included a blend of four bourbons, including 20 year old distilled by Booker, 14 year old by Fred, and 7 year old by Freddie, while the latter included 22 year old distilled by Booker, 10 year old by Fred, and 7 year old from Freddie. With these whiskeys Freddie then blended the unique Edition III components, among them a 23 year old Knob Creek distilled by Booker (the oldest component ever included), 11 year old Knob Creek made by Fred, and 9 year old Baker’s distilled by Freddie. 

The Infinite Edition III is bottled at 59.15% ABV, and available for $200. If Booker’s is Beam’s ode to small batch, cask strength whiskey, Little Book is its tribute to blending. New “Chapters” are released annually, and they highlight Freddie’s creative license. The most recent release, Chapter 10: “All the Wiser,” seems a blueprint for the third release of Edition III, as it too blends Knob Creek and Baker’s bourbons (as well as Booker’s, Basil Hayden, and Jim Beam).
glenlivet-12-year-old-provence-edition-r:
Speyside scotch distiller Glenlivet is no stranger to cask finishing, with its core Signature Collection prominently finishing single malts with cognac, Caribbean rum, and Limousin French oak, and some of its higher-end bottlings following suit. But last year the distillery put this method under the microscope with Beyond Speyside, a travel-themed series that re-imagines the distillery’s iconic 12 year old with cask finishes inspired by destinations around the world. The inaugural release was Jamaica Edition, which aimed to echo Caribbean flavors by finishing in barrels that previously held high-ester Jamaican rum. For the second release in the series, the distillery is turning its eyes to the Provence region of southern France, finishing its latest whisky in a series of wine casks from the area. 

The French Connection

Like its predecessor, Glenlivet Provence Edition starts with a base of Glenlivet 12, which was aged in a mix of American and European oak casks. After maturation, a portion of the whisky was finished for an undisclosed span of time in three types of French wine casks. The first type previously held white wine from Château Sainte Marguerite, a prominent Côtes de Provence vineyard known for its cru classé cuvée whites and rosés. The second type is rivesaltes, an AOC-protected aged fortified wine from Languedoc-Roussillon. The third type is sauternes, a sweet dessert wine from the Graves subregion of Bordeaux that’s made from grapes affected by noble rot—a beneficial fungus that dehydrates the grapes while sharply increasing their sugar and acid concentrations— creating a sweeter wine. 

Though not nearly as common as their sherry and port counterparts, French wine casks are sometimes used to finish whisky—most often popping up among single malt distillers in Ireland and Scotland. When used skillfully, these casks can help create impressive expressions. Sauternes is one of the most popular styles, prized by distillers like Glenmorangie, Bowmore, Kilchoman, Arran, and others for notes of honeyed fruit and concentrated sweetness. Bordeaux red wine casks are also very much in the picture, contributing lush red fruits to standout bottlings from Glen Scotia, Isle of Harris, Kavalan, Bushmills, and Glenfiddich. The Rivesaltes casks used to finish Glenlivet Provence Edition are far and away the rarest ones of the Provence Edition trio, with only a handful of distillers like Tomatin, Clonakilty, Teeling, and Bruichladdich having used them before.

Beyond these specific cask types, other French wine casks have also been used for finishing vessels. Aberfeldy is one of the leaders in the space, with several impressive expressions in its Wine Cask series, including Sémillon Cadillac white wine, Côte-Rôtie, Pomerol, Languedoc, and Pauillac. In terms of specific styles, Burgundian pinot noir also shows up occasionally, with examples from Bowmore Appellations Collection, Bushmills, and Tullibardine. Another underrated example is pineau des charentes—a fortified dessert wine from the Cognac region—which Balvenie, Old Pulteney, and Teeling have used to great effect. 

How Does Glenlivet Provence Edition Taste?

91 points—Glenlivet 12 year old Provence Edition Speyside Single Malt

ABV: 40%
SRP: $55
Availability: Limited, but nationwide

An interesting mélange of fruit greets the nose, including grape jam, plums, baked peach, dried cranberries, and marmalade, alongside cloves and marzipan. Grape and plums reemerge for a light but flavorful palate, with apricot rings, cinnamon, vanilla, and pleasant tannins. It ends fairly mellow, with baked orchard fruits, red berries, candied orange peel, and peach, with softer tannins providing balance and structure. A thoroughly pleasurable experience, with delicious flavors that are somewhat restrained by the low proof.
how-to-shop-for-bottom-shelf-whiskey:
Everybody’s been reaching for premium, allocated, and single barrel bottlings in recent years, but what about the whiskeys on the lower shelves, even the bottom shelf? If you’re looking to discover some gems at the bargain end, here are 10 tips to help you get the most out of it.

1. Jump Right In

Scan the bottom shelf and look for the cheapest bottle there. Examine it to determine whether it’s worth drinking. Then buy it or don’t; move on to the next cheapest, and so on.

2. Start With the Label

You may be in the bourbon section, but make sure bourbon is what’s in the bottle. Be on the lookout for blended bourbon, which is half bourbon and half neutral spirit (i.e., vodka). Though usually in its own section, American blended whiskey sometimes appears on the bottom shelf in the bourbon section too, but it’s typically only 20% whiskey and 80% neutral spirit, plus coloring and flavoring. So-called light whiskey might even slip in there. Spirit whiskey is another red flag. It’s only 5% whiskey.

3. Read the Fine Print

All this information must be on the label, but sometimes it’s hard to find. There’s nothing wrong with any of the above-mentioned if that’s what you like, but you don’t want to buy one thinking it’s straight bourbon or rye. If you see straight whiskey on the bottom shelf, that’s a good sign. You should also look for an age statement: you may have to look carefully to find it because the required age statement for whiskey under 4 years old is usually not displayed prominently. Suntory’s Old Crow bourbon, for example, is 3 years old.

4. Look for These Good Signs 

The best thing to find on the bottom shelf is straight bourbon without an age statement, because that means it’s at least 4 years old. Also, the word “Kentucky” on the label doesn’t necessarily make it better, but it probably means it came from a major distillery, so it shouldn’t be too bad.

5. Check Out That ABV

Everything on the bottom shelf will probably be 40% ABV, so if you spot something higher down there, give it a look. The 50% ABV versions of Heaven Hill’s J.T.S. Brown or MGP/ Luxco’s Rebel can sometimes be found there.

6. Color Is Important

This is also a good time to look at color. Unlike scotch, American straight whiskeys can’t include caramel coloring, so color means something. Color doesn’t always track with flavor, but there are no guarantees in any of these suggestions anyway. They’re just ways of increasing your odds of success.

7. Brave the Unknown

When it comes to brands on the bottom shelf, you can never be sure what you’ll find. Don’t be afraid of unfamiliar labels. Especially now, with American whiskey stocks having moved from shortage to surplus, unknowns may be great finds. Some will be house brands, others will be independent bottler brands. They may be a one-off, so if you find one you like, stock up.

8. Bottom Shelf Kings

Among national brands, Sazerac’s Benchmark is the king of the bottom shelf. Though not distributed as widely, Sazerac’s Very Old Barton is a perennial bottom-shelf gem. Their Ancient Age is another one. They are three different recipes, too. Some brands have both top-shelf and bottom-shelf expressions. Heaven Hill’s 80° proof Old Fitzgerald Prime is bottom shelf, as is Four Roses bourbon. For rye whiskey, Suntory’s Jim Beam and Old Overholt are usually the best deals, but here too the brand you’ve never heard of might be a better bet.

9. Check Those Sales and Closeouts!

Careful shoppers will often find that something on sale is the best value in the store. Jim Beam white label isn’t normally bottom shelf, but it’s frequently on sale, so it might be just as inexpensive. After browsing the bottom shelf, make sure you check all the case stacks and end caps. Many stores also have a closeout area that’s worth a look.

10. Have Fun with It, No Matter What

If you get something you don’t particularly care for, have fun with it: Doctor it with vanilla or pancake syrup, use it in a cocktail that isn’t whiskey-forward, add it to an infinity barrel or a house blend, etc. There are no guarantees on the bottom shelf, but at least it’s low risk and offers the potential to find yourself an affordable favorite.
