redemption-single-barrel-bonded-bourbon-:
There won't be one Redemption Single Barrel Bonded bourbon released this year. There will be somewhere around 600 of them.

That's because every bottle of Redemption's newest bourbon comes from a single barrel, with roughly 550 to 600 individual casks expected to roll out nationally this year. Each will share the same rye-heavy mashbill, the same bottled in bond designation, and, thus, 100 proof. What they won't necessarily share is exactly the same flavor.

Rolling out nationally at retailers and online this month with an SRP of $50, Single Barrel Bonded is Redemption's first bottled in bond whiskey and the beginning of an ongoing single barrel program. Each bottle carries its barrel number, distilling season, mashbill, and age statement. All are at least 6 years old, though master blender Alan Kennedy says most land in the 7 to 8-year range.

For Kennedy, the conceit behind the new expression goes back to what made single barrel bourbon interesting in the first place. “There’s an idea of a single moment expressing time,” he says. “By not blending it, you get to see what’s happening through nature and the rickhouses. The true creator of whiskey is time and Mother Nature.” 

Kennedy points to Blanton’s, which helped establish the modern single barrel category under Elmer T. Lee, and Four Roses’ single barrel program. Single barrel bottled in bond bourbon itself isn't new—Henry McKenna has offered a 10 year old version since the 1990s. Redemption’s spin on the format is to lean into the differences among the barrels. While private barrel selections have exploded in popularity, Kennedy says buying an entire barrel has become increasingly difficult for many bars, restaurants, and liquor stores, both financially and in terms of inventory.

The whiskey is distilled at Ross & Squibb Distillery in Lawrenceburg, Indiana, using Redemption’s rye-heavy bourbon mashbill of 60% corn, 36% rye, and 4% malted barley. Each barrel must also meet the bottled in bond requirements: produced by one distiller during a single distilling season, aged at least 4 years in a federally bonded warehouse, and bottled at 50% ABV.

Kennedy considers the last requirement revealing. “That’s kind of the litmus test,” he says. “That’s the point in proof and flavor of the truest expression of what it can be. If it’s not good at (50% ABV), a lot of times that means it’s got faults.”

The proof also suits Redemption’s unusually high percentage of rye. Kennedy considers 6 to 10 years a sweet spot for this particular 36% rye mashbill, before extended aging begins sanding away some of its more assertive qualities. “It’s vibrant and spicy, and it hasn’t toned down,” he says. “It has fight left in it.”

That fight is evident in barrel No. 0130, distilled in fall 2018, which I tasted for this story. At 8 years old, the bourbon’s nose is immediately spice-driven, with cinnamon, ginger, and clove mingling with old leather, oak, burnt sugar, and barrel spice. It’s medium-weight but surprisingly creamy, hitting the center of the palate with baking spice before warmth slowly spreads down the sides of your tongue. Crème brûlée provides sweetness and lift against the drier leather and rye flavors. The finish changes direction again, with tart berries dusted with dark chocolate shavings emerging and lingering well after the sip. It’s pleasing, punchy, and well-integrated. It has enough age to temper harsh edges, but it’s still wide and multi-dimensional.

Another barrel will, by design, tell a slightly different story. But that’s Kennedy’s whole point.
glenmoranige-50-year-old-whisky:
Glenmorangie’s newest whisky comes from a distillery that no longer exists. Not literally. But when the spirit that became Glenmorangie 50 year old first ran from the stills back in the mid-1970s, the distillery had only two stills, malted its own barley, and dried that barley with a small peat fire. None of that is true of Glenmorangie today.

Which makes the oldest single malt whisky the Highland distillery has ever released something more interesting than merely old. Limited to a scant 149 bottles and priced at $36,000, Glenmorangie 50 year old has a unique flavor, distinct from what it produces today.

“The original tall two pot stills were fitted in 1887, so the stills that this spirit has been distilled in were almost certainly replacements, as the copper would be very unlikely to have lasted 90 years,” Glenmorangie’s director of whisky creation Dr. Bill Lumsden, MBE, tells us, adding that at that time, “there was just one wash still and one spirit still.” (It doubled to four during a 1977 expansion, then doubled again to eight in 1990, and reached its current 12 in 2009.)

The stills would’ve affected the character of mid-1970s new make at Glenmorangie, though not as much the barley. Home-malted barley would be dried over a small peat fire, “giving it a gentle background smokiness,” says Lumsden, “not tar or creosote notes like you get with Ardbeg, for example, but a lovely, subtle woodsmoke.”

 

Lumsden joined Glenmorangie in 1995, when this whisky was already old enough to order itself a drink. In 1999, a handful of bourbon barrels and a single sherry butt were combined at a ratio of 75% bourbon-matured to 25% sherry-matured whisky and transferred to a secondary marrying cask. This decision was partially because Lumsden says the sherried flavors, “such as toffee, sultana, and brown sugar, balance out the spiciness and the smokiness from the floor-malted barley.”

The first sample from that married cask wasn't drawn until 2014, some 15 years later, when the whisky was 38 years old. As the whisky approached its fifth decade, Lumsden and his team began checking it at increasingly shorter intervals, particularly from age 47 onward. The danger at this point wasn't that the whisky needed more maturity. It was that another year—or perhaps another season—might be one too many.

For Lumsden, the decision to bottle came when the equilibrium was ideal. “It was deemed ready when the balance between wood influence and base fruity flavors was right,” he says, “avoiding the heavy wood dominance often seen in other old bottlings.”

The final cask yielded enough whisky for exactly 149 bottles of Glenmorangie 50 year old, plus a small amount reserved for sampling. According to Lumsden, that particular cask is now empty, with nothing stashed away for an encore. There is, however, a tantalizing footnote about the sibling casks that fed the 1999 marriage cask. “There is a very small amount of remaining stock from that era, which is being monitored closely,” says Lumsden, adding there are currently no plans for it.

According to the brand’s tasting notes, Glenmorangie 50 year old opens with amber, cardamom, sultanas, nutmeg and baked orange, followed by toffee, leather, and a faint herbal note. The palate brings pepper, stewed Assam tea, birch tar, cinnamon, grape must, and oak tannin, before a long finish of aniseed, treacle toffee, and eucalyptus.

As for the bottle’s encasement, American ceramic artists Peter and Laurie Pincus were commissioned to create 149 individual display vessels, a three-year project that involved developing new techniques and 50 custom pigments inspired by the whisky’s tasting notes. Each vessel has a unique hand-applied pattern, but the 149 pieces also fit together into a single tessellated artwork titled “Together in Spirit.”
torabhaig-taigh-review:
One of the most fascinating new distillers to emerge in the modern scotch landscape is Torabhaig, which has a very unique approach to making whisky. When the tiny outpost fired up its stills in 2017, it became only the second single malt distillery on the Isle of Skye, which is also home to Talisker. Production is headed up by founder and industry veteran Neil MacLeod Mathieson (master blender for Torabhaig’s sister labels Mossburn and Caisteal Chamuis), who leads a large group of distillers, many of whom are Skye residents from other walks of life who were hired without prior experience in the field.

Since Torabhaig is so young, it lacked sufficient aged inventory to support a core range of expressions. Instead, the distillery has The Legacy Series, a collection of limited annual releases that gives drinkers a chance to follow the distillery as it works toward creating its house style step by step. It kicked off in 2021 with the release of Chapter 1: 2017, which served as a jumping-off point for future expressions, each having slight tweaks to the original recipe while gradually increasing the age. Those whiskies have been nothing short of mind-blowing: Chapter 2: Alt Gleann Batch Strength scored 95 points with our tasting panel while last year’s Chapter 4: Sound of Sleat gave the distillery its first-ever Top 20 honor—both championing the idea that scotch doesn’t have to be old to be delicious. This year the distillery surprised everyone with news that it's finally ready to debut its first permanent release, which we recently got a chance to taste.

Years in the Making

The new expression is called Taigh (pronounced “tie”), the Scottish Gaelic word for “home” or “house.” According to the brand, this whisky epitomizes Torabhaig’s house style and will serve as the blueprint for all future releases. The majority was aged in first-fill bourbon barrels, but there are also some refill barrels and madeira casks thrown into the mix too. That latter portion includes parcels that were finished in madeira casks after an initial maturation in bourbon barrels, and others that were aged entirely in madeira casks. It was made from malted barley smoked with Highland peat from Aberdeenshire, non-chill filtered, no added coloring, and bottled at 46% ABV. 

Torabhaig’s barley typically has a peat content that hovers around 78 phenol parts per million—nearly twice as much as Laphroaig, and almost four times higher than its neighbor Talisker—but its whiskies don’t taste nearly as smoky as those. The secret lies in the distillation, with the team running the stills slowly and tightening their cuts around the heart of the spirit, which serves to lighten its body while stripping some of the key phenols responsible for heavier industrial smoke notes. Torabhaig also uses a long fermentation (around 70–100 hours depending on the batch), which lends concentrated fruit notes early on in the process.

Taigh is technically not part of The Legacy Series, but it does take some production cues from those earlier releases, with a particular focus on aging. First-fill bourbon barrels have always played a role at the distillery, which largely used them for early expressions like 2017 Vintage and Alt Gleann. The distillery notably tried including PX and oloroso casks for Cnoc Na Moine, and virgin toasted American oak for Sound of Sleat, but both of those have been set aside this time around. The madeira casks are a fairly surprising addition, marking the first time Torabhaig has used these vessels for a mainline release. Madeira casks were previously used for a few one-off expressions, including retailer barrel picks and for Club Reserve No. 3, which sported a 6-month finish and was bottled exclusively for Torabhaig Club members.

The goal of The Legacy Series was always to arrive at a 10 year old flagship expression. Taigh is understood to be slightly younger than that, but the distillery isn’t giving up on the mission just yet. Torabhaig estimates that it’s roughly two years away from having sufficient inventory to make that dream a reality.

How does Torabhaig Taigh Taste?

94 points - Torabhaig Taigh Isle of Skye Single Malt Scotch

ABV: 46%
SRP: $50
Availability: Nationwide

Gentle wisps of earthy campfire smoke serve as a welcome mat for a pleasant nose that also includes roasted nuts, dried fruits, citrus, nutmeg, clove, and other assorted spices. The smoke reveals itself more on the palate, coiling around hazelnuts, vanilla, dried apricot, caramel apple, and bitter Seville oranges. The dram saves its best for the finish, adding hot cocoa and red berries to the mix, along with gentler woodsmoke and vanilla. A very tasty dram, with great flavors that continue to shift and evolve without stepping out of balance as you sip.
gary-linden-agave-surfboards:
Gary Linden doesn’t drink anymore, but he spends every day with agave. The 76 year old surf legend’s life has revolved around the pursuit of riding waves. He once ran the Association of Surfing Professionals (now the World Surf League), and later founded the Big Wave World Tour—a circuit that sanctions the largest big-wave contests on Earth, including Jaws, Nazaré, and Mavericks, where he still judges today.

But Linden is also renowned for his skill at making surfboards. He’s been crafting boards since he was 17 and has operated Linden Surfboards out of an Oceanside, California workshop since 1978. Yet the thing that may define the final chapter of his board-shaping career has nothing to do with foam or fiberglass.

Agave Boards

Since 2003, Linden has been building his boards from agave. He first became attracted to the idea when a doctor brought him some small surfboard blanks (the board’s core that still needs shaping and finishing) that had been made from agave. “They were rough, but they were beautiful,” he says. “I couldn’t throw them away. I showed the doctor how to make proper blanks and then started making them myself.”

Linden sources stalks from a 33,000-acre farm in Kenya and from canyon backyards in Southern California, milling and shaping every board by hand. Linden notes that there are about 26 to 30 varieties of agave. The ones in Kenya are sisal, whose fibers can be used for netting and rope. Blue Weber is, of course, the variety used for tequila, while mezcal is made from espadín and about 10 other varieties. “In California, what I’m working with is the century plant, which is used to make fencing,” he says. “They’re all different.” Linden uses dried quiotes or stalks of the plant to create the blanks for the boards. The boards are made entirely from the dried stalks. Agave grown for tequila is harvested before the plant produces a quiote.

After roughly a thousand boards, he’s just now approaching scaling his operation, so you may see more Linden agave boards in the ocean soon. “In making boards from agave, it doesn’t matter too much whether you drink the stuff or not,” he says. “It’s easier to explain to a tequila drinker about the plant and how I use it, and easier to explain what a surfboard core is made of to a surfer. With everyone else, you’re starting from scratch on both ends. The spirits drinkers get the plant. The surfers get the board. The overlap is small, but those are the people that really get it.”

Asked whether agave stocks from Kenya or California are best for surfboards, Linden says both are good. “The strength and flexibility in each are superior to what you’d usually make surfboards from—polyurethane foam, which is fairly brittle. Even though [polyurethane boards] have a wooden streak down the middle, they’re prone to breakage. Since an agave stalk is solid—closer to a reed—it’s much less susceptible to breaking.”

In either case, Linden argues that both the Kenyan and Californian agave boards will outlast traditional foam boards by five or more years. “California has a bigger stalk, a larger plant with an extraordinary range of colors,” he says. “I love putting them together in ways that complement or contrast each other—art pieces, I call them. The Kenya boards are less colorful, but are lighter and more workable for performance. California is more for the soul.”

So how does an agave surfboard actually ride? Linden explains it by referencing Goldilocks. “Balsa is too stiff; it doesn’t flex at all. Foam flexes too much—hit a wave and watch the energy dissipate,” he says. “Agave is just right. It flexes when you want it to and holds when you don’t want any movement. That gives you speed, stability, and a smoother ride. It’s like an old Cadillac compared to a bouncy VW bug. They’re best in big waves, like at Nazaré or Jaws. Foam boards chatter, while agave glides.”

Multi-Use Plant

In general, Linden marvels at the sheer diversity of the agave plant’s uses. “You can squeeze the juice from the heart to make a beverage, the leaf tip is a needle that has its own thread attached, and pulp from tequila production can be pressed into paper. Ranchers use the leaves for fencing. The mash can be repurposed into diesel fuel. It requires no irrigation because it collects moisture from the night air; it’s essentially a carbon filter that grows on its own.” He’s also worked alongside a Fender custom master builder to create Stratocaster guitars from agave, and even collaborated with Jose Cuervo to make a 100% agave surfboard.

Asked if there is a mezcal connection to surfing beyond agave’s use for boards, Linden gives a spiritual response. “When I’m on my board out in the ocean, sitting on a piece of nature that took 20 years to grow and that I got to shape, there is something spiritual about it,” he says. “Surfing is my meditative state. I sit on the water, watch the horizon, and wait for a wave. I want to be with nature. I used to drink raicilla [known as Mexican moonshine] while I was building. My favorite brand was Lorena. I’d have a small glass, and I’d start shaping it. I gave up alcohol at 70 for health reasons. I miss it. But I’m still making the boards.”
smores-whiskey-cocktail-recipe:
Step outside on any given night this time of year, and you're apt to breathe in the comforting scent of a fire pit. Those smoky wafts feel like a warm, soft blanket, coaxing you to relax and slow down.

Whether you have a fire pit or not, it's the perfect nudge to make a drink that transports you to a fireside gathering. And Tipsy S'mores, created by Armando Acevedo, bar captain at Sungold in Brooklyn, New York, will do just that. “I wanted to capture the essence of those cozy fall nights spent by a fire, roasting marshmallows and making s'mores,” Acevedo says. “The toasted marshmallow rim brings forward smoky, nostalgic aromatics, and the banana liqueur adds a hint of unexpected flavor.”

Rich and creamy, it's a great adult dessert in a glass for sweater weather, complete with a chocolate-graham cracker-marshmallow garnish.

Tipsy S'mores

  • 1 1/2 oz. Maker’s Mark (or other wheated bourbon)
  • 1 oz. banana liqueur
  • 1 1/4 oz. marshmallow root tea (recipe below)
  • 1 1/2 oz. condensed milk
  • 4 dashes coffee bitters
  • Chocolate syrup, crushed graham cracker, and torched marshmallow for garnish

Rim a coupe with chocolate syrup, then roll in graham cracker. Set aside. Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice. Shake vigorously for about 15 seconds. Double strain into prepared glass and garnish with a skewered marshmallow.

Marshmallow Root Tea

  • 2 Tbsp. dried marshmallow root
  • 1 cup cold or room-temperature water

Place marshmallow root in a mason jar, then pour water over top to fill the jar. Cover and steep for 4 to 8 hours or overnight at room temperature or in the fridge. (The liquid may turn a soft yellow color.) Strain into an airtight container. Keep refrigerated for up to 3 days.
