Back in May, Texas distiller Garrison Brothers kicked off its new Ranch Reserve series with a pair of sherry cask-finished bourbons. Now the distillery is releasing single cask versions of those whiskeys, representing a selection of 27 barrels from the original batch that master distiller Donnis Todd held back for their bold, distinctive profiles.

These barrels yielded around 3,000 bottles for each expression. The first 984 bottles of each will be available at a tailgate at the distillery on October 17th, coinciding with the Texas Longhorns vs. Florida Gators college football game. The remaining bottles will be made available at retailers nationwide.

O.H. Ingram River Aged Flagship Bourbon (Batch 6)

ABV: 56.9%
SRP: $80
Availability: Select retailers and at the distillery

The Ingram Distillery, a Kentucky producer best known for its river-aging process that matures barrels on floating rickhouses moored to the banks of the Mississippi River, has a fresh batch of its annual Flagship bourbon. This one comprises a blend of 25 barrels, including four from upper decks and 21 that were aged on the lower decks. It has a mashbill of 70% corn, 21% wheat, and 9%, and it carries a 7-year age statement.

Brother Justus Founder's Reserve IV American Whiskey

ABV: 55%
SRP: $150
Availability: At the distillery, online, and retailers in Minnesota and Illinois

Minneapolis craft distillery Brother Justus is back with its annual Founder’s Reserve expression. It was distilled entirely from malted two-row pale ale barley and aged for 2–4 years in new charred Minnesota oak barrels. The total batch accounts for 25 barrels, which yielded fewer than 1,000 bottles.

2XO Collectible Series Rapper’s Delight The Hip-Hop Blend Kentucky Straight Bourbon

ABV: 52%
Price: $80
Availability: Nationwide

2XO’s Icon Series, since renamed the Collectibles Series, highlights the personal memories, passions, and hobbies of founder and master blender Dixon Dedman. The seventh release in the limited-edition collection taps into Dedman’s love of rap music through a collaboration with the Sugarhill Gang. Named for the group’s seminal 1979 hit, “Rapper’s Delight,” the expression blends two bourbon mashbills: a high-rye (35%) bourbon comprising 90% of the blend and a moderate-rye (18%) bourbon making up the remaining 10%. It follows several high-scoring releases in the collection, notably the Vinyl Blend (2025), the Kiawah Blend, which landed at No. 14 on our 2024 Top 20, and the Tribute Blend (2023).

Wilderness Trail 10 year old Symphony of Disruption Bourbon

ABV: 61.45%
SRP: $190
Availability: 414 bottles

Wilderness Trail 8 year old Cask Strength Rye

ABV: 58.05%
SRP: $80
Availability: 408 bottles

The first of Wilderness Trail’s two new ultra-limited releases is a bourbon that celebrates co-founders Dr. Pat Heist and Shane Baker in light of their induction into the Kentucky Distillers’ Association Bourbon Hall of Fame. Named “Symphony of Disruption”—a reference to the distillery’s championing of sweet mash fermentation as opposed to the more standard sour mash—the new bourbon is a 10 year old wheater comprised of three barrels. Just 414 bottles are available, and they’re exclusive to the Wilderness Trail Distillery in Danville, Kentucky.

The second release is an 8 year old rye that was selected by Wilderness Trail national brand ambassador Haley Perros and the distilling team. Made from the distillery’s signature rye mashbill of 56% rye, 33% corn, and 11% malted barley, the new rye is also a distillery exclusive, limited to 408 bottles.

Copperworks Craft Malt Month 2026 (Cask 488) American Single Malt

ABV: 63.2%
SRP: $90
Availability: Limited

In commemoration of Craft Malt Month, which comes every September, Washington-based Copperworks has debuted a new single cask American single malt. The new whiskey is distilled from baronesse barley grown by Joseph’s Grainery in Colfax, Washington, and malted by LINC Malt in Spokane. It aged for 5 years in a rye whiskey barrel, marking the first time Copperworks has matured one of its whiskeys in a rye cask. For every bottle sold, $10 will go directly to the Craft Maltsters Guild.

Pursuit x Shortbarrel Found Footage Blended 

ABV: 56.2%
Price: $100/700-ml bottle
Availability: Limited

Louisville, Kentucky-based Pursuit Spirits and Atlanta-based Shortbarrel have teamed up for a collaborative barrel-proof expression. The blend combines a barrel of Pursuit’s Double Oak rye from its United lineup and Shortbarrel’s Sapsquatch, a maple syrup barrel-finished bourbon. Its name, Found Footage, references a fictional tale in which a beast guarding the maple-finished bourbon is lured out by the United rye, with grainy “recovered” camera footage inspiring the release’s name and custom label. The whiskey debuted at the Kentucky Bourbon Festival, with the remaining bottles from the small run allocated to the brands’ respective subscription clubs, P. Club and The Shortlist.

The Maven Kentucky Straight Bourbon

ABV: 47%
Price: $200
Availability: Limited

The Maven Distillery, the newly completed Shelbyville, Kentucky facility commissioned by IJW Whiskey Company, has debuted the flagship Kentucky straight bourbon for its new label, The Maven. The 7-plus year old, high-rye blend of six whiskeys puts a large emphasis on oak. The bourbon combines whiskeys aged entirely in toasted American oak with others initially matured in traditional charred American oak, then finished in toasted barrels made from four species of oak from around the globe: Kentucky chinkapin, Pacific Northwest garryana, French, and Japanese mizunara. Master blender Steve Hughes developed a proprietary toasting profile for the casks, designed to draw additional caramelized sugars and flavor from the wood.

While IJW Whiskey Company has historically operated under the radar as a non-distilling producer, sourcing and storing barrels, it has begun releasing whiskey under its own labels in recent years, including Bondstone, First Call, MacFarlane’s Reserve, and Old Emmer. The Maven represents its first national brand—and most oak-focused—addition. It’s currently available at retailers in Kentucky, with rollout to California and New York coming this October.

Silver Brothers 3 year old Rye (Batch 2)

ABV: 46%
Price: $78
Availability: New York retailers and online

Silver Brothers Whiskey has unveiled a 3 year old rye, the third expression in its rapidly growing portfolio that launched earlier this year. A marriage of six 30-gallon barrels, the rye marks the distillery’s first release made predominantly with estate-grown grain, a major milestone for the regenerative farm-focused operation. The mashbill comprises 80% rye from the label’s first-year harvest, namely the AC Hazlet varietal, said to have a lighter flavor profile than other rye varieties. The remaining 20% is malted barley.

Situated on a picturesque 220-acre farm, Hudson Valley's Silver Brothers Whiskey opened its doors with the inaugural Empire Rye whiskey this past June, followed by an American single malt in July. It focuses on creating terroir-driven whiskeys using estate-grown and New York grain. In 2020, the husband-and-wife team of Matthew Greitzer and Kimberly Driessen-Greitzer purchased the property. Their first grain harvest was in 2022, and spirits production began in 2023.

Dublasé Signature No. 9 V 5 year old bourbon 

ABV: 50.15%
Price: $55

Dublasé Signature No. 9 VII 7 year old bourbon

ABV: 54.3%
Price: $70

Dublasé Signature No. 9 X 10 year old bourbon

ABV: 54.45%
Price: $90

Availability: Florida, California, Washington D.C., Maryland, and online shipping to 38 states.

Jacksonville, Florida-based DuBlasé launched in 2021 with a vanilla-flavored whiskey, later adding its signature No. 11 Bourbon in 2023. Now, it’s debuting three new age-stated bourbons: 5, 7, and 10 year olds. All three were aged primarily in Indiana, with the exception of the 5 year old No. 9 V, which spent two years there before traveling to Florida for three-plus years of maturation in the subtropical climate. The V and VII share a mashbill of 75% corn, 23% rye, and 2% malted barley, while the 10 year old X leans further into rye at 60% corn, 38% rye, and 2% malted barley.

Giving back is central to the label’s mission: A portion of bottle-sale proceeds supports the DuBlasé Foundation, which funds STEM education, scholarships, and youth innovation programs.
best-new-bourbon-rye-september-2026:
September is a great month to be a bourbon fan. National Bourbon Heritage Month signifies the commencement of fall’s allocation run, a stretch through the holidays when distilleries ship their scarcest annual releases and retailers start calling their waitlists. The Kentucky Bourbon Festival, held mid-month in Bardstown, the bourbon capital of the world, doubles as a launch pad for a slew of expressions, with distillers pouring new whiskeys for the crowds before they reach distillery gift shops and liquor stores.

Labels revived from company archives, century-old family brands, and anniversary blends from Kentucky's biggest distilleries all arrive within weeks of each other, leaving drinkers with more worthwhile bottles than shelf space. These five are worth the chase.

Bluegrass Distillers Elkwood Reserve 19 year old bourbon, 64.5%, $450

It’s a steep price, but this 19 year old Kentucky straight bourbon is well worth it. It’s one of three single barrels Bluegrass Distillers has been hanging onto since it acquired a parcel of 30 Barton 18-year barrels. “We thought these could handle another year of age,” says Ben Franzini, Bluegrass Distiller’s co-founder. He was correct. This particular barrel, at 64.5%, is a fresh Dr Pepper bomb, fizzy and heavy on the cherry syrup, with plenty of grip but nowhere near over-oaked. Released as part of a trio of barrels at Kentucky Bourbon Fest, and with a little less than 100 bottles per barrel, this is one to hunt. Will there be a 20-year next year? “Who can say?” Franzini smiles.

Castle & Key Cask Strength Wheated Bourbon, 54.9%, $70

Despite the 7-year age statement on this cask strength release, it’s almost entirely 8 and 9 year old liquid, says Brett Connors, Castle & Key’s head blender. “It’s the best wheated we’ve done so far. It’s silky, sexy, and easy drinking.” The mouthfeel is hefty, and there’s a nice punch of aged oak upfront, followed by stone fruit, golden raisins, dates, peach, and apricot. There’s plenty of grip without being too biting, and a longer finish than a typical 7 year old whiskey has. “I opt for a really good toast density on our casks, which helps pull more developmental sugars from the wood,” says Connors. With lower entry proof—this liquid is 53.5% at the time of filling—the extra sugars help sweeten the final product. Pour it over ice, and you may mistake it for an Old Fashioned.

Dark Arts 19 year old Mizunara Finished bourbon, 57.5%, $500

Lexington-based non-distiller producer Dark Arts has been on a heater streak. Last year’s release of 16 year old BuffTurkey was a sought-after banger. This September, Dark Arts dropped a series of offerings, including a $200 21 year old MGP-made light whiskey finished in custom French oak called Supernova at 71.35 proof (it drinks far sweeter and creamier than the hazmat proof would indicate) and another hazmat 11.5 year old bourbon named Flight of the Icarus. But the buzz is louder for its Cuvée 19-year Kentucky straight bourbon finished for 7 years(!) in Japanese mizunara oak casks. “We put the blend together in a way where there wasn’t too much tannic structure,” says Dark Arts owner and chief alchemist Macaulay Minton. This one-off experimental Jim Beam mashbill (75% corn, 21% rye, 4% malted barley) gives light sandalwood, salted caramel, toasted marshmallow, and barrel spice that’s all remarkably balanced.

Pursuit Spirits x Shortbarrel Found Footage, 56.2%, $100

What happens when bourbon aged in maple syrup barrels meets double-oaked rye featuring tobacco staves? Deliciousness. Found Footage marries two barrels of Sasquatch, the maple barrel finished bourbon,from Atlanta-based Shortbarrel, with two rye barrels from Louisville producer Pursuit Spirits, leaving you with a sip that’s a harmonious blend of sweetness and rye. Ryan Cecil, Pursuit co-founder and master blender, calls it a drinkable maple-bacon doughnut. All those notes pop up in the effervescent whiskey, along with some grape Nerds candy notes, and some sweet pepper on the finish. For the release, 660 bottles went to the Kentucky Bourbon Festival, with another few hundred going to Seelbach’s. “We release new quarterly products to our P.Club first,” says Kenny Coleman, Pursuit’s other co-founder, so look for similarly tasty barrel mashups there.

Very Olde St. Nick Pirate Booty Rye, 55.4%, $200

Preservation Distillery doesn’t miss, and all of its six releases for the Kentucky Bourbon Festival prove it, but one interesting expression stands out: Pirate Booty Rye. Per Kyle Lloyd, Preservation Distillery’s master of maturation, Pirate Booty is built from some of the oldest rye barrels made at owner Marci Palatella’s farm. “When Preservation started pot distilling rye, we laid a very small number of casks down across a spread of toast and char profiles to see what each one would do,” says Lloyd. “Pirate Booty combines a few of those barrel profiles in a way we haven't put into a Preservation-distilled rye before.” The result is a semi-traditional rye profile—you’ll pick out herbaceous dill notes amid the rye bread nose—with a little more sweetness on the palate, perfectly balancing out the spice.
dram-central-spirits-lounge:
When Brandy Library opened in lower Manhattan back in 2004, owner Flavien Desoblin realized he had a location problem. The bar, an elegant shrine to whisky in New York’s Tribeca neighborhood, was far away from Midtown, where many of its customers worked. Even back then, Desoblin thought about creating a more centrally located whisky oasis—a place where the whisky-minded could spend time after a day at the office. That long-awaited idea has now come to fruition with Dram Central Spirits Lounge, Desoblin’s newest and most ambitious project yet.

Located at 14 E 44th Street, just a few blocks from Grand Central Station, Dram Central opened in August with a vibe that will be instantly familiar to anyone who’s visited Brandy Library or Copper & Oak (a bar also owned by Desoblin, also in lower Manhattan). Copper accents, dark wood, and warm, orange-hued backlighting set the space aglow, and shelves of bottles—mostly whisky, but also high-end tequilas, mezcals, cognacs, and more—line the walls, much as they do at both Brandy Library and Copper & Oak. But Dram Central has more to offer, including a full kitchen, multiple private event spaces, and, of course, a great deal more whisky and other spirits.

The Dram Central space is twice the size of Brandy Library, so Desoblin had plenty of empty shelf space to fill. The whisky list alone fills 200 pages, spanning the major whisky countries as well as others like New Zealand and Denmark. The main focus, though, is on single malt scotch and American whiskey, and that’s where you’ll find the most precious bottles. “If we look at single malts, there are about 50 different Ardbeg expressions, and just about every single Octomore release since the first one,” Desoblin says. He calls out a few more single malt highlights—every Dalwhinnie Distiller’s Edition ever made, all of the Lagavulin Distiller’s Editions, vintage-dated Glenmorangie going back to 1975, and an impressive selection of Springbank and Hazelburn—and also points to Dram Central’s varied array of single grain scotch whiskies.

Bourbon lovers will also find plenty to like at Dram Central; Desoblin has amassed just about every limited edition of Four Roses, from Marriage Collection to Secretariat 40th Anniversary to single barrel selects, all of the Buffalo Trace Antique Collection whiskeys, every Old Forester Birthday bottling, and scores of Pappy, Michter’s, and Russell’s Reserve releases, among countless others. There are also numerous ryes, American single malts, wheat whiskeys, and more, from both historic and craft American distillers. Irish and Canadian whiskies are also plentiful, and they’re joined by sizable French and Japanese contingents, as well as Indian and other world whiskies. In all, more than 2,000 unique whiskies are available, priced anywhere from $20 to $1,900 (for Black Bowmore 1964) for a 1-ounce pour.

While Brandy Library and Copper & Oak both have limited selections of other spirits, Dram Central takes things much further. As with the whiskies, these aren’t just any spirits. “We’re looking for the special ones—in tequila, that means we’re staying away from what’s really commercial, because there are so many other beautiful tequilas out there,” he explains. “Same thing for mezcal, we’re looking for the small production bottles, the one-offs, the unique pechugas, the different villages and odd and rare agaves.” The agave spirits list fills 20 pages, with tequila and mezcal rounded out by sotol, pechuga, and raicilla pours. High-end cognacs, armagnacs, calvados, and brandies are plentiful too, as are rums from around the world. A bespoke cocktail list and flights complete the drinks menu. Not to worry if it sounds like an overwhelming array of choices: The staff, as at Desoblin’s other venues, is well-versed in the menu and can provide a helping hand during the selection process. 

Dram Central also has something new for Desoblin: a full-service restaurant. Scotch eggs, steak tartare, tequila ceviche, and wedge salads are among the featured starters, while the main courses are meat-centric and spirits-accented—there’s filet mignon with a cognac peppercorn sauce, pepper-crusted duck magret made with a Grand Marnier reduction, and pan-seared chicken breast served with Speyside scotch sauce, to name a few examples. In the future, Desoblin sees ample opportunity for bourbon dinners, tequila pairing tastings, and similar things, with the lounge’s second floor exclusively available for private events.

When Desoblin opened Brandy Library, the world of fine spirits looked a little different. “It was all about single malt scotch [in 2004],” he says. “Then in 2008, it was all about bourbon. But in the last seven or eight years, it’s opened up to tequila and mezcal and armagnac and more, and now we’ve got them all in one place. That’s the most exciting thing for me—because it means at long last, people are taking hard liquor more as a fine spirit than as just hard liquor. And being right here—where people work and then make their way home—makes the most sense.” Of course, Dram Central’s Midtown location makes it easily accessible to whisky-loving tourists visiting landmarks like Grand Central, Times Square, Bryant Park, or similar. The lounge is open from 3 p.m. to 1 a.m. Tuesday through Saturday; reservations aren’t required, but can be made here.
whisky-and-px-sherry-cocktails:
Pedro Ximénez (PX) is a luscious dessert-style sherry produced in southern Spain. PX-cask finishing is adored by whisky lovers, enveloping the spirit with flavors of dates, raisins, figs, toffee, and coffee. Bartenders lean into this natural affinity by adding PX sherry to whisky cocktails to unlock new depths of flavor in the whisky. The rich, sticky viscosity of PX also enhances a cocktail’s mouthfeel. “Swapping PX sherry for vermouth makes a Manhattan incredibly velvet-like and accentuates the rye whiskey’s spice notes,” says Max Schikora, bar manager at Echelon Kitchen and Bar in Ann Arbor, Michigan, who recommends pairing it with chocolate-based desserts.

Even a small pour can transform a drink. “Out of the seven sherry varietals, PX works well with whisky as it substitutes sugar and adds an entirely new flavor profile to any cocktail,” explains Janina Silva, beverage director at Pomona Kitchen in West Palm Beach. “The notes of sweet dark fruits from PX sherry play very well with grain spirits.” Rich in sweetness, depth, and texture, PX adds a luxurious touch to any cocktail, making it an inspired and strategic choice for your bar cart.

PX Marks the Spot 

Created by Janina Silva, beverage director, Pomona Kitchen, West Palm Beach 

  • 1½ oz. Nomad Outland (or other blended scotch)
  • ½ oz. Gonzalez Byass Nectar PX sherry
  • ¼ oz. Vecchio Amaro del Capo Red Hot
  • 2 dashes chocolate mole bitters
  • Orange twist and amarena cherry, for garnish

Stir all ingredients into a rocks glass with a large ice cube. Garnish with orange twist and amarena cherry.

Borrowed Time

Created by David Perez, assistant general manager & beverage director, Agnes and Sherman, Houston

  • 1½ oz. Iwai 45 (or other Japanese blended whisky)
  • ¾ oz. El Maestro Sierra PX sherry
  • ½ oz. Matsui Umeshu plum liqueur
  • 2 dashes Kaffir lime leaf tincture
  • Lime coin, for garnish

Stir ingredients in an Old Fashioned glass; serve over a mound of crushed ice and garnish with a quarter-size lime coin.

PX Manhattan

Created by Max Schikora, bar manager, Echelon Kitchen and Bar, Ann Arbor, Michigan

  • 2 oz. Rittenhouse (or other bottled in bond rye)
  • 1 oz. PX sherry
  • 3 dashes Angostura bitters
  • Orange peel
  • Maraschino cherry, for garnish

Stir all ingredients with ice for 10-12 seconds, then strain into a chilled coupe. Express an orange peel over the top, discard, and garnish with a maraschino cherry.


Red Winter Dram

Created by Cheech Kinsway, general manager at Palm Valley Cocktails, Dubin, Ohio

  • 1¼ oz. Middle West (or other wheat whiskey)
  • ½ oz. PX sherry
  • ½ oz. banana liqueur
  • ½ oz. orange oleo saccharum (recipe below)
  • ¼ oz. lime juice
  • Orange coin, for garnish

Shake, then strain into a rocks glass over a large ice cube. Garnish the ice with expressed orange coin

Orange Oleo Saccharum

Combine equal parts by weight of orange peel and sugar. Coat the peels with the sugar, muddle them, cover, and let sit for 1-2 days. Strain and discard peels
mgp-chapter-one-out-of-the-shadows:
Behind many of the non-distilling producers in the U.S.—and even some that make their own whiskey—lies a single name: MGP (Midwest Grain Products). The Lawrenceburg, Indiana-based distillery, capable of producing millions of proof gallons per year (making it among the biggest distilleries in the U.S.), has sent its whiskeys to be bottled under countless brand names. Throughout it all, MGP has remained largely behind the scenes, cited on many labels only as “Distilled in Indiana.” Now, MGP has decided to release its own branded line of whiskeys, the very first to prominently feature “MGP” on the bottle.

The first release, simply called “MGP Chapter One: Out of the Shadows,” is a 10 year old bourbon that clocks in at 55.5% ABV. It’s made from MGP’s signature high-rye bourbon mashbill: 60% corn, 36% rye, and 4% malted barley (a recipe also used by Hirsch, James E. Pepper, and within the distillery’s Ross & Squibb lineup, among others). Every barrel of Out of the Shadows is aged in MGP’s Rickhouse G, a brick warehouse built in 1936. MGP Chapter One is available now in limited quantities nationwide for $70. There will be other releases down the road, though those details aren’t available yet.

This whiskey, like all MGP whiskeys, whether they’re for the distillery’s own releases or contract distillation, was made by master distiller Ian Stirsman, who joined the distillery in March 2014. While he started at MGP as a production shift manager, he began distilling in 2015 and was named master distiller in 2021. He took the reins from Greg Metze, who ran the distillery for 38 years before leaving the role in 2016. MGP did not name a master distiller between Metze’s retirement and Stirsman’s start in the role.

While this is MGP’s first whiskey to put its name front and center, it’s not the company’s first move into branding; that came in 2021, when it changed its name to Ross & Squibb Distillery and released the proprietary Rossville Union, Remus Repeal Reserve, George Remus, Eight & Sand, and Tanner’s Creeks labels (it also purchased Penelope Bourbon in 2023, having supplied whiskey for the brand since its inception). But those whiskeys didn’t tout the MGP name as this one does. The Chapter One release marks an about-face for MGP, which is dropping the Ross & Squibb Distillery name and reinstating MGP, in alignment with the release of this new whiskey.
elmer-t-lee-40th-anniversary-edition-bou:
Four decades after the brand launched, Buffalo Trace Distillery will release Elmer T. Lee 40th Anniversary Edition this fall, the first version of the single barrel bourbon bottled without dilution or chill filtration. Suggested retail is $99.99, and it can only be purchased through the Buffalo Trace Bottle Draw lottery system.

The barrels run from 124.8 to 138.6 proof, wide enough that structure and intensity shift noticeably from one to the next. That’s markedly up from the regular Elmer T. Lee proof of 90, the Elmer T. Lee 15 year old Single Barrel Reserve proof of 93, and the Elmer T. Lee 100 Year Tribute at 100 proof.

As for the man behind the label, Lee joined what was then the George T. Stagg Distillery in 1949 as a maintenance engineer, arriving with a University of Kentucky degree and a stint in World War II behind him. Over the next four decades, he worked his way to master distiller, steering the plant through its postwar modernization. Lee had a habit of pouring guests bourbon drawn from single barrels in the middle tiers of the metal-clad Warehouse H, and in 1984 he formalized this practice when he introduced Blanton's, the first commercially marketed single barrel bourbon and the template for nearly every premium expression that followed. Two years later, the distillery put his name on a single barrel bourbon of its own.

Master distiller Harlen Wheatley, who worked under Lee early on, said he was "fortunate to learn from Elmer" and described the anniversary bottling as a privilege for the distillery. Erica Bovard, senior brand director for American whiskey, said the uncut format keeps the whiskey "true to the standards Elmer set." Buffalo Trace frames the choice as a nod to how Lee assessed barrels during Blanton's selection, tasting them straight from the wood. (No mention of how Lee famously liked to drink his whiskey mixed with Sprite.)

The 40th Anniversary Edition joins a short list of commemorative and allocated Elmer T. Lee bottlings: the 90th Birthday Edition in 2009, the Commemorative Bottle in 2013, the year Lee died at 93, and the 100 Year Tribute in 2019, marking what would have been his centennial. Standard Elmer T. Lee Single Barrel remains in ongoing limited production, released as individual barrels are ready.

Getting a bottle requires a trip to Buffalo Trace in Frankfort. The distillery is allocating the limited release through the newly minted Buffalo Trace Bottle Draw system, a lottery the gift shop built after visitor complaints about its previous first-come system. Registration opens at 10 a.m. ET on September 15 and closes at 11:59 p.m. ET on September 17, with one entry per person and no advantage to entering early. An independent partner draws names on September 22, and everyone who enters is notified either way. Winners have from September 28 through October 11 to come to the distillery during visitor hours and buy their bottle in person. Buffalo Trace has said it will collect feedback from participants and adjust the format for future drawings.

At $99.99, Elmer T. Lee 40th Anniversary Edition is a steal, given it’s an uncut single barrel. However, being part of the Buffalo Trace lineup, it will trade for several multiples of that figure the moment it leaves the gift shop. The lottery structure and in-person pickup mandate are the distillery's attempt to mitigate secondary market flipping, though neither does much for anyone who can’t drive to Kentucky within the two-week window.
2026-parkers-heritage-kentucky-boy-and-m:
This week brings several commemorative releases. Heaven Hill returns with the 20th edition of Parker’s Heritage, the annual series that honors late master distiller Parker Beam. From Brown-Forman comes Kentucky Boy, a resurrected bourbon brand that celebrates master distiller emeritus Chris Morris’ 50th year with the company. Chicken Cock has added two new bourbons, both in recognition of its 170th anniversary. There are also a couple of bottles celebrating 10-year milestones: Four Roses is toasting the 10th year of its Salt River cleanup, while Jeptha Creed is commemorating a decade in the business with a new solera-aged bourbon. And from Neeley Family Distillery is a 10 year old triple pot-distilled bourbon that pays homage to master distiller Royce Neeley’s grandfather and mentor, Earl Sizemore. Elsewhere, Penelope has added a new chapter to its Cigar Sessions series, Middle West has a new vino de naranja cask finish, and WhistlePig returns with the 13th edition of The Boss Hog.

Parker’s Heritage 20th Edition: 14 Year Old Kentucky Straight Bourbon (2026 Release)

ABV: 59%
SRP: $200
Availability: Limited

For the 20th edition of Parker’s Heritage Collection, a series that honors late Heaven Hill master distiller Parker Beam, current master distiller Conor O’Driscoll pulled 100 barrels distilled between October 2011 and January 2012 that aged across the 2nd floor of Rickhouse A; the first and second floors of Rickhouse KK; and the third floor of Rickhouses L and M. The 14 year old whiskey is made from a mashbill of 78% corn, 10% rye, and 12% malted barley, and is unique in that it incorporated rye backset—a portion of rye left over after distillation—during the fermentation as opposed to bourbon backset, which is more typical of Heaven Hill (rye is only periodically made at the distillery, which puts the brunt of production toward bourbon). According to O’Driscoll, this switch-up imbues the whiskey with more depth and spice character. The 2026 edition of Parker’s Heritage is available nationwide; as with every release in the series, Heaven Hill will donate a portion of the proceeds from each bottle sold to the ALS Association in honor of Beam. To date, the distillery has donated more than $1.4 million to the organization.

Kentucky Boy Bourbon

ABV: 50%
SRP: $100
Availability: Limited

Brown-Forman master distiller emeritus Chris Morris is celebrating his 50th year with the company; to mark the milestone, Woodford Reserve master distiller Elizabeth McCall and Old Forester assistant master distiller Caleb Trigo resurrected the Kentucky Boy brand, creating a bourbon that nods to some of Morris’s most iconic releases.

The new bourbon—named after a brand originally made at Louisville’s Lynndale Distillery, which Brown-Forman acquired in 1923—blends three Morris mainstays: Old Forester Birthday Bourbon, King of Kentucky, and Woodford Reserve Double Oaked. Birthday Bourbon, one of Old Forester’s most coveted releases, debuted back in 2002 under Morris's watch; he later spearheaded the creation of an enduring Woodford classic, Double Oaked, in 2012, and revived the King of Kentucky brand in 2018.

McCall and Trigo developed the whiskey in secret, keeping it hush-hush until a recent companywide event commemorating Morris’s 50th anniversary. Now the public is privy to Kentucky Boy as well—the bourbon launched at the Kentucky Bourbon Festival in Bardstown on September 10th, and starting today (September 11th), bottles will be available at the Old Forester Distillery on Louisville’s Whiskey Row, as well as through the distillery’s website and at various Kentucky retailers. As an added bonus, Morris will be at the distillery tonight for the Kentucky Boy release party. A portion of the net proceeds from Kentucky Boy sales will go toward Second Stride, a nonprofit focused on the rehabilitation, retraining, and placement of retired thoroughbred racehorses. It’s a fitting alignment, given that the brand was marketed with a thoroughbred racing theme in the 1940s, and features the same theme under its new lease on life.

Four Roses Salt River Clean Up Private Barrel Selection bourbon

ABV: 61.8%
SRP: $120
Availability: Limited; distillery exclusive

Ten years ago, Four Roses partnered with the Kentucky Waterway Alliance for its first-ever Salt Water Clean Up, a project that brought the two forces together to protect and restore the 150-mile-long Salt River in Kentucky. In commemoration of the decade-long collaboration, master distiller Brent Elliot has selected a 10 year old barrel of Four Roses’ OESQ bourbon—made from the distillery’s mashbill E (75% corn, 20% rye, and 5% malted barley) and the delicate, floral yeast strain Q. The whiskey will be available starting Thursday, September 17th at 12:30 p.m., which is when this year’s cleanup is taking place. Half of the proceeds will go to the Kentucky Waterway Alliance, and each purchase will include a commemorative Salt River Clean Up water bottle.

Chicken Cock 170th Anniversary Limited Edition Rooster Decanter

ABV: 57.5%
SRP: $200
Availability: Limited

Chicken Cock 170th Anniversary Edition Legacy Kentucky Straight Bourbon

ABV: 57.5%
SRP: $100
Availability: Limited

Chicken Cock’s latest whiskey celebrates both the 170th year since the brand’s founding and its founder, James A. Miller. The 6 year old bourbon features Miller’s name on the label, a noteworthy inclusion given that his name hasn’t appeared on a Chicken Cock bottle in over 100 years (it disappeared from all branding during Prohibition). Alongside this release is the debut of a ceramic rooster decanter, Chicken Cock’s first such collectible piece, which is filled with 8 year old Kentucky bourbon—some of the first bourbon the brand laid down in Bardstown through contract distillation with Bardstown Bourbon Co. Only 1,200 decanters were made. Both limited releases will be available at the Kentucky Bourbon Festival (running September 10th-13th in Bardstown, Kentucky), as well as online and at retailers nationwide.

Penelope Cigar Sessions Chapter 2 Blended American

ABV: 58.7%
Price: $80
Availability: Nationwide

Penelope Bourbon has teamed up with cigar maker Alec Bradley for the second release in its annual Cigar Sessions series. While last year’s inaugural edition blended bourbon, American single malt, and American light whiskey after testing 19 mashbills with cigar makers Cynn Coburn and Lee Marsh, Chapter 2 takes a step away from blending as a single-component expression: a 6 year old American whiskey made from a 69% corn, 19% rye, and 12% malt mashbill. Developed in partnership with Alec Bradley’s cigar blenders specifically to stand up to medium and full-bodied cigars, it’s bottled at a high 58.7% ABV.

Middle West Vino De Naranja Cask Finished Single Barrel Blend

ABV: 61.1%
SRP: $100
Availability: Ohio retailers and online

This expression from Middle West’s Double Cask Collection is a 50/50 blend of the distillery’s straight wheat and Dark Pumpernickel rye whiskeys. It was aged for a minimum of 5 years, spending the first four in new charred American oak before being finished for 1–2 years in casks that previously held vino de naranja orange wine. It follows in the footsteps of other Middle West finished expressions, including whiskeys finished in port, oloroso, sherry, and calvados casks.

Jeptha Creed Solera Aged Bourbon

ABV: 50%
SRP: $80
Availability: At the distillery and online

Shelbyville, Kentucky grain-to-glass producer Jeptha Creed celebrates its 10th anniversary this year. The distillery is marking the occasion with a new solera-aged bourbon that includes all nine heirloom corn varieties grown on the farm, including Bloody Butcher, Bruce’s Blue, Blue Clarage, Hopi Blue, Hickory King, Jimmy Red, Oaxacan Green, Pink Heirloom, and White Cob White. The final product has a derived mashbill of 75% heirloom corn, 20% malted rye, and 5% malted barley. It’s set to debut this weekend at the Kentucky Bourbon Festival and is expected to launch at the distillery and its online retail shop on September 17th.

Neeley Family Distillery 10 year old Papaw’s Legacy Triple Pot-Stilled Bourbon

ABV: 55%
SRP: $300
Availability: Distillery exclusive

This claims to be the world’s oldest triple pot-distilled bourbon in existence. It was released by master distiller Royce Neeley in honor of his grandfather, Earl Sizemore, or PaPaw, who guided Royce during his formative years as a distiller. The liquid was pulled from a steel blending tank that contains some of the barrels the pair distilled together before Sizemore’s passing in 2024. The whiskey debuts today at the Kentucky Bourbon Festival and at the distillery, with a 10% discount offered to any buyers who dress up like PaPaw.

WhistlePig The Boss Hog XIII: The Golden Pharaoh Egyptian Black Honey Barrel Finished Straight Rye

ABV: 51.3 - 52.8% ABV
Price: $600
Availability: Nationwide beginning September 29th

Vermont-based WhistlePig is looking to ancient Egypt for the 13th edition of its Boss Hog series. This year’s single barrel iteration is a straight rye finished in casks seasoned with Egyptian black honey (sugarcane molasses) and tiger nuts, root tubers with an almond and coconut-like flavor, inspired by a tiger nut cake recipe found on an ancient tomb. It also features a King Tut-inspired topper, with a select number of bottles decorated with a rare gold version. The release continues the series’ penchant for experimental finishes, following 2025’s Mexican chocolate, chile, and pulque-seasoned casks and 2024’s Indian thandai-seasoned casks.
stranahans-first-bottled-in-bond-america:
A quick look at the American whiskey landscape and you’d be hard-pressed to find many bottled in bond releases that stretch past the double-digit mark in the craft whiskey world. The majority of the older bonded whiskeys hail from well-established distilleries; think Heaven Hill, which has produced countless ultra-aged Old Fitzgerald bottled in bond bourbons in its day, not to mention a 10 year old Henry McKenna and 11 and 13 year old William Heavenhills, among others. Also, somewhat unusual are bottled in bond whiskeys that aren’t bourbons—the Old Overholt and Rittenhouse bonded ryes are ubiquitous, yes, and George Dickel has a number of age-stated bottled in bond Tennessee whiskeys, but the style is by and large dominated by bourbon. Denver, Colorado-based distillery Stranahan’s has now gone against the grain on both counts with the debut of its first-ever bottled in bond whiskey, an 11 year old American single malt.

This isn’t the first bottled in bond American single malt; others include Portland, Oregon’s Westward 7 year old, Baltimore-based Old Line Spirits 5 years old, and one from Town Branch, which lays claim to being the oldest-ever released at 15 years old. But as one of the country’s most prolific American single malt makers, Stranahan’s take on the style carries its own kind of weight.

For starters, this is the oldest unfinished whiskey from Stranahan’s hitherto—it’s bookended by 10 and 12 year old Mountain Angel single malts, the latter of which is finished in port casks (the 10 year old spends the entirety of its maturation in new charred oak, just like the bottled in bond). While Stranahan's got its start back in 2004, it hadn't before released a bottled in bond whiskey by virtue of its penchant for blending (bonded whiskeys are made in a single distilling season). In making the whiskey, master blender Justin Aden turned to barrels distilled in the spring of 2015. He tasted about 212 of them; of those, he selected just 35 barrels for the final blend, with many coming from either January or June. “There’s this soft round note that comes through really well in the finished blend, and a sort of caramel texture and flavor that all came out of January,” he explains. “And alongside that, there’s this mustiness—I say that with love—that I found in the June barrels; it evoked a lot of notes from childhood, like dusty camping gear and a cottage coat closet. The harmony of those two things just seemed to hit the right, very American note for this occasion.”

The “occasion” he speaks of is two-pronged, referencing both the country’s 250th anniversary and Colorado’s own 150th anniversary of statehood, celebrated on August 1st (the same day the whiskey made its debut). Aden’s notes—well-worn camping gear, cottage closet—are certainly present in the whiskey and evocative of Americana in their own way, but there are more broadly American flavors to latch onto as well, including apple pie, vanilla soft serve, and a touch of root beer sweetness. The palate is silky, with mouth-coating wood spice joined by swirls of caramel syrup, baked apple, butterscotch, a little chocolate truffle, and a crack of black pepper. A lengthy finish, where more silken spice meets chocolate and baked stone fruit, makes for a deeply enjoyable sipping experience.  

While there are no concrete plans for additional bottled in bond whiskeys at this time, Aden isn’t without ideas. “What’s so fun about bottled in bond is you have the opportunity to create a series from two different perspectives; we could either do an 11 year old next year using 2016 barrels, or we could follow these 2015 barrels as they became 12, 13, 14 year old, and so on,” he says. With any luck, such future bottlings will come to fruition, as the new whiskey is a bit scarce outside of Colorado—you’ll have the best luck finding a bottle ($150) at either the distillery in Denver or the Stranahan’s Aspen Whiskey Lodge, though retailers in Florida, Texas, and California have also received distribution. In the meantime, Aden teases that there will be other exciting releases coming down the pike later this year, including the distillery’s oldest single malt yet.
whisky-lovers-travel-guide-to-british-co:
From a distance, Victoria, BC has all the hallmarks of a sleepy government town, from its quaint, cozy bistros and boutiques to its easily strollable downtown and the eye-catching turquoise domes of the 19th-century Parliament buildings. But up close, this scenic provincial capital offers more for lovers of quality beers and spirits than meets the eye.

A visit to Victoria should begin at the city’s original brewpub, Spinnakers, perched spectacularly above Lime Bay and only a short drive or 25-minute waterside walk from downtown’s Harbour Airport. Known locally as “Spins,” Spinnakers was born as a British-style pub and brewery, but since its founding in 1984 it has expanded to include a restaurant, guest suites, a bottle shop, and most recently, a distillery.

Although many of Spinnakers’ spirits are produced from 100% malted barley, just like its Mitchell’s Extra Special Bitter and Nut Brown ales, you won’t find any single malt whisky in its cellar. Instead, there is the bright and pleasantly phenolic Knot single malt spirit, aged 18 months in the brewery’s charred stout casks, hence not old enough to be called whisky, as well as Chocoholic crème de cacao, a complex, not-too-sweet chocolate liqueur made from the same malt spirit that’s been macerated with spent cacao husks from a local chocolatier before being sweetened and proofed to 25% ABV.

A short walk from Spinnakers is Driftwood Brewery and Distillery, home to the unapologetically old school Fat Tug IPA. Fat Tug is ubiquitous in Victoria—and throughout southern British Columbia, for that matter— so it’s best to focus on the brewery’s ever-evolving slate of seasonal and limited releases, as well as the distillery’s pair of gins and unique Oyster Spirit, a creamy, briny clear liquor infused with whole oysters.

Crossing the harbor on the Johnson Street Bridge, you come to the city’s finest beer bar, the comfortably rustic Drake Eatery, where spirits take a back seat to 29 rotating taps of British Columbia beer, and the menu is so local that it lists the names of many of the ingredient growers and suppliers. This is your opportunity to sample the wares of British Columbia’s finest and sometimes most obscure breweries, such as Burnaby-based Dageraad and Howe Sound of Squamish.

Almost directly opposite Drake is Fan Tan Alley. Narrow, uneven, and very photogenic, its northern end leads to Fisgard Street and Canada’s oldest Chinatown. Continue across Fisgard to the atmospheric Dragon Alley. From there, it is just a quick two blocks further on Government Street to arrive at Phillips Brewing and Malting.

Another of Victoria’s breweries that branched into distilling, 25 year old Phillips Brewing added a distillery in 2014 and its own malting plant a year later, making it one of the very few brewery-distillery-maltings in North America, and perhaps the only one in a city center. A partnership with local sandwich legend Roast has elevated the taproom menu and aesthetic, while the addition of distiller-blender Kevin Titcomb has helped improve the distillery’s Sanctuary Signature Edition single malt—a light but lively and complex blend of 5 to 9 year old whiskies aged in whisky, wine, and beer casks.

A few blocks around the Upper Harbour, in Victoria’s more industrial district, is the Brass Monkey Taproom, formerly Moon Under Water. Visitors can sample the full assortment of Brass Monkey beers and Moon spirits, but the diverse range of Antifogmatic Bliss whiskies, whether corn, rye, malted barley, or wheat, is not to be missed.

A visit to Macaloney’s Island Distillery does require a taxi or rideshare, but as one of Canada’s finest whisky producers, it’s well worth the journey. Scottish ex-pat founder Graeme Macaloney is the master distiller, and his devotion to single pot still and single malt whisky is unwavering. Of particular note is the Peat Project range, featuring malts smoked on-premise with Pacific Northwest peat.

No trip to Victoria is complete without a visit to Clive’s Classic Lounge and Strath Liquor Merchants, respectively the city’s finest whisky bar and shop, conveniently located around the corner from one another. Add a meal at the nearby, very BC whisky-friendly Courtney Room, and your journey to western Canada’s whisky paradise will be complete.

Hit the Road, Whisky Lover

Outside of Victoria proper, the 150 coastal miles between the city and Campbell River to the north offer a quartet of creative, innovative, and impressive whisky distilleries, beginning with Shelter Point at the northernmost end.

Shelter Point is a true farm-to-bottle operation, growing the majority of the barley it uses. Its flagship 7 year old Classic single malt can rival many of Scotland’s youthful coastal- influenced whiskies, but visitors would be advised to explore the distillery’s more limited releases, like the fruity marzipan-and marmalade-accented 12 year old and the alligator- char oak-aged Ripple Rock single malts.

Just a half-hour south in Courtney is Wayward Distillery, which claims to have been the first distillery in Canada to produce spirits from honey, and donates 1% of its sales to Pollinator Partnership Canada in appreciation of the bees. Its flagship is the floral, buttery Drunken Hive rum, but equally noteworthy is the distillery’s newer whisky program that includes the bourbon-style Unruly Suburban, with sweet and fruity charred oak aromas and a full body that seems more akin to Tennessee whiskey than bourbon.

An hour south of Wayward, in Nanaimo, is Arbutus Distillery & Cocktail Lounge, where single malt whisky shares the stage with a 100% Canadian rye and a blend of separately distilled and aged barley, wheat, and rye whiskies aptly called Canadian 3-Grain. For aficionados of lighter Lowland malts, its Canadian single malt will check several boxes, while the rye sits halfway between the relatively soft Canadian approach and the punchier American straight version. It’s with the 3-Grain, however, that the distillery has really hit its stride, with an attractive citrus-spice nose and medium-bodied orange toffee palate.

An overnight stop in Nanaimo makes for a fine respite from a day of driving and tasting, and provides the opportunity to sample several versions of that famous Canadian sweet, the Nanaimo bar. This is a three-layer square with a base of graham cracker, coconut, and cocoa, a middle layer of custard cream, and a top layer of chocolate ganache, and is almost as popular as the butter tart. Consider the Coast Bastion Hotel as a base, convenient to the city’s Art Gallery and Nanaimo Museum, with higher floors providing stellar views.

The final southward stop is Stillhead Distillery in Duncan, about 45 minutes from Nanaimo. Not quite a decade old, Stillhead has made a name for itself with intriguing cask finishes, like its limited spring release Garry Oak single grain rye, aged 3 1/2 years in charred oak before being finished in once-used barrels crafted from Quercus garryana, the Garry oak, which imbues the whisky with a deep color, clove aroma, and vaguely rum-like character, minus the sweetness. Not to be missed is the distillery’s flagship Islay Cask single grain rye, with a smoked herb aroma and rich flavors of salt, spice, plum, and smoke.

IF YOU GO

Flights to Victoria typically connect through Vancouver, except for Alaska Airlines, which flies direct from Seattle, and numerous Canadian airlines that fly direct from major Canadian hubs. Harbour Air offers frequent downtown-to-downtown service from Vancouver.

Ferries operate from Seattle and Port Angeles, Washington, as well as from Tsawwassen, BC, about 45 minutes from the U.S. border. If walking rather than driving onto the ferry, passengers can take a BC Transit bus or taxi into the city, or rent a car at the terminal.

Driving is unnecessary in central Victoria, as the compact downtown is easy to traverse on foot. In inclement weather or for longer distances, public transit, electric taxis, bike rentals, and rideshares are all options.

Suggested hotels include the historic Fairmont Empress, the luxurious Magnolia and Grand Pacific, more budget-friendly Strathcona—home to the Strath—and cottagey Spinnakers.

In addition to distilleries, the city is home to a large number of highly accomplished breweries, including Hoyne, Île Sauvage, Whistle Buoy, and Herald Street, and is considered a whale-watching paradise, with numerous companies offering tours. For the horticulturally inclined, the world-famous 55-acre Butchart Gardens is a must. With its impressive scenery and attractions, Victoria appeals to every visitor, whisky lovers included.
summer-whiskey-cocktails-recipes:
There’s a 19th-century colloquialism about whisky, likening it to “liquid sunshine.” If whisky captures sunshine in the glass, summer supplies everything else. The season is rich with ripe fruit and garden-fresh produce that naturally complement whisky's spectrum of flavors, making it one of the most versatile spirits for warm-weather cocktails. Here, we’ve selected whisky cocktails that put the spotlight on these standout summer ingredients.


Corn Fed Cowboy 

This cocktail is based on the Elote Old Fashioned, a twist on the classic in which the typical sugar cube is replaced with corn liqueur, and pays homage to the sweet and savory flavors of Mexican street corn. Julianna Parsons, beverage director at Alcove Social in Alpine, Texas reaches for more corn flavor in a butter-fat-washed Balcones Baby Blue corn whiskey. The 46% ABV foundation, chosen for its “highly flavorful profile of tropical fruits, creamy vanilla, and toasted nuts with a thick oily mouthfeel,” has enough heft to stand up well to the corn liqueur, spicy simple syrup, and lime bitters.

  • 1 ½  oz. fat-washed Balcones Baby Blue (or other corn whiskey)
  • 1/2 oz. Nixta corn liqueur
  • 1/2 oz. spicy simple syrup (1:1:3 Tajin, demerara, water)  
  • 4-5 dashes Fee Brothers lime bitters
  • Baby corn and lime wheel for garnish

Fat-wash your whisky using this method. Pour ingredients into a mixing glass. Add ice. Stir until chilled. Pour into a rocks glass over a large ice cube. Garnish with lime wheel and baby corn rolled in Tajin, if desired.

Leaves of Grass

Served at Manhatta in New York City, this citrus-forward cocktail gets its name from a collection of Walt Whitman poems. “This drink evokes his celebration of nature, individuality, and interconnection of all things. It mirrors that ethos, highlighting freshness, complexity, and the poetry of flavors.” Added depth comes from shiso simple syrup and its subtle coconut sweetness, making it perfectly refreshing on a summer day,” notes bar manager Cameron Johnson. 

Yuzu ponzu—an umami-packed combination of soy sauce, rice vinegar, and yuzu—is easier to find than you’d think, as it's usually in the international section of grocery stores. Think of it as a brighter, citrusy version of soy sauce.

  • 2 oz. Toki (or other Japanese blend) 
  • ¼ oz. Faccia Brutto Centerbe (or chartreuse or génépy) 
  • ¾ oz. Shiso syrup (recipe below)
  • 4-5 dashes Shiso bitters (or celery bitters)
  • ¼ oz. Yuzu Ponzu
  • Lime wheel for garnish

Add all ingredients and ice to a shaker; shake well. Strain into a coupe and serve. Garnish with lime wheel, if desired. 

**The glass rim pictured is pickled plum powder; it can be replaced by a lime wheel 

Shiso Syrup

Bring ½ cup water and ½ cup sugar to a boil in a pot over medium heat. Remove from heat and add 1 cup tightly packed red or green shiso leaves (about 10-15 leaves). Cover and infuse 30 minutes to 4 hours. Strain into a clean container and store in an airtight container for up to 2 weeks. 


The Orchard Aviator 

Lead bartender Juya Ebrahami at Tampa’s Oak & Ola created this summery peach riff on a classic Paper Plane, dedicated to the culinary and seasonal-forward thinking culinary icon Ina Garten, better known as the Barefoot Contessa. French peach liqueur is married with bittersweet orange notes from Aperol and Amaro Nonino, resting on an Angel's Envy canvas, accentuating the fruit-forward cocktail with its signature port finish. Don’t skip on the garnish, it’s an enviable treat floating atop the glass. 

  • ¾ oz. Angel’s Envy (or other port-finished bourbon) 
  • ¾ oz. Aperol
  • ⅜ oz. Amaro Nonino
  • ⅜ oz. Giffard Pêche de Vigne
  • ¾ oz. lemon juice
  • Brûléed peach garnish (see below)

Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice, pour into the prepared coupe. Garnish with a toothpick of 2 brûléed peach pieces. 

Brûléed peach garnish

  • 2 Tbsp. sugar
  • ½ peach (pit removed)
  • 1 Tbsp. freeze-dried pulverized strawberries

Sprinkle the peach half with 1 tablespoon of sugar and broil in the oven until caramelized, 1-2 minutes. Cut into 4 pieces (eat the leftover brûléed peach as a snack, or keep in the fridge tightly wrapped, for up to 2 days).

Combine remaining 1 tablespoon each of sugar and freeze-dried strawberries in a small bowl, and spread on a plate. Rim a coupe with mixture.


Key Lime Sour 

Created by Brian Bolter, owner and beverage director of Maryland’s Dry 85, this Key Lime Sour taps into the classic summer dessert, Key Lime pie, with a layered recipe of graham-cracker-infused bourbon, lime juice, and an unexpected addition of black walnut bitters. He opts for budget-friendly Evan Williams Black as the vanilla, caramel, and brown sugar-forward canvas for the toasty wheat graham infusion. The infusion gets brightened and balanced by the key lime’s sweet acidity, creating a “rich, nostalgic sweetness and creamy texture to feel indulgent without weighing you down in the heat,” Bolter says. 

  • 2 oz. Graham cracker-infused Evan Williams (recipe below)
  • ¾ oz. key lime juice
  • ¾ oz. simple syrup 
  • ½ oz. egg white 
  • 1 dash black walnut bitters 
  • Graham cracker crumbs and lime wheel for garnish (optional) 

Vigorously shake all ingredients in a shaker. Strain into a coupe. Garnish with graham cracker crumbles and dehydrated lime wheel.

Graham Cracker-infused bourbon

  • 375 ml Evan Williams, or other bourbon.
  • ¾ cup graham cracker crumbs 

Add graham cracker crumbs and bourbon in a large bowl. Stir well. Infuse for 2 hours, agitating the mixture at least twice. Double-fine strain into a large sealable container. Store for up to 1 month at room temperature.
new-zealand-whisky-distilleries:
New Zealand, the ruggedly beautiful, isolated nation of around 600 islands, is best known for beer and wine (and “Lord of the Rings”), but it’s also home to a growing single malt whisky scene. Since the start of the millennium, the country has gone from zero single malt distilleries to 20 and counting. The total barrelage is still tiny, and only a few distillers are exporting, but the Kiwis are putting their own stamp on single malt.

Given New Zealand’s Scottish roots, you might think the country’s whiskies are the southern hemisphere’s answer to scotch, but a variety of climactic factors combine to create whiskies with their own terroir and national character.

“We have a fantastic climate and fertile soils for barley here,” says Sarah Elsom, head distiller at Cardrona Distillery. “We’re predominantly all working with barley. There’s a little play with rye and wheat by some, but it’s at an experimental level. Barley grows exceptionally well in the Canterbury plains of [South Island], so much so that it’s often a site used by the UK in their off-season for seed development trials.”

The barley of choice for New Zealand’s distillers is the laureate varietal, which is also used in scotch. But the grain expresses itself far differently in New Zealand. “Laureate grown in New Zealand is much sweeter than the laureate that’s grown in Scotland, and that’s because of the growing conditions,” says Pōkeno Whisky founder Matt Johns. “If you’re starting with a sweeter barley, that’s going to positively affect your spirit. For ours, it definitely means a fruitier spirit.” This idea is echoed by The New Zealand Whisky Collection general manager and head distiller Michael Byars, who notes that while all New Zealand whisky makers are creating unique single malts, laureate barley is what binds them together. “We’re all slightly different, but there’s one category that’s all the way through in every single malt distillery: our grain,” says Byars. He cites an overwhelming creaminess and oiliness that’s present within many of New Zealand’s single malts, and attributes it directly to the barley.

In letting the laureate barley shine, many New Zealand distillers also employ longer fermentations and slow distillations, in what Elsom calls an “unhurried approach.” At Cardrona, fermentation was around 115 hours, though these days it skews closer to the more standard 72. “We have quite a fruit-driven flavor profile, and the way that we ferment and distill our barley very much encourages those fruit-forward esters,” she notes. At Pōkeno, the mash is fermented for around 90 hours, and Johns keeps the spirits run to around 9 hours. Similarly, The New Zealand Whisky Collection’s, Byars pushes fermentation over a week long and runs distillation by smell and taste, not by numbers. “I want to extract as much character from the grain and new make as possible, and the resulting spirit is creamy and rich and full of grain character,” he explains.

North vs. South

While these production similarities exist from distillery to distillery, you won’t find a signature style of New Zealand whisky— at least not yet. That’s due in part to the country’s dramatic differences in climate. It’s about a thousand miles from the southernmost tip of South Island to the northern reaches of North Island, a distance that takes nearly 30 hours to traverse by car and around 4 hours by plane. This translates to subtropical conditions on North Island, and a cooler, more temperate climate on South Island.

“We have a more rapid maturation on North Island, with an angels’ share of 9.5% per year,” explains Pōkeno’s Johns. “If you go to a distillery like Cardrona on South Island, they’ll be sitting at a 3.5% angels’ share. We’ll never get to the age statements that the South Island distilleries will, but that’s great because it illustrates this regionality all around New Zealand.” The warm, humid temps around Auckland mean more tropical fruit in Pōkeno, especially in its younger whiskies; conversely, Elsom points to Cardrona’s more delicate honeyed and floral notes, brought about by higher altitude and temperature swings.

Distinctly Kiwi

The other key factor driving the diversity of New Zealand single malts is something the Kiwis call the “number-8 wire.” While it’s a type of wire used in agricultural fencing, it became a catchword for a ‘can-do’ national mindset of inventiveness, creativity, and resourcefulness as they adapted the wire for uses far beyond its original purpose. “New Zealand is a long way from everywhere else, so we have to be creative and innovative,” says Johns. “That’s what the number-8 wire approach is about. The Kiwis have always batted above their weight [because of it].”

So, if number-8 wire calls for thinking outside the box, New Zealand’s distillers have done that in spades. Take Pōkeno—a hunt for barrels made from native New Zealand wood led the distillery to establish its very own cooperage—the only one in the country—enabling it not only to make barrels from local totara and kauri trees, but to also build a coopering business that supplies other distilleries, wineries, furniture makers, and even film sets. At The New Zealand Whisky Collection, Byars opted not to import sherry barrels from Spain, and instead took New Zealand pinot noir casks and oxidized them himself to create the sherry character he wanted.

For others, following the number-8 wire mentality has meant incorporating more of New Zealand’s natural resources into the whisky-making process. Native manuka wood—famous for its potent antibacterial honey—is used by Pōkeno, Scapegrace, and others to smoke malt. “Manuka-smoked malt gives the distillate this smoky, sweet, savory flavor that’s distinctively New Zealand in nature; it’s an aroma you’d smell if you were camping out here,” says Scapegrace co-founder Mark Neal. The manuka-smoked malt has so far appeared in Anthem, one of Scapegrace’s inaugural single malts, and Neal expects it to play a role in future releases as well. A handful of distillers, Thomson and Waiheke among them, are making smoky whiskies with locally sourced New Zealand peat, but those releases have yet to reach the American market.

Given New Zealand’s robust wine industry, it’s no surprise that distillers have turned to local winemakers for barrels too. Both Byars and Elsom came into distilling from wine backgrounds and have built connections with local wineries for casks. Thus far, Elsom has used port, pinot noir, sauternes, and chardonnay casks for Cardrona’s single malts, emphasizing first-fill maturation rather than finishing. The New Zealand Whisky Collection has gone in a more traditional direction, using New Zealand pinot noir, merlot, syrah, and others for cask finishing, not entire maturation periods.

Small But Dynamic

For U.S. whisky drinkers, one of the biggest issues with New Zealand whisky is its limited availability. Few Kiwi distilleries have direct routes to the market. The New Zealand Whisky Collection has entered and exited the American market multiple times, and has been absent here since COVID. Põkeno, imported by ImpEx Beverages since 2022, is among the most available, and ImpEx founder Sam Filmus makes a point to get not only the distillery’s flagships in American stores, but its limited releases as well. Scapegrace is now distributed in a handful of states (it’s handled by Sazerac’s 375 Park Avenue distribution arm), and Cardrona was purchased by International Beverage in 2023, giving it a firm foothold on the global stage. But with such small production out of those three, there’s not a lot of New Zealand whisky to go around.

As they steadily build their stocks and consider routes to export markets, New Zealand whisky makers have time to consider the trajectory of their single malts. Cardrona’s oldest whisky turned 10 last year, a milestone for the distillery. “We’re seeing these rolling waves of character that are just developing, and I think we’ll have to be open to allowing what we believe is the signature profile to evolve, and play with it and work with it in a way that’s not moving away from what we’ve celebrated so far,” Elsom muses. At Pōkeno, Johns is of a similar mindset. “The jury is still out for us—is age a friend or an enemy for the quality of our spirit? We don’t really know yet, but we’re finding out.” In an industry so young, the sky’s the limit.

Temperance Legacy

Whisky making came to New Zealand in the 1830s with the arrival of Scottish settlers. But high taxes and other major obstacles, including a ban on stills, effectively drove the industry underground or wiped it out in some places altogether, and late in the century a strong temperance movement took hold. By the 20th century, New Zealanders were mostly drinking imported whiskies. Gradually, local production restraints began to loosen, but by then the country had just one distiller of consequence: Willowbank, producer of the Wilson’s brand. It was acquired by global drinks giant Seagram in 1981 and sold to Australian brewer Foster’s Ltd. in 1997, which promptly shut it down. Foster’s eventually sold its remaining casks to The New Zealand Whisky Collection in the early 2000s—right around the time when the country’s smaller independent distillers were starting up, as was happening in other countries around the world.

New Zealand’s single malt production began to take off in 2009, when home distiller Matthew Thomson (yes, home distilling is legal there) co-founded Thomson Whisky, initially as an independent bottler sourcing stocks from Willowbank. A year later, The New Zealand Whisky Collection, another independent bottler, launched. They began bottling and exporting in limited quantities. By 2014, Thomson had opened his own distillery just north of Auckland, and down on the South Island, gin maker Scapegrace began producing small amounts of its own single malt. A year later, the distilling resurgence continued with Cardrona, South Island’s first single malt distillery with export aspirations.

More distilleries followed, very gradually. Pōkeno Whisky joined Thomson Whisky on the North Island in 2019, becoming the largest single malt distillery in the country with production capacity of 66,000 gallons (for comparison, Buffalo Trace’s annual production capacity is estimated at 2.65 million gallons). By 2021, The New Zealand Whisky Collection established Dunedin Distillery in leased space within Speight’s Brewery in Dunedin and started distilling its own single malt on South Island, while Scapegrace opened a state-of-the-art facility in 2024, capable of producing 160,000 cases of single malt each year. Finally, Waiheke Whisky set up shop east of Auckland on Waiheke Island in 2024, rounding out the modern class of more substantial New Zealand whisky distillers.
