Spas-For-Whisky-Lovers:
We can all think of various ways to enjoy whiskey, but the idea of mixing it into a body scrub isn’t one that usually springs to mind. Yet applied to the skin, whiskey in this form can be surprisingly beneficial. According to McKenna Lamons, spa concierge at Ama Spa at the Edwin Hotel in Chattanooga, Tennessee, “Whiskey is filled with phenolic compounds like ellagic acid, which are believed to have potent antioxidant effects to cleanse the body.”

Several spas around the country feature whiskey-infused scrubs on their treatment menus, while others offer whiskey to sip while you unwind. A few even tout both experiences.

For some retreats, whiskey is a natural fit because of the location. Ama Spa features locally made Chattanooga whiskey in its body scrub. “Whiskey is Tennessee’s signature spirit, so using Chattanooga whiskey connects guests to the local products and stories we want to highlight,” says Merrily Bell, general manager of the Edwin Hotel.

It’s a similar story for spas in Kentucky. “We’re located in central Kentucky, right in the heart of bourbon country, and we love bringing that local heritage into our services to help enhance the senses,” says Kenna Trent, spa manager at The Kentucky Castle in Versailles.

In Louisville, the appropriately named Bourbon & Blush Salon and Spa offers several bourbon-infused treatments and even collaborates with local distilleries for tastings. “In Kentucky, bourbon is more than a spirit—it’s a tradition. Bourbon & Blush was created to celebrate that heritage while pairing it with something equally meaningful: self-care,” says owner Melissa Jacobi. “Incorporating bourbon elements allows us to offer guests an experience that feels uniquely Kentucky while still being refined and spa-forward.”

Jacobi adds that whiskey and spas are more aligned than you might think. “We love that bourbon and self-care share the same philosophy: slowing down, savoring the moment, and enjoying something crafted with intention,” she says. “The time and artistry that goes into bourbon mirrors the care behind luxury self-care treatments.”

Whether touting a bourbon-infused full-body scrub or offering guests a pour of whiskey—or both—the sanctuaries on this list are sure to entice the wellness-minded whiskey fan. A couple of the spas compiled here are even on the same grounds as distilleries, making the whiskey connection that much stronger.

ÁHSI’ DAY SPA AT TURNING STONE RESORT & CASINO

Verona, New York

There’s a wide range of massages and skin treatments on this spa’s menu, but the whiskey enthusiast will be most interested in the body treatments, one of which includes a guest-favorite bourbon scrub, comprising Kentucky bourbon, brown sugar, rice bran oil, and vitamin E that leaves skin exfoliated and soft. From Monday through Thursday, a 50-minute scrubbing session is $130 and an 80-minute session is $180; from Friday through Sunday, it’s $140 and $200, respectively. To keep the whiskey experience going, both TS Steakhouse and Wildflowers restaurants at Turning Stone offer exceptional whiskey menus as well as Wine Spectator- awarded wine lists. 

AMA SPA AT THE EDWIN HOTEL

Chattanooga

This retreat offers a Whiskey & Wellness treatment ($275 for 120 minutes) that aims to improve circulation, calm muscle tension, and revive dull skin with its Bourbon Bubbler sugar scrub infused with locally made bourbon from Chattanooga Whiskey. After the scrubbing, a warming body wrap is applied, followed by a full-body custom pressure massage. Once you’re sufficiently relaxed, head to the hotel’s rooftop Whiskey Thief bar for seasonal small bites and a high-end cocktail or a dram or two from a selection of more than 150 labels.

BOURBON & BLUSH SALON AND SPA

Louisville

This bourbon country spa is an ideal stop after a long day of distillery tours. The Bluegrass Bourbon body scrub ($145 for 50 minutes) is a full-body exfoliating treatment that will leave skin smooth, refreshed, and glowing. The service begins with gentle dry brushing to stimulate circulation and lymphatic drainage, then exfoliation with a locally made bourbon-infused sugar scrub, followed by a eucalyptus steam shower, and finished with an ultra-rich body butter application. Another option is the Bluegrass Bourbon pedicure ($80), which includes a mineral sea salt soak, hot towel compressions, bourbon scrub treatment, and a lower leg and foot massage. In addition to spa and salon treatments, this spot offers customized bourbon tastings, curated pairing events, and treatment collaborations with local bourbon brands. 

THE EDGE SPA AT THE LODGE AT BLUE SKY

Wanship, Utah

On the grounds of this sprawling, 4,000-acre mountain resort just outside Park City, you’ll find a cliffside wellness sanctuary as well as High West Distillery. At the spa, the High West Whiskey Rubdown ($504 for 90 minutes) begins with a whiskey, salt, and sage foot soak while you sip a High West whiskey, followed by a massage that includes warm towel compressions to loosen muscles, proprietary hydrating body butter, and scalp invigorator. Or you can opt for the Whiskey on the Rocks experience ($780 for up to 2 guests; $420 per additional guest), which starts with a cold plunge—assisted by a certified breathwork coach—and a visit to the outdoor sauna, after which you’ll be joined by a High West whiskey ambassador for a private tasting. To complement your whiskey-fueled wellness journey, stop by the distillery for a tour, then enjoy a meal and craft whiskey cocktail at the distillery’s restaurant, The Refectory. 

FOUR SEASONS NEW ORLEANS

New Orleans

Situated on the Mississippi River, this Four Seasons is home to a spa that blends self-care and the rich cocktail culture of New Orleans with its signature offering, The Southern Gentleman ($365 for 80 minutes, $500 for 110 minutes). This treatment includes a deep therapeutic massage focusing on the neck, shoulders, and back to release tension and restore ease, plus a foot exfoliation and massage using targeted pressure-point techniques that incorporate a locally sourced cypress-scented oil. To complement the experience, guests are offered a date-infused Old Fashioned.

THE KENTUCKY CASTLE

Versailles

Another bourbon country spot, this hotel is owned by Angel’s Envy co-founder Wes Henderson and serves as the current home away from home for his new whiskey brand, True Story, while its distillery is being built next door. The hotel serves True Story bourbon and rye at its bar, and also hosts tastings and pairing events. This connection to whiskey extends to the hotel’s spa as well. The Warm Bourbon and Honey Body Drench ($205 for 90 minutes) is a relaxing, refreshing massage experience featuring a warm, soothing bourbon-and-honey-scented oil. The spa also offers a full-body bourbon-and-honey-scented scrub followed by a body butter application ($145 for 60 minutes). The scrub can also be purchased in the spa’s retail shop to take home.

SPA TERRA AT THE MERITAGE RESORT AND SPA

Napa Valley

This 22,000 square-foot wine country spa is located within a centuries-old estate cave. Appropriately, it offers plenty of wine-related treatments, but there’s also something for the whiskey fan to enjoy. The Bourbon Bubbler body treatment features a vanilla bourbon scrub that relieves tension in the feet, neck, and shoulders; controls excess oils; and calms the skin. From Monday through Thursday this 50-minute treatment is $245; from Friday through Sunday it’s $270.

SEAHILL SPA AT THE CAVALIER HOTEL

Virginia Beach 

This historic oceanfront hotel conveniently houses both a spa and Tarnished Truth Distillery, specializing in small-batch bourbon, among other spirits. At the spa, a full-body treatment with a Tarnished Truth bourbon-infused scrub, followed by a warm detoxifying mineral soak and a moisturizing lotion application can be enjoyed while relaxing on a heated quartz table ($200 for 50 minutes), as part of a multi-sensory hydro capsule treatment ($180 for 50 minutes), or as part of a couples service ($380 for 50 minutes). After your treatment, you can enjoy a tour and tasting at Tarnished Truth, then visit the adjacent Hunt Room tavern for a cocktail or bourbon flight. 

THE UNDERGROUND SPA AT THE LOGAN HOTEL

Philadelphia

At this retreat, you’ll be offered a complimentary glass of bourbon (or wine, prosecco, or non-alcoholic beverage) with every treatment. The bourbon selection rotates. For men, the Beard & Bourbon Experience ($420 for 100 minutes) aims to renew skin tone and texture while soothing and restoring devitalized, sun-damaged, or razor-burned skin. The treatment includes a 50-minute Nirvana stress relief massage and a 50-minute hot towel facial with special attention to beard care—or, for men who don’t have a beard, extra attention to the skin. Afterward, enjoy your glass of bourbon in the Relaxation Room. This package also gives you a 20% discount on beard products available in the spa shop. In addition, any guest can add a 25-minute full-body bourbon-bubbler scrub treatment to any service for $125.
four-roses-bakers-13-ardbeg-trudernish-a:
The art of the blend is on full display this week, as several distillers have chimed in with new and innovative whiskies that combine different mashbills. Four Roses is back with a Limited Edition Small Batch that blends four ultra-aged bourbons; Chattanooga married two bourbon recipes to replicate the flavors of s’mores; Remus has a new Repeal Reserve batch that mixes three bourbon mashbills (alongside the label’s first rye); Shortbarrel blended four bourbons for its latest Cigar Batch; and Town Branch experimented with blending pot-still and column-still distillates. Elsewhere, Baker’s 13 year old Single Barrel has returned, Basil Hayden tries its hand at cognac cask finishing, Virginia Distillery Co. continues its work with craft beer casks, and Joseph Magnus has a new 10 year old rye. Looking to scotch, Ardbeg welcomes a new core-range 15 year old, Glendronach has a 14 year old that commemorates its 200th anniversary, and Dalmore has a trio of ultra-aged malts finished in madeira casks.

Four Roses Limited Edition Small Batch Bourbon (2026 Release)

ABV: 54.6%
SRP: $249
Availability: Nationwide, starting next month

Next month, Four Roses is set to release the 19th edition of its annual Limited Edition Small Batch expression. This year’s iteration has four blending components, each of which pull from one of the distillery’s 10 distinct bourbon recipes that encompass five yeast strains and two mashbills. The ingredients are as follows:

  • 14 year old OBSK (60% corn, 35% rye, 5% malted barley; slightly spicy “K” yeast)
  • 14 year old OESK  (75% corn, 20% rye, 5% malted barley; slightly spicy “K” yeast)
  • 15 year old OESV  (60% corn, 35% rye, 5% malted barley; delicate fruits “V” yeast)
  • 23 year old OESK  (75% corn, 20% rye, 5% malted barley; slightly spicy “K” yeast)

The total batch accounts for around 16,800 bottles, available at retailers nationwide and at the distillery’s Lawrenceburg visitor center starting October 10th. 

Baker’s 13 year old Single Barrel Bourbon (2026 Release)

ABV: 53.5%
SRP: $150
Availability: Limited

Baker Beam, the grandnephew of whiskey legend Jim Beam, celebrated his 90th birthday in July. Now the distillery is marking the occasion by re-releasing a fan-favorite expression from his namesake bourbon label. Baker’s 13 was initially released in 2019 when the brand transitioned away from a vatted model in favor of the single barrel format it currently uses. After a brief hiatus, it returned in 2023 with a notably impressive batch, and has since turned into an annual release.

Basil Hayden Cognac Cask Reserve Bourbon

ABV: $40
SRP: $50
Availability: Limited

Basil Hayden has added to its stable of finished whiskeys—which currently includes Toast, a bourbon finished in toasted barrels—Cognac Cask Reserve. The new bourbon follows the same template as other Basil Hayden bourbons, in that it retains the brand’s signature high-rye mashbill, but is then finished in French oak barrels that previously held cognac for 20 to 25 years. This is the first time that Basil Hayden has brought an international finish into the fold. Though it is a limited release, the new bourbon will be available at retailers nationwide.

Virginia Distillery Co. The Brewer’s Coalition: The Bruery Black Tuesday Stout Cask Finished American Single Malt

ABV: 50%
SRP: $55
Availability: At the distillery, online, and select retailers

Virginia Distillery Co. The Brewer’s Coalition: Revolution Brewing Straight Jacket Barleywine Ale Cask Finished American Single Malt

ABV: 50%
SRP: $60
Availability: At the distillery, online, and select retailers

Virginia Distillery Co. has added two new American single malts to its ongoing The Brewer’s Coalition series, which focuses on finishes in inventive craft beer barrels. The first newcomer spent time in casks that previously held Black Tuesday, an annual bourbon barrel-aged imperial stout from The Bruery in California. The second one was finished in barrels that previously held Straight Jacket, a barleywine from Chicago’s Revolution Brewing. Both whiskeys were initially aged for 5 years in bourbon barrels prior to finishing.

Chattanooga Bottled in Bond Bourbon (Fall 2022 Vintage)

ABV: 50%
SRP: $53
Availability: At the distillery and retailers in select states

Yesterday, Tennessee craft distiller Chattanooga Whiskey released its latest Bottled in Bond Vintages bourbon. This one blends two new mashbills that have never before been used for the series. The first one is “Barrel 54”, which uses malted spelt and huskless malted oats for flavoring grains. The second one, “Barrel 177”, uses a pair of specialty brewing malts called Melanoidin and Carafa to contribute notes of chocolate. According to distiller Grant McCracken, the marriage of mashbills gives the final product a profile that’s reminiscent of s’mores.

Remus Repeal Reserve Series X Straight Bourbon

ABV: 53.5%
Price: $80
Availability: Nationwide

MGP-owned Remus is marking the 10th anniversary of its Repeal Reserve Series, an annual blended bourbon release known for celebrating the end of Prohibition that historically pulls from rare ultra-aged stocks. Remus’s highest-proof release yet at 53.5% ABV, Series X is aged 9 to 18 years. It’s comprised of three mashbills: LBSV, MGP’s flagship high-rye bourbon (60% corn, 36% rye, 4% malted barley); LESV, a low-rye (75% corn, 21% rye, 4% malted barley); and LISV, its “highest-rye” bourbon (51% corn, 39% rye, 10% malted barley), first featured in Remus Highest Rye releases, launched in 2023. 

Remus Repeal Reserve Straight Rye

ABV: 55.5%
Price: $80
Availability: Nationwide

Also joining the Remus Repeal Reserve lineup is the label’s inaugural rye. The limited-edition straight rye draws from 2015 and 2016 reserves of MGP’s signature 95% rye, 5% malted barley mashbill—the same high-rye recipe behind whiskeys including Rossville Union Rye and Bulleit Rye, including its recently released 20 year old.

Joseph Magnus 10 Year Cask Strength Rye

ABV: 56.72%
SRP: $75
Availability: Nationwide

While Joseph Magnus has made a modern name for itself in bourbon and blends, this is the brand’s first rye since 1918. Head blender Will Fabry—who has taken over production at Jos. A. Magnus since master blender Nancy Fraley left earlier this year—focused on a 95% rye, 5% malted barley mashbill for the whiskey, calling it “a natural progression” given that the brand’s bourbon has a high-rye content.

When Joseph Magnus started his spirits business in the 1800s, rye whiskey was a staple of American whiskey. The style fell to the wayside following Prohibition, as more distilleries turned to bourbon, but Magnus' reintroduction of a rye—its first since the brand relaunched in 2015—points to rye's revival in the U.S.

Shortbarrel Cigar Batch No. 4 Blend of Bourbons

ABV: 53.5%
SRP: $90
Availability: Limited

The fourth release of Shortbarrel’s Cigar Batch incorporates more than 50 separate armagnac, cognac, rum, tawny port, and sherry casks (marking the first time the brand has used sherry within the blend). The liquid is a blend of aged whiskeys sourced from Kentucky and Indiana, made from four distinct mashbills:

  • 60% corn, 36% rye, and 4% malted barley
  • 70% corn, 21% rye, and 9% malted barley
  • 75% corn, 21% rye, and 4% malted barley
  • 91% corn and 9% malted barley

Each individual whiskey component underwent its own secondary maturation before being blended together at the Shortbarrel blending facility in Georgia. While the whiskey is designed to pair with cigars—Shortbarrel calls out Arturo Fuente Don Carlos Robusto, Padrón 1964 Anniversary Maduro Exclusivo, and Liga Privada No. 9 Toro—the blending house also notes that it took inspiration from the production process of premium cigars in making the whiskey.

Town Branch Imperium MMXXVI Kentucky Straight Bourbon

ABV: 57.55%
SRP: $120
Availability: Limited

For the third edition of its Imperium series, Town Branch has crafted a wheated bourbon blend.. The 2026 release kicks off with a column-distilled wheater base made from 70% corn, 22% wheat, and 8% malted barley (accounting for 50% of the blend) that’s blended with a column-distilled bourbon made from a mash of 72% corn, 15% rye, and 13% malted barley, and a pot-distilled bourbon of the same mashbill. A total of eight barrels were selected for the blend, ranging from 6 to 9 years old.

The whiskey is a limited release that will be available at the distillery in September in a custom flight featuring all three Imperium releases, as well as at the 2026 Kentucky Bourbon Festival in Bardstown (Friday, September 11th through Sunday, September 13th). It'll also have limited distribution at retailers across the U.S.

Ardbeg Trudernish 15 year old Islay single malt

ABV: 48.8%
SRP: $90 
Availability: Nationwide; imported by Moët Hennessy USA

Ardbeg’s core range is getting a major shake-up, led by a new peaty 15 year old. Matured in bourbon, charred new oak, and oloroso sherry casks, it is named after the ancient settlement of Trudernish on Islay’s southeast coast, where reputedly, there is a well that never freezes.

Trudernish is Ardbeg’s fourth age-stated core range expression, slotting neatly between the 10 and 25 year old. Its release heralds a complete refresh of the Ardbeg core range look, with lighter green cartons bringing the brand’s storytelling to life through woodcut-style illustrations, their canine mascot Shortie, expanded tasting notes, and cask recipes. A QR code tucked inside each carton lid also makes it easier to join the Ardbeg Committee. Islay fans have been treated to a run of major new releases recently, with Ardbeg Trudernish 15 year old following the launches of the new Laphroaig 15 year old, Bowmore 20 year old, Bruichladdich Greener Still, and Octomore Series 17 releases.

Glendronach Boynsmill House Edition Highland single malt

ABV: 46.8%
SRP: $125
Availability: Limited

In celebration of its 200th anniversary, Glendronach has released a 14 year old single malt named after founder James Allardice’s home estate. The whisky is matured in a combination of casks, including oloroso and Pedro Ximénez—both beloved by Glendronach—as well as a number of Bordeaux red wine casks, in a nod to the wine that would’ve been served at Allardice’s dinner parties. According to the distillery, the Bordeaux casks imbue the whisky with unmistakable red berry fruit and elegant complexity.

In tandem with its anniversary celebration, Glendronach has restored the Boynsmill House, turning it into an invitation-only experience for guests. Glendronach, by way of parent company Brown-Forman, has invested heavily in its public-facing sites this decade, unveiling a visitor center renovation at Glendronach back in 2020, in addition to these Boynsmill House renovations.

Dalmore Cask Curation Series: The Madeira Cask Edition Highland single malt scotch

SRP: $47,000
Availability: Limited edition global release of 150 sets

The fourth and final release in Dalmore’s Cask Curation Series is a collaboration with Blandy’s Madeira, which, for seven generations, has been creating madeira on the Portuguese island. Master whisky maker Dr. Kirstie McCallum decided to finish each Highland whisky in a different type of madeira pipe to accentuate different facets of Dalmore’s spirit.

  • Dalmore The Madeira Cask Edition 30 year old, 49.3%, was initially matured in bourbon barrels for 29 years before an 8-month finish in a 2010 Terrantez madeira pipe, an elegant and semi-dry style of madeira.
  • Dalmore The Madeira Cask Edition 34 year old, 44.5%, was finished in a 2018 Bual madeira pipe following its initial maturation in bourbon barrels. Bual is a richer and more rounded style of madeira.
  • Dalmore The Madeira Cask Edition 45 year old, 40.7%, is the oldest whisky in the entire series. After 44 years in bourbon barrels, it was finished for 3 months in a 2012 Malvasia madeira pipe, the richest and most decadent style of traditional madeira.

The annual Cask Curation Series debuted in 2023, and each release has featured a distinctive trio of rare high age statement whiskies in collaboration with Dalmore’s exclusive cask partners, including González Byass, Graham’s Port, and Château Mont-Redon. Each set is presented in colorful leather cases inspired by the golden age of travel, handcrafted in Saffiano leather in Florence by Italian luggage makers AB Florence. In April, Dalmore reopened its doors, welcoming small groups for private tours of its new luxury visitor experience.

The 20 highest hammer prices for the first eight months of 2026 topped $7 million, outperforming the same period in 2025 and 2024. The combined total for August was $644,528, up 16% compared to this month last year, led by the record-setting Macallan TIME:SPACE 84 year old hammer price of $128,487. While competition at the top was tight in July, this sale helped Macallan pull away from rivals and consolidate its lead.

American whiskeys had a strong month with nine entries, the highest number since January 2026, including three Willett bottlings, Van Winkle rarities such as Old Advocate Special Reserve 15 year old, and a gold wax A.H. Hirsch Reserve 18 year old. Five Japanese whiskies made August’s list, including three bottles of Karuizawa, a Hanyu Jack of Clubs, and a Yamazaki Junshin. Hirsch Reserve 18 year old (Est. $20,000–$30,000). Unicorn Auctions enters the fray with high-value Macallan expressions including Macallan in Lalique 55 year old, Macallan Millennium 1949 50 year old, and a Macallan Red Ribbon 1938.  With this formidable array of rarities now heading to auction, the secondary market looks set to finish 2026 on a high.

grilling-with-whisky-recipes:
Fewer things go together better than whisky and food cooked over a fire. Most grill enthusiasts know what they like to drink alongside the barbecue. Yet whisky can also add depth as an ingredient, in marinades, sauces, glazes, and desserts, if it’s used with restraint. We’ve asked the former executive chef of New York City’s Hill Country Barbecue, consultant, cookbook author, and grilling authority Elizabeth Karmel for tips on how to make whisky stand out not only next to, but on the grill. A self-described bourbon lover, Karmel shared her approach to cooking with whisky, along with recipes that showcase it in a cocktail, main dish, sauce, and a dessert. She enjoys a pour of whisky in a glass as much as in a measuring cup, appreciating its ability to lend depth and complexity.

“Cooking and baking are all about balance and restraint. Using just enough whisky to make a difference in the flavor but not so much that it slaps you in the face,” Karmel says. She recommends starting with one to two tablespoons of whisky in most recipes, adjusting only for marinades, where a greater volume adds flavor and tenderizes the meat.

Quality is paramount when drinking whisky, and it's the same when cooking with it. Provenance is important to Karmel both in sourcing seasonal ingredients and determining a spirit’s origin to go with it. While recreating a smoked salmon dip inspired by a trip to Scotland, she found American smoked salmon lacked the gentle salinity she remembered. A splash of smoky Laphroaig supplied the missing sense of place to the more rustic American-smoked salmon she was using. “It added a terroir-specific smoky element that took it from good to extraordinary.”

PICKING YOUR GRILL WHISKY

Flavor Comes First:  When developing recipes for Hill Country Barbecue Market in New York, Karmel settled on Maker’s Mark bourbon for a sweet potato mash after testing a dozen bourbons with different price points, finding it was the only one with the full-bodied, intense vanilla flavor she was after. Her advice: Cook with something that you enjoy in your glass, but no need to reach for your finest; save those for sipping. 

Go With Subtle: Karmel generally gravitates toward softer whiskies that emphasize flavor over heat. She tends to avoid heavily smoky expressions. Whatever style you choose, look for a whisky with flavors that complement the rest of the dish rather than compete with it.

Practically Speaking: Never pour whisky directly onto food over an open flame or lit grill. “The high-alcohol content can easily flare up and turn into a big flame,” Karmel warns. Glazes and sauces made with whisky are safe to use because the spirit is diluted, but apply them with a long-handled brush rather than pouring or squirting them over the food to help prevent flare-ups.

RECIPES FOR GRILLING WITH A WHISKEY TWIST  

Lemon's bright acidity gets a charred makeover in this classic summer refresher, Photo by Elizabeth Karmel

Bourbon and Grilled Lemon Arnold Palmer

The Arnold Palmer is a summertime staple, but this whiskey-spiked take starts on the grill. Charring the lemons deepens their sweetness and softens their acidity, creating a richer foundation that pairs naturally with the caramel, vanilla, and toasted nut flavors of a double oaked bourbon.

Makes 4 cocktails

  • 2 oz. 2XO American Oak straight bourbon
  • 1½ oz. grilled lemon juice (see below)
  • 3 oz. chilled sweet tea
  • Squeeze of fresh lemon
  • Grilled lemon wheel for garnish

Grilled Lemons

  • 3 to 4 large lemons, halved
  • 1 large lemon, cut into wheels, ends reserved
  • Olive oil, for brushing

Preheat grill to medium-high heat (375-450°F).

Lightly brush the lemon halves, reserved ends, and wheels with olive oil. Set aside one lemon half and cut it into wedges for finishing the cocktails.

Place the halved lemons and ends cut-side down on the grill. Cook until deeply marked, lightly charred around the edges, and warmed through, 2 to 4 minutes. Grill the lemon wheels briefly on each side until marked. Remove and cool for 10 minutes. Juice the halves. Strain the juice through a fine-mesh sieve to remove seeds and charred bits.

For each cocktail, combine the bourbon, grilled lemon juice, sweet tea, and a squeeze of fresh lemon from the reserved wedges. Stir, pour over ice into a tumbler, and garnish with a grilled lemon wheel.

, Photo by Elizabeth Karmel

Whiskey Joe Steak Marinade

This marinade was inspired by Karmel’s favorite steak rub of espresso coffee and black pepper. The spiced rye stands up to the strong coffee and cuts through the rich beefy hanger steak. “Try this preparation once, and it will become your signature preparation for any cut of beef or steak. Although I prefer using it for hanger steak, it is equally good on any cut of steak. Just remember, the more tender the cut, the less time you want to marinate before cooking,” Karmel advises.

  • 1 cup espresso or very strong brewed black coffee
  • ½ cup WhistlePig Piggyback (or other rye whiskey)
  • 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard
  • 2 Tbsp. dark brown sugar
  • 1 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce
  •  4 garlic cloves, grated
  • 1/2 cup extra-virgin olive oil
  • 2 tsp. coarsely ground black pepper
  • 1 tsp. cinnamon chips or whole cinnamon stick
  • 2 ½ tsp.Kosher salt
  • 1 1-2 lbs. preferred cut of steak

In a medium non-reactive bowl, mix together all ingredients until well blended. The marinade will keep, tightly covered, in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. 

Place steak in a zip-lock bag or shallow non-reactive dish and pour marinade over. Cover tightly. Marinate 2–3 hours refrigerated. 

Preheat the grill to medium-high heat, about (375-450°F). 

Remove steak from marinade. Discard marinade.

Place meat directly over the heat for about 4-5 minutes. Turn steak and continue cooking for about 4-5 more minutes for medium rare, depending on size. 

Remove the steak from the grill and rest for 5 minutes, but no longer than 10 minutes, before carving. 

Slice the steak against the grain and serve, preferably with the compound butter, but it's just as delicious on its own. 

NOTE: If you don’t have access to an outdoor grill, sear the steak in a hot cast-iron pan over medium-high heat and then finish cooking it in a preheated 400°F oven for about 7 minutes.

, Photo by Elizabeth Karmel

Whiskey Compound Butter

Few grilling upgrades are as effortless, or as rewarding, as whiskey compound butter. Decadent on everything from steaks and chops to seafood and vegetables, it transforms as it melts, carrying the whiskey's flavors into every bite. Karmel favors Irish whiskey, such as Kilbeggan, because of its lighter profile, which adds depth without overpowering the food.

  • 1 shallot, minced
  • 3 tsp. Kilbeggan (or other Irish whiskey)
  • 2 sticks unsalted butter, softened
  • 3 tsp. minced parsley
  • ½ tsp. Worcestershire sauce
  • ½ tsp. Dijon mustard
  • ½ tsp. sea salt
  • White pepper to taste

Soak minced shallot in whiskey for 5 minutes

Combine butter, whiskey-soaked shallot, parsley, Worcestershire, mustard, salt, and pepper. Mix well.

On a piece of plastic wrap or parchment paper, drop butter in spoonfuls to form a log. Roll butter in plastic wrap or paper, then smooth it out to form a log.

Refrigerate until hard and easy to slice into coin-shaped pieces, about 1 ½ to 2 hours.

When meat is ready, cut butter into ¼-inch coins, and while grilled meat is still hot, place one to two coins on each steak, allowing the heat to melt it slightly before serving.

Store leftovers, well-wrapped, in the freezer for 1 month or refrigerator for up to 1 week.

, Photo by Elizabeth Karmel

Whisky-Glazed Grilled Pineapple with Toasted Coconut and Whisky Caramel

“Indri Trini single malt’s triple-cask maturation—bourbon, French wine, and Pedro Ximénez sherry casks—brings notes of caramelized pineapple, black tea, and toasted almond that make it a natural match for grilled fruit,” Karmel says. Here, the whisky does double duty, flavoring both the pineapple glaze and a salted caramel sauce. Grilling concentrates the fruit’s sweetness and adds smoky caramelization, while toasted coconut lends a nutty finish.

Serves 4

Grilled Pineapple

  • 1 fresh pineapple, peeled, cored, and cut into ¾-inch rings
  • 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil
  • 3 Tbsp. Indri Trini single malt
  • 2 Tbsp. light brown sugar
  • ½ tsp. ground cinnamon
  • ¼ tsp. ground cardamom
  • Pinch of sea salt flakes

Whisky Caramel

  • 1 cup homemade or store-bought caramel sauce
  • 3 Tbsp. Indri Trini single malt
  • ½ tsp. sea salt flakes
  • ½ cup toasted coconut flakes
  • Vanilla ice cream (optional)

Preheat the grill to medium-low heat (275-325°F). 

In a bowl, whisk together the olive oil, whisky, brown sugar, cinnamon, cardamom, and salt. Place the pineapple rings in a resealable plastic bag, pour in the glaze, and turn to coat evenly. Lay the bag flat so the pineapple is submerged in the sauce and marinate for 20 to 30 minutes. If preparing ahead, refrigerate after marinating.

Meanwhile, toast the coconut flakes on a parchment-lined baking sheet in a 250°F oven until golden, 7 to 10 minutes. Cool completely. The coconut can be prepared up to five days ahead and stored in an airtight container.

To make the whisky caramel, gently warm the caramel sauce so it’s slightly runny.  Remove from heat, then gradually stir in the whisky until smooth and glossy. Stir in the salt and set aside.

Grill the pineapple for about 2 minutes per side, or until deeply marked and lightly caramelized. Avoid moving the rings as they cook to allow the sugars to caramelize without sticking.

Transfer to a serving platter. Drizzle generously with the whisky caramel, sprinkle with toasted coconut, and serve warm or at room temperature with vanilla ice cream, if desired.
octomore-17-details:
Islay whisky Octomore is famous for having some of the world’s highest peat levels. Distilled from heavily peated barley and bottled at relatively high proof, it has all the makings of a smoke bomb. But it’s in fact more complex than that, and stands out more for the purity of its spirit than its high smoke content. This year’s Octomore release, the four-bottle Series 17, uses considerably less peat than previous collections.

In keeping with tradition, the first single malt in the release, (labeled as “.1”) serves as a reference point for the rest of the series. 17.1 was distilled entirely from Concerto barley grown on the Scottish mainland that was peated to 81 phenol parts per million (PPM). It was aged 5 years in first-fill bourbon barrels, and bottled at 59.7% ABV.

Next comes 17.2, which focuses on maturation. It uses the same distillate as 17.1 (Concerto barley peated to 81 PPM), but it was parceled then aged in a completely different arrangement of casks. This one spent 4 years in French oak barrels that previously held California red wine and were briefly used to finish bourbon. After that, the whisky was finished for 1 year in first-fill port barriques. It was bottled just a touch lower at 59.5% ABV. According to the distillery, this is the first time Octomore has been aged in this arrangement of casks.

Octomore 17.3 puts local grain in the spotlight, showcasing Concerto barley from one harvest that was grown on a single field on Octomore Farm. This one has the highest peat content for the 2026 lineup at 132.1 PPM. It also has a fairly interesting maturation, having been matured full-term in a mix of first-fill bourbon, second-fill Ribera Del Duero Spanish wine, sauternes, ice wine, and syrah casks. It was bottled at 60.9% ABV.

For the first time, Octomore has released a “.4” edition in the U.S., with previous expressions having been set aside as distillery exclusives or for specific markets abroad. 17.4 also taps mainland Concerto barley, though it has a higher peat content of 108.2 PPM. At 7 years old, it’s also the oldest whisky in this year’s collection, having been aged in first-fill oloroso casks and finished in virgin French oak. It was bottled at 62.6% ABV. 

Octomore’s peat content varies year to year, but they almost always fall somewhere in the triple digits. The high-water mark for the series is 2017’s Octomore 8.3, which had an eye-watering peat content of 309.1 PPM. But this year’s .1 and .2 expressions use notably less peat than previous years, with some of the lowest PPMs we’ve seen from the brand in recent memory. As master blender Adam Hannett explains, smoke is one of the few production aspects that the distillery doesn’t have complete control over, with the work being carried out at a malting house in Inverness. He says it's a fickle process that poor weather can affect—Scotland’s strong winds can disrupt the chimney’s airflow, raise the temperature, speed up the process, and ultimately reduce peat content.

The drop in PPM might upset some fans of the series, but double-digit peat levels aren’t unprecedented at Octomore. As Hannett points out, the brand’s first-ever production run was even lower at 80 PPM. There’s also Octomore 13.4, an experimental release that was aged for 3 years in virgin French oak, and had a PPM of 88. While the newcomers seem lightly peated by Octomore standards, it’s worth mentioning that they’re still considerably smoky when looking at the wider scotch landscape. For reference, 17.1 and 17.2 have about twice the PPM as Bruichladdich’s own Port Charlotte 10, and about four times more peat than Highland Park 12.

Octomore 17.1, 17.2, and 17.3 are available online and at select retailers nationwide for suggested prices of $205, $245, and $280, respectively. 17.4 is expected to release exclusively online on October 1st, with a suggested retail price of $250.
fee-brothers-fat-wash-drops-review:
Fat washing has always been a project. You add melted bacon fat or brown butter to a spirit, let the two get acquainted for a few hours, then freeze until you can remove the congealed fat and strain what's left. The payoff is real: A fuller mouthfeel, savory depth, and flavors that regular cocktails never achieve. But the process requires patience (and planning) most home bartenders don't have on a random evening. Conveniently, bitters king Fee Brothers just unveiled three fat wash drops that take the labor out of the equation, allowing you to make incredibly complex drinks instantly. 

Their new fat wash drops come in three flavors, Browned Butter, Roasted Duck, and Bacon, and each delivers the same unctuousness, umami, and savory-salty backbone that used to take a full day of prep. Since I picked them up a month ago, I’ve been running them through a number of cocktails, always with fantastic results. My friends ask for thirds, and we’ve been having a blast experimenting with how far we can push any cocktail’s flavor.

Regardless of the specific flavor, these drops add dimensions most cocktails don’t hit. Sweet, sour, bitter, and boozy are the usual attributes in your glass. Savory and salty rarely surface, and umami almost never does. A few dashes from one of these bottles changes that, layering in richness and a rounded, mouth-coating body without the freezer, the cheesecloth, or the wait.

Here are three of my favorite drinks to make with Fee Brothers fat wash drops. One thing before you start concocting: Wash your mixing glass between fat wash varieties. A quick water rinse won't cut it. The residual fat lingers and will haunt your next drink, so give it a real scrub.

Browned Butter Fat Washed Maple Old Fashioned

  • 2 oz. bourbon
  • 1/4 oz. maple syrup
  • 4 dashes Fee Brothers Browned Butter fat wash
  • Lemon peel for garnish

Add all ingredients with ice to a mixing glass, stir, strain over one large cube in a rocks glass, and garnish with a lemon peel.

The smell hits before anything else. While I was building this drink, the browned-butter aroma took over my entire kitchen, the way it does when you've got the best pie crust or a tray of brown butter cookies in the oven. For the whiskey, I used a 12 year old Peg Leg Porker, a 93-proof Tennessee straight bourbon filtered with hickory charcoal, for a barbecue note. Before adding the drops, the cocktail has a great aroma on its own from the Peg Leg and the maple syrup, and the drops only amplify it.

The drops give the glass a nice haziness, the same cloudy look you get from a proper fat wash. Express a lemon peel over the top and the nose becomes brown butter, with a hint of barbecued pork, and a bright edge of citrus. The mouthfeel is velvety and silky, coating everything as the butter and barbecue roll over your palate.

If you want that kick of oomph from the whiskey, stay at four drops. If you're after something sweeter and creamier, add a fifth, which starts to overshadow the drink. Either way, this one lands closer to dessert in a glass.

Roasted Duck Fat Boulevardier

  • 2 oz. bourbon or rye
  • 1 oz. Campari
  • 1 oz. sweet vermouth
  • 5 dashes of Fee Brothers Roasted Duck fat wash
  • Orange peel for garnish

Combine all ingredients over ice in a mixing glass, stir, strain into a coupe, and garnish with orange peel.

This is savory, earthy, and spirit-forward. For the whiskey, I used High West Bourye, bourbon and rye in the same bottle at 46% ABV, the best of both worlds. For sweet vermouth, I like Vermut Cueva Nueva, a Spanish offering featuring 88 botanicals.

The duck fat takes the Boulevardier from a clear, grapefruit-red to a hazy ruby, and that opaqueness reads as elegance in the glass. It's fantastic; 11 out of 10. The fat smooths the sharp edge off the Campari so it folds into the Bourye instead of fighting it, and a light gaminess comes through underneath, acting as a bridge between every other ingredient. Make this when you want savory over sweet and don't want the base spirit to be hidden.

 

Bacon Vieux Carré

  • 3/4 oz. rye
  • 3/4 oz. sweet vermouth
  • 3/4 oz. cognac
  • 2 tsp. Benedictine
  • 4 dashes bitters
  • 4 dashes Bacon fat wash
  • Lemon twist for garnish 

Combine all ingredients over ice in a mixing glass, stir, and strain into a rocks glass. Garnish with lemon twist.

The longstanding classic, the Vieux Carré, is already a busy drink, but the dashes of bacon fat wash give an umami thread that harmonizes well. I used Red Top Rye, which has a 100% Kentucky rye mashbill that comes in more floral than the herbaceous, minty ryes you might be used to. At 105 proof, it stands up in a cocktail. For the cognac, I went with White X Cognac, a collaboration between rapper Quavo and Sazerac.

Add the fat wash, and the drink goes cloudy enough that half a floating lemon peel vanishes into it, pulling you in. There's just a hint of bacon on the nose, present but never elbowing the rest of the cocktail aside. The fruitiness of the Red Top Rye sits in the background and nudges the whole thing a touch sweeter than it would be with, say, Old Overholt.

The bacon tempers the sweetness with a savory counterweight, and the result is a perfectly layered drink. It opens sweet from the Benedictine and cognac, moves into acidity from the bitters, picks up a little spice from the rye, then finishes savory with bacon. It ticks every box. This is the drink for someone who wants balance, nuance, and a little of every major flavor sensation in one glass.
deanston-17-orange-wine-cask-fnish-revie:
Set on the banks of River Teith around an hour’s drive northwest of Edinburgh, Deanston Distillery is an often-overlooked whisky maker—partly because it hasn’t been producing for very long. The distillery was once home to a cotton mill built in 1785 that operated for 180 years before it was converted into a distillery in 1965. Production began the following year, but was relatively short-lived, as an industry-wide downturn forced its closure in 1982.

Deanston reawakened in 1991 under new ownership, and since then it has been making some very impressive whiskies. Its core range includes a 12 year old and an 18 year old (both aged in bourbon barrels) alongside Virgin Oak, a non-age-stated expression finished in new American oak. Its limited releases feature interesting casks, including a 2002 vintage 20 year old aged in re-charred American oak and a 15 year old finished in tequila barrels. Its latest goes in a similar direction, finished in rare orange wine casks. 

Waves of Citrus

The newcomer is a 17 year old that matured 15 years in bourbon barrels before being transferred into vino de naranja casks for 2 years. It was bottled at 53.6% ABV, which is a slight uptick from its tequila barrel-finished counterpart.

Unlike orange wines, which get their name from their amber color that results from fermenting white grapes with their skins, vino de naranja is a flavored wine. In fact, it’s the only aromatized wine  protected by a Denominación de Origen (DO) in Spain, coming from Huelva and Málaga, two areas in the Andalucía region in the southern part of the country. It starts with a base of fortified white wine, infused with macerated peels of local Seville oranges (a bitter variety widely used to make British-style marmalade) for at least 6 months, and aged in a solera system for a minimum of 2 years.

Vino de naranja often has a complex profile that melds the sweetness from the fortification process with bitter notes from the oranges. Those flavors sound like a natural fit for finishing whisky, but vino de naranja casks are fairly uncommon. That’s likely because the wine is a relatively niche offering and represents a very small fraction of the region’s overall wine production, which also includes sherry, moscatel, and other fortified wines. Plus, as is the case with many of those other fortified wines, producers are reluctant to part with casks that are vital to maintaining their solera systems. 

But some whisky makers have used vino de naranja casks to great effect. They’re most often seen among American distillers, with examples including Blue Note Special Reserve, TX Whiskey Experimental Series, Penelope Valencia, Middle West Double Cask Collection, 15 Stars 8 year old Vino De Naranja Cask, and others from Sagamore, Castle & Key, Lasso Motel, Smooth Ambler, and more. They’re far rarer in scotch, with only a handful of expressions like Compass Box Canvas, a previous Scallywag Winter Edition from independent bottler Douglas Laing, and a very limited Kilchoman 100% Islay that was released exclusively for the German market. Some world whisky producers have also dabbled with these casks, including New Zealand’s Pōkeno, The Lakes Distillery in England, and Milk & Honey Distillery in Israel.

While vino de naranja casks are certainly interesting from a flavor perspective, Deanston master blender Julieann Fernandez also chose them for a sentimental reason. She has family ties to southern Spain, with both of her parents having originally met in Andalucía and some family members still living in the area. " I spent part of my childhood surrounded by the sights, smells, and flavors of Andalucía, and those memories have always stayed with me,” she says. “Working with vino de naranja casks allowed us to bring that influence into Deanston’s spirit in a very natural way.”

How Does Deanston 17 year old Orange Wine Cask Taste?

92 points—Deanston 17 year old Orange Wine Cask Finished Highland Single Malt

ABV: 53.6%
SRP: $132
Availability: 7,000 bottles globally, available nationwide 

Honeydew and apricot tango with lemon sorbet, candle wax, grape jam, and a bit of marmalade on the nose. The citrus influence from the casks truly comes through on the palate, which combines burnt oranges, candied orange peel, and Jaffa cakes with plum, more apricot, honey, and snickerdoodles. These flavors linger for a medium-to-long finish that also adds orange spice tea. The vino casks seem to be a great match for the distillery's sweet and fruity spirit.
balvenie-88-year-old:
The record is undeniable. At 88 years old, Balvenie’s latest release is the oldest single malt whisky ever brought to market, surpassing the 85 year old Glenlivet released by Gordon & MacPhail in 2025. Only 17 bottles exist.

The whisky within Cask 239 did not remain in oak for nearly nine decades so Balvenie could win an age-statement contest. Malt master Kelsey McKechnie stopped its maturation in 2019, two years short of 90 and within sight of 100. For her, the more consequential number was not its age, but the point at which further maturation might begin to take something away.

The whisky was transferred to glass in 2019, fixing its age at 88. Some 95 years have now passed since the cask was filled, but none of that time in glass counts as maturation.

Filled on March 5, 1931, and fully matured in a European oak refill sherry butt sourced from Jerez. At the time, its spirit was probably destined for blending rather than release as a Balvenie single malt. How it escaped that fate cannot be reconstructed from the surviving records. McKechnie describes it as having been “hidden in plain sight,” watched over by generations of distillery workers while nearby casks were emptied.

When she sampled it, McKechnie deliberately set its reputation aside. “I had absolutely no expectation whatsoever,” she says. Whisky approaching 90 years is beyond the familiar boundaries of maturation, where knowledge of wood extraction, ester development, and declining alcohol strength becomes less predictive. “It’s absolutely doing its own thing.”

Nevertheless, Cask 239 had retained the distillery character. Honey and toffee remained beneath mint, damp bracken, worn leather, and aromatic oak. Bottled at a natural strength of 43.2% ABV, it tasted old without being overcome by wood.

I tasted it at the distillery. Its age was evident in its earthiness, leather, and drying oak, but it kept moving: buttery fudge gave way to woodland notes, then unexpected freshness and dark fruit. It felt less like a record-breaking age statement or something fixed in time, and instead something evolving and fresh. In McKechnie’s words, “a little nugget of scotch whisky history.”

McKechnie inherited the cask from her predecessor and mentor David Stewart, who could have released it during his own tenure. Instead, its stewardship passed to her. “I absolutely see my role as the guardian of the stock,” she says. McKechnie is “exceptionally proud” that Cask 239 was bottled during her tenure, but considers it “bigger than the malt master role”—the accumulated work and restraint of almost a century of people.

The 88 year old is part of The Balvenie 1931 Collection, accompanied by a 12 year old made with 100% on-site floor-malted barley and a 15 year old made entirely with barley grown and malted at the distillery. Both connect the release to 1931, when The Balvenie’s floor maltings opened. The 88 is available to private clients and collectors only at an undisclosed price, and most bottles have already been purchased. The 15 year old is available exclusively through global Travel Retail, while the 12 year old is available in selected markets.

Records will eventually fall; another cask may reach 89, 90, or 100 years. What cannot be repeated is the decision McKechnie made in 2019: to accept that the world’s oldest single malt was already old enough.
oldest-whiskey-pre-prohibition-tasting-s:
“You hear that hiss?” says Zev Glesta as he jimmies the Ah So wine opener down the sides of the cork. “That’s 113 year old air escaping, baby!” The assistant vice president, whiskey North America for Sotheby’s, is jazzed. The seal on this 33 year old Chicken Cock whiskey—distilled in 1880 and bottled in 1913—held tight enough to sound off when it gave, and Glesta deftly opened five straight pre-Prohibition whiskey bottles without a single cork disintegrating, and it appears his streak will continue.

More cajoling and the sixth cork’s remnants slide free. Glesta beams, holding up his tiny foe. “There we go,” says Bill Carmean, clapping from across Sotheby’s conference table. “You can have as much as you want, Bill,” Glesta says, drizzling the motor oil-colored whiskey—the darkest I have ever seen—into a Glencairn and sliding it to Carmean. “It is your bottle…”

How a Lawyer Bought a Whiskey Dynasty’s Best for $365

In the ’80s and early ’90s, Carmean worked as a lawyer for National Distillers, shepherding them through the transition to Quantum Chemical, a sale to Jim Beam, and a merger with Hanson PLC. In 1993, Carmean ate lunch in the company’s executive dining room, “an opulent wood-paneled room, surrounded by a collection of 120 special bottles, called the National Distillers Museum of Old Bottles,” he recalls. “It was a beautiful sight.”

The new bosses didn’t agree. They wanted it gone but had no idea what it was worth. Carmean, a whiskey fan, volunteered to get it appraised. “The whole lot was assessed at $250, which felt like a steal, so I said I’d take it. They said okay, but I’d have to pay the $115 appraisal fee, too,” Carmean smirks.

And so, for $365, Carmean took possession of the 120 bottles, a third of which were made pre-Prohibition. A bunch were empty, others had such low and hazy fills, “you knew you’d get sick if you drank them,” says Carmean. He stored them with his fine wine, in an old Victorian house outside New York City.

 

The collection became a working one. At parties, friends skipped pressuring him to open bottles and opened them themselves. “One fellow grabbed a corkscrew and opened a 1920 cognac,” Carmean laughs. “Afterward, I figured you may as well have some old bourbon so we opened one of those, too.”

A tenth of the collection dwindled over the decades, but when Carmean and his wife wanted to move to the city, “she wanted more space, and that meant giving up some bottles,” he says. Carmean consigned 21 bottles to Sotheby's for its September 2026 Whisky & Whiskey auction. Six more missed the cut for pronounced ullage—they now loom large on our table.

Ullage kills auction value, but a bottle you can't sell is a bottle you can (gingerly) pull the cork on. So the bottles Carmean is letting me try may be 30%-plus lighter, but they’re the apex of any whiskey geek’s dream drinking list.

Inside National Distillers, the Disney of American Whiskey

There’s the 33-year Chicken Cock. And an Old Hermitage, made by W.A. Gaines in the 1880s. A Mount Vernon rye, crafted somewhere in the early 1900s, an Old Crow and Jefferson, each distilled in 1914. And a 16 year old Old Grand-Dad, distilled in 1916, bottled in 1932.

If that lineup sounds like the Oscars of pre-Prohibition whiskey, it’s because National Distillers is more a dynasty than a distillery. Its roots run back to the Whiskey Trust of the 1880s, and with a huge share of aged bourbon still in bond at Repeal, president Seton Porter made a crucial choice to keep National Distillers' high-end brands instead of chasing bottom-shelf volume.

Old Crow was the country’s best-selling bourbon for a stretch. Old Grand-Dad, whose label swore it was “unexcelled for medicinal purposes,” remains lauded today. Old Taylor, Old Overholt, Mount Vernon, Old Sunny Brook, Mellwood, Bourbon DeLuxe, and more; brands rivals built companies around, and National had them all. Owning that portfolio was the whiskey equivalent of Disney owning Marvel, Star Wars, and Pixar.

What Evaporation Leaves Behind

Our first tipple is the Old Hermitage, a straight bourbon from W.A. Gaines of Frankfort, with no indication of age beyond a pre-1900 lead seal and a three-mold bottle. The evaporation is considerable, and what was bottled north of 100 proof may now sit closer to 80, Glesta muses. The nose has ample pure old-style rye: medicinal, herbal, and minty beyond belief; synthetic mint tea; a little household cleaner; synthetic lemon; and, 10 minutes in, some matzah ball soup, says Glesta. 

The straw-light liquid has a decent palate, minty with a zippy spice that sharpens as it opens. The finish is mint, lemon, and tea leaves, like a cup of Lipton gone dry. “I’m blown away by the extraordinary flavors in here,” Carmean says, swirling the Old Hermitage. “It’s like taking a sip of a sunrise. It explodes in your mouth.”

Next, Mount Vernon. This quart, labeled “a fine whiskey blend from choice stock,” is hard to pin down. It’s marked Philadelphia, so it’s likely late 1800s or very early 1900s. Glesta reads it as pure rye that predates the square bottlings, from an era when the Mount Vernon operation bought up everything around it.

The nose opens on wet cardboard and mint, then turns to maple syrup, caramel, and vanilla. The palate is lively, albeit thin, with rancio, leather, dried golden raisins, and dates appearing later, a spectacular nose riding over tired liquid, which is what low fill levels will do. Ten minutes later, it completely dies in the glass. A shame, but that’s the craps game that is drinking pre-Prohibition whiskey; sometimes you win, sometimes you roll snake eyes.

The fifth of Old Crow straight bourbon is 90 proof, distilled in 1914 and bottled in 1920, on the doorstep of Prohibition. This 6 year old was an export bottle, so chances are it was bound for Canada. The youngest pour yet, and the biggest and roundest; oxidized bubble gum, like the dried stick from an old baseball-card pack, plus shoe polish, banana, and mint. It’s a pleasant pour that stands up over 15 minutes. Upon revisiting, the nose moves into polished leather, and the finish—a pop of baking spice—lingers longer.

“It’s funny,” says Carmean as we swap tasting notes. “All these words in our language, and we still don't have specific ones to express whiskey’s palate and bouquet. We use bizarre comparisons, old rubber, shoe polish. The Inuit languages have two dozen words for snow and ice. We've got nothing like that for this." He nods at the Old Crow, the bourbon Ulysses S. Grant drank by the case and Mark Twain praised by name. “If anyone, Twain would have found the words.”

On to the 16 year Old Grand-Dad, distilled in 1916 and bottled in 1932. This bottled in bond bottle features a National Reform Association sticker and a New York State tax stamp. The metal tamperproof cap hides a cork layer that helps preserve the liquid, and this opens up magnificently. Notes of Snickers, orange, caramel, and dusty basement entwine with buttercream, fresh-cut wood, anisette, and lavender. It’s a notable Prohibition pint for a reason. “We have a 1911 quart of this from Bill in gorgeous shape in the sale,” Glesta says. Locate that buyer and beg for a taste.

The Jefferson whiskey, 100 proof, distilled in 1914, bottled in 1919, pours startlingly dark, a deep tawny that looks older than its 5 years. The whiskey is alive: it hisses on opening, and the nose charges out robust and bright: a little rye, rose, bubble gum, banana, and a green edge. “That’s the rush before Prohibition,” Glesta says, “when distillers filled barrels of poorly seasoned green wood as fast as they could to get whiskey into oak.” The palate is full, rich, and lively, lemongrass riding on top.

What 1880 Chicken Cock Tastes Like 146 Years Later

Onto the main course: the 33 year old Chicken Cock distilled in 1880, the year Edison patented the light bulb. The telephone was four years old. Karl Benz wouldn’t build a practical automobile for another five. The oak this Chicken Cock would go into? From a felled tree some 300 years old, germinated from an acorn in the 1500s.

American whiskey aged over 30 years is a novelty—and was in 1913, too—one that yields unpredictable and often less-than-stellar results. Accordingly, this blend of unknown whiskies is rough around the edges. The sludgy liquid resembles prune juice when swirled, coating the glass with thick purple-hued legs from the wood oils. “Or at least we hope it's wood oils,” Glesta jokes. “1913 was late enough to mean this was likely unadulterated.”

The nose, closed off at first, opens rapidly. “It’s pretty weird,” Carmean says, picking out old tires and molasses. It’s woody, fruity, astringent, and minty all at once. Within minutes, the nose is actually nice. There’s bubble gum, old lipstick, prune, and cherry, too.

Sip to discover none of those aromas are present on the palate. Instead, there’s oak, more oak, and some burnt lumber with added water, as if a rickhouse was aflame and the fire department hosed it all down, then turned that used water into whiskey. Someone mentions it’s like accidentally eating patchouli, and that fits. The finish is… oak, and it only grips harder over time as the 146 year old oils release. Carmean adds water and the dram goes instantly opaque, drawing a chuckle. The earliest produced whiskey I’ve ever tasted landed on snake eyes. Again.

Would it have tasted better in 1914? Probably not. Though Chicken Cock’s producer, Old J.A. Miller, was known for quality, “good whiskey then was very different from good whiskey now,” says Glesta. “I doubt this flavor drifted far from what the profile was back then, but it makes you wonder what it was actually used for,” meaning it could’ve pulled double duty as medicine, a bitter, a tincture, or even a household solvent.

Ruminating on 1880s production methods—of men cutting grains with scythes, hand-hammering casks, moving grains by wagon—gets Carmean wistful. “So much of this was so great, and they didn’t have any of the computers or systems we have now,” he says. “This is as analog as it gets,” Glesta echoes.

A Steal That Turns Into a Gift

Ask if Carmean has any consignor’s remorse, and his eyes dart to the Old Hermitage. “I always knew this would be an amazing bottle," he says. "I wish I'd left it for me and my friends." "This is not your regret meal, Bill,” Glesta jokes. “You spent $365, and you are about to do a lot of good for the world."

That’s because all of Carmean's net sale proceeds are bound for World Central Kitchen. Caring for those in need is a cause that runs close to home for him: Carmean’s mother lived with psychiatric illness, and without his family's support, he says, she would have ended up on the street.

While the six bottles open on the table aren’t among the lots, given the hit rate, the bottles from Carmean’s collection that did make the sale should be superb.

The Sotheby’s Whisky and Whiskey | Featuring The Wax Top Collection Auction runs from September 3rd through the 18th. Check out the lots and register to bid here.
whiskey-berry-jam-crumble-bars-recipe:
There’s a strong pull that brings even the most developed palates back to favorite childhood snacks, and none compare to the classic peanut butter and jelly sandwich. As lunchboxes are dusted off to start the school year, this childhood staple gets an adult upgrade in the tipsy berry crumble bar. Anchored by a peanut shortbread, the homemade quick berry jam on top is spiked with bourbon and underpinned by a hit of woodsy thyme blanketed by a crisp, buttery crumb topping.

These bars are easy to portion and sturdy enough to travel, working well at a tailgate, potluck, or tasty snack. Use a full-flavored bourbon or rye to bake with; high-proof expressions tend to retain more character once baked. They’re best served alongside a fruit-forward or nutty whisky that complements its sweet, jammy flavors. A growing number of whisky producers use wine casks for finishing because they reinforce the tart berry character already present in the spirit. Virginia Distilling Co. is one example; its Cabernet Cask Select is a modestly priced single malt at $45, resplendent with tart red berries, raisins, and baking spice thanks to a finish in cabernet sauvignon barrels from France and California.

Sherried whiskies work well with these bars, too, with bramble fruit notes in a scotch like Isle of Arran single malt sherry cask ($80), or Lux Row Sherry finished bourbon ($60), loaded with red berry flavors. If you’re looking for an extra-indulgent dram, a pour of 15 Stars 10 year old sherry cask-finished bourbon ($180) will not disappoint. It’s oozing with overripe berries and a hint of peanut. These three hover around 55% ABV, which makes for a rich, full-bodied dram that pairs well with the flavors in the dessert.

If you pile on the peanut butter on your PB&J, reach for a whiskey that does the same. Charles Goodnight 6 year old, a high-rye Texas-made bourbon, is riddled with peanut butter cookie and peanut butter flavor, rounded out with a bit of berry ripeness for the closest thing to PB&J in a glass. California’s Redwood Empire Rocket Top bottled in bond ($80) and Knob Creek’s 12 year old bourbon ($60) offer similar nutty profiles with an earthy spice that complements the thyme.

Stewed, jammy fruits and whisky are familiar territory, with several brands now making their own whisky-infused jams that work beautifully in place of homemade jam to cut prep time. For the most similar flavor, reach for New York-based Great Jones and Brooklyn Jam Stand’s collaborative Blueberry Bourbon jam ($14.50). For a hit of stone fruit, opt for Stranahan’s peach jam, infused with the label’s Rocky Mountain single malt.

Not a fan of blueberries? Swap them out in equal measure for blackberries, raspberries, or strawberries, setting aside a tablespoon of strawberry jam filling to make a Strawberry Patch Smash, a perfect cocktail to drink alongside the bars.

Tipsy Berry Jam Crumble Bars

Shortbread 

  • ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter
  • ½  cup creamy, all-natural peanut butter
  • ¾ cup powdered sugar
  • 2 tsp. vanilla extract
  • Zest from 1 orange
  • 2 ¾ cups all-purpose flour
  • 1 ½ Tbsp. cornstarch

Blueberry Whiskey Jam

  • 1 ⅓ cups blueberries, fresh or frozen
  • ½ cup granulated sugar
  • ½ Tbsp. cornstarch
  • 2 Tbsp. thyme, wrapped in kitchen twine
  • 3 Tbsp. high-proof bourbon or rye

Preheat the oven to 350°F. Grease and line an 8-inch square baking pan with parchment.

In a standing mixer, or with a hand mixer, with the paddle attachment, beat the butter, peanut butter, sugar, vanilla, and orange zest until light and fluffy, about 3 to 5 minutes. Add the flour and cornstarch and mix just until a dough forms.

Press three-quarters of the dough evenly into the bottom of the prepared pan. Lightly cover with plastic wrap. Wrap the remaining dough in plastic wrap and refrigerate both for at least 30 minutes.

Meanwhile, combine the blueberries, sugar, cornstarch, and thyme bundle in a saucepan over medium heat. Cook, stirring frequently, until thickened, 15 to 20 minutes. Remove the thyme, stir in the bourbon, and let cool slightly.

Remove the pan from the refrigerator. Spread the jam over the chilled dough in the pan. Crumble the remaining dough into dime and quarter-sized pieces evenly over the top, leaving a few gaps for the jam to peek through. 

Bake until the topping is lightly golden and the filling is bubbling, about 40 minutes. Cool completely, then refrigerate for at least 1 hour before slicing into 16 bars.

Store in an airtight container for up to 3 days at room temperature or 4 days in the refrigerator.
one-mans-johnnie-walker-collection-to-be:
Some collectors focus on a particular whisky style; others pursue rarity, prestige, or investment potential. Rarer still are single-brand collectors who seek not just exceptional bottles but also packaging variations, advertising, memorabilia, and obscure releases that tell the brand's story. California-based Frans Op den Kamp took that approach with Johnnie Walker, the world’s No.1 scotch whisky brand, amassing a comprehensive collection spanning bottlings from around the globe.

The result of his two-decade pursuit of Johnnie Walker comes to market this September, when Whisky Auctioneer presents the largest and most comprehensive collection of Johnnie Walker ever offered at auction. Transferred from California to Scotland for the sale, the collection consists of more than 600 miniatures, 1,000 pieces of original advertising and memorabilia, and 1,600 full-sized bottles, offering collectors an unusually detailed look at the evolution of one of scotch whisky’s most recognizable brands. Op den Kamp’s fascination with Johnnie Walker began in 1999, when he bought a $130 bottle of Blue Label on his way home from a business trip to New York. That first purchase grew into a 20-year collecting project spanning rare releases, market-specific bottlings, historical labels, and whisky ephemera chronicling the story of the Striding Man.

For Op den Kamp, selling this collection marks the end of a personal journey rather than simply dispersing his whisky cellar. “Parting with the collection is certainly not easy, but I feel I have achieved what I set out to do,” he said in a statement. “I hope these bottles find their way to collectors who discover something that resonates with them, whether that’s a particular whisky, a moment in Johnnie Walker’s history or simply the thrill of the hunt.” He added, “Most of all, I hope it inspires a renewed appreciation for the art of blending and the story of scotch whisky.”

Diageo owns the world’s largest Johnnie Walker archive, and visitors to Johnnie Walker Princes Street in Edinburgh can view an archivist’s display. Whisky Auctioneer has not publicly revealed the estimated value for the Op den Kamp collection, but the scale of its contents will likely attract bidders with a wide range of budgets. More than 500 bottles of Black Label, 280 of Blue Label, and 200 of Red Label offer ample opportunity to pick up older bottles and packaging variations at relatively accessible prices. The collection reaches back more than a century, and early 20th century examples of Old Highland whisky, the original name for the blend, will be on the block. The sale also includes a number of Johnnie Walker-adjacent single malts from Mortlach, Talisker, and Cardhu that reference John Walker & Sons on the label. From cartoons to figurines, the memorabilia and advertising material may well generate sufficient competition. Whisky Auctioneer’s previous highest hammer price for Johnnie Walker memorabilia was $4,880 in 2016 for three scrapbooks of Johnnie Walker labels from 1930–1960.

For dedicated Johnnie Walker collectors, this sale, which runs from September 11th –21st, will provide a chance to fill long-standing gaps, while those hunting the brand’s rarest and most valuable releases will find plenty to keep them watching.

Below is a list of standout bottlings included in this sale, with a guide to the previous highest hammer prices achieved by Whisky Auctioneer for each expression: 

  • Johnnie Walker 1805 Celebration Blend ($24,628 in 2021)
    One of 200 bottles, this was created to commemorate the 200th anniversary of John Walker’s birth.
  • John Walker & Sons Signature Blend Vodafone McLaren Mercedes Edition ($17,561 in 2016)
    Signed by F1 world champion Jenson Button, one of 25 bottles.
  • Johnnie Walker Swing ($13,021 in 2018)
    Bottled to commemorate the opening of the new premises of John Walker & Sons Ltd at Hill Street, Kilmarnock on September 11, 1956.
  • Johnnie Walker The Director’s Blend 2008 ($6,652 in 2019)
    Part of a series of annual bottlings released between 2008–2013, these were gifted to individuals by Diageo, but never available for sale. The Johnnie Walker Collection sale includes a complete set.
  • Johnnie Walker Blue Label Robert Burns ($4,844 in 2019)
    A bottling engraved with words from the Bard, bottled for a commemorative dinner held in 2008.
  • Johnnie Walker Commemorative 1920 Edition ($2,554 in 2023)
    The fifth release in the Epic Dates series, the Johnnie Walker Collection sale includes a complete set.
  • Johnnie Walker Red Label Old Highland Whisky ($1,535 in 2026)
    A 1930s bottling with a driven cork closure.
outdoor-excursions-for-whisky-lovers:
“Aye, you’ve gon’ and caught the bank,” says Macallan’s head ghillie Richard Whyte. He rushes over, moving fast for a man in a three-piece tweed suit and galoshes, and carefully unhooks the fly and fishing line from the earth beside Scotland’s River Spey, where I had lodged it seconds earlier. Sheepishly, I fling the tip of the 12-foot rod in the general direction of the river, and hear a whoosh as the line flies over my head. The fly lands in the rushing water, though not where I intended. “Better, but watch ye don’ hook yer head,” Whyte says, with a wink. “Happens more than ya’d think.”

Whyte’s thick Scottish accent means even his admonishments and safety warnings sound charming. I’ve fly-fished only once before, in the wilds of Alaska, using a shorter rod and vastly different technique. Whyte runs through a list of reasons why fly-fishing here in the Scottish Highlands is more complicated. The rods are longer, and the casting techniques are an elaborate series of maneuvers designed to keep the fly dancing atop the river’s surface without letting the line itself disturb the surface tension—“Scare ‘em off like that”—and the fish put up prolonged fights after being hooked.

Like his father, Whyte has spent his whole life as a ghillie, the Gaelic term for someone who shepherds you on a fishing or hunting expedition. He’s been head ghillie at Macallan for the past four years, overseeing fishing on the Estate’s property that extends to the banks of the River Spey.

For around £100/$134 a person, anyone can use Macallan’s website to book an afternoon with Whyte and his team—today, relief ghillie Jim Grant and apprentice ghillie Thea Stronach join. A Macallan Estate Bentley Bentayga collected us from our hotel for the excursion, and took us to a quaint wooden hut beside the river. Here, over sandwiches, sausage rolls, tea, and various Scottish delicacies, Whyte explains that the fly-fishing package is actually a deal, considering rods, waders, and lunch are included. (Whisky is not.) Neighboring fishing beats—the term for a privately owned stretch of river where fishing is permitted—charge more and don’t provide gear or meals, he says.

While his black doodle Kobe sprints up and down the riverbank, stick in mouth, Whyte demonstrates proper technique, showing how to wield the rod to cast. The tip of the rod dances in the air, zipping this way and that before the fly touches down. It looks like a masterful execution to me, but Whyte says it could be better and recasts. His second throw of the day sees the line drifting toward shore. “Caught on a rock here, I think,” he says, tugging.

“No, wait. We got a fish, lads!”

Sure enough, thrashing in the water reveals a sizable dorsal fin. “He’s still got fight in ‘im. You want ‘im in quick, but ye don’t wanna rush it,” Whyte says. “C’mon, then! Let’s have ya,” he says to the fish. For 10 minutes, Whyte balances letting the line out and reeling his catch in. Stronach shows up toward the end, net in hand, and scoops the fish. It’s a whopper: 36 inches long and about 16 pounds.

Whyte says it’s an older fish, one that’s made its way to fresh water and back upriver again. Because it’s only catch-and-release on the Spey, after photos, Whyte’s scaly adversary is freed, while Kobe barks in protest.

The rod is then handed to me. The only thing I snag over the next few hours is the bank and river grass. When I quip to Whyte that I’m better at drinking scotch than fishing, he grins. “Well, this is the right place. Drams are in yer future.”

There’s a certain logic to pairing whisky and the outdoors. The landscapes that shape whisky—rivers, barley fields, peat bogs, rolling hills—are also worth exploring on foot, on horseback, or on skis. These five experiences underscore that drams taste better when you’ve earned them.

Fly-Fishing in the Catskills, New York

With a population of about 500, Roscoe is a charming small town about two hours north of Manhattan. This tiny Catskills village is also known as Trout Town USA, due to five legendary trout streams converging within minutes of Roscoe’s Main Street. One of those, the Beaverkill, is to American fly-fishing what the Spey is to Scotland: hallowed water.

Certain eddies and pools are geared toward experienced fishers, while others are well-suited to first-timers. In town, a slew of stores will square you away with all the kit you need, and guides are available to create any kind of day you’d like, from one of casual casting to a pro angler’s nirvana.

Once your cooler is full, head to Do Good Spirits in town, a veteran-owned distillery that operates out of a former firehouse. Authenticity abounds here—the founder is an angler, and the distillery’s Beaverkill straight whiskey is a tribute to the fishing culture that defines the town. Nearby Beaverkill Valley Inn offers private river access for fly-fishing, hiking, winter activities, and a tavern with a selection of local whiskeys.

Visit the Heart of Scotch by Walking the Speyside Way

For those willing to walk, this is the pilgrimage. The Speyside Way is a 70-plus-mile self-guided walking trail through the heart of scotch whisky country, putting you inside the landscape that’s the spiritual home of single malt. You’ll trace along the Spey, the second-longest river in Scotland, passing distilleries including Glenfiddich, Glenlivet, Macallan, and Cardhu, among others.

The full trail takes most people four to six days, threading through river valleys, moorland, and small market towns. (Shorter routes are options, too.) While on the trail, you’ll see everything from ospreys to golden eagles to dolphins. The dolphins congregate to feed on salmon from May to September at the river’s northern terminus, Spey Bay, where it meets the ocean.

Several tour operators offer fully supported packages that book your lodging at various B&Bs, transport your luggage from stop to stop, and help you arrange distillery visits along the way. All you need to do is show up, walk, and drink. Plan accordingly, as in the off-season—November through March—it can be harder to find open accommodations. However, Scotland’s “right to roam” law means that you’re legally allowed to camp on any land that isn’t private property.

Tasting WhistlePig at Spruce Peak, Vermont

Skiers and snowboarders who are whisky fans should check out WhistlePig’s Tasting Shack at Spruce Peak in Stowe, Vermont for apres-ski. Spruce Peak is a proper luxury resort—ski-in, ski-out lodge, spa, geothermal- powered village—where you can spend a morning on the mountain before warming up with a glass or flight of whisky.

The shack, situated in the village center, is a short walk from the lifts. The vibe there is low-key, perfect if you’re tired from a day of runs. The shack lives up to its name; it’s cozy, with seating for up to eight people. Walk-ins are welcome, but reservations are advised for the 30-minute private tasting ($25 per person). There’s a retail corner where you can buy bottles from the full WhistlePig portfolio, including limited releases like Boss Hog, at standard retail prices. Also available are barrel-aged maple syrup and WhistlePig merchandise.

Looking for a bite with your beverage? Try the nearby WhistlePig Pavilion, also mountainside at Spruce Peak. Here, a medley of barbecue dishes, craft beers, cocktails, raclette, and, of course, whisky is on offer. And the fun doesn’t stop when the season’s over. The Stowe area becomes a hotspot for golf, hiking, mountain biking, and more. The Tasting Shack is open year-round, while the Pavilion is seasonal.

Saddle Up For a Ride Into The Grand Tetons

This one operates at a different level, literally. Mason Walker and the team behind luxury experiential group Bourbon Lore will immerse you in the Grand Tetons lifestyle—and whiskey. Your day starts in downtown Jackson, where you create a custom cowboy hat at famed milliner Kemo Sabe, then it’s over to the roughly 300,000-acre Gros Ventre Valley to meet your steed. American mustangs, specifically. Wranglers and Bourbon Lore concierges will lead you on a two-hour horseback ride through the area before arriving at a glamping site.

Here, you’ll be treated to fireside cocktails, a seven-course meal with wine and rare spirit pairings, then a Wyoming Whiskey tasting flight of limited releases. Its craft whiskey utilizes locally grown grains and matures in the same high-altitude air you’re breathing. Post-meal, Bourbon Lore has one more treat: an acoustic country music performance under the stars. Custom-rolled cigars are available, as are additional whiskies. Luxury comes at a price; here it’s $35,000 and up for six people.
all-inclusive-resorts-with-great-whisky-:
It’s far less stressful to know in advance how much your vacation will cost, and the best way to do that is to go all-inclusive. It’s long been a popular idea for spring break and low-budget party vacations, but now the idea has gone upscale—and believe it or not, these all-inclusives also cover the bar tab. Here’s a roundup, listed in order of price from highest to lowest.

JUMBY BAY

Antigua

This resort occupies its private 300-acre island with a mix of luxury cottages, ultra-luxury villas, and palatial estate homes. The island is a tropical paradise for guests, with amenities like sailing, coral reefs, racquet clubs, a kids club, and the house specialty: luxury picnics on private beaches.
