There are several fine dining restaurants focused on local specialties and seafood. Given the Caribbean location, it’s not surprising that they have more than three dozen included rums, with some Cubans you can’t get at home, and around 25 whiskies, with a focus on scotch. Labels include Macallan, Glenfiddich, and Ardbeg, plus Maker’s Mark, Woodford Reserve, and Gentleman Jack on the American list. From $2,950/night for two. 

TWIN FARMS

Barnard, Vermont

This country estate occupies the 300-acre former farm of Nobel Prize-winning writer Sinclair Lewis and journalist Dorothy Parker, and has been described as a summer camp for grown-ups because so many activities are included, from hiking and cross-country skiing to biking, fly-fishing, and canoeing. A top-flight culinary staff will meet you at the lake for a cookout, or mid-hike with a gourmet picnic basket and champagne. The 29 lodging options include hotel rooms, uniquely themed houses, and new luxury treehouses, all decorated with museum-quality art. The meals are made from the bounty of extensive chef’s gardens, with other products sourced from local artisan farms, and there are more than 80 whiskies included, plus rare selections on their reserve list with a surcharge. But the inclusions are enough for most whisky fans with a nice mix of American, Irish, Japanese, Canadian, and plenty of scotch, including several 18 year olds (Glenlivet, Talisker) and 16 year olds (Balvenie, Lagavulin), along with Glenfiddich Fire & Cane, Glenmorangie Nectar d’Or, Dalwhinnie 15, Oban 14, and more. Notable bourbons include Blanton’s Gold Edition, E.H. Taylor Barrel Proof, Jefferson’s Ocean, and Thomas S. Moore Port, Chardonnay, and Cabernet finishes. It is Vermont, so there is also local Mad River rye, Rectified bourbon, and several WhistlePig options, including 10, 12, and Farmstock, with more on the reserve list (15, 18, Boss Hog 7, X Commandments). From $2,950/night for two (adults only). 

RANCH AT ROCK CREEK

Philipsburg, Montana

This guest ranch takes the term all-inclusive to the extreme, offering equine activities, fishing, hiking, yoga, and more. In winter, downhill and cross-country skiing are also included. The food and accommodations are true standouts, as is the spirits selection. About 70 whiskies are offered at no extra charge, from classic standbys like Macallan 12 year old and Dalwhinnie 15 to High West Campfire, Weller Special Reserve, and several locally made expressions, like Mama Tried high-rye and wheated bourbons, Wildrye Fire Drops, and Montgomery Sudden Wisdom 3 year old rye. From $2,829/night for two.

FOUR SEASONS NAVIVA

Punta Mita, Mexico

Punta Mita is a 1,500-acre private peninsula with two golf courses, a pier, and just about every imaginable amenity. But hidden on 50 private gated acres is a second one-of-a-kind enclave, an all-inclusive called Naviva. It has only 15 rooms—if by rooms you mean tented villas starting at 1,250 square feet, with private plunge pools, indoor and outdoor showers, and jetted tubs. Want to do yoga? Call, and an instructor will join you at the outdoor ocean-view platform. Want to go fishing? Call, and a guide will take you. Rates even include a spa treatment and temazcal sweat lodge experience. Naviva has its own trail network, private beach, and chef ready to prepare whatever and whenever you want. While the bar embraces agave spirits, having a fine selection of tequila and mezcal, it offers more than 50 whiskies in its all-inclusive package, including standouts from Japan that can be hard to find, such as Yamazaki 18, Hakushu 18, and Nikka Miyagikyo single malt. There is the local Mexican 100% corn whisky Abasolo, plus other notable indulgences like Johnnie Walker King George V and a flight of Macallan (12, 15, and 18). From $2,800/night for two (adults only).

CLAYOQUOT WILDERNESS LODGE

Vancouver Island, Canada

A legendary “North American safari” destination, Clayoquot occupies 600 acres of pristine island wilderness that is home to bears, whales, sea lions, otters, and eagles, with all lodging in 25 luxury African safari-style glamping tents. Clayoquot is also a famous culinary destination known for sourcing fine organic meats, seafood, and produce in partnership with local ranchers and First Nations tribes. In this same vein, they showcase local craft breweries, dozens of Canadian wineries, and more than 20 British Columbia distilleries, including Wayward, Macaloney’s, Arbutus, Shelter Point, and Sheringham. There are about 20 others, ranging through Hibiki Harmony, Dalwhinnie 15 year old, Oban 14 year old, Macallan 12 year old, and Crown Royal Northern Harvest rye. Sunsets on Vancouver Island are spectacular, and sunset cocktails are a big thing at Clayoquot—try the Ursus (Bearface whisky, red wine syrup, and bitters). From $2,335/night for two. 

JADE MOUNTAIN

St. Lucia

Jade Mountain has an unusual rate structure that allows guests to choose a regular room, a Modified American plan with breakfast and dinner, or an all-inclusive package. The all-inclusive whisky selection is limited but premium, with scotch options from Macallan, Dalmore, Glenlivet, Glenfiddich, Oban, Johnnie Walker, Glenmorangie, and Glengoyne, and bourbon from Woodford Reserve, Knob Creek, and Maker’s Mark. While the whisky list is not a top-tier standout among luxury all-inclusives, Jade Mountain is simply one of the most spectacular such properties, and one of the finest escapes in the Caribbean, all-inclusive or not. A stunning fantasy designed by its architect-owner and perched on a high tropical peak, the suites, called sanctuaries, have an open, non-existent “fourth wall” framing stunning views over its curved, tiled, private infinity pool (carefully angled so there is no place anyone can look in at you from). You also get an on-call butler. It’s a tremendous honeymoon, anniversary, or celebratory choice, and Jade Mountain guests seeking more activities can take a shuttle to the larger but less fancy 600-acre sister beach resort below, Anse Chastanet, where they get full run of the food, beverage, and amenities, which include a PADI 5-Star scuba dive center, watersports, and tropical mountain biking trail system. From $2,035/night for two (adults only).

BRUSH CREEK RANCH

Saratoga, Wyoming

This 30,000-acre property is another full-service family-friendly luxury dude ranch with horses and a vast slate of summer and winter activities, plus unique lodging options including rooms, cabins, glamping tents, and an adults-only boutique resort. It has a basic list of no-fee spirits, about a dozen standard premium options (Maker’s Mark, Woodford Reserve, Chivas Regal, Jameson), but adds something no other all-inclusive offers: its own distillery, so they also pour their own Brush Creek bourbon and rye. The distillery is part of The Farm, a culinary compound that also includes a bakery, cheesemaking dairy, organic greenhouses, a 30,000-bottle wine cellar, and several restaurants, including Cheyenne Club, specializing in incorporating house-made spirits into food, such as roasted wild game with bourbon demi-glace. The Farm offers distillery tours, cooking, baking, and cheesemaking classes, and is home to the Spirits Vault, a top-shelf lounge (not included in the all-inclusive rate) that has about 100 rare and hard to find whiskies beyond the included basics listed above, with Pappy Van Winkle Family Reserve 23 year old ($400/ oz.) and many single barrel bottlings from Weller, Willet, Blanton’s, Buffalo Trace, Elijah Craig, and more. There are also notable imports like 21 year old Hibiki ($170), Dalmore Constellation 1969 ($1,510), and Glenfiddich 50 year old Old Rare Collection ($1,820). From $1,770/night for two at the Main Lodge. 

TRIPLE CREEK RANCH

Darby, Montana

This dude ranch has a massive slate of outdoor activities—including downhill skiing in winter—along with a full complement of horseback options, yoga, cooking classes, clay shooting, and offbeat choices such as panning for sapphires, geocaching, and frontier skills including axe throwing and fire building. Its high-level culinary emphasis includes on-site chef’s gardens and orchards, and the food is amazing. Wash it down with 30-plus whiskies, with a focus on Montana (Montana Whiskey Company straight whiskey, Montgomery single malt, Willie’s Devil’s Brigade, Glacier Distilling North Fork rye) and other Americans (Michter’s US*1 Small Batch, Woodford Double Oaked), plus scotch and Irish (Glenlivet 12, Laphroaig 10, Green Spot 10, Redbreast 12). From $1,770/night for two (adults only).

GRAND VELAS RESORTS

Mexico

Grand Velas was the first major independent luxury all-inclusive brand, with four large beachfront resorts in Mexico, from the east coast Riviera Maya to the west coast Los Cabos. Every property has multiple restaurants, including fine-dining options and inclusive 24/7 room service. The resorts are all suites with hot tubs, plunge pools, or infinity pools on private terraces. All four locations are luxurious, but the Los Cabos resort is the fanciest (and priciest) and has a list of about 15 premium whiskies, mostly scotch, including Glenfiddich 12, Buchanan’s 12, Old Parr 12, and Glenmorangie 10. From $770/night per person. 

IMPRESSION ISLA MUJERES BY SECRETS

Cancun, Mexico

For its highest-end foray into all-inclusive, Hyatt created a fancier tier of its Secrets brand, Impression by Secrets, with two locations opened so far. Impression features dedicated butler service, 24-hour room service, unlimited dining at seven restaurants, and a bottle of sparkling wine daily. The best whisky selection is at the all-suites Impression Isla Mujeres, on an island off the coast of the Riviera Maya south of Cancun that also includes transfers from the mainland on its private catamaran. The included list is on the shorter side compared to resorts charging twice as much, but still solid for an all-inclusive, with about 20 whiskies like Suntory Hibiki Harmony, Buchanan’s 18, Glenlivet Founders Reserve, and Glenmorangie 10 among other single malts, plus several Irish, Canadian, and American offerings such as Gentleman Jack and Woodford Reserve. From $700/ night per person (adults only). 

DUNTON HOT SPRINGS

Rico, Colorado

Dunton, founded in 1885, was once a booming mining town in the San Juan Mountains. Its silver days were short-lived; by 1918 it was abandoned and languished as a ghost town for almost eight decades until the current owners restored it. The resort is a Wild West village with accommodations and venues in cabins and buildings like the stagecoach depot, sheriff’s office, dance hall, and saloon. It has mineral-rich hot springs and tons of outdoor activities in both summer and winter. Outlaw Butch Cassidy hid out here and carved his initials into the bar, and you can take that in while enjoying an inclusive list heavy on Colorado whiskeys (10 labels from Laws, Distillery 291, Breckenridge, Leopold Brothers, and Storm King) along with a dozen other American labels (Michter’s rye and bourbon, Booker’s, High West, and more), a couple of Japanese including Hibiki, and several scotch options, like Talisker Storm and Laphroaig 10 year old. From $1,165/night for two.
steal-my-sunshine-whisky-cocktail:
Given the role sherry casks play in aging and finishing many whiskies, it’s understandable that sherry works well with whisky in cocktails. Aside from the complementary flavors, splitting a base between sherry and whisky leads to a complex drink that's light enough for summer. Case in point: Steal My Sunshine, created by Alexandra Somers, bar manager at Ovide, Hotel Effie Sandestin, in Miramar Beach, Florida.

The name gives a nod to the desire to hold on to carefree moments—the ones that so commonly occur during the summer with a cool drink in hand.

“This cocktail is bright, layered, and incredibly refreshing,” Somers says. “It opens with tropical notes of pineapple and passion fruit, balanced by fresh citrus and a touch of richness from demerara. The bourbon brings a soft, approachable warmth, while the sherry adds a subtle salinity and nutty depth. Served over crushed ice, it's light, juicy, and effortlessly sippable.”

Steal My Sunshine

  • 1 oz. Basil Hayden (or other straight bourbon)
  • 1 oz. sherry (manzanilla, amontillado, or oloroso recommended)
  • 1/2 oz. Chinola passion fruit liqueur
  • 3/4 oz. pineapple juice
  • 1/2 oz. fresh lemon juice
  • 1/2 oz. rich demerara syrup (recipe below)
  • mint sprig and orange twist for garnish

Add all ingredients to a shaker. Add 3 to 4 ice cubes and hard shake for about 8 seconds. Strain into a rocks glass and pack the glass with crushed ice. Garnish with mint sprig and orange twist.

Rich Demerara Syrup

  • 1/2 cup turbinado cane sugar
  • 1/4 cup boiling water 

In a small nonreactive bowl, add water to sugar and whisk until completely dissolved, about 1 to 2 minutes. Transfer to an airtight container. Keep refrigerated for up to 1 month.
new-whiskey-from-bowmore-barrell-and-mor:
This week brought an interesting mix of new releases, as some producers dropped fresh batches of old favorites while others went out of their comfort zone by experimenting with new styles. In the U.S., New Riff has a new batch of its sherry cask-finished malted rye, Barrell announced a new iteration of its fan-favorite New Year blend, Dublasé has a trio of aged bourbons, blending house Filmland Spirits bottled its first American single malt, craft producer Branch & Barrel distilled its first rye whiskey aimed at bourbon drinkers, and Koopers finished a well-aged bourbon in toasted Texas oak. Over in Scotland, Bowmore released a 20 year old single malt in partnership with New York design studio Snarkitecture.

Bowmore x Snarkitecture 20 year old Oak Voyage Islay Single Malt

ABV: 50.8%
SRP: $360
Availability: Limited; from September

Part of Bowmore’s new Captivo Collection, Oak Voyage aims to highlight the influence of different casks. It matured in bourbon barrels for 20 years before a finish in oloroso sherry-seasoned American oak butts, keeping the focus on one type of oak while changing the seasoning of the wood.

The new series is a collaboration with New York-based design studio Snarkitecture, with the artwork created to act as a portal into the world of Bowmore. The collection consists of two 20 year olds, with the second release, Bowmore Captivo Collection 20 year old Sherry Cask Pursuit, expected to go on sale in Global Travel Retail later this year, bottled at 51.8% and costing $380.

With its distinctive black and red packaging, Bowmore Oak Voyage is totally different from Bowmore Voyage, a non-age statement, cask strength expression released in 2000, which was finished in port pipes.

New Riff Sherry Finish Malted Rye

ABV: 58.65%
SRP: $70
Availability: Limited

The latest iteration of New Riff’s oloroso and Pedro Ximénez-finished malted rye continues on the path forged by its forerunners: It’s made from a mashbill of 100% malted rye, and aged for 6 years. Cask finishes are more of an anomaly for New Riff, which has made a name for itself with single barrel and bottled in bond releases over the years. Even so, they’ve shown a growing prowess for secondary maturation with this whiskey, which has improved upon its scores since its first release in 2022. 

Barrell New Year Blend of Straight Bourbons

ABV: 58.3%
SRP: $85
Availability: Limited

The latest edition of Barrell’s New Year blend of straight bourbons includes components from 7 different states, among them Indiana, Kentucky, Tennessee, Wyoming, Maryland, Texas, and Ohio. The exact blend breakdown is as follows:

  • 7, 8, 9, and 10 year old Indiana bourbon
  • 7 and 8 year old Kentucky bourbon
  • 10 and 16 year old Tennessee bourbon
  • 13 year old Wyoming bourbon
  • 7 and 8 year old Maryland bourbon
  • 5 year old Texas bourbon
  • and 5 year old Ohio bourbon

The derivative mashbill is a four-grain, comprised of 73% corn, 22% rye, 4% malted barley, and 1% wheat. This is the 11th edition of Barrell New Year, which, per the name, is a celebration of the new year to come, and often blends whiskeys from many states and of a variety of ages. It’ll be available nationwide (though in limited quantities) starting next month.

Filmland Spirits The Malted Mummy American Single Malt

ABV: 43%
SRP: $75
Availability: Limited

Los Angeles independent bottler Filmland Spirits, which takes its creative inspiration from B-movies, has blended and bottled its first American single malt. It was sourced from an undisclosed distillery in Iowa and aged for 5 years in oak barrels that previously held IPA. It’s set to make its debut on August 29th.

Filmland may not be a mainstream name in the independent bottler landscape, but it should be on your radar. It has been on a roll in recent years, releasing some very impressive whiskeys like the 92-point Ryes of the Robots and 93-point White Port Wolf. We got an early chance to taste the new whiskey, and it’s another winner, scoring 90 points with our tasting panel. Be sure to check out the full review, and many others, in our upcoming Fall issue, which hits newsstands next month. 

Dublasé Signature Bourbon Trio

ABV: Varies
SRP: Varies
Availability: Limited

Founded by entrepreneur Darrin Eakins back in 2020, Dublasé Whiskey has launched a trio of new bourbons. The whiskeys are demarcated by age and are as follows:

  • Signature No. 9–V: a 5 year old Indiana bourbon (75% corn, 21% rye, 4% malted barley) that spent 2 years aging in Indiana, and the rest of its maturation in Florida, where Dublasé is based
  •  Signature No. 9–VII: a 7 year old Indiana bourbon (75% corn, 21% rye, 4% malted barley) that aged entirely in Indiana
  • Signature No. 9–X: a 10 year old Indiana bourbon (60% corn, 36% rye, 4% malted barley) that aged entirely in Indiana

The new whiskeys will be available online at Dublase’s website, as well at select Florida retailers, starting September 1st (when prices will also go live). They join a 3 year old bourbon and a vanilla-flavored whiskey in the Dublasé lineup.

Part and parcel of Dublasé is a philanthropic mission. A portion of all sales of the Signature Trio will go to the Dublasé Foundation, a non-profit Eakins created in an effort to support minority students pursuing the science, technology, engineering, art, and mathematics fields. So far, Dublasé Whiskey and the Dublasé Foundation have created opportunities that have engaged 175,000 students throughout northeastern Florida.

Branch & Barrel Straight Rye

ABV: 44%
SRP: $35
Availability: Colorado exclusive

Centennial, Colorado’s Branch & Barrel Distilling has released its first whiskey. It was aged for a minimum of 3 years and has a low-rye mashbill of 51% rye, 40% corn, and 9% malted barley. According to master blender Mitchell Nester, he chose the mashbill with bourbon drinkers in mind. “This build is a bit corn-heavy for a rye,” he explains. “But we’re bourbon people, so we’re bringing those bourbon sensibilities to this bottle to create something uncommonly smooth and drinkable.”

The rye for this release was sourced from local growers in the San Luis Valley, where the grain is grown as a cover crop to protect the soil during winter. It’s a variety we’ve seen other whiskey makers use before, with fellow Colorado resident Laws Whiskey House tapping San Luis Valley rye throughout its portfolio.

Koopers Whiskey 8 year old Texas Oak Bourbon

ABV: 57.4%
SRP: $70
Availability: Online and at the tasting room

Texas independent bottler Koopers Whiskey will unveil a new bourbon finished in local oak. The base is an 8 year old MGP bourbon with a mashbill of 75% corn, 21% rye, and 4% malted barley, which was finished in toasted oak barrels constructed from Texas-grown white oak and built by Standard Cooperage—the Lone Star State’s first cooperage—in Blanco.
glamping-near-whiskey-distilleries:
When it comes to touring a distillery, you’ve likely taken the easy route. The one where you fly or drive, stay in a chain hotel, shuffle through the hour-long tour, hear a few new facts about the mashbill and production process, get your three or four included drams, then maybe snag a bottle on your way out of the gift shop. And that’s a perfectly fine way to experience whisky.

But you’re leaving something on the table by not immersing yourself in what the region itself imparts on the whisky. What’s special about this valley, this microclimate, this water source are essential elements that only begin revealing themselves when you stay on or near the land where the whisky is made. Whisky tourism is on the rise internationally, and one corner of the practice offers a deeper connection to what’s in your glass: glamping.

That portmanteau sometimes translates literally as a well-appointed camping tent, though increasingly it’s become more inventive and creative: bourbon-barrel cabins, Airstreams, geodesic domes, and shepherd’s huts. There’s a format for everyone’s level of acceptable ruggedness, but all share the common trait of being positioned within the terroir that shapes the liquid you’re there to enjoy.

That connection between great whisky and its land of origin becomes seared into memory in a way that breezing through a distillery with a friendly tour guide simply can’t replicate. It’s where you are that matters. The land shapes character, so the best way to understand and appreciate what’s in the bottle is to spend the night in the place where it came from.

12 Superb Glamping Sites with Whisky Options 

KENTUCKY

Stay in the Heart of Bourbon Country

Lawrenceburg, Kentucky sits within striking distance of 22 distilleries—Four Roses, Wild Turkey, Woodford Reserve, and Buffalo Trace among them—making it a practical bourbon base camp and a must-visit for serious bourbon pilgrims. Before you start plotting your route, fuel up at Heaven’s to Betsy!, a deli and bakery on Main Street whose sandwiches have derailed more than one carefully scheduled distillery itinerary. Then stay in one of the three more inventive lodging concepts in American whiskey travel that have taken root here.

Get the best sense of what your whiskey undergoes during maturation by sleeping inside a barrel. Bourbon Barrel Retreats offers exactly what the name implies. The custom-built barrel cabins have king beds, private bathrooms, kitchenettes, and air conditioning (vital for humid Kentucky summers). Arranged around fire pits and communal gathering spaces with an on-site restaurant and tasting room, they’re the most Instagram-ready whiskey accommodation on the planet. You can contact management about group rates for four or more barrels, and also tap into the property’s concierge for help with planning your distillery tours and transportation.

Bourbon Barrel Cottages and Tours takes a different approach. Seven private two-bedroom cottages are available, each set on two acres, and each with a private hot tub, fire pit, grill, and covered porch. You can simply stay and enjoy the cottage, or have them book distillery tours for you. If you choose the latter, a Mercedes Sprinter limo shows up at your door and drives you wherever you want to go on the trail. There’s even an option to blend a custom bottle of bourbon at J. Mattingly Distillers.

Looking for something rustic and unusual? EarthJOY Village in Brooksville offers whimsical treehouses, including one designed by Pete Nelson of “Treehouse Masters,” on a 285-acre working farm. Swinging bridges, hammock lounges, composting toilets, and a short walk to a shower provide a proper off-grid sensibility. It’s within striking distance of northern Kentucky’s bourbon scene, near distilleries including Augusta, Old Pogue, and Ohio’s Northern Yankee Moonshine, but the energy here is less barrel room and more deep woods.

Breathtaking views of the Tennessee Valley, heated bathroom floors, stocked mini-fridges, and more await glampers at Treetop Hideaways in Tennessee.

TENNESSEE

Where the Mountains Meet the Mash

The Tennessee Whiskey Trail maps the state’s distilleries against its waterfalls, state parks, and river corridors, then connects them to outdoor accommodations in ways that feel perfect. The result is an itinerary that threads together drams with trail dust and waterfall mist. No need to choose between a hike and a tasting. Enjoy both.

Pick your ideal dwelling at the Little Arrow Outdoor Resort in Townsend: Glamping tents, Airstreams, cabins, tiny homes, and RV hookups are all available at the foot of the Great Smoky Mountains. You’re within minutes of Company Distilling’s 4,000 square-foot tasting room on the Little River, so whiskey is never far away. Tubing, hiking, and biking are all built into the resort’s programming, and there are on-site pools, hot tubs, fishing and swimming holes, and more.

Thinking about a treehouse, but perhaps on the more upscale side? Treetop Hideaways perches luxe abodes on Lookout Mountain, complete with heated bathroom floors, stocked mini-fridges, s’mores kits, and dramatic views of the Tennessee Valley. Chattanooga Whiskey’s Experimental Distillery is right in town, the city’s food scene is underrated, and the overall vibe is more couples retreat than group distillery crawl.

You can also stay in a converted school bus, a covered wagon, or a geodesic dome, as Tennessee Glamping has all three options spread across two locations: one near Savage Gulf State Natural Area for serious hikers, and one at Center Hill Lake for people who’d rather be on the water. Both Cascade Hollow and Rolling Oak Distilleries are nearby, anchoring the whiskey portion of the trip.

In Bon Aqua—this is Johnny Cash country, where the Man in Black himself kept a farm—Piney River Resort offers affordable glamping tents with air conditioning and private bathrooms, tiny homes that are drenched in sunlight, and RV spots. Bon Aqua is perfectly positioned between Nashville’s bustling distillery scene and the Middle Tennessee trail stops.

TEXAS

A Different Kind of Whiskey Country

Spend enough time in Kentucky or Tennessee, and you might forget that serious American whiskey happens elsewhere, so Texas is a flavorful reminder. Treaty Oak Distilling sits on a 28-acre ranch called Ghost Hill, 30 minutes southwest of Austin. The surrounding Dripping Springs corridor has slowly become a distillery district, with Desert Door Sotol and Dripping Springs Vodka springing up as neighbors. Geodesic domes, Hill Country bell tents, and the gypsy wagons at Ranch 3232 all serve as outdoor accommodations. Add live music, serious Texas barbecue, and nighttime visibility that bourbon country can’t match, and you have a whiskey trip with an entirely different energy.

SCOTLAND

The Land Behind the Liquid

For those itching for a new stamp in their passport, decamp across the pond to stay where the Water of Life originated. For peat lovers, Islay is where you want to be, and Islay Glamping Pods is where you want to stay. Featuring both pods (micro-houses) and bothies (small cottages), you’re situated on Lagavulin Bay with views of Dunyvaig Castle and direct access to the Three Distilleries footpath connecting Lagavulin, Laphroaig, and Ardbeg. Three of the most iconic names in single malt scotch are walkable from your pod. Herons, seals, otters, and white-tailed eagles are regular visitors. The combination of peat smoke drifting from the distilleries and the Atlantic light cast over the bay makes for an idyllic setting.

Venture to the mainland and the Speyside region to book a stay with Cairnty Lodges and Glamping Pods. You’ll stay along the Malt Whisky Trail with Glenfiddich, Glenlivet, Macallan, and Cardhu all within easy reach, and Cairngorms National Park, with all its golden eagles, red deer, and ancient Caledonian pine forest as the backdrop. This is serious wildlife and hiking territory. Venture toward the abandoned railway that used to connect all these distilling greats, which has been repurposed as a walking trail, or book a fly-fishing session at a fishing beat along the River Spey. You won’t be disappointed.

Looking for more adventure than camping can provide? Try the Hebridean Sea Safari, a four-night sea expedition offered through Glenapp Castle in Ayrshire. During the days, you’ll travel by boat through Jura, Islay, Eilean Mòr, and Gigha. Your nights are spent in luxury tents pitched by the staff in remote locations, and your meals are prepared by a private chef. Distillery visits to Lochranza and Lagg on Arran are built in. So are possible sightings of basking sharks, dolphins, and minke whales. Keep your camera or phone close; it’s a tremendously cinematic trip.

NORTHERN IRELAND

The Oldest and Wildest

Old Bushmills Distillery has a long history of whiskey making along the Causeway Coast that surrounds the grounds and covers 120 miles of UNESCO-designated coastline past the Giant’s Causeway, the Carrick-a-Rede rope bridge, and the Dark Hedges, the tree-tunnel road that doubled as King’s Road in “Game of Thrones.”

Multiple glamping operations have sprung up across the landscape. Pods, wigwams, shepherd’s huts, and log cabins are scattered from Bushmills village to working farms by the Dark Hedges. Thornfield Farm’s pods sit on a working property directly adjacent to that iconic avenue of trees. Causeway Country Pods in the village itself has private hot tubs and fire pits, with the Bushmills tasting room just minutes away.

The scenery is among the most dramatic in the British Isles. Sipping a Bushmills 16 year old single malt while watching the sun drop into the sea from a coastal pod is its own special argument for slowing down and contemplating the good fortune that brought you to an amazing place like this.
20-whiskies-rated-90-points-or-higher-pr:
Looking for good, solid whiskies that won’t break the bank? These recent releases are worth stepping out of your go-to lane and exploring something new. All these whiskies have a suggested retail price of $75 or less, and all scored 90 points or above.

93 points - Filmland Spirits Moonlight Mayhem! 2 The White Port Wolf bourbon, 47%, $65

This white port cask-finished 7 year old bourbon comes from Los Angeles-based non-distiller producer and blender Filmland Spirits, which takes inspiration from B-movies. It features a high-rye mashbill, with 75% corn, 21% rye, and 4% malted barley.

93 points - Knob Eli Manning Bold Pick Cask Strength Single Barrel bourbon (2026), 58.2%, $70

For the NFL fans out there: this Knob Creek single barrel bourbon was made in collaboration with former Giants quarterback Eli Manning. As part of the partnership, Manning tasted through a variety of Knob Creek barrels alongside master distiller Freddie Noe; the two selected a 9 year old bourbon with notes of vanilla, butterscotch, cherry, and espresso, among others.

93 points - Two Stacks Triple Sherry Cask Finish Irish Single Pot Still, 43%, $49

This was aged in bourbon barrels, then parceled and individually finished in oloroso, amontillado, and Pedro Ximénez sherry casks (hence the name Triple Sherry). Two Stacks doesn’t make its own whiskey, but aims to honor Ireland’s history of sourcing, aging, and blending distillate.

92 points - Elijah Craig Barrel Proof (A126) bourbon, 60.2%, $75

Elijah Craig Barrel Proof rye stole our hearts in 2025, when it was named our Whisky of the Year, so it shouldn’t come as a surprise that the second edition keeps a good thing going. This one is quite a bit hotter than the first release, coming in at 60.2% ABV (compared to 2025’s decidedly lighter 54% ABV).

92 points - Maker’s Mark 7 year 2 month old Cask Strength bourbon, 56.3%, $50

With this whiskey, Maker’s marked a first: it added an age statement to one of its bourbons. While the cask strength has existed since 2014, it’s now a loud and proud 7 year old.

92 points - Killowen Rum & Raisin Irish single malt, 55%, $70

This was distilled at Great Northern Distillery, aged in bourbon barrels, and ultimately finished in a combination of Pedro Ximénez sherry butts and Killowen’s dark rum casks. Consider trying this alongside or over some rum and raisin ice cream.

92 points - Skellig Six 18 Small Batch PX Cask Finished Irish blend, 40%, $40

For this release, Skellig blended sourced single pot still and single grain whiskeys, then gave it a Pedro Ximénez sherry cask finish. Skellig, based in the coastal town of Cahersiveen, takes its name from Skellig Michael, where 6th-century monks carved 618 steps into rock before building their monastery at the summit.

91 points - Wheel Horse Cigar Blend Sherry, Port, & Armagnac Cask Finished bourbon, 50.5%, $40 

The latest cigar blend bourbon from Wheel Horse is its oldest yet at 5 years old; it consists of sourced whiskeys from unnamed Kentucky distilleries, and is finished in a combination of port, cognac, sherry, and armagnac casks. Light up your favorite stogie and enjoy it with a pour of this.

91 points - Lagavulin 11 year old Sweet Peat Bourbon Cask Aged scotch single malt, 43%, $70

We’re well aware that the word peat can be an instant turn-off for some, but Lagavulin wants to ease you into your peat journey with Sweet Peat, which was made with approachability in mind and pulls out sweet notes alongside the peated ones.

90 points - Bardstown Bourbon Co. Origin Series Bottled in Bond bourbon, 50%, $50

Bardstown Bourbon Co.’s 6 year old bottled in bond bourbon is a wheater, featuring a mashbill of 68% corn, 20% wheat, and 12% malted barley. It’s part of the distillery’s Origin Series, which highlights its own-make distillate.

90 points - Bulleit Mesquite Smoked Malt bourbon, 46.5%, $50

Bulleit took a leap with this bourbon: it’s the distillery’s first-ever departure from its signature high-rye bourbon mashbill, instead consisting of 65% corn, 30% mesquite-smoked barley, and 5% malted barley. That mesquite-smoked barley means there’s earth and smoke at play here, making for a fun twist on a classic whiskey.

90 points - Buzzard’s Roost Double Oak bourbon, 50%, $45

In making this bourbon, Buzzard’s Roost sourced distillate from MGP, then finished it in proprietary casks that are specially toasted and feature a lighter char. The resulting whiskey is dessert in a glass.

90 points - Carlyle Master Blender's Selection 16 year old blended scotch, 40%, $35

At just $35, this might be the best value you’ll see for a 16 year old scotch. It’s a blend of more than 20 components, and spent its maturation in bourbon barrels.

90 points - Chattanooga Barrel Finishing Series Triple Islay Cask Finished Blend of Straights blended American whiskey, 55.5%, $90

Part of Chattanooga’s Barrel Finishing Series, this release celebrates Islay. First is the whiskey itself: it’s a 5 year old custom blend of three different peated whiskeys, each made with a unique peated malt sourced from three different UK malthouses. The finish leans into peat even more, with the whiskey seeing secondary maturation in three types of scotch casks from three of the island’s distilleries—a peaty promised land!

90 points - Clan Colla Uasis The Triple blended Irish whiskey, 43%, $46 

This sourced blend from Galway’s Ahascragh Distillery contains 50% grain, 25% single pot still, and 25% single malt Irish whiskeys.

90 points - Loch Lomond Triple Oak single malt scotch, 40%, $45

This isn’t a new Loch Lomond, per se, but it did get a facelift and is now part of the brand’s The Original Series. As the name suggests, it’s aged in three types of American oak: first-fill, refill, and re-char.

90 points - Shelby Co. Peaky Blinders bourbon, 45%, $45

If you’ve ever tuned into the Peaky Blinders television series, perhaps you’ll want a taste of the Peaky Blinders whiskey, which was distilled by Kentucky’s Green River Distillery but has Irish influence by way of an Irish whiskey-soaked oak stave finish. The best of both worlds!

90 points - Shortbarrel Four Grain bourbon, 46%, $40

This is a blend of Kentucky bourbons made from corn, rye, wheat, and malted barley. Before bottling, the whiskey saw additional maturation at Shortbarrel’s Atlanta, Georgia-based distillery and tasting room.

90 points - Stoll & Wolfe Pennsylvania rye, 45%, $48

Made from the same recipe and process passed down by legendary Pennsylvania master distiller Dick Stoll, this rye is corn heavy, with a mashbill of 60% rye, 30% corn, and 10% malted barley.

90 points - Traveller No. 40 Full Proof blended American whiskey, 60.5%, $40

The second whiskey from Buffalo Trace and musician Chris Stapleton is bottled at a bold 60.5% ABV, much higher than the flagship’s 45% ABV. The result is a whiskey with more panache than the original, if you can handle the heat.
thunder-bird-whiskey-cocktail-recipe:
“Most summer cocktails are either too sweet or too simple,” says Max Schikora, bar manager at Huna in Ann Arbor, Michigan. So, he set out to create a drink that is refreshing but has weight. For inspiration, he thought back to a rye whiskey-based Jungle Bird riff created by one of his mentors.

“I kept the rye—because that’s where my story starts—but brought rum back into the conversation to reconnect with the original Jungle Bird. It's a split-base drink, but it's also a split timeline: part homage, part evolution,” he says.

His Thunder Bird has a bright, juicy hit of pineapple and lime up front, then Campari slides in with just enough bitterness to keep the drink honest, while rye brings spice and structure. “You’ve got sweetness, acid, bitterness, and a surprising amount of structure, all working together without stepping on each other,” Schikora says. “And it drinks easier than it should for something with this much proof behind it. I usually say it tastes like a vacation—one you actually remember!”

The Thunder Bird

  • 3/4 oz. Rittenhouse bottled in bond rye (or other 100-proof rye)
  • 3/4 oz. Jamaican rum
  • 3/4 oz. Campari
  • 1/2 oz. fresh lime juice
  • 1/2 oz. demerara syrup (recipe below)
  • 2 oz. pineapple juice
  • pineapple wedge for garnish

Add all ingredients to a shaker with cubed ice. Shake for 5 to 8 seconds. Strain over fresh ice in a double Old Fashioned glass. Garnish with pineapple wedge.

Demerara Syrup

  • 1/2 cup demerara sugar
  • 1/4 cup hot water

In a nonreactive bowl, stir until fully dissolved (this should take less than 5 minutes). Let cool, then transfer to an airtight container. Keep refrigerated for up to 2 weeks.
jameson-single-pot-still-garrison-cowboy:
Atop this week’s new releases is a single pot still whiskey from Jameson, an Irish brand that’s best known for its flagship blend. While the whiskey, which is matured in five different cask types, is brand new to the U.S., it’s not actually new to Jameson—it’s been on European shelves since 2022, and takes inspiration from a recipe written by John Jameson II back in 1826. From neighboring Scotland comes a single malt from Bruichladdich, the final expression in its trio of releases celebrating its 25th anniversary. Elsewhere, Garrison Brothers has the latest iteration of its uncut, unfiltered Cowboy bourbon, Redemption has debuted its first-ever bottled in bond whiskey, Chattanooga has introduced a blend finished in Moldovan ice wine casks, and Breckenridge has added a peach-flavored whiskey to its stable.

Jameson Distiller’s Batch Irish Single Pot Still

ABV: 46%
SRP: $50
Availability: Nationwide beginning in September; imported by Pernod Ricard USA

Jameson’s newest addition is a single pot still whiskey, not a blend, departing from its long-standing profile. There is historical precedent for this move: one of the earliest recipes in the Jameson archive is a mashbill for single pot still whiskey written by John Jameson II in 1826, when Jameson was made at Bow Street Distillery in Dublin. Fast forward 200 years, and Jameson master distiller Kevin O’Gorman has created this triple-distilled single pot still whiskey made from a mash of malted and unmalted barley at Midleton Distillery, near Cork. It’s matured in five cask types, including first and second-fill bourbon, oloroso from the Antonio Páez Lobato cooperage, and three types of virgin oak: Irish, American, and European.

Jameson Distiller’s Batch will introduce more people to single pot still whiskey, Ireland’s signature whiskey style, at a friendly price point. Originally released in Europe in 2022 as Jameson Single Pot Still, Distiller’s Batch joins other single pot still whiskeys in the Irish Distillers portfolio, including Redbreast, Spot Whiskeys, and select expressions from Method and Madness, Powers, and Midleton Very Rare.

Bruichladdich Greener Still Islay single malt

ABV: 51.6%
SRP: $160
Availability: Limited

The last of Bruichladdich’s 25th anniversary celebration bottlings has arrived, following in the footsteps of Yellow Submarine III and Old Skool. Greener Still is a 15 year old unpeated single malt that’s distilled from organic, biodynamic, and bere barleys. The organic barley was grown on the Scottish mainland, the biodynamic barley was sourced from Yatesbury House Farm in Wiltshire, England—marking Bruichladdich’s sole exception to its rule of using 100% Scottish barley—and the bere barley, developed in partnership with the University of the Highlands Islands’ Agronomy Institute, was grown on Orkney. Greener Still matured entirely in first-fill bourbon casks. The whisky is the fourth addition to the distillery’s Still Series, which previously included Blacker Still, Redder Still, and Golder Still, all of which put the spotlight on the distillery’s experimental cask maturation.

The name Greener Still, as well as the combination of barleys used, is a nod to Bruichladdich’s longtime commitment to environmentally conscious practices, both at the agricultural level and within the distillery. Since re-opening the distillery 25 years ago, Bruichladdich has trialed various ways to reduce its impact, ranging from regenerative agriculture and experimentation with low-carbon biofuels to exploring renewable heating solutions. Ultimately, its goal is to eliminate its carbon dioxide emissions entirely.

Garrison Brothers Cowboy Bourbon

ABV: 70.5%
SRP: $250
Availability: 16,000 bottles

The 12th edition of Garrison Brothers Cowboy bourbon is here. The whiskey is among the Hye, Texas-based distillery’s most highly coveted. Year-to-year, Cowboy bourbon generally follows the same blueprint: Bourbon aged at least 8 years, and bottled at cask strength. A distillery event for the bourbon also comes around each release; this year, it’s kicking off at 8 a.m. on September 12th. There’ll be coffee, breakfast, and lunch available at the distillery’s on-site restaurant The Whiskey Shack, as well as live music, bottle signings, specialty cocktails, tastings, and tours. While there are 16,000 bottles total of this year’s Cowboy, 1,000 of those are relegated to the launch event, and another 279 will be available on the distillery’s online store starting Friday, September 18th (the vast majority will be available nationwide).

Redemption Single Barrel Bonded Bourbon

ABV: 50%
SRP: $50
Availability: Limited

Redemption’s latest bourbon is its first bottled in bond whiskey. The new release is a Ross & Squibb-sourced distillate aged for 6 years; each barrel was hand-selected by master blender Alan Kennedy, then bottled by Redemption in Frankfort, Kentucky. The bourbon also marks the relaunch of Redemption’s Higher Marques collection, which features some of the brand’s more elevated and limited edition whiskeys (previous releases included the Cognac Cask Finish high-rye bourbon and wheated bourbon). It’ll begin rolling out next month, both in stores and reservebar.com.

Alongside the bottled in bond bourbon comes the return of Redemption’s Ancient Series 18 year old bourbon, which originally debuted last summer. When it appears on shelves once more this coming fall, it’ll have a $400 price tag, keeping it in line with last year’s release. Like the original, this is a blend of ultra-aged barrels distilled at MGP (back when it was Lawrenceburg Distillers Indiana).

Chattanooga Moldovan Ice Wine Finished Blend

ABV: 47.5%
SRP: $60
Availability: At the distillery and online

Chattanooga Whiskey has unveiled the eighth entry in its Barrel Finishing Series. This one was finished in ice wine casks sourced from an undisclosed winery in the hills of Moldova overlooking the Black Sea. It’s a blend of five different malt whiskeys and one bourbon, all of which contain specialty malted grains including barley grown on the Italian coast near Venice and two varieties of malted wheat.

Ice wine is a relatively rare style of wine because it requires certain weather conditions. It’s produced from grapes—typically white, but sometimes red—that are frozen on the vine and pressed without being thawed, yielding a very concentrated and sweet wine that’s rife with notes of honey, lychee, stone fruits, and bright citrus. Ice wine casks are quite rare in the whisky world, but a handful of distillers use them to craft decadent, dessert-like drams. Examples include Barrell Craft Spirits, Two Stacks, Writer’s Tears, and Glenfiddich 21 Winter Storm.

Breckenridge Peach

ABV: 36%
SRP: $35
Availability: Nationwide

The second flavored whiskey from Colorado’s Breckenridge Distillery takes inspiration from the state’s late-summer harvest, when peaches ripen by the thousands. The new release begins with a base of 5 year old Breckenridge—instead of proofing the whiskey down solely with water, locally sourced Palisade peach juice is also incorporated. According to master distiller Hans Stafsholt, this allows the peach flavors to more fully integrate with the bourbon’s notes. Breckenridge Peach is currently available at Colorado retailers; it'll go nationwide this fall.

Breckenridge first dabbled in flavored whiskey in 2025, when it released a honey-infused limited edition variant in collaboration with the Denver Broncos NFL team. That was followed by a permanent Honey whiskey earlier this year, also infused, but with Goldswarm raw honey from Nigeria.
whisky-auction-results-august-14-2026:
Collectors brought some much-needed excitement to the auction scene in early August with the return of several heavyweight expressions, signaling a shift in momentum from July. Unicorn Auctions brought a huge haul of Willett bottles to auction and smashed the world record for Willett Family Estate 23 year old Bourbon “Bigfoote” Private Barrel B57 with a winning hammer price of $39,200. Chef Sean Brock named this bottling “Bigfoote” after Edwin Foote, the former master distiller at Old Fitzgerald (Stitzel-Weller) and Bernheim Distilleries. Unicorn’s first sale of Willett Family Estate 18 year old Bourbon “Soppressata” Private Barrel 79, a bottling selected by Bill Thomas, owner of Jack Rose Dining Saloon, sold for $28,900. The first bottle of LeNell’s Red Hook Rye 23 year old Barrel No. 1 to appear since January sold for $32,600.

Whisky Auctioneer set a new record for Macallan TIME:SPACE 84 year old at $128,487. This is the highest auction price for Macallan so far this year, and represents a 26% increase over the previous record set in March, when it sold at auction for the first time in Hong Kong. The Whisky Auctioneer auction also included a dazzling 1.5-liter decanter of Glenfarclas Pagoda Ruby Reserve 1954 62 year old, which fetched $20,287. Antique scotches also performed well; a bottle of Glamis 10 year old Unblended Pot Still Malt (pronounced “Glams”) distilled in the 1930s sold for $14,201, a bottle of Berry Bros. & Co. Talisker 8 year old produced in the 1940s fetched $11,496, while a screwcap bottle of Laphroaig 10 year old from the 1960s took $7,844. McTear's, Glasgow sold a Macallan in Lalique 72 year old Genesis Decanter for $37,828, an even higher sum than July's sale, which delivered the month's highest hammer price.

Lot of the Week

In 2021, Glenturret marked the 60th anniversary of the E-Type Jaguar, the iconic sports car launched in 1961, with a commemorative bottling. The Highland single malt inside is 30 years old and was created by Glenturret whisky maker Bob Dalgarno from three oloroso-seasoned European oak butts and an amontillado-seasoned American oak quarter cask. This was a release of 265 bottles, a tactical limited edition honoring the 265bhp original specification of the E-type models. Originally, this whisky was only available via the Glenturret website, priced at £1,500, and auction values have varied both higher and lower. The label features the elegance of the E-Type Jaguar with its long, sculpted bonnet, compact cockpit, and sweeping lines to the rear. The launch was celebrated for the 700-mile overnight drive from Coventry to Geneva, known as “The Mad Dash” undertaken by Norman Dewis, Jaguar chief development engineer, in 11 hours, just in time to demonstrate the E-Type to the assembled press and potential buyers at the Geneva Motor Show. Since the Glenturret E-Type release, the distillery has released Glenturret C-Type Jaguar 70th anniversary, a 32 year old single malt composed of oloroso-seasoned European oak hogsheads and a single Pedro Ximénez American oak hogshead, which is rarer still; just 220 bottles were released to reflect the 220bhp of the 24 Hours of Le Mans winner.

dubai-chocolate-and-whisky-pairing:
If you’ve been on TikTok or strolled into a chocolate shop in the past few years, you’ve likely encountered Dubai chocolate. The silky chocolate bar, jam-packed with bright green pistachio cream, tahini, and crunchy fried phyllo dough, has become the most viral sensation in the confectionery world—so much so that its popularity has actually contributed to pistachio shortages worldwide.

It may come as no surprise that Dubai chocolate is a relatively recent invention. In 2021, a then-pregnant British-Egyptian engineer named Sarah Hamouda started a side hustle inspired by her food cravings and began developing a chocolate bar filled with the aforementioned ingredients with the help of her friend and culinary consultant Nouel Catis Omamalin. The following year, Hamouda and her husband Yezen Alani opened FIX Dessert Chocolatier in Dubai with their flagship chocolate bar, Can’t Get Knafeh Of It, before adding a slew of other confections to the FIX portfolio.

Creating chocolate took elements of a popular Middle East delicacy called ‘knafeh’ and wrapped it in high-end Belgian chocolate. “Knafeh has a base of kataifi, which is a dried and shredded phyllo dough that gets fried in butter to make it crunch, says Todd Robinson, director of operations at Robinson Confections in Hayden, Ohio. “For knafeh, you’d make sort of a crust out of this and then fill it with pistachio cream mixed with tahini (ground sesame seed), and add other things like cheese or cream.” In Dubai chocolate’s case, the cheese and non-pistachio cream are left out.

As Robinson puts it, “If you are a pistachio lover, [Dubai chocolate] is quite literally one of the best things you’ll ever eat in your entire life.” As good as it is on its own, we feel that a dessert so decadent deserves an equally decadent dram to go with it. So here are stellar whiskies that pair perfectly with the myriad textures and rich, nutty flavors of Dubai chocolate. 

7 Whiskies to Pair With Dubai Chocolate

95 points - Rampur Barrel Blush Indian Single Malt, 45%, $105

This hails from the Himalayan foothills, where extreme temperature fluctuations cause barrel influence to set in rapidly. That means intense flavors from both bourbon barrels and Australian shiraz wine casks. Pistachio, chocolate, rose, raspberry, and vanilla are a flavor combo made in heaven, and those notes are all present when you snack on a Dubai chocolate bar and wash it down with sips of Rampur Barrel Blush.

94 points - Port Charlotte 18 year old Scotch Single Malt (2025 Release), 51.5%, $200

This single malt from Islay’s Bruichladdich Distillery contains a healthy dose of peat, so a note of earthy campfire smoke is present from start to finish. However, this feature only amplifies the whisky’s flavors of salted caramel, butterscotch, dried figs, and ginger. With peat and an ensemble of barrels ranging from bourbon and sherry to French oak casks all at play, sipping this between bites of the chocolate is like having a s’more layered with tahini and pistachio cream.

94 points - Wild Turkey Rare Breed Barrel Proof Straight Rye, 56.1%, $60

For those looking to pair Dubai chocolate’s hallmark pistachio-and-chocolate flavors with mint, citrus, and oak, seek out Wild Turkey Rare Breed Barrel Proof straight rye. The whiskey’s nose doubles down on woodsy notes of cedar, oak, and mint, while the palate offers waves of oranges, barrel char, and myriad herbs. Unlike most Wild Turkey products, this expression is non-chill filtered, ensuring a rich texture that contrasts with the chocolate bar’s crunch. 

93 points - Kentucky Peerless Double Oak Bourbon, 54.35%, $95

Kentucky Peerless Double Oak is no shrinking violet. It’s bottled at cask strength and spends at least 4 years in a charred new oak barrel before being transferred to another charred new oak barrel for further aging. The result is a bourbon chock-full of oak influence with a rich, luscious texture that complements Dubai chocolate’s nuttiness and counteracts its satisfying crunch. The whiskey’s flavors of apple pie, raisins, and gingerbread only add more to explore. 

92 points - Hibiki Japanese Harmony, 43%, $100

Not all whisky and Dubai chocolate pairings need to be big and bold. For something a bit more delicate and understated, reach for Hibiki Japanese Harmony. This blend consists of multiple malt and grain whiskies from three of Suntory’s distilleries in Japan and contains whiskies aged in various cask types, including mizunara oak—prized for its rarity and unique notes of sandalwood and coconut. The final product is a smooth sipper with plenty of fruit, vanilla, and spice.

92 points - Redbreast 12 year old Irish Single Pot Still, 40%, $70

Hailing from Ireland’s Midleton Distillery, Redbreast 12 year old is the brand’s flagship expression. It’s a triple-distilled single pot still blend crafted from malted and unmalted barley that’s aged in both bourbon and oloroso sherry casks. The resulting profile dishes up plenty of pot still baking spice notes, along with bourbon barrel sweetness and nutty, dried-fruit flavors courtesy of the sherry casks. The whiskey’s nutty notes help enhance pistachio and tahini flavors in the chocolate. 

90 points - High Wire Distilling Co. 7 year old Jimmy Red Limited Edition Wheated Bourbon (Batch 6), 53.5%, $100 

South Carolina’s High Wire Distilling Co. has been using the once nearly extinct Jimmy Red corn varietal to make bourbon since the brand’s inception in 2013. While every Jimmy Red release is unmistakably “bourbon” in profile, the prized corn brings a nice peanut butter flavor into the mix, and few things pair better with chocolate than peanut butter. This particular expression contains wheat in its mashbill, which softens the bourbon and adds further complementary flavors of cherry gelato and caramel.
first-west-explorer-reviewed:
Since father-son team Rick and Ricky Johnson set out to make whiskey seven years ago, the focus has been on heirloom corn. Their shared passion for grains stems from the family’s high-end popcorn business, which gave them experience in working with unusual types of corn, most notably a proprietary black variety named Baby Black. They enlisted Bardstown Bourbon Co. to contract distill these heirloom grains, as well as some more traditional varieties.

As those stocks were maturing, the Johnsons turned to blending ultra-aged sourced whiskeys, which they bottled under the 15 Stars label. These blends were excellent—of the 11 expressions we’ve tasted, most have earned ratings of 92–93 points, with none scoring below 90—but drinkers remained curious about how the brand’s Baby Black bourbons would turn out. Now they’ll get a chance to taste it for themselves, with the Johnsons finally putting their black corn distillate on display with a permanent expression called First West Explorer.

Black Beauty

Explorer is the brand’s first expression to entirely use contract-distilled liquid from Bardstown Bourbon, with previous bottlings always containing some whiskey sourced from elsewhere. It’s a blend of two bourbons: The base is a more traditional wheated bourbon, with a mashbill of 70% yellow dent corn, 18% wheat, and 12% malted barley. The other component is a ryed bourbon with a mashbill of 70% Baby Black corn, 18% rye, and 12% malted barley. It’s age-stated as 5 years old on the back label, but it also contains slightly older liquid, including some of the stocks the Johnsons laid down seven years ago. It was bottled under the First West brand, a sister label to 15 Stars that focuses on heirloom grains, and debuted last August with three permanent expressions. 

Baby Black is a very unfamiliar variety of corn, and there’s a good reason for that. This heirloom grain—just like the red, white, and blue corn used for First West—was developed exclusively for the Johnsons. The Johnsons grow some of these grains on their own farms, with the rest cultivated on contract by farmers in Kentucky and Indiana. As the name suggests, Baby Black corn has striking onyx-colored kernels that are surprisingly tiny, measuring about a quarter of the size of their yellow counterparts, with ears that grow 5 or 6 inches long. Flavor-wise, the Johnsons say that Baby Black contributes butter, peppermint, and sweetness. But the defining characteristic is its natural viscosity, boasting a rich, creamy mouthfeel that emerges in the new make, making it an attractive blending component. 

With that in mind, the Johnsons plan to continue using Baby Black bourbon as a blending component for other First West expressions. They believe the black corn bourbon is strong enough to stand on its own, but the viscosity and flavors go a long way in elevating the complexity of other whiskeys in a blend. They haven't completely ruled out the possibility of showcasing that distillate on its own. They’re exploring the possibility of eventually bottling it—alongside other heirloom and non-heirloom mashbills—in a single barrel format, with the intention of giving drinkers the ability to taste the individual blend components.

Beyond this specific proprietary variety, black corn is still exceedingly rare in the whiskey world. Other examples include the Mexican Sierra Norte, which produces a single barrel whisky made from native Oaxacan black corn, and Don Michael Distillery in Lima, Peru, which widely uses Andean black corn in its Black Whiskey brand.

How Does First West Explorer Taste?

92 points—First West Explorer Kentucky Straight Bourbon

ABV: 47.5%
SRP: $50
Availability: Nationwide as a permanent release

The nose offers ginger, dried herbs, generous cinnamon spice, caramel, baked apple, vanilla, and barrel char, leading to a mellow, smooth palate with nutmeg, almond, vanilla coconut ice cream, and a halo of mellowed sweetness. The warm, full finish is loaded with chocolate, spice, and peanuts, plus the flavors of the palate continuing. This one just keeps on coming with an excellent follow-through; it’s well balanced and delicious.—David Fleming
louisville-rickhouse-whiskey-co-tastings:
The barrels are the first thing you notice. Two hundred of them, stacked on ricks in a government-bonded room in the middle of Louisville's NuLu district. The barrel heads are facing you, so you can be impressed when you see the stencils of Jim Beam, Barton, Campari, O.Z. Tyler (now Green River), staring back at you. That transparency is the point. Louisville Rickhouse Whiskey Co., which opened in late July, wants you to see its fantastic sourcing before you taste it.

The company is the Kentucky offshoot of Nashville Barrel Company, the Tennessee non-distilling producer that co-founder Mike Hinds and his partners Casey Kostrzebski and James Davenport built into a national name through single-barrel selection and small-batch releases. Coming to Louisville was always the goal. “We wanted to get to the mecca of bourbon tourism,” says Hinds. After years of perfecting the craft in Nashville, the team wanted to share its aged whiskey with a bigger audience, in the city with the deepest claim to it.

A Tennessee company opening in the bourbon capital could read as an intrusion. Hinds heads it off by leaning into Kentucky rather than around it. “Some of our favorite bourbons are from Kentucky. And location matters. We want to make sure we’re a welcome addition to the neighborhood,” Hinds laughs. For the new space, 90% of the barrels in Louisville Rickhouse are from legacy Kentucky distillers, with the remaining 10% from outside the state, including Tennessee and Indiana. Guests can taste through six, seven, or eight Kentucky and Indiana distilleries in one visit, a spread few single-brand tasting rooms can offer.

Three Ways to Taste at Louisville Rickhouse

What sets the space apart from a conventional distillery tour is the level of education that Hinds and the team have imbued into the three ticketed experiences, which allow guests to taste straight from the barrel (a fourth tasting of a curated flight is also available). There’s a Rare and Allocated Tasting ($75), which allows participants to select four self-pulled pours of whiskey aged over 10 years. The current lineup includes a 19 year old Tennessee bourbon, a 15 year old Indiana rye, a 12 year old double-oaked Kentucky bourbon, and a 12 year old Indiana bourbon. Hinds expects to always have ultra-aged stock available. “We’re giving you some of the best whiskey made, not just our core items,” he said.

The Single-Barrel Experience ($150), ported from Nashville, walks guests through a blind barrel pick usually reserved for stores, bars, and “rich people,” Hinds quips. Guests sample four barrels, choose their favorite, and leave with a bottle of it. Interestingly, participants aren’t given the opportunity to select a favorite mashbill or age range; constraints that are deliberate. “After watching this for five years [at the Nashville distillery], most people pick what they say they don’t like,” Hinds says. Guests arrive certain they hate rye and leave converts, he says, adding that each barrel is between 7 and 10 years old and typically includes three bourbons and a rye, though precise options are up to the guides helming the experience. 

The third tasting, The Experimental Deep Dive ($50), presents four barrel-finished pours of honey, maple, madeira, and cognac casks, with a maple rye often in the rotation. “While you taste, we tell you about the process. How to know when to dump it, what you’re looking for from this kind of finish, and more,” says Hinds. These are mostly bourbons, though Hinds has a soft spot for maple-finished ryes.

Pick a Whole Barrel, Bottle It the Same Day

The engine underneath all of this is the barrel program that made Nashville Barrel's name. A group can walk in, pick a full barrel, and leave with the bottled result the same day. At $10,000 to $30,000 a barrel, depending on the age and bottle yield, it’s not a cheap proposition, but it’s certainly an interesting one, considering it takes up to 6 months to receive single barrel selections from most major distilleries. And Hinds’ inventory moves. Two weeks ago, with buyers and groups cycling through, the company sold 20 barrels in a single day.

The Same Great Nashville Barrel Co. Standard, Now in Kentucky

The room holds between 150 and 200 barrels, roughly 5% of the company’s total stock, and serves as the last mile for whiskey that is mature and designated as ready for consumption. Most of it is 7 years or older, and the climate-controlled space slows further profile swings. 

The bonded status puts Louisville Rickhouse in company with Angel's Envy, Old Forester, and Michter's, all of which run bonded spaces in the city. “Being bonded brings a huge set of challenges to clear, so it’s pretty cool to have a few hundred barrels sitting in the middle of Louisville,” Hinds says.

While there’s no kitchen, guests can bring their own food. And plenty of good options abound in the Nulu neighborhood. For non-whiskey drinkers accompanying loved ones, there’s a limited list of wine, cocktails, and bubbles, ranging between $12 and $20 per glass. And some merchandise is available, including a very fun hat that simply reads “HAZMAT,” a nod to those who like their whiskey above 140 proof.

Louisville Rickhouse Hazmat Bottle Exclusives

Hazmat hounds will rejoice at Hinds’ launch exclusives: hazmat 19 year Kentucky bourbon. “We knew when we launched here, we wanted to bring the heat,” Hinds says. “We’re sourcing, but we have the best. Not many companies have 19-year Kentucky bourbon, let alone at hazmat proofs.” Hinds declined to comment on the source of these, but you can assume it’s from a heritage distillery with four numbers in its name.

Each run is a single cask, with many being short barrels, and costs $499 per bottle. “We launched with a 54-bottle cask; the one I’m bottling now is 65 bottles. We had one that was 13 bottles at 158 proof, so that ended up being a personal barrel for us,” Hinds says. We tried two of the available cask offerings and were blown away at how underproof they drink. Hinds says he has enough to keep the 19-year run “going for several months.” What’s after that? “We’ll figure that out when we get there,” he laughs.
macallan-glenfiddich-jack-daniels-and-mo:
Scotch takes center stage in this week’s list, headlined by a new Glenfiddich 16 year old released in collaboration with Aston Martin Formula One Team—marking the pair’s second joint project—finished in a mix of bourbon, sherry, port, and wine casks. Macallan concludes The Harmony Collection with two coconut-inspired single malts, while Isle of Raasay has selected Hungarian oak oloroso casks for its latest Oak Species Maturation Series release. Across the pond, Old Forester ages its Louisville’s Whiskey Row distillate in super heavily charred barrels, Jack Daniel’s taps high angels’ share barrels from Coy Hill for its latest Distillery Series expression, Old Overholt has a new 11 year old Extra Aged rye, Wyoming Whiskey celebrates America’s 250th birthday, and Colorado’s Branch & Barrel has a fresh batch of its flagship 5 year old bourbon.

Glenfiddich & Aston Martin Formula One Team 16 year old Limited Edition (Release 2)

ABV: 43%
SRP: $80
Availability: Limited

For the second edition of Glenfiddich’s partnership with the Aston Martin Formula One Team, Glenfiddich malt master Brian Kinsman and Aston Martin Formula One team managing technical partner Adrian Newey experimented with different casks, putting 16 year old Glenfiddich into a combination of first-fill bourbon barrels, port pipes, oloroso sherry casks, unspecified wine casks, and fino sherry butts. In contrast, the first release aged in virgin American oak, bourbon, and American oak casks that previously held an undisclosed type of wine. Next up, Formula One heads to Zandvoort, Netherlands for the Dutch Grand Prix.  

Macallan The Harmony Collection VI Speyside single malt

Macallan The Harmony Collection Inspired by Fresh Coconut

ABV: 46.3%
SRP: $185
Availability: Nationwide

Macallan The Harmony Collection Inspired by Toasted Coconut

ABV: 43.3%
SRP: $185
Availability: Travel Retail exclusive

Evoking the flavors of coconut, Macallan has unveiled the final pair of whiskies in The Harmony Collection. Master whisky maker Kirsteen Campbell crafted the single malts using a combination of sherry-seasoned American oak and bourbon barrels, balancing cask types and whiskies of varying ages to bring coconut notes to the forefront. The Harmony Collection debuted in 2021 and comprises 12 non-age statement whiskies introduced over six years, with two contrasting expressions each year: one for the domestic market and the other for global travel retail. Over the years, the series has drawn inspiration from chocolate, coffee, nature, oak, tea, and coconut, and featured innovative packaging materials that gave new life to organic waste. In 2021, the first release included Rich Cacao and Fine Cacao; Intense Arabica and Smooth Arabica arrived in 2022. The distillery collaborated with Stella and Mary McCartney for the third release, with Amber Meadow and Green Meadow in 2023, and partnered with Cirque du Soleil to mark the release of Vibrant Oak and Guardian Oak during the distillery’s 200th anniversary year. Whiskies inspired by JING tea were released in 2025, adding Phoenix Honey Orchid Tea and Organic Cherrywood Lapsang Tea editions, before the 2026 series conclusion of this pair of coconut-inspired whiskies, which incorporate discarded coconut fibers in the packaging.

Isle of Raasay Hungarian Oak Islands single malt scotch

ABV: 50%
SRP: $110

Hungarian Oak is the latest release in Isle of Raasay’s Oak Species Maturation Series, which explores how different oak varieties influence flavor and texture. For this edition, the distillery turned to oloroso sherry casks made from Quercus petraea, or sessile oak, sourced from Hungary’s Zemplén Mountains. Valued by coopers for its slow growth and tight grain structure, Hungarian oak typically imparts spicy notes to whisky, but seasoning the casks with oloroso sherry tempers the wood's more assertive characteristics and adds layers of dried fruit and sweetness. Isle of Raasay is known for the complexity of its recipes and its innovative approach to multi-cask maturation. Here, peated and unpeated spirits distilled in 2021 were matured separately in Hungarian oak sherry casks before being married together. The result is a whisky that showcases both the influence of this uncommon oak species and Isle of Raasay's signature lightly peated house style.

Isle of Raasay’s Oak Species Maturation Series debuted in 2024 with a whisky fully matured in virgin Colombian oak.
