sam-heughan-actor-and-distillery-owner:
For actor, author, and spirits entrepreneur Sam Heughan, the past decade has been defined by a single name: Jamie Fraser. The Highland warrior at the heart of “Outlander” has become one of television’s most enduring characters: romantic, resilient, and rooted in Scotland’s cultural imagination. But as the eighth season draws to a close on Starz, Heughan finds himself at a turning point. “It has been 12 years playing this character, a quarter of my life,” he reflects. Shooting the final episodes was emotional, as the cast said farewell to locations, fellow actors, and crew. “Looking back, what an amazing job it was, and what a wonderful experience to work in Scotland,” says Heughan. “People will always revisit this show; it’s something that will live on forever.”

In “Waypoints,” Heughan’s 2022 memoir, he describes the challenges he faced trying to break into the acting industry after drama school. He held down numerous temporary jobs, including bartending, while attending countless auditions in London and Los Angeles. “It’s about persistence and luck,” he says. Then his big break came when he was cast as Jamie Fraser, turning him into a household name. He credits Diana Gabaldon, author of the “Outlander” book series, for capturing the public’s imagination, but also understands what made Jamie Fraser resonate so powerfully with fans. He’s an iconic character; Heughan says, “Jamie is stoic and heroic, but he’s got great emotional intelligence. He can be funny, tempestuous, and impulsive.” Scotland is also a major draw, showing a romantic world within pivotal historical events. The series sparked a surge in tourism—dubbed the Outlander Effect—as set-jetting visitors flocked to explore Scotland’s ancient monuments, battlefields, and historic buildings.

For the role, Heughan had to master horsemanship and swordsmanship, hone his firearms skills with pistol and musket, and deliver lines in French and Gaelic. Jamie Fraser is portrayed over four decades, starting in 1743, ahead of the Jacobite Rebellion, and his character takes part in the battles of Prestonpans, Culloden, and Saratoga. Heughan has some mementos from the show, including a full Jamie Fraser outfit of kilt, jacket, waistcoat, sporran, and boots, and his back scars from season one, which hang on his wall. He developed a fascination with antique pistols and began collecting them. “It’s remarkable to hold a weapon that dates back 200 years,” says Heughan. “That’s what’s amazing about Scotland; the history is tangible.” Whisky runs through the storylines in “Outlander,” as Jamie Fraser becomes a wine and spirits merchant, whisky smuggler, and eventually a distiller.

Heughan discovered his own passion for whisky in his early 20s. Feeling homesick while living in London, a fellow Scot took him to a pub on Burns Night and ordered him a single malt. “There was something about it that captured my imagination,” he recalls. “It was evocative; it reminded me of Scotland and transported me back. Whisky holds a real emotional connection for me.” While filming “Outlander,” Heughan deepened his interest in whisky. First, he explored single malt scotch, developing a love of peated and Campbeltown malts, then branched out to Japanese and Indian whiskies. “I started collecting, then realized I’d rather drink them, so all the good stuff is gone,” admits Heughan. “If I’ve got a really fine bottle and there’s a great occasion, I’ll open it.”

One night, inspiration struck Heughan and business partner Alex Norouzi over a whisky in Glasgow’s The Ben Nevis Bar. Having turned down offers from scotch distillers to bottle a whisky in his name, they decided to create their own brand. The Sassenach is named after Jamie Fraser’s affectionate name for his wife Claire, played by Caitriona Balfe, though it’s traditionally used as a derogatory term for the English, or outlanders (outsiders). Heughan chose Michael Henry, master blender at Loch Lomond Group, to create an approachable, balanced blend suited to his palate. “He’s such an amazing talent and understood exactly what I was looking for,” says Heughan. Additional Sassenach spirits followed: Wild Scottish gin, Fine Scottish vodka, and Sassenach Select reposado tequila from El Tequileño. Heughan travels regularly to Mexico and arranged a visit with third-generation master distiller Tony Salles in Jalisco. Over glasses of their respective scotch and tequila, they decided to join forces and create a bespoke tequila. To mark the “Outlander” finale, Sassenach Spirits launched The Jamie Fraser Collection, a limited-edition whisky that includes a letter from Heughan to Fraser reflecting on their shared journey.

The plan was always to find a home for The Sassenach brand, which drew Heughan back home to Galloway. “This historic part of Scotland has ties to Ireland and England, stone circles, castles, lochs, and hills. It really is a magical place.” Heughan took ownership of Galloway Distillery in 2025. Founded by Crafty Distillers in 2013, it’s where Sassenach gin has been produced, and plans are now underway to expand the site and welcome more visitors. “We’ve got 3 year old whisky in casks now, and it tastes amazing. Our first single malt release will be a huge moment, representing Galloway and everything that’s unique about it.”

“I started collecting, then realized I’d rather drink them, so all the good stuff is gone."

After “Outlander,” Heughan played the lead in “Macbeth” with the Royal Shakespeare Company, and will next star as a tough British soldier in “Embassy,” a six-part thriller featuring Anna Kendrick and J.K. Simmons. Heughan has also authored “The Cocktail Diaries,” a collection of fresh, accessible drinks recipes inspired by his global adventures. It’s a refreshing guide to the joy of making cocktails at home, and the antithesis of those dense, technical mixology tomes that can seem intimidating to non-professionals. “I am an enthusiast,” states Heughan. “I’ll flip the book open, see what I have, and play around with it. I’m not really into process; there’s so much to explore with just three ingredients. Choose a mezcal, tequila, or whisky, and it changes the nature of the cocktail itself. It doesn’t need to be difficult; anyone can do it.”
stetson-bourbon-review:
It may surprise you to learn that the Western brand Stetson has never had an official whiskey. The inventor of the cowboy hat and America’s spirit seem meant for a partnership, but the closest we’ve seen was the now-discontinued John B. Stetson Bourbon, launched back in 2012 by a New Jersey wine company that licensed Stetson’s name and logo. This week, Stetson launched Stetson Bourbon, a 7 year old, 100-proof, high-rye offering that’s made by combining Green River Distilling and Bardstown Bourbon Company bourbons, a first-ever collaboration for those two producers.

At a launch fete at Keen’s Steakhouse, Robert Dundon, CEO of Stetson, told attendees that he and his business partners had spent three years traveling the country, searching for the ideal production partner for this whiskey. “We tried bourbons from producers in Texas, North Carolina, Indiana, Ohio, Washington, Tennessee, and Colorado. But Kentucky, as the birthplace of American bourbon, really felt like the right place for us,” he said.

Dundon explained Stetson’s vision was precise and unwavering. “Something that was ultra-premium; that you can drink neat, over ice, or in a cocktail without it getting lost. And we wanted high-rye.” Ultimately, Dundon and Stetson tapped Bardstown Bourbon’s master blender Dan Callaway to craft a proprietary blend for them. Over the course of 100 iterations, Callaway worked with Dundon and the team to create something balanced and distinctly unique, with a focus on the finish.

Callaway, also at the dinner, told the room that “this project was back and forth right up until the very end, swapping barrels,” adding that Stetson was exceptionally committed to getting the product right. That meant pulling in barrels from Bardstown’s sister company, Green River. “Green River always gives those lovely fruit notes, and Bardstown brings more of the barrel character, more structure, more vanillin, and balances this blend nicely,” Callaway said.

The sum of these efforts is good; the bourbon is tasty. On the bright, vibrant nose, there’s ample caramel, green apple, cinnamon, orange zest, baking spices, and a little bit of cherry. The liquid’s rounder and richer than its light weight would have you believe. It takes a second to open up, but then caramel, buttery oak, cherry syrup, and vanilla wafers emerge, and a little rye spice blossoms toward the end of the sip to balance the sweetness and creaminess.

The finish isn’t terribly long, but it starts sweet before fading into baking spices as a final note. It drinks a little higher than its 100 proof, though category newcomers won’t find it aggressive. We tried it neat and in a few cocktails, including a riff on a Manhattan and an Old Fashioned, and it indeed doesn’t get lost when mixed.

Each bottle features an etching on the back, a depiction of “The Last Drop from His Stetson”, a painting by Western artist Lon Megargee from the 1920s that shows a cowboy giving his horse a drink from his hat.

Stetson Bourbon retails for $75 and will be available at the company’s retail store in Texas and online at stetsonbourbon.com, shipping to 40 states.
red-white-blue-corn-bourbons:
In the early days of American distilling, bourbon producers made whiskey from whatever corn was planted nearby, so local corn strains were often the only available source. By the middle of the 20th century, as the bourbon industry consolidated and ramped up production to a national scale, corn was needed in far greater volumes. Local varieties fell by the wayside in favor of high-yielding mass-production hybrids—notably the No. 2 yellow dent hybrid (known for a slight dimple or dent at the top of the kernel). Most major bourbon distillers came to use this efficient, sturdy hybrid, and still do today.

But the craft distilling movement in the 2000s brought a revival of traditional methods, including the use of heirloom strains. While there is no legal definition of heirloom corn in the U.S., they are naturally pollinated varieties—not hybrids—usually passed down through generations. Heirloom corn is best known for its brightly colored kernels of red, blue, purple, black, pink, orange, and other hues, though some types come in the more traditional colors of white and yellow.

Color Combinations, American Style

Texas whiskey maker Still Austin, founded in 2015, has long made heirloom and non-GMO grain a focus of its craft, perhaps more so than any other non-farm distiller. In a 2019 blog post titled “Realness in Red, White, and Blue,” head distiller John Schrepel revealed his mission of focusing on grain and drilling down on regional identity. He foresaw 100% of Still Austin’s grain being grown in Texas, and that is indeed the case today. His ideas called for “new Jimmy Red and ultra-high rye blue corn bourbons, as well as a white corn bourbon.” Still Austin’s first whiskey to feature 100% Texas-grown grain was its straight bourbon released in 2020, beginning the path to making all its whiskeys from local grain.

Still Austin’s most prominent heirloom and non-GMO expressions can be found in its bottled in bond range. The bottled in bond Red Corn bourbon has a mashbill of 36% Jimmy Red and 34% white corn, 25% rye, and 5% malted barley, and was a Whisky Advocate Top 20 whisky in 2024. The distillery’s bottled in bond Blue Corn bourbon is made from 26% blue and 25% white corn, 44% rye, and 5% malted barley, and scored a 93 with our panel. Its bottled in bond bourbon is made of 70% non-GMO white corn, 25% rye, and 5% malted barley, and notched a 92-point rating. The non-GMO white corn it uses is the same as that used for the tortillas made in Austin.

Still Austin also has a bourbon that features the patriotic combination of its red, white, and blue corn expressions: Tanager Cigar Blend, first released in late 2024, is a 6 year old blend of all three. The primary ingredient is its Blue Corn bourbon, which creates most of the sweet flavors, according to master blender Nancy Fraley, while the Red and White Corn bourbons contribute fruit, nuttiness, and spice. Tanager scored 92 points with our tasting panel.

Waving The Colors

While Still Austin is certainly a prominent player in the heirloom corn space, one whiskey maker that’s totally committed to heirloom grains is Shelbyville, Kentucky-based Jeptha Creed. Its involvement began when co-owner Joyce Nethery began growing heirloom tomatoes, which ultimately led her to heirloom corn. Today, the family harvests around 2,000 acres annually on its farm. Bloody Butcher (a red-hued dent variety) is its most prominent heirloom, but the family also grows Hickory King white corn and Bruce’s Blue corn, among others.

Jeptha Creed has also gone all-in on heirloom corn’s patriotic color combination, as its work ultimately led it to create what’s arguably the standout Jeptha Creed expression: Red, White & Blue straight bourbon. Launched in 2021, it’s made from a mashbill of 25% Bloody Butcher, 25% heirloom white, and 25% Bruce’s Blue corn, with 20% malted rye and 5% malted barley. It’s aged 4 years, and, living up to its patriotic theme, a portion of its sales supports veterans’ causes.

In Charleston, South Carolina, husband-and-wife Scott Blackwell and Ann Marshall founded High Wire Distilling in 2013 with a mission to explore the flavors of long-forgotten grains. High Wire went all-in on the Jimmy Red varietal, a strain grown for years on James Island near Charleston. It scaled up sourcing of this once-forgotten grain to the point where today High Wire has hundreds of acres of Jimmy Red planted under contract. Jimmy Red straight bourbon is made from 100% Jimmy Red, and the whiskey is noted for its smooth texture and enhanced flavors, including cherry, marzipan, and almond.

Back in Texas, the state’s original purveyor of heirloom corn whiskey is Balcones, best known for its Baby Blue corn whiskey, the distillery’s inaugural release launched in 2009. Baby Blue is made of 100% roasted blue corn, at first Hopi Blue from New Mexico and later Texas-grown blue flint corn. Fellow Texas distillery Ironroot Republic utilizes heirloom corn varietals “like a spice rack” to enhance flavor, according to co-founder and distiller Jonathan Likarish. The distillery’s flagship Harbinger bourbon’s mashbill includes Andean purple corn from Indiana and Bloody Butcher. Its Hubris and Icarus corn whiskeys also include purple, red flint, and non-GMO yellow dent corn.

Down On the Farm

Other farm distillers besides Jeptha Creed, of course, play a big role in the heirloom scene. Illinois farm-distiller Whiskey Acres has released single corn varietal bourbons made from Oaxacan green corn, blue popcorn, and sweet corn. Its Artisan Series includes a Blue Popcorn and a Bloody Butcher bourbon, which are very limited annual releases that sell out quickly.

There are many smaller farm distillers experimenting with heirloom varietals, and plenty of non-farm distillers who’ve made exciting heirloom corn expressions. Kentucky’s New Riff Distilling has a program exploring older heirloom strains, and its releases have included its Yellow Leaming and Blue Clarage corn expressions. Brooklyn, New York-based Widow Jane began growing an heirloom variety back in 2013 at its upstate New York location, and it even has its own proprietary strain: Baby Jane, an orange-colored heirloom derived from a cross of Bloody Butcher and Wapsie Valley yellow corn. Widow Jane’s Baby Jane bourbon, first released in late 2024, is a blend of its own distillate made from the Baby Jane strain and bourbon sourced from Kentucky.

Mexico’s Bounty

Sierra Norte Distillery, based in San Agustin de las Juntas in the Mexican state of Oaxaca, is among the early pioneers in working with native heirloom corn varieties in a host of different colors. Founder Douglas French can map out the flavor profile for each: white (green husks, peanuts, toasted oak, pepper), yellow (dried chiles, maple syrup, marmalade), black (banana peels, earth, ginger, and roasted corn), red (graham cracker, spices, buttered corn), purple (brisket, peanut shells, star anise), and rainbow, which combines corn from multiple varietals (sweet corn, dried fruits, spice, vanilla). All the corn is from local Oaxacan farmers, and each varietal is distilled in individual batches of 85% corn and 15% malted barley.

Amid this flurry of heirloom corn over the past two decades, the question remains whether heirloom grains actually improve the flavor of a whiskey. Distillers sometimes take opposite sides on the issue, though many whiskeys made from heirloom corn have scored highly. The use of heirloom strains will remain confined to smaller-scale operations or to very limited releases by larger distillers because cost and supply make it difficult to produce large volumes. So expressions made from heirloom corn will remain a small but very interesting and enjoyable part of the whiskey scene—and one whose value and fan appreciation are very likely to grow.
how-to-store-tequila-bottles:
You’ve invested in some premium añejo—maybe that new delicious El Tesoro Mundial Yamazaki finish—or scored a limited-release blanco. You want it to taste exactly as the distiller intended, not flat, faded, or off. Tequila storage follows whisky’s basic playbook: keep it upright, away from heat and light. But ensuring agave spirits never lose their punch involves more nuance than that. For expert guidance, we tapped Tommy Patrick, owner of the renowned Seattle bar The Ballard Cut, which runs deep on both agave and whisky.

The Basics: Upright, Cool, and Dark

Start with the fundamentals. Always store tequila bottles upright, never on their side. Prolonged contact between high-proof alcohol and cork or synthetic closures will degrade the seal over time, potentially affecting the flavor and causing leaks. This applies to both unopened and opened bottles.

Keep them out of direct sunlight or consider a UV tint. “We can’t avoid the sun,” says Patrick, “so we use a 99.999% UV blockage on our windows.” Consider the humidity and temperature—a consistent 55-65°F is ideal— but also the airflow in your storage space. “Having too much air moving can really wick away any moisture and shrivel up corks faster than you think,” says Patrick.

Don’t Leave It Opened Too Long

Once you crack the seal, you’re on the clock. Exposure to air triggers oxidation, which will gradually dull the agave spirit’s vibrant flavors. “The first 10% of any bottle is typically very ‘tight,’ requiring breathing like wine,” says Patrick. The next 20% of the bottle starts to hit its stride, and “the following 30% pours pleasantly, very open and smooth—type and expression dependent,” he says. “The remaining 40% starts to mellow significantly, but many people love this section due to the smoothness.”

Once the bottle is at the 50% mark, you should finish it within a year, Patrick advises, “Given agave’s super-high phenolic particle numbers—think beets, celery, peaty scotch— after this point, it’ll lose its vegetal deliciousness if it softens out too much.” Higher proofs mean longer shelf life, but the halfway mark is your sign to drink the rest of the bottle. Tequila won’t go bad to the point where you’ll ever get sick, but it definitely won’t taste great. And don’t save the last two ounces for a big occasion that’s five years down the road. “It won’t taste anything like what made it special in the first place,” he says.

Skip the Parafilm

Some pros like to parafilm the closures of prized bottles to help thwart oxidation, but Patrick prefers an alternative. “If you’re worried about degradation, replace the closure— cork, synthetic, or glass stopper—with a full contact seal,” he says. You can also take a page from fine wine collectors and replace any air in the bottle with a layer of neutral gas (argon or nitrogen) to slow oxidation.

Others prefer to decant the remaining tequila into progressively smaller bottles, filling them to the top and tightly securing the caps to minimize oxygenation.

The Pros and Cons of Condensation

Seeing little water droplets in your bottle? “It’s good in that it indicates your seal is intact and airtight,” Patrick says. “But condensation means it’s being stored in an area that has too much heat and internal pressure... altering the flavor.” Time is not on your side in this situation; change the storage area’s temperature or move your bottles immediately to remedy the issue.

How to Know If the Bottle Has Turned

Even properly stored tequila can deteriorate over months or years. Each bottle will vary, but there are clear signs if your agave is past its prime. Watch for significant color changes, such as darkening. “If a previously clear blanco becomes cloudy, that’s not good,” says Patrick. “Sediment formation can be natural, but if you come back to a bottle that all of a sudden looks like you just washed your hands after a day at the beach, you should toss it immediately.”

Also, watch out for the palate becoming metallic or flat, and the nose moving into sharp or rancid notes. With any bottle of distillate, if you try it and then ask yourself, “Should I be drinking this?” that’s a giveaway, too. “The answer,” says Patrick, “is most likely no.”
european-oak-barrels:
European oak has shaped scotch whisky since the 18th century, long before American oak (Quercus alba) bourbon barrels entered the picture. Coopers primarily work with pedunculate (Quercus robur) and sessile oak (Quercus petraea), with distillers seeking both new barrels and casks that previously held sherry, port, cognac, or wine. These casks impart whisky with the sweet spiciness of cinnamon, nutmeg, and clove, layered with dried fruits, orange, nuts, and caramel. Sustaining this character depends on healthy forests, yet European oak faces mounting threats from drought, flooding, storms, fires, ecological change, pollution, and pests. As pressure on supply grows, responsible distillers increasingly demand fully traceable oak, knowing that felling less mature trees not only undermines sustainability but can negatively alter the flavor profile of their whisky.

Quercus robur vs Quercus alba

Quercus robur offers higher tannins and greater porosity than its American counterpart, yielding richer colors and deeper flavors. Its slow growth and softer structure make it both prized and more expensive; it’s the OG of scotch whisky maturation vessels.


Distillers’ Favorite

These major distillers regularly use European oak casks, primarily Quercus robur, to mature their whiskies: Bowmore, Dalmore, Kavalan, Macallan, Midleton (for Redbreast), and Yamazaki. Quercus petraea is more commonly used to make wine barrels.

A Tree that Outlives Empires

European oak trees can live for more than 1,000 years. For cooperage-grade timber, only trees that are at least 100-200 years old are considered suitable for felling.

Reaching Higher

European oak trees grow tall and straight, reaching 80-130 feet, while American oaks have a broader canopy and grow to 80-100 feet tall.

Forest Finder

These mighty oaks are native across Europe, spanning from the Atlantic coast to the Ural Mountains. Coopers and distillers particularly prize Spanish and French oak for producing high-quality casks.
peach-and-whisky-cocktail-recipes:
Stone fruit flavors are commonly found in a variety of whisky styles, so it’s only natural that peach shines in whisky cocktails. Keven Stehl, lead bartender at Smith Tower Observatory Bar in Seattle, calls the two “an iconic combination,” noting that, especially when peach is mixed with American whiskey, the resulting cocktail evokes classic Southern flavors. “The caramel notes of bourbon and the spice of rye pair beautifully with the sweet, rich character of peach,” he adds.

Stephen Burgess, lead bartender at Virtue restaurant & bar in Chicago, loves to mix peach with scotch. “The depth of flavor from stone fruits highlights the natural fruit and vanilla character that comes from barrel aging and the subtle peat in some scotches,” he says. “Ripe peaches also have a fantastic balance of acidity and sweetness that provides lift and roundness to punchy whiskies.”

No matter your whisky preference, pairing it with peach in a summery cocktail is a surefire way to beat the heat.

Peach & Peat

Created by Stephen Burgess, lead bartender, Virtue restaurant & bar in Chicago

Shrubs are generally made days in advance, but this cocktail can be made with a same-day variation. In a blender, add the peaches, sugar, and honey and blend until somewhat smooth, then add the vinegar and pulse a few times. Let sit at room temperature for 30 minutes, then strain. “You’ll definitely get a rounder, more flavorful peach taste with the full recipe, but this option is for when you’re short on time but still want a great peachy cocktail,” Burgess says.

  • 2 oz. Monkey Shoulder (or other scotch blended malt)
  • 2 oz. coconut water
  • ½ oz. peach shrub (recipe below)
  • Peach slice or peach rose for garnish

Combine all ingredients in a Collins glass, then fill with ice and give a quick stir. Garnish with a peach slice or peach rose.

Peach Shrub

  • 1½ cup ripe, finely chopped peaches (about 2 medium peaches)
  • 1 cup sugar
  • 2½ Tbsp. honey
  • 1 cup apple cider vinegar

In a bowl, muddle peaches, sugar, and honey. Stir, cover, and refrigerate overnight. The next day, stir in the apple cider vinegar. Cover and refrigerate 1–3 days. Strain through cheesecloth or a fine mesh strainer, pressing gently to release liquid without pushing the pulp through. Keep refrigerated up to 2 weeks.

The Pioneer’s Peach

Created by Keven Stehl, lead bartender, Smith Tower Observatory Bar in Seattle

“Black tea brings a gentle tannin that complements the rye’s oak and spice, and a touch of peach and bright lemon lifts the finish, creating a summer sipper reminiscent of sun-warmed peach iced tea—refined, but easygoing,” Stehl says.

  • 2 oz. Earl Grey tea-infused Old Forester 100 proof rye (or other higher-proof rye; recipe below)
  • ¼ oz. Giffard Pêche de Vigne peach liqueur
  • ¼ oz. Demerara simple syrup
  • 2 dashes Angostura bitters
  • 1 dash orange bitters
  • Lemon peel for garnish

Stir all ingredients with ice. Strain into an Old Fashioned glass over a large ice cube and garnish with a lemon peel.

Earl Grey Tea-Infused Rye

  • 17 oz. Old Forester 100 proof rye
  • 1 ½ tsp. loose Earl Grey tea
  • Steep tea in rye for 2-4 hours, then strain.

Peach Whisky Smash

Created by Will Murphy, general manager, The Falls in Falls Church, Virginia

“Fresh peach and honey-thyme syrup highlight the delicate floral character of Japanese whisky in this light, refreshing Smash designed for easy, elegant sipping at home,” Murphy says.

  • 2 oz. Suntory Toki (or other Japanese blend)
  • 2–3 fresh peach slices
  • ½ oz. honey-thyme syrup (recipe below)
  • 4–6 fresh mint leaves
  • ½ oz. fresh lemon juice
  • Splash soda water (optional)
  • Mint sprig for garnish

Add peach slices and simple syrup to a shaker and gently muddle. Add mint leaves and lightly press to release aroma. Add whisky, lemon juice, and ice. Shake briefly and strain into a rocks glass over fresh crushed ice. Top with a splash of soda water, if desired, and garnish with a mint sprig.

Honey-Thyme Syrup

  • 1 cup honey
  • 1 cup warm water
  • 2 thyme sprigs

Combine honey and water; add thyme sprigs and stir until honey dissolves. Steep for 30 minutes, then remove thyme sprigs and let syrup cool before using. Keep refrigerated for up to 1 month.

Peachy Keen

Created by Kelly Duong, general manager, Kyojin in Washington, D.C.

White peach–infused bourbon is balanced with aromatic pandan syrup and bright lime juice in this smooth and refreshing cocktail.

  • 2½ oz. white peach–infused Maker’s Mark (or other bourbon; recipe below)
  • ½ oz. Tram Phan Tram Salted Pandan syrup
  • 1 oz. fresh lime juice
  • 2 dashes saline solution
  • 2 fresh peach slices for garnish

Shake all ingredients with ice. Strain into a double rocks glass over fresh ice and garnish with peach slices.

White Peach–Infused Maker’s Mark

  • 1½ cups sliced white peaches
  • 12½ oz. Maker’s Mark

Combine peaches and bourbon in a sealed container and refrigerate for 8 hours. Fine strain into a glass bottle and store refrigerated for up to 7 days.

The Mumbai Sour

Created by Patrick Nikel, bar manager, Brass Peacock in Georgetown, Texas

“Indri gives notes of mellow grain in harmony with sweet baking spices. As soon as I tasted it, I knew that a Peach Sour would be an excellent way to utilize the spirit to its full potential. Campari and Chareau bring balance and introduce notes of aloe and mint, making for a fantastic summer drink to either introduce someone new to single malts or bring a welcome change for the aficionado,” Nikel says.

  • 1½ oz. Indri (or other Indian single malt)
  • ¼ oz. Campari
  • ¼ oz. Chareau aloe vera liqueur
  • 1 oz. Liber and Co. Yakima Valley peach syrup
  • 1 oz. fresh lemon juice
  • 2 dashes Regan’s No. 6 orange bitters
  • 1 small pinch salt
  • Mint sprig for garnish

Shake all ingredients with ice. Strain into a double rocks glass over a large ice cube and garnish with mint sprig.
old-elk-bib-and-tucker-and-more-new-whis:
This week’s new whiskeys are dominated by age-statement American releases of all styles. From Old Elk, there are three 10 year olds, a bourbon, a wheater, and a wheat whiskey, while Dancing Goat Distillery also has two decade-old whiskeys under its new Stillman’s Sonder brand. Bib & Tucker, too, has a new 8 year old bourbon. Rounding out the new releases are a new peach brandy cask-finished American single malt from Root Shoot and a single malt scotch from Streathearn. 

Old Elk 10 Year Old Collection

ABV: 51.5-52.5%
SRP: $70
Availability: Nationwide

Old Elk has rolled out its 10 Year Old Collection with a bourbon (52.5% ABV), wheated bourbon (52.5% ABV), and wheat whiskey (51.5% ABV). The bourbon has a high-malt mashbill of 51% corn, 34% malted barley, and 15% rye; the same as the brand’s flagship blended bourbon. The wheater has a mashbill of 51% corn, 46% wheat, and 3% malted barley, having just a smidge higher wheat content than its core wheated bourbon. The wheat whiskey has a mashbill of 96% wheat and 4% malted barley. All three whiskeys were contract distilled by MGP early in Old Elk's history. But the brand has already started distilling these same mashbills at Middle West Distillery, which acquired it back in May of last year. 

Bib & Tucker 8 year old Bottled in Bond Bourbon

ABV: 50%
SRP: $65
Availability: Nationwide

While this 8 year old bottled in bond whiskey was distilled in spring 2018 at Tennessee Distilling Group, it was blended by Bib & Tucker apprentice blender James Joseph—marking his first release for the brand. It features a Tennessee high-rye bourbon mashbill, with corn sourced from within 100 miles of the distillery. As a Tennessee whiskey, it was filtered through maple charcoal (a method known as the Lincoln County Process). The new bottled in bond bourbon will be available next month.

This isn’t the first Tennessee whiskey from Bib & Tucker—the brand previously launched a 15 year old bourbon, The Golden Spike, in 2024, which was also distilled at Tennessee Distilling Group. Bib & Tucker is owned by Deutsch Family Wines & Spirits, which also owns Redemption Whiskey. Master blender Alan Kennedy oversees both.

Stillman’s Sonder 10 year old Bourbon

ABV: 47%
SRP: $70
Availability: Online and select retailers

Stillman’s Sonder 10 year old American Single Malt

ABV: 48.2%
SRP: $70
Availability: Online and select retailers

These are the inaugural expressions from Dancing Goat Distillery’s new Stillman’s Sonder brand. Both were sourced from MGP, specifically from experimental stocks distilled between 2010 and 2016. The bourbon sports a dual maturation, having been aged in a mix of American and rare Andean oak barrels. The American single malt was finished in a mix of barrels including virgin oak, bourbon, Wisconsin brandy, cognac, and calvados.

Root Shoot Spirits Peach Brandy Cask Finished American Single Malt

ABV: 49%
SRP: $70
Availability: 480 bottles; Colorado exclusive

Colorado malting house Root Shoot has released a new cask finish. The base whiskey is the brand’s flagship 4 year old American single malt, made from barley grown and malted on-site and distilled in partnership with Boulder Spirits. It was finished in casks that previously held Palisade peach brandy from Peach Street Distillers in Colorado.

Strathearn (Batch 03) Highland Single Malt Scotch

ABV: 50%
SRP: $115
Availability: Limited release available at Total Wine and K&L Wines

Strathearn's third batch signals the next chapter for Douglas Laing & Co.'s distillery, as lead distiller Angela Brown continues to fine-tune the emerging house style for this Highland whisky maker. Presented in its signature acorn-shaped bottle, the third batch revisits the bourbon, virgin oak, and sherry cask recipe of its predecessors, but with a heightened sherry cask influence to enhance its depth and richness.

Strathearn opened as a microdistillery in 2013 in Methven, Perthshire, not far from Glenturret and Aberfeldy Distilleries, releasing its debut whisky in 2016. Douglas Laing & Co. acquired the distillery in 2019, marking the independent bottler’s first move into distilling. The company upgraded the distillery’s capacity but continued the founder’s handcrafted approach; each production shift at Strathearn produced enough spirit to fill a single barrel. The first Strathearn release of the Douglas Laing era was released in 2024. Batch 03 is drawn from 31 casks, selected from both inherited stocks and spirit distilled under Douglas Laing's ownership.
whisky-auction-update-july-2026-20-highe:
At a total of $365,984, July delivered the lowest combined value for the 20 highest hammer prices of the month since August 2024. Macallan in Lalique 65 year old set the highest hammer price of the month at $25,228 at McTear’s, Glasgow. Although nearly $10,000 below the bottle's original $35,000 release price, this sale helped Macallan overtake Yamazaki and reclaim the top spot in our rankings, albeit by the narrowest of margins. Elsewhere, Just Whisky sold bottle No.13 of Blair Castle whisky for $20,129. That cache of bottles first came to auction in 2023, hailed at the time as the world’s oldest whiskies, although the credibility of the evidence supporting the claim drew criticism online.

Japanese whisky comprised 20% of the 20 top bottles, with the sale of a third bottle of Hibiki 40 year old and three bottles of Karuizawa, led by a winning bid of $17,378 for the Karuizawa Aqua of Life 1969 50 year old Cask No. 538.

After a couple of months in which the 20 highest hammer price lists were dominated by single malts, Kentucky bourbon made more of an impact in July. Bottles of Buffalo Trace’s O.F.C. did well, with the 1980 vintage fetching $18,600 and the 1985 vintage making $16,600, plus a bottle of Eagle Rare 30 year old landed at $17,600, still trading 40% above its suggested retail price. No Van Winkle whiskeys have made the list for two months now. Michter’s had one of its most successful months at auction, securing two of the five highest hammer prices of the month with a bottle of Michter’s 25 year old Single Barrel rye selling for $21,500, and a second bottle for $20,100. Additionally, a bottle of Michter’s Celebration Sour Mash 2013 Release took $15,200, and a bottle of Michter’s 20 year old Single Barrel bourbon L14L709 narrowly missed a top 20 place with a bid of $13,200. If you’ve always wanted to try aged Michter’s expressions like these, get your tickets for the WhiskyFest Afternoon Seminars as Michter’s 20 year old bourbon is just one of the incredible whiskies you can look forward to tasting.

whistlepig-opens-develpment-depot-in-lou:
Vermont-based WhistlePig has been making moves in Kentucky. Last December, the distillery opened the Development Depot, a production facility in Brandenburg—a city on the banks of the Ohio River just under an hour southwest of Louisville—that’s capable of distilling 50,000 gallons a year. That same month also saw the debut of the WhistlePig Vault, a brand home in Louisville’s NuLu neighborhood that features whiskey tastings, bespoke cocktails, and a retail space.

The 4,000-square-foot Development Depot, which opened to the public earlier this month, features a 270-gallon still that’s designed predominantly for experimentation—more one-off mashbills and innovative flavors. Each batch will amount to about 600 gallons of whiskey. Apart from its production capabilities, the site has a tasting room and a retail area that sells single barrel releases made on-site. It’s open Wednesdays through Saturdays from 12 p.m. to 4 p.m.

But WhistlePig’s main Kentucky attraction is still The Vault in Louisville. A 5,000-square-foot space, previously known as the WhistlePig PiggyBank, The Vault is housed within a restored former bank vault built in 1911. Central to the site are three tasting experiences: a standard tasting of WhistlePig’s signature whiskeys hosted in its Bank Lobby Bar; a more premium, private experience that features some of the distillery’s older, more exclusive whiskeys; and a prestige tasting aimed at collectors, held within the building’s vault and takes guests through the rarest WhistlePig releases, including the full Boss Hog collection. If a tasting isn’t in the offing, guests can post up at the Bank Lobby Bar for bespoke cocktails or neat pours.

For now, these two sites will serve as WhistlePig’s sole Kentucky outposts. Until recently, the distillery also had a barrel aging site in Moriah, New York, but it was sold for $17 million following months of back-and-forth with neighbors over whiskey fungus-related concerns (though the state did recently renew its distilling license with New York State). Its home base is still in Shoreham, Vermont, on a 500-acre farm where much of its rye and other grains are grown, and it also owns a tasting room in Queechee, as well as a tasting and retail outpost in Stowe.
bourbon-room-saratoga-springs-new-york:
The heart of Saratoga Springs is its welcoming downtown main street, Broadway, about six blocks lined with shops, restaurants, cafes, and hotels, full of small-town charm. One of the few cross streets is Caroline, nicknamed “Saratoga’s Bourbon Street” in a nod to New Orleans, as it has more than a dozen bars in a short two-block stretch. But only one of these is an actual bourbon bar, and while it sits just a 30-second stroll from the heart of town’s action, it has a hidden gem vibe, with a dark interior and low-key, old-school neighborhood tavern atmosphere. From the outside, its name, The Bourbon Room, is the only clue that it offers a roughly 500-label whisky list.

Once you step through the door, it’s a different story. While many whisky bars proudly display their impressive collections amidst other premium spirits on library-style shelving behind the bar, here there is nothing else, and although it has a full bar, every other spirit is hidden away, with three sections of ornate dark brown wooden shelving full of whiskey. The establishment is narrow and deep; the centerpiece is a marble-topped bar lined with about a dozen high-backed stools, while parallel to this, on the exposed-brick wall behind the bar seating, is a narrow wooden shelf ledge with more stools, plus a handful of tables and seating in the front and back. It’s classy but comfortable and intimate, the walls decorated with barrel ends engraved with whiskey logos, the space capped by a vintage pressed-tin ceiling. Were it not for the preponderance of American whiskeys, the bar would be right at home in Dublin or Edinburgh.

Brian Miller, the founder, was a bartender and owner of a liquor store a few towns over when he was approached by the landlord to open a Martini bar at the height of vodka’s popularity over a dozen years ago. But he noticed the fast-rising popularity of brown spirits and decided to open a whiskey bar in 2014. Many regulars are glad he did, especially since Saratoga is home to the oldest active horse racetrack in the nation, dating back to 1863. It’s a popular classic that has made substantial improvements, significantly expanded its race season, and recently hosted the Triple Crown Belmont Stakes, and whose signature event, the Travers, is known as the “Midsummer Derby.” This attracts a steady flow of horse lovers from Kentucky, especially the heart of the state’s bourbon region, Louisville and Lexington, home to much of the thoroughbred industry and two similarly iconic tracks, Churchill Downs and Keeneland. Horse racing and whiskey have a long history, and Miller carries many labels made by producers who also own racehorses and visit Saratoga, such as Pinhook.

A cocktail lover, he has staked out an interesting middle ground between fancy mixology and the basic bar, with a focus on offering a value proposition. He makes dehydrated fruits and brews craft coffees and espresso to create whiskey-and-coffee drinks, riffs on the Espresso Martini, but stops short of fat washes and homemade bitters. The specialty whiskey cocktails use well-regarded but not overly expensive American whiskeys. For instance, the House Manhattan uses Elijah Craig rye, the Old Fashioned includes Bulleit bourbon, and the Paper Plane is made with Angel’s Envy bourbon. All are priced at $14 ($11 at Happy Hour, from 4 p.m. to 6 p.m. daily, along with $7 select whiskies).

A create-your-own flight program lets you pick any three whiskies from the list. The third Thursday of every month is “Flight School,” when a brand representative comes in and serves a flight and a specialty cocktail for $30. There is live acoustic music every Friday and Saturday, and in summer, when both the track and the famed Saratoga Performing Arts Center concerts are held, the town gets jammed and so does the bar, and it often stays open until the legal closing time of 4 a.m.

The whisky list is especially deep in a few brands such as Taconic Distillery, Penelope, Templeton, Pinhook, Old Forester, Michter’s, Kentucky Owl, and Colonel E.H. Taylor, with 6-10 labels from each. It skews heavily toward American, but includes around 40 whiskies from Scotland, Ireland, England, Canada, and Japan. All are offered in 1.5 or 2-ounce pours, and span from lower cost offerings like Puncher’s Chance bourbon ($11), Pinhook rye ($12), Dalmore 12 year old ($13), and Tenjaku blended Japanese whisky ($13) to rarer options such as Ardbeg 25 year old ($125), Barrell Craft Gray Label 24 year old ($129), and Pappy Van Winkle 23 year old ($250). But most of the options sit comfortably in the $15 to $30 range, including the likes of Rabbit Hole Dareringer bourbon ($20), Abraham Bowman Port finished bourbon ($19), and  Oban 14 year old scotch single malt ($25).
bulleit-87-bourbon-rye-blend:
Since the advent of High West Bourye in 2009, bourbon-rye blends have been part of the American whiskey universe; these days, they’re more prolific than ever before. Many an American distiller or blender has tried their hand at a blend of the two styles, ranging from James B. Beam Distilling (Knob Creek Bourbon X Rye) to Blue Run (Flight Series) to Cedar Ridge (Slipknot No. 9 Reserve) to Wild Turkey (Forgiven) and more. The latest to throw its hat in the ring? Bulleit, which has introduced Bulleit ’87.

The new Bulleit blends two disparate components: Bulleit bourbon, distilled, barreled, and aged in Shelbyville, Kentucky, and rye distilled and aged at MGP in Indiana. Both whiskeys are aged 4 years and finished separately with toasted American oak and French oak staves for 4 to 6 weeks—an anomaly for Bulleit, which has never before finished its whiskeys with staves. Whiskey R&D manager Phil Gelineau refers to the resulting whiskey as “like a cake” in its construction, with bourbon acting as the sponge, rye as chocolate shavings, and the staves as buttercream. Unlike its flagship bourbon and rye, which are often found in cocktails, the distillery is recommending the new whiskey be sipped neat or on the rocks for optimal enjoyment. At just $30, it’s a release that doesn't break the bank.

The whiskey’s name refers to the year Bulleit was founded (1987). Since that year, just two whiskeys have been part of the core portfolio—Bulleit bourbon and Bulleit 95 rye—making Bulleit ’87 only the third permanent whiskey introduced by the distillery in its nearly 40-year history. It'll be on shelves starting in September. As part of the release, Bulleit is taking the whiskey on a sampling tour, hitting 15 cities, including New York City, Los Angeles, Austin, New Orleans, and Louisville, along the way (stops will be announced on Bulleit's Instagram).

Bulleit’s foundation is built on high-rye bourbon and 95% rye, 5% malted barley rye—two whiskeys that, when the distillery got its start, weren’t nearly as common as they are today. The bourbon held down the fort for the distillery’s first 24 years, before rye was added in 2011. Over the past decade, numerous limited editions have also joined the Bulleit lineup, many of them with age statements—including a 20 year old rye released earlier this month. While all of the distillery’s rye remains sourced from MGP, it ramped up its bourbon capabilities with two new distilleries toward the end of the 2010s, one in Shelbyville, Kentucky capable of producing 3 million proof gallons and the other, a mammoth operation in Lebanon with capacity for 10 million proof gallons per year (though that distillery temporarily paused production last year).
still-austin-quarter:
Music has always had a role to play at Still Austin. The flagship bourbon is named The Musician in a nod to the distillery’s hometown of Austin, Texas, the self-proclaimed “live music capital of the world.” Still Austin regularly holds concerts on an outdoor stage just outside its tasting room, which often features up-and-coming local musicians. Last year, the live music program was expanded thanks to a partnership with legendary blues joint Antone’s Nightclub on a collaborative concert series that spotlights local and national acts each month. Now the distillery is set to open a brand new, music-themed visitor center of its own.

Making Music

Named The Still Austin Quarter, the 15,000-square-foot center will serve as the distillery’s visitor experience, alongside its existing whiskey garden patio and tasting room/retail shop. The building is divided into four spaces—the Music Room, the Vinyl Lounge, the Atrium, and a private event space—each with a unique concept. At full capacity, it will accommodate around 500 guests, including some 125 seats outside.


The Music Room is the crown jewel, purpose-built to host intimate concerts and other events. It’s home to The Musician’s Stage, which was inspired by the stage at Steamboat 1874, a legendary Austin nightclub that was a favorite haunt of rock legend Stevie Ray Vaughan that closed in 1999. The room is lined with a collection of original posters donated by  Danny and Leslie Crooks, who previously owned Steamboat 1874. Still Austin enlisted the help of Steven Durr—a music industry veteran who has designed studios for stars like Garth Brooks, Mark Ronson, and Willie Nelson—to handle the acoustics. Concerts are expected to be held nightly from Thursday through Sunday, featuring both local and national artists.

As for the center’s other components, the Vinyl Lounge will be home to the distillery’s vinyl record collection, which spans more than 5,000 albums across multiple genres. The distillery plans to continue growing the collection over time, with the goal of adding as many Austin musicians as possible. Visitors will have a chance to listen to some of those albums (plans call for having a DJ host every night). While The Atrium is geared toward daytime get-togethers, with happy hours during the week and lunches/brunches on weekends.

Each of these spaces will have its own bar, and Still Austin plans to make cocktails a main focus. The beverage program will include drinks made from the distillery’s flagship expressions, though there will also be a rotating list of archival pours and limited expressions. The menu also includes an agave spirit sourced by the distillery and aged in its own barrels, as well as aperitifs, amaros, and herbal liqueurs, all distilled in-house. There will also be a food program, with details to be announced.

Distilling Expansion

The new visitor facility isn’t the only area where Still Austin has been in expansion mode, as the company has been navigating the current whisky slump with strong gains. Last year it broke a volume milestone by selling over 50,000 cases (just north of 600k bottles), up 43% over 2024, according to Whisky Advocate’s research arm Impact Databank. 

This year is also showing positive trends. In February, the distillery signed a partnership with construction logistics company Fero to fuel its growth. The deal, which covers $20 million in working capital (with Still Austin retaining total ownership), will see the distillery scale up its production. On that front, plans have been discussed for building a larger distillery that would increase Still Austin’s capacity nearly sevenfold. The place currently produces 8,500 barrels annually, and the new facility would boost that number to 58,500 barrels, with capacity for further expansion over time.

The new Still Austin Quarter’s operating hours will be Wednesday and Thursday from 4 p.m. to 10 p.m., Friday and Saturday from 11 a.m. to 12 a.m., and Sunday from 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. For more information, visit Still Austin’s website.
peated-whisky-cocktail-for-summer:
If you could take some of the classic summer sensory memories—smoke from a charcoal grill, the sweetness of perfectly ripe pineapple, the fresh notes of herbs from the garden—and stir them into a Collins glass, you’d have the Charred Garden Smash.

“This cocktail is an exercise in contrast,” says creator Kendall Salgado, bar manager and beverage director at Current Charcoal Grill in Birmingham, Alabama. “The initial sip is bright and tropical, driven by the pineapple and lime, but it quickly gives way to a sophisticated, earthy finish. The light peat smoke from the whisky creates a charred effect that grounds the sweetness of the falernum and pineapple, resulting in a crisp cocktail with surprising depth and a silky, refreshing, spice-flecked texture.”

It’s ideal for serving at a barbecue or for shaking up on any hot day. The layered ice technique—regular cubes on the bottom and pebbles on top—slows the overall dilution while ensuring an intensely cold sip from the start, so every taste quenches your thirst.

Charred Garden Smash

  • 4-5 fresh basil leaves
  • 1 1/2 oz. Suntory Toki Black (or other lightly peated Japanese whisky)
  • 3/4 oz. John D. Taylor's Velvet Falernum
  • 1/2 oz. fresh lime juice
  • 1 oz. pineapple juice
  • 1 pinch sea salt
  • Dehydrated lime wheel and fresh pineapple frond or basil sprig for garnish

Add basil to a Collins glass and gently press to release oils. Add remaining ingredients to a shaker with ice. Shake well for about 10 seconds, then strain into prepared glass. Fill glass with fresh ice and use a barspoon to gently agitate basil leaves so they distribute throughout the drink. Garnish with lime wheel and pineapple frond or basil sprig.
new-whisky-from-deanston-barrell-and-mor:
Many of our new release roundups are dominated by American whiskey, but this week’s edition is a bit different. Sagamore’s High Rye bourbon is the only one on the list, now available nationwide after a limited launch last year. In Irish whiskey, Sailor’s Home has a new triple-casked blend and Dublin’s Pearse Lyons has a brown ale barrel-matured single malt that's part of a larger single cask series. Elsewhere, Highlands distillery Deanston has an orange wine cask-finished 17 year old and Barrell Craft Spirits has an ultra-aged Canadian whisky.

Deanston 17 year old Orange Wine Cask Finished Scotch Single Malt

ABV: 53.6%
SRP: $132
Availability: Limited

Deanston’s second expression in its Experimental Whisky collection was matured for 15 years in bourbon barrels before undergoing a 2-year finish in vino de naranja (orange wine) casks sourced from southern Spain. This is an unusual cask finish for a scotch whisky, to say the least, as this is only one of a few. It’s also the second unconventional finish for Deanston in recent years, following the release of its tequila cask-finished expression in late 2023.

Barrell Decade 2 Canadian whisky

ABV: 70.65%
SRP: $200
Availability: Limited 

A year after debuting its first Decade release, Barrell is back with the second batch. It’s crafted from the same barrels as the inaugural edition: Canadian whiskies distilled each year from 1995 to 2005, finished in a combination of Spanish brandy and Hungarian oak casks. The whisky is part of the brand’s Black Label series, which also includes ultra-aged whiskies like 21 year old Toasted Single Barrel bourbon and 33 year old Canadian whisky finished in French oak and oloroso sherry casks. It’s available online at Barrell’s website, as well as at select retailers nationwide.

Sagamore High Rye Straight Bourbon (2026 Release)

ABV: 54%
SRP: $50
Availability: Nationwide

Sagamore Spirit, which has recently rebranded as Sagamore Whiskey, has announced that its High Rye bourbon is now available nationwide starting this month, following a limited launch last year. The new batch has the same 60% corn, 25% rye, and 15% malted rye mashbill and 6 years of aging, but it’s bottled at a slightly lower proof compared to the original’s 59% ABV.

Sailor’s Home Journey Blended Irish

ABV: 43%
SRP: $35
Availability: Arkansas, Connecticut, New Jersey, and New York; imported by Park Street Imports

This sourced, triple-distilled Irish whiskey undergoes a distinctive triple cask maturation process. Part of the Explorer Series, Irish grain whiskey is first aged in virgin American oak casks, then re-casked into bourbon barrels, and blended with bourbon cask-matured Irish malt whiskey. The blend is then finished in Jamaican rum casks for 6 months. 

Inspired by the historic Sailors' Home in Limerick, founded in 1856, the brand takes its name from this building, which was created to welcome and support visiting seafarers. The recipe was devised by Dr. Jack Ó'Sé, an Irish whiskey maker, who began his career in the spirits industry in 1979. Previously, Ó'Sé worked for Alltech and commissioned the Pearse Lyons Distillery in Dublin, before consulting for other Irish distilleries

Pearse Lyons Camino Collection Kentucky Bourbon Barrel Ale Single Cask No. M 14–C398 KA Irish single malt

ABV: 54.3%
SRP: $125
Availability: Single cask releases will be available from either Pearse Lyons Distillery, Ireland or Town Branch Distillery, Lexington.

Pearse Lyons Distillery is launching its first-ever single cask series of double-distilled Irish whiskeys, drawing inspiration from the Camino de Santiago pilgrimage. The distillery opened nine years ago, housed within the beautifully restored St. James's Church in Dublin's historic Liberties district. For centuries, the church served as a gathering place for Irish pilgrims beginning their journey to Santiago de Compostela in Spain. Every traveler completing the Camino follows the same broad route across the network of pilgrim trails, but experiences their own unique journey: Pearse Lyons uses that idea as a metaphor for single cask maturation. Each Camino Collection whiskey is fully matured in its respective cask; no finishing takes place.

The whiskeys come from the Kentucky-made Vendome stills that operated at the Alltech Carlow Distillery between 2012–2015, and were moved to the new distillery in St. James’s Church from 2017 onward. The debut U.S. release, an Irish single malt matured in a Kentucky Bourbon Barrel Ale cask, will be available at Town Branch Distillery in Kentucky. The collection also includes Oloroso Hogshead Single Cask No. PS 21–118 0 Irish single pot still and Pedro Ximénez Hogshead Single Cask No. M 19–043 PX Irish single malt, which are available at Pearse Lyons Distillery in Dublin, while  More single casks will be available for selection by Pearse Lyons’ partners, while further single casks will be selected as distillery exclusives under the Pearse Lyons Irish whiskey portfolio.
buffalo-trace-2026-prohibition-collectio:
It all began with a box destined for a dumpster. When a Buffalo Trace employee combing through distillery castoffs happened upon a trove of mint-condition copies of every label the plant had released during Prohibition—when it operated as George T. Stagg Distillery—five such labels were reimagined as the first Buffalo Trace Prohibition Collection, launched in 2023. 

The second edition of the Prohibition Collection landed in January 2025. This time the focus narrowed to brands tied to the George T. Stagg era. Buffalo Trace’s lead archivist Nicolas Laracuente worked from a book of rescued Stagg-era labels, matching each defunct name to a flavor profile from existing barrels, since no original tasting notes or bottles survived. Like the first edition, it moved off shelves nearly as fast as it hit them.

Now comes the 2026 Prohibition Collection release, its third edition. Five more forgotten names return: Henry Watterson, Kentucky River, John G. Carlisle, Walter B. Duffy, and Cove Spring, each tied to a real figure or landmark from the Albert B. Blanton era. (Blanton helmed the George T. Stagg distillery during Prohibition.) As with prior releases, the 2026 Prohibition Collection bottles are scaled down to a period-appropriate 375-ml size. The set comes in a wooden case featuring archival imagery, and each carton keeps the prescription cut-out symbolizing where a physician would’ve signed to authorize a medicinal purchase. Priced at $1,000 for the set, these began shipping through Sazerac's distributor network to select retailers, bars, and restaurants in June 2026.

We got samples of each expression. Here are our 2026 Prohibition Collection tasting notes.

John G. Carlisle straight bourbon, 50%

Named for the congressman who helped write the Bottled in Bond Act of 1897, this one nails classic bourbon structure. The nose leads with rye spice, cinnamon, and baking chocolate, with tobacco leaf sitting underneath. It’s a classic candy bar nose; one that doesn’t disappoint with repeated whiffs. The medium-weight pour hits the back of the palate first, oily and coating, rewarding you with a proper Kentucky hug on the way down. Caramel popcorn, baking spice, and stewed pears keep it in a darker register, though a sweetness pushes through. The lengthy finish dries as it zips down the sides of the tongue, closing on caramel, rye spice, and a touch of oak.

Walter B. Duffy blend of 10 and 14 year old straight bourbons, 53.5%

In 1893, after Stagg's death, Duffy took sole ownership of the distillery, then named Old Fire Copper (O.F.C.), and later appointed Blanton president. This noses brighter and more floral than the Carlisle: cinnamon, peaches, pears, and ripe orchard fruit show up at first, then it coalesces into an inescapable note of Mott’s cinnamon applesauce. The palate is rich and heavy. Tobacco and strong spice bloom in the back, joined by dark chocolate, toffee, and coffee. It’s an oily, thick whiskey with a light chew to it. The protracted finish is drying and warm, ending on dark chocolate and tobacco leaf, leaving you with a final Fig Newton note.

Kentucky River straight whiskey, 50% 

My favorite of the set. The nose is a pastry shop: honey, graham crackers, vanilla wafers, biscuit dough, and a trace of green tea. The mouthfeel is heavier and sweeter, coating the palate with cherry syrup, Kellogg’s Honey Smacks, and a light undercurrent of oak. There's wheat whiskey in here somewhere, judging by the softness and the way it balloons out. Shortbread and fresh graham-cracker pie crust round it off. The finish is medium long; it gets in and gets out, but leaves you a welcome cherry hand pie note before it vanishes.

Cove Spring Uncut wheated straight bourbon, 60.1%

My second favorite. The nose is a little closed off at this strength, offering soft honey wheat toast on the back end, a fair amount of oak, cherry, and baking chocolate. The palate of this heavyweight liquid, however, explodes with lush and fruit-forward flavors, including bright cherry, sweet corn pudding, and biscuits with jam. The finish runs long, round, and vibrant, landing on buttered corn on the cob and cherry cobbler. A summer picnic in a single sip.

Henry Watterson straight rye, 70.3%

This is the highest-proof rye in the distillery's modern history. It’s named for the anti-Prohibition congressman and Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist, who supported many distilleries. The nose is textbook rye, evergreen and mint over the herbaceous, dill-backed profile you'd know from a Sazerac or a Handy, with lemon and orange zest brightening the top and an earthy undercurrent below. For a hazmat rye, it hides its ethanol well; deep inhales lead to a York Peppermint Pattie note. Its medium-weight palate is green through and through, with dill first, then mint and pine, with a sweetness arriving at the tip of the tongue once the herbs settle, then a little lemon, rye spice, and barrel oak seeping in behind. It finishes long and warm with more dill and spice.
low-barrel-entry-proof-flavor-impact-on-:
Of the many methods used in the whiskey-making process, one that’s relatively unfamiliar is barrel entry proof (BEP), which refers to a distillate’s strength prior to entering the barrel for maturation. Most American whiskeys are barreled at the legal maximum of 125 proof. Some distillers, however, add more water before the distillate goes into the barrel—lowering the proof to 115 or less. They argue that it increases the extraction of desirable barrel flavors and smooths out a whiskey as it ages, and many of these low-entry proof whiskeys have built a quality reputation among aficionados.

The issue came to the fore in 1935, when the federal government established new standards of identity for whiskey, hoping to better regulate an industry that was getting back on its feet after Prohibition. Back then, the maximum entry proof was 110, and most distillers tended to barrel at or just under that number. But in 1962, at the behest of distillers, the government raised the limit to 125, helping some struggling producers to improve their margins by using fewer barrels to produce the same volume of aged whiskey.

Maker’s Mark was one of the very few that has stuck with its barrel entry proof, the original 110 that Bill Samuels, Sr. implemented in 1954. The lower BEP helps the distillery to truly shine in two areas that fans of the brand tend to gravitate toward: extended aging and stave finishing. On the finishing front, the additional water in the barrel helps extract more flavors from the staves—including spice from French oak in expressions like Maker’s 46 and The Heart Release, or vanilla and caramel from American oak in The Keepers Release and others. It has also played a key role in paving the way for the distillery’s annual Cellar Aged series, which features some of its oldest and most impressive blends that, despite the double-digit ages of their components, are remarkably vibrant and complex without being overly tannic.

For Wild Turkey, the change was more gradual. The distillery had long barreled its whiskey at 107 proof, since that’s the way master distiller Jimmy Russell had always done things. But that changed in the early to mid-2000s, when Jimmy’s son Eddie began playing a larger role in production, and more labels like Russell’s Reserve were introduced. During this time, the distillery raised its barrel entry proof twice—first to 110 in 2004 and then to 115 in 2006. Wild Turkey doesn’t disclose what BEP it uses today, but it claims that it still uses a low entry proof to help maintain complexity and reduce the amount of water needed to proof the whiskey post-maturation. In our tastings, we’ve found that certainly suits the house style, with notable examples including the 8 year old Jimmy Russell 70th Anniversary bourbon and Rare Breed Barrel Proof straight rye, which both made appearances on our Top 20 lists with scores of 94 points.

Buffalo Trace is another historic distillery that uses low entry proof, albeit in somewhat limited fashion. While its rye whiskeys and most of its bourbons are barreled at the standard 125 proof, Buffalo Trace drops it to 117 for its wheated labels like W.L. Weller. Buffalo Trace also explored other entry proofs in a limited fashion, using its Experimental Collection to release wheated and ryed bourbons in 2013 and 2014, barreled at varying proofs between 90 and 125. Master distiller Harlen Wheatley found that the entry proof had a significant impact on flavor, with higher BEPs generally yielding spicier profiles, while lower entry proofs produced sweeter, fruitier characters. Those whiskeys may be hard to find now, but a worthy alternative exists in its more accessible W.L. Weller Full Proof, which is proofed back down to its entry proof of 114 prior to bottling.

Modern Marvels

Outside those historic distilleries, a few newer ones have also adopted the practice. One of the most prominent is Michter’s, which began distilling its own liquid in 2014 and barrels all of its distillate at a relatively low 103 proof. (Its 20 year old and 25 year old are a completely different story, coming from stocks sourced earlier that were barreled at indeterminate proofs.) According to Michter’s master of maturation Andrea Wilson, low BEP is one of the most significant parts of the distillery’s process. “Water is a powerful hydrolyzer for wood sugars and other soluble compounds,” she explains. “This way, every barrel begins with a beautiful catalyst for a lot of wonderful chemistry, and allows each barrel to extract more from the wood to increase the complexity and flavor of the final product.” Wilson works with wood that’s open-air seasoned for 18-60 months to further soften any astringent, bitter, or green flavors that can sometimes come from oak during maturation. The result is a distillate that shines at all levels of the proof spectrum, with its US*1 Single Barrel rye (91 points/42.4% ABV) and its barrel strength counterpart (93 points/54.9% ABV) both carrying complexity, power, and grace that belie their respective bottling strengths.

Kentucky Peerless has been barreling its whiskey at 107 proof since it began producing in 2013, though the team briefly considered barreling at 123 proof instead. According to master taster and single barrel curator John Wadell, the decision was rooted in a desire to showcase the distillery’s use of sweet mash. “The first thing we thought about is the need to respect the grains and fermentation,” Wadell says. “With lower barrel entry proof, you allow the grain character to stay more prominent, the fermentation esters to survive, and the yeast-driven fruit and spice to shine through more.” He also notes that the process helps preserve some of the natural oils that add viscosity, especially if the whiskeys aren’t chill-filtered. We certainly found that to be the case with the distillery’s Double Oak bourbon, noted for its syrupy texture and complexity, which led to a 93-point score from our tasting panel.

For Peerless it all comes back to flavor. “Your water will pull more of those wood sugars: the vanillins, the caramelized hemicellulose, and your baking spice compounds. Whereas a high entry proof will extract more dried oak, bitter tannins, and some of those sharp astringencies you may have,” Wadell argues. “Our water becomes an ingredient, not a dilution, in this process.”

heaven-hill-double-mash-bottled-in-bond-:
Heaven Hill is one of American whiskey’s most prolific distillers, producing numerous whiskey styles for a wide range of brands. At the top end are its sought-after unicorns, like the annual Parker’s Heritage Collection, Old Fitzgerald Decanter Series, and Heaven Hill Heritage label. Its high-strength middle-tier offerings like Elijah Craig Barrel Proof and Larceny Barrel Proof seem to get all the attention, with both taking home our Whisky of the Year award over the years. Even its bottom-shelfers are popular, with Mellow Corn and Evan Williams bottled in bond beloved by bartenders and home mixologists for their affordability and mixability.

With all of its other brands having devoted fan bases, Heaven Hill’s namesake label often doesn’t get a chance to shine. The line has historically been anchored by Heaven Hill Bottled in Bond, the distillery’s flagship bourbon that launched in 1939 and was a key growth driver throughout the company’s early years. It has undergone some changes over the decades, but the current version carries a 7-year age statement—a $40 gem that scored 92 points and was named our No. 4 Whisky of 2019. Now there is Double Mash, which blends two of the distillery’s most popular mashbills.

Blender’s Art

Two-thirds of Double Mash’s blend is Heaven Hill’s signature low-rye mashbill (78% corn, 10% rye, and 12% malted barley), which is widely used throughout its portfolio for bourbons like Elijah Craig, Evan Williams, Henry McKenna, and Heaven Hill Bottled in Bond. The other third represents the distillery’s wheater mashbill (68% corn, 20% wheat, and 12% malted barley) that’s featured in Old Fitzgerald and Larceny. The entire blend adheres to the standards outlined in the Bottled in Bond Act of 1897 and was aged for 9 years.

Heaven Hill says Double Mash was created to explore the various flavor profiles within the bonded designation. Indeed, by limiting their options to barrels distilled within a single season, whiskey makers can showcase their blending skills. Some whiskey makers take advantage of that regulation to create some truly innovative whiskeys. One notable example is Angel’s Envy Bottled in Bond, which holds the distinction of being both bottled in bond and cask strength. Master blender Owen Martin accomplished that by targeting whiskeys with lower barrel entry proofs and varying strengths, which allowed him to naturally bring the final product to 50% ABV through blending alone without using any water. Jack Daniel’s reaches across styles with Bonded Triple Mash, an interesting blend that combines bonded bourbon, rye, and American malt whiskey. There’s also RIOT from Neil Giraldo’s Three Chord brand, which  two bottled in bond ryes from MGP and Bardstown.

Heaven Hill isn’t especially known for blending multiple mashbills like this, but there are a few other examples across its portfolio, particularly in its annual Parker’s Heritage line. The closest comparison to Double Mash is 2012’s Parker’s Heritage 6th Edition, an 11 year old non-bonded expression that similarly blended Heaven Hill’s ryed and wheated mashbills. Last year’s Parker’s batch ventured even further than that, blending wheated bourbon with very old corn whiskey and a rare two-grain rye whiskey.

Heaven Hill Double Mash Bottled in Bond Bourbon
